explanation:
This problem mainly uses the knowledge of $\text{conditional expectation}$ and $\text{expectation}$. The key idea is to verify that the limit of $E(X_n\mid\mathcal{A})$ satisfies the two defining properties of the conditional expectation of $X$ with respect to $\mathcal{A}$: $\mathcal{A}$-measurability and the integral identity on every set in $\mathcal{A}$. The monotone convergence theorem is needed because both $X_n\uparrow X$ and, correspondingly, $E(X_n\mid\mathcal{A})$ form an increasing sequence.

First, for each $n$, $E(X_n\mid\mathcal{A})$ is $\mathcal{A}$-measurable by the definition of conditional expectation. Therefore the pointwise limit
$\lim_{n\to\infty}E(X_n\mid\mathcal{A})$
is also $\mathcal{A}$-measurable.

So it remains to prove that for every $A\in\mathcal{A}$,
$$\int_A \lim_{n\to\infty}E(X_n\mid\mathcal{A})\,dP=\int_A X\,dP.$$
Once this is shown, the limit will satisfy the defining property of $E(X\mid\mathcal{A})$ and hence must equal $E(X\mid\mathcal{A})$ almost surely.

Next, since $0\le X_1\le X_2\le\cdots\le X$ a.s., the monotonicity property of conditional expectation gives
$$0\le E(X_1\mid\mathcal{A})\le E(X_2\mid\mathcal{A})\le\cdots\le E(X\mid\mathcal{A})\quad \text{a.s.}$$
Thus $\{E(X_n\mid\mathcal{A})\}$ is a nondecreasing sequence of nonnegative $\mathcal{A}$-measurable random variables.

Now fix any $A\in\mathcal{A}$. By the monotone convergence theorem,
$$\int_A \lim_{n\to\infty}E(X_n\mid\mathcal{A})\,dP
=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_A E(X_n\mid\mathcal{A})\,dP.$$
By the defining property of conditional expectation, because $A\in\mathcal{A}$,
$$\int_A E(X_n\mid\mathcal{A})\,dP=\int_A X_n\,dP.$$
Hence,
$$\int_A \lim_{n\to\infty}E(X_n\mid\mathcal{A})\,dP
=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_A X_n\,dP.$$
Since $0\le X_1\le X_2\le\cdots\le X$ and $X_n\to X$ a.s., we again apply the monotone convergence theorem to obtain
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_A X_n\,dP=\int_A \lim_{n\to\infty}X_n\,dP=\int_A X\,dP.$$
Combining the above equalities yields
$$\int_A \lim_{n\to\infty}E(X_n\mid\mathcal{A})\,dP=\int_A X\,dP,
\qquad \forall A\in\mathcal{A}.$$
Therefore $\lim_{n\to\infty}E(X_n\mid\mathcal{A})$ is an $\mathcal{A}$-measurable random variable whose integral over every $A\in\mathcal{A}$ equals $\int_A X\,dP$. By the uniqueness of conditional expectation,
$$E(X\mid\mathcal{A})=\lim_{n\to\infty}E(X_n\mid\mathcal{A})\quad \text{a.s.}$$
This proves the result.

answer:
(i) Put $Y_n=\inf_{m\ge n}X_m$. Then $0\le Y_n\uparrow\liminf_nX_n$. For every $m\ge n$,
$$
E(Y_n\mid\mathcal A)\le E(X_m\mid\mathcal A),
$$
hence
$$
E(Y_n\mid\mathcal A)\le\inf_{m\ge n}E(X_m\mid\mathcal A).
$$
Conditional monotone convergence now gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
E(\liminf_nX_n\mid\mathcal A)
&=\lim_nE(Y_n\mid\mathcal A)\\
&\le\lim_n\inf_{m\ge n}E(X_m\mid\mathcal A)
=\liminf_nE(X_n\mid\mathcal A)
\end{aligned}
$$
a.s.

(ii) Since $|X_n|\le Y$ and $X_n\to X$ a.s., also $|X|\le Y$ a.s. Apply (i) to the nonnegative sequence $Y+X_n$:
$$
E(Y+X\mid\mathcal A)
\le\liminf_nE(Y+X_n\mid\mathcal A).
$$
By linearity,
$$
E(X\mid\mathcal A)\le\liminf_nE(X_n\mid\mathcal A). \tag{1}
$$
Apply (i) to $Y-X_n$:
$$
E(Y-X\mid\mathcal A)
\le\liminf_n\{E(Y\mid\mathcal A)-E(X_n\mid\mathcal A)\}.
$$
Since $\liminf(a-Z_n)=a-\limsup Z_n$,
$$
\limsup_nE(X_n\mid\mathcal A)\le E(X\mid\mathcal A). \tag{2}
$$
Combining (1), (2), and $\liminf\le\limsup$ yields
$$
E(X_n\mid\mathcal A)\longrightarrow E(X\mid\mathcal A)\quad\text{a.s.}
$$
explanation:
For (i), the tail infima $Y_n=\inf_{m\ge n}X_m$ increase to $\liminf X_n$. Monotonicity and conditional monotone convergence give the conditional Fatou inequality in the stated direction:
$$
E(\liminf X_n\mid\mathcal A)\le\liminf E(X_n\mid\mathcal A).
$$

For (ii), both $Y+X_n$ and $Y-X_n$ are nonnegative. Applying the preceding inequality to $Y+X_n$ gives
$$
E(X\mid\mathcal A)\le\liminf E(X_n\mid\mathcal A).
$$
Applying it to $Y-X_n$ and using
$\liminf(a-Z_n)=a-\limsup Z_n$ gives
$$
\limsup E(X_n\mid\mathcal A)\le E(X\mid\mathcal A).
$$
These are the two required opposite bounds. They force the conditional expectations to converge almost surely to $E(X\mid\mathcal A)$.

question: Let $X$ and $Y$ be integrable random variables on the probability space $\left( {\Omega ,\mathcal{F}, P}\right)$ and $\mathcal{A} \subset \mathcal{F}$ be a $\sigma$ -field. Show that $E\left\lbrack {{YE}\left( {X \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack = E\left\lbrack {{XE}\left( {Y \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack$ , assuming that both integrals exist.
answer:
(1) The problem is much easier if we assume that $Y$ is bounded. When $Y$ is bounded, both ${YE}\left( {X \mid \mathcal{A}}\right)$ and ${XE}\left( {Y \mid \mathcal{A}}\right)$ are integrable. Using the result in Exercise 37 and the fact that $E\left\lbrack {E\left( {X \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack = {EX}$ , we obtain that$$
E\left\lbrack {{YE}\left( {X \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack = E\{ E\left\lbrack {{YE}\left( {X \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) \mid \mathcal{A}}\right\rbrack \}
$$$$
= E\left\lbrack {E\left( {X \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) E\left( {Y \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack
$$$$
= E\{ E\left\lbrack {{XE}\left( {Y \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) \mid \mathcal{A}}\right\rbrack \}
$$$$
= E\left\lbrack {{XE}\left( {Y \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack .
$$
(2) Assume that $Y \geq 0$ . Let $Z$ be another nonnegative integrable random variable. We now show that if $\sigma \left( Z\right) \subset \mathcal{A}$ , then $E\left( {YZ}\right) = E\left\lbrack {{ZE}\left( {Y \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack$ . (Note that this is a special case of the result in Exercise 37 if $E\left( {YZ}\right) < \infty$ .)
Let ${Y}_{n} = \min \{ Y, n\} , n = 1,2,\ldots$ Then $0 \leq {Y}_{1} \leq {Y}_{2} \leq \cdots \leq Y$ and $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}{Y}_{n} = Y$ . By the results in Exercises 35 and ${39},0 \leq E\left( {{Y}_{1} \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) \leq \; E\left( {{Y}_{2} \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) \leq \cdots$ a.s. and $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}E\left( {{Y}_{n} \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) = E\left( {Y \mid \mathcal{A}}\right)$ a.s. Since ${Y}_{n}$ is bounded, ${Y}_{n}Z$ is integrable. By the result in Exercise 37,$$
E\left\lbrack {{ZE}\left( {{Y}_{n} \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack = E\left( {{Y}_{n}Z}\right) ,\;n = 1,2,\ldots
$$
By the monotone convergence theorem,$$
E\left( {YZ}\right) = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}E\left( {{Y}_{n}Z}\right) = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}E\left\lbrack {{ZE}\left( {{Y}_{n} \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack = E\left\lbrack {{ZE}\left( {Y \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack .
$$
Consequently, if $X \geq 0$ , then the result follows by taking $Z = E\left( {X \mid \mathcal{A}}\right)$ . (3) We now consider general $X$ and $Y$ . Let ${f}_{ + }$ and ${f}_{ - }$ denote the positive and negative parts of a function $f$ . Note that$$
E\left\{ {\left\lbrack XE\left( Y \mid \mathcal{A}\right) \right\rbrack }_{ + }\right\} = E\left\{ {{X}_{ + }{\left\lbrack E\left( Y \mid \mathcal{A}\right) \right\rbrack }_{ + }}\right\} + E\left\{ {{X}_{ - }{\left\lbrack E\left( Y \mid \mathcal{A}\right) \right\rbrack }_{ - }}\right\}
$$
and$$
E\left\{ {\left\lbrack XE\left( Y \mid \mathcal{A}\right) \right\rbrack }_{ - }\right\} = E\left\{ {{X}_{ + }{\left\lbrack E\left( Y \mid \mathcal{A}\right) \right\rbrack }_{ - }}\right\} + E\left\{ {{X}_{ - }{\left\lbrack E\left( Y \mid \mathcal{A}\right) \right\rbrack }_{ + }}\right\} .
$$
Since $E\left\lbrack {{XE}\left( {Y \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack$ exists, without loss of generality we assume that$$
E\left\{ {\left\lbrack XE\left( Y \mid \mathcal{A}\right) \right\rbrack }_{ + }\right\} = E\left\{ {{X}_{ + }{\left\lbrack E\left( Y \mid \mathcal{A}\right) \right\rbrack }_{ + }}\right\} + E\left\{ {{X}_{ - }{\left\lbrack E\left( Y \mid \mathcal{A}\right) \right\rbrack }_{ - }}\right\} < \infty .
$$
Then, both$$
E\left\lbrack {{X}_{ + }E\left( {Y \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack = E\left\{ {{X}_{ + }{\left\lbrack E\left( Y \mid \mathcal{A}\right) \right\rbrack }_{ + }}\right\} - E\left\{ {{X}_{ + }{\left\lbrack E\left( Y \mid \mathcal{A}\right) \right\rbrack }_{ - }}\right\}
$$
and$$
E\left\lbrack {{X}_{ - }E\left( {Y \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack = E\left\{ {{X}_{ - }{\left\lbrack E\left( Y \mid \mathcal{A}\right) \right\rbrack }_{ + }}\right\} - E\left\{ {{X}_{ - }{\left\lbrack E\left( Y \mid \mathcal{A}\right) \right\rbrack }_{ - }}\right\}
$$
are well defined and their difference is also well defined. Applying the result established in (2), we obtain that$$
E\left\lbrack {{X}_{ + }E\left( {Y \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack = E\left\{ {E\left( {{X}_{ + } \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) {\left\lbrack E\left( Y \mid \mathcal{A}\right) \right\rbrack }_{ + }}\right\} - E\left\{ {E\left( {{X}_{ + } \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) {\left\lbrack E\left( Y \mid \mathcal{A}\right) \right\rbrack }_{ - }}\right\}
$$$$
= E\left\lbrack {E\left( {{X}_{ + } \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) E\left( {Y \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack ,
$$
where the last equality follows from the result in Exercise 8. Similarly,$$
E\left\lbrack {{X}_{ - }E\left( {Y \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack = E\left\{ {E\left( {{X}_{ - } \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) {\left\lbrack E\left( Y \mid \mathcal{A}\right) \right\rbrack }_{ + }}\right\} - E\left\{ {E\left( {{X}_{ - } \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) {\left\lbrack E\left( Y \mid \mathcal{A}\right) \right\rbrack }_{ - }}\right\}
$$$$
= E\left\lbrack {E\left( {{X}_{ - } \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) E\left( {Y \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack .
$$
By Exercise 8 again,$$
E\left\lbrack {{XE}\left( {Y \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack = E\left\lbrack {{X}_{ + }E\left( {Y \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack - E\left\lbrack {{X}_{ - }E\left( {Y \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack
$$$$
= E\left\lbrack {E\left( {{X}_{ + } \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) E\left( {Y \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack - E\left\lbrack {E\left( {{X}_{ - } \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) E\left( {Y \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack
$$$$
= E\left\lbrack {E\left( {X \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) E\left( {Y \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack .
$$
Switching $X$ and $Y$ , we also conclude that$$
E\left\lbrack {{YE}\left( {X \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack = E\left\lbrack {E\left( {X \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) E\left( {Y \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack .
$$
Hence, $E\left\lbrack {{XE}\left( {Y \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack = E\left\lbrack {{YE}\left( {X \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right\rbrack$ .
explanation:
This problem uses conditional expectation, expectation properties, and the tower property. The key idea is to first prove the identity in an easier bounded case, then extend it to nonnegative variables by monotone convergence, and finally handle general integrable variables through positive and negative parts.

Step 1: First treat the case where $Y$ is bounded.

If $Y$ is bounded, then both $Y E(X\mid \mathcal{A})$ and $X E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})$ are integrable. Since $E(X\mid \mathcal{A})$ is $\mathcal{A}$-measurable, we compute
$E\left[YE(X\mid \mathcal{A})\right]
=E\left(E\left[YE(X\mid \mathcal{A})\mid \mathcal{A}\right]\right)$.
Using the property that an $\mathcal{A}$-measurable factor can be taken out of the conditional expectation,
$E\left[YE(X\mid \mathcal{A})\mid \mathcal{A}\right]
=E(X\mid \mathcal{A})E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})$.
Hence
$E\left[YE(X\mid \mathcal{A})\right]=E\left[E(X\mid \mathcal{A})E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]$.
Similarly,
$E\left[XE(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]
=E\left(E\left[XE(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\mid \mathcal{A}\right]\right)
=E\left[E(X\mid \mathcal{A})E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]$.
Therefore, when $Y$ is bounded,
$E\left[YE(X\mid \mathcal{A})\right]=E\left[XE(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]$.

Step 2: Extend to the case $Y\ge 0$.

Let $Z\ge 0$ be another integrable random variable such that $\sigma(Z)\subset \mathcal{A}$. We show that
$E(YZ)=E\left[Z E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]$.

Choose a bounded increasing approximation $Y_n=\min\{Y,n\}$, $n=1,2,\dots$. Then
$0\le Y_1\le Y_2\le \cdots \le Y$, and $Y_n\uparrow Y$ a.s.
By monotonicity of conditional expectation,
$0\le E(Y_1\mid \mathcal{A})\le E(Y_2\mid \mathcal{A})\le \cdots$ a.s.,
and
$E(Y_n\mid \mathcal{A})\uparrow E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})$ a.s.
Since each $Y_n$ is bounded, $Y_n Z$ is integrable. By the bounded-case result,
$E\left[Z E(Y_n\mid \mathcal{A})\right]=E(Y_n Z),\qquad n=1,2,\dots$
Now apply the monotone convergence theorem:
$E(YZ)=\lim_{n\to\infty}E(Y_n Z)
=\lim_{n\to\infty}E\left[Z E(Y_n\mid \mathcal{A})\right]
=E\left[Z E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]$.
Thus, for any nonnegative integrable $Z$ that is $\mathcal{A}$-measurable,
$E(YZ)=E\left[Z E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]$.

Now suppose $X\ge 0$. Take
$Z=E(X\mid \mathcal{A})$.
Then $Z\ge 0$, $Z$ is integrable, and $Z$ is $\mathcal{A}$-measurable. Therefore,
$E\left[Y E(X\mid \mathcal{A})\right]
=E\left[E(X\mid \mathcal{A})E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]$.
So the desired identity holds when $X\ge 0$ and $Y\ge 0$.

Step 3: Handle general integrable $X$ and $Y$.

Write
$X=X_+-X_-$,
where $X_+=\max\{X,0\}$ and $X_-=\max\{-X,0\}$.
Also decompose $E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})$ into positive and negative parts. Then
$\left[XE(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]_+
= X_+\left[E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]_+ + X_-\left[E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]_-$,
and
$\left[XE(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]_-
= X_+\left[E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]_- + X_-\left[E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]_+$.
Since $E\left[XE(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]$ exists, one of the positive or negative parts has finite expectation; without loss of generality assume
$E\left(\left[XE(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]_+\right)
=E\left(X_+\left[E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]_+\right)+E\left(X_-\left[E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]_-\right)<\infty.$
Then both
$E\left[X_+E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]
=E\left(X_+\left[E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]_+\right)-E\left(X_+\left[E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]_-\right)$
and
$E\left[X_-E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]
=E\left(X_-\left[E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]_+\right)-E\left(X_-\left[E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]_-\right)$
are well defined.

Now apply the result from Step 2 to the nonnegative random variables $X_+$ and $X_-$. We obtain
$E\left[X_+E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]
=E\left[E(X_+\mid \mathcal{A})E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right],$
and similarly
$E\left[X_-E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]
=E\left[E(X_-\mid \mathcal{A})E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right].$
Subtracting gives
$E\left[XE(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]
=E\left[X_+E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]-E\left[X_-E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]$
$=E\left[E(X_+\mid \mathcal{A})E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]-E\left[E(X_-\mid \mathcal{A})E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right]$
$=E\left[E(X\mid \mathcal{A})E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right].$

By symmetry, exchanging the roles of $X$ and $Y$ yields
$E\left[YE(X\mid \mathcal{A})\right]=E\left[E(X\mid \mathcal{A})E(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right].$
Therefore,
$E\left[YE(X\mid \mathcal{A})\right]=E\left[XE(Y\mid \mathcal{A})\right].$

Hence the statement is proved.

question:
Let $X,X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be integrable random variables on $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$, and let $\mathcal A\subset\mathcal F$ be a $\sigma$-field. Suppose that
$$
E(X_nY)\longrightarrow E(XY)
$$
for every bounded random variable $Y$. Show that, for every bounded random variable $Y$,
$$
E\{E(X_n\mid\mathcal A)Y\}
\longrightarrow E\{E(X\mid\mathcal A)Y\}.
$$
answer:
Fix a bounded random variable $Y$ and put
$$
Z=E(Y\mid\mathcal A).
$$
Then $Z$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable and bounded, with $|Z|\le\|Y\|_\infty$. Hence the hypothesis may be applied to $Z$:
$$
E(X_nZ)\longrightarrow E(XZ). \tag{1}
$$
All products below are integrable because $X_n,X$ are integrable and $Y,Z$ are bounded. Since $Z$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable,
$$
E(X_nZ)=E\{E(X_n\mid\mathcal A)Z\}.
$$
Since $E(X_n\mid\mathcal A)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable,
$$
E\{E(X_n\mid\mathcal A)Y\}
=E\{E(X_n\mid\mathcal A)E(Y\mid\mathcal A)\}
=E\{E(X_n\mid\mathcal A)Z\}.
$$
Thus
$$
E(X_nZ)=E\{E(X_n\mid\mathcal A)Y\}.
$$
The same calculation with $X$ gives
$$
E(XZ)=E\{E(X\mid\mathcal A)Y\}.
$$
Substitution in (1) proves the required convergence.
explanation:
The statement is made for bounded test variables, which guarantees that every product occurring in the proof is integrable. For bounded $Y$, the conditional expectation $Z=E(Y\mid\mathcal A)$ is also bounded. The hypothesis therefore applies to $Z$.

By the defining property of conditional expectation, first conditioning $X_n$ and then conditioning $Y$ yields
$$
E[X_nE(Y\mid\mathcal A)]
=E[E(X_n\mid\mathcal A)E(Y\mid\mathcal A)]
=E[E(X_n\mid\mathcal A)Y].
$$
The identical formula holds with $X$ in place of $X_n$. Consequently the assumed convergence tested against $E(Y\mid\mathcal A)$ is exactly the desired convergence tested against $Y$ after conditioning $X_n$ and $X$.

question:
Let $X$ be a nonnegative integrable random variable on the probability space $\left( {\Omega ,\mathcal{F}, P}\right)$ and $\mathcal{A} \subset \mathcal{F}$ be a $\sigma$ -field. Show that$$
E\left( {X \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) = {\int }_{0}^{\infty }P\left( {X > t \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) {dt}.
$$
Note. For any $B \in \mathcal{F}, P\left( {B \mid \mathcal{A}}\right)$ is defined to be $E\left( {{I}_{B} \mid \mathcal{A}}\right)$ .
answer:
From the theory of conditional distribution (e.g., Theorem 1.7 in Shao,2003), there exists $\widetilde{P}\left( {B,\omega }\right)$ defined on $\mathcal{F} \times \Omega$ such that (i) for any $\omega \in \Omega ,\widetilde{P}\left( {\cdot ,\omega }\right)$ is a probability measure on $\left( {\Omega ,\mathcal{F}}\right)$ and (ii) for any $B \in \mathcal{F}$ , $\widetilde{P}\left( {B,\omega }\right) = P\left( {B \mid \mathcal{A}}\right)$ a.s. From Exercise 23,$$
\int {Xd}\widetilde{P}\left( {\cdot ,\omega }\right) = {\int }_{0}^{\infty }\widetilde{P}\left( {\{ X > t\} ,\omega }\right) {dt}
$$$$
= {\int }_{0}^{\infty }P\left( {X > t \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) {dt}\text{ a.s. }
$$
Hence, the result follows if$$
E\left( {X \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) \left( \omega \right) = \int {Xd}\widetilde{P}\left( {\cdot ,\omega }\right) \text{ a.s. }
$$
This is certainly true if $X = {I}_{B}$ for a $B \in \mathcal{F}$ . By the linearity of the integration and conditional expectation, this equality also holds when $X$ is a nonnegative simple function. For general nonnegative $X$ , there exists a sequence of simple functions ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},\ldots$ , such that $0 \leq {X}_{1} \leq {X}_{2} \leq \cdots \leq X$ and $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}{X}_{n} = X$ a.s. From Exercise 38,$$
E\left( {X \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}E\left( {{X}_{n} \mid \mathcal{A}}\right)
$$$$
= \mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}\int {X}_{n}d\widetilde{P}\left( {\cdot ,\omega }\right)
$$$$
= \int {Xd}\widetilde{P}\left( {\cdot ,\omega }\right) \text{ a.s. }
$$
explanation:
This problem uses the ideas of conditional expectation, conditional distribution, and expectation. The key is to represent the conditional probability $P(B\mid \mathcal{A})$ by a regular conditional probability, and then apply the tail-integral formula for a nonnegative random variable under that probability measure.

Step 1: Introduce a regular conditional probability.
By the theory of conditional distribution, there exists a function $\widetilde P(B,\omega)$ on $\mathcal F\times \Omega$ such that:
(1) for each fixed $\omega\in\Omega$, $\widetilde P(\cdot,\omega)$ is a probability measure on $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$;
(2) for every $B\in\mathcal F$, one has
$\widetilde P(B,\omega)=P(B\mid \mathcal A)\quad \text{a.s.}$
In particular, for the event $\{X>t\}$,
$\widetilde P(\{X>t\},\omega)=P(X>t\mid \mathcal A)\quad \text{a.s.}$

Step 2: Apply the tail-integral formula under $\widetilde P(\cdot,\omega)$.
For each fixed $\omega$, since $\widetilde P(\cdot,\omega)$ is a probability measure and $X\ge 0$, the usual formula for nonnegative random variables gives
$\int X\,d\widetilde P(\cdot,\omega)=\int_0^{\infty}\widetilde P(\{X>t\},\omega)\,dt.$
Using the identification above, we obtain
$\int X\,d\widetilde P(\cdot,\omega)=\int_0^{\infty}P(X>t\mid \mathcal A)\,dt\quad \text{a.s.}$
Therefore, it remains to show that
$E(X\mid \mathcal A)(\omega)=\int X\,d\widetilde P(\cdot,\omega)\quad \text{a.s.}$

Step 3: Verify the equality first for indicator functions.
If $X=I_B$ for some $B\in\mathcal F$, then
$\int X\,d\widetilde P(\cdot,\omega)=\int I_B\,d\widetilde P(\cdot,\omega)=\widetilde P(B,\omega)=P(B\mid \mathcal A)=E(I_B\mid \mathcal A)\quad \text{a.s.}$
So the desired equality holds for indicator random variables.

Step 4: Extend to nonnegative simple functions.
Let $X=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i I_{B_i}$ with $a_i\ge 0$. By linearity of both integration and conditional expectation,
$\int X\,d\widetilde P(\cdot,\omega)=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\int I_{B_i}\,d\widetilde P(\cdot,\omega)
=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i E(I_{B_i}\mid \mathcal A)
=E\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i I_{B_i}\mid \mathcal A\right)
=E(X\mid \mathcal A)\quad \text{a.s.}$
Hence the equality also holds for all nonnegative simple functions.

Step 5: Pass to a general nonnegative random variable by monotone approximation.
For general $X\ge 0$, choose nonnegative simple functions $X_1,X_2,\dots$ such that
$0\le X_1\le X_2\le \cdots \le X,\qquad X_n\to X\quad \text{a.s.}$
By the monotone convergence property of conditional expectation,
$E(X\mid \mathcal A)=\lim_{n\to\infty}E(X_n\mid \mathcal A).$
Since the equality has already been proved for each $X_n$,
$E(X_n\mid \mathcal A)=\int X_n\,d\widetilde P(\cdot,\omega).$
Again by monotone convergence for the integral with respect to the probability measure $\widetilde P(\cdot,\omega)$,
$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int X_n\,d\widetilde P(\cdot,\omega)=\int X\,d\widetilde P(\cdot,\omega).$
Therefore,
$E(X\mid \mathcal A)=\int X\,d\widetilde P(\cdot,\omega)\quad \text{a.s.}$

Step 6: Combine the two parts.
From Step 2 and Step 5,
$E(X\mid \mathcal A)=\int X\,d\widetilde P(\cdot,\omega)=\int_0^{\infty}P(X>t\mid \mathcal A)\,dt\quad \text{a.s.}$

Hence,
$E(X\mid \mathcal A)=\int_0^{\infty}P(X>t\mid \mathcal A)\,dt.$

question:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent integrable random variables on a probability space and $f$ be a nonnegative convex function. Show that $E\left\lbrack {f\left( {X + Y}\right) }\right\rbrack \geq E\left\lbrack {f\left( {X + {EY}}\right) }\right\rbrack$ .
Note. We need to apply the following Jensen's inequality for conditional expectations. Let $f$ be a convex function and $X$ be an integrable random variable satisfying $E\left| {f\left( X\right) }\right| < \infty$ . Then $f\left( {E\left( {X \mid \mathcal{A}}\right) }\right) \leq E\left( {f\left( X\right) \mid \mathcal{A}}\right)$ a.s. (e.g., Theorem 9.1.4 in Chung, 1974).
explanation:
This problem uses the keypoints of conditional expectation, independence of random variables, and Jensen's inequality. The main idea is to condition on $X$, apply Jensen's inequality to the conditional expectation, and then use the independence of $X$ and $Y$ to simplify $E(Y\mid X)$ to $EY$.

We prove the required inequality in two cases.

First, if $E\left[f(X+Y)\right]=\infty$, then since $f$ is nonnegative, the left-hand side is $\infty$, and therefore
$E\left[f(X+Y)\right] \geq E\left[f(X+EY)\right]$
holds automatically.

So it remains to consider the case where $f(X+Y)$ is integrable. In this case, we may use conditional expectation and Jensen's inequality.

By the tower property of conditional expectation,
$$
E\left[f(X+Y)\right]=E\left(E\left[f(X+Y)\mid X\right]\right).
$$

Now apply Jensen's inequality for conditional expectations to the convex function $f$ and the random variable $X+Y$, conditioning on $\sigma(X)$ (equivalently, conditioning on $X$). This gives
$$
E\left[f(X+Y)\mid X\right] \geq f\left(E\left[X+Y\mid X\right]\right) \quad \text{a.s.}
$$
Taking expectation on both sides yields
$$
E\left(E\left[f(X+Y)\mid X\right]\right)
\geq E\left(f\left(E\left[X+Y\mid X\right]\right)\right).
$$
Hence,
$$
E\left[f(X+Y)\right]
\geq E\left(f\left(E\left[X+Y\mid X\right]\right)\right).
$$

Next simplify the conditional expectation inside $f$:
$$
E\left[X+Y\mid X\right]=E\left[X\mid X\right]+E\left[Y\mid X\right]=X+E\left[Y\mid X\right].
$$
Therefore,
$$
E\left[f(X+Y)\right]
\geq E\left[f\left(X+E(Y\mid X)\right)\right].
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are independent, $Y$ is independent of $\sigma(X)$, so
$$
E(Y\mid X)=EY \quad \text{a.s.}
$$
Substituting this into the previous expression gives
$$
E\left[f(X+Y)\right]
\geq E\left[f\left(X+EY\right)\right].
$$

Thus the required inequality is proved:
$$
E\left[f(X+Y)\right] \geq E\left[f(X+EY)\right].
$$

question: Let $X$ be an integrable random variable with a Lebesgue density $f$ and let $Y = g\left( X\right)$ , where $g$ is a function with positive derivative on $\left( {0,\infty }\right)$ and $g\left( x\right) = g\left( {-x}\right)$ . Find an expression for $E\left( {X \mid Y}\right)$ and verify that it is indeed the conditional expectation.
keypoint: 连续型随机变量的条件分布
answer:
Let $h$ be the inverse function of $g$ on $\left( {0,\infty }\right)$ and$$
\psi \left( y\right) = h\left( y\right) \frac{f\left( {h\left( y\right) }\right) - f\left( {-h\left( y\right) }\right) }{f\left( {h\left( y\right) }\right) + f\left( {-h\left( y\right) }\right) }.
$$
We now show that $E\left( {X \mid Y}\right) = \psi \left( Y\right)$ a.s. It is clear that $\psi \left( y\right)$ is a Borel function. Also, the $\sigma$ -field generated by $Y$ is generated by the sets of the form ${A}_{a} = \{ y : g\left( 0\right) \leq y \leq a\} , a > g\left( 0\right)$ . Hence, it suffices to show that for any $a > g\left( 0\right)$ ,$$
{\int }_{{A}_{a}}{XdP} = {\int }_{{A}_{a}}\psi \left( Y\right) {dP}.
$$
Note that$$
{\int }_{{A}_{a}}{XdP} = {\int }_{g\left( 0\right) \leq g\left( x\right) \leq a}{xf}\left( x\right) {dx}
$$$$
= {\int }_{-h\left( a\right) }^{h\left( a\right) }{xf}\left( x\right) {dx}
$$$$
= {\int }_{-h\left( a\right) }^{0}{xf}\left( x\right) {dx} + {\int }_{0}^{h\left( a\right) }{xf}\left( x\right) {dx}
$$$$
= {\int }_{h\left( a\right) }^{0}{xf}\left( {-x}\right) {dx} + {\int }_{0}^{h\left( a\right) }{xf}\left( x\right) {dx}
$$$$
= {\int }_{0}^{h\left( a\right) }x\left\lbrack {f\left( x\right) - f\left( {-x}\right) }\right\rbrack {dx}
$$$$
= {\int }_{g\left( 0\right) }^{a}h\left( y\right) \left\lbrack {f\left( {h\left( y\right) }\right) - f\left( {-h\left( y\right) }\right) }\right\rbrack {h}^{\prime }\left( y\right) {dy}.
$$
On the other hand, ${h}^{\prime }\left( y\right) \left\lbrack {f\left( {h\left( y\right) }\right) + f\left( {-h\left( y\right) }\right) }\right\rbrack {I}_{\left( g\left( 0\right) ,\infty \right) }\left( y\right)$ is the Lebesgue density of $Y$ (see the note in Exercise 17). Hence,$$
{\int }_{{A}_{a}}\psi \left( Y\right) {dP} = {\int }_{g\left( 0\right) }^{a}\psi \left( y\right) {h}^{\prime }\left( y\right) \left\lbrack {f\left( {h\left( y\right) }\right) + f\left( {-h\left( y\right) }\right) }\right\rbrack {dy}
$$$$
= {\int }_{g\left( 0\right) }^{a}h\left( y\right) \left\lbrack {f\left( {h\left( y\right) }\right) - f\left( {-h\left( y\right) }\right) }\right\rbrack {h}^{\prime }\left( y\right) {dy}
$$
by the definition of $\psi \left( y\right)$ .
explanation:
This problem uses conditional expectation, conditional distribution in the continuous case, and the change-of-variable method. Since $Y=g(X)$ with $g$ even and strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$, each value of $Y$ comes from the two points $\pm h(y)$, so $E(X\mid Y)$ should be a Borel function of $Y$ obtained by averaging these two possible values with density weights.

Let $h$ be the inverse of $g$ on $(0,\infty)$. Define
$\psi(y)=h(y)\frac{f(h(y))-f(-h(y))}{f(h(y))+f(-h(y))}$.
We claim that
$E(X\mid Y)=\psi(Y)$ a.s.

First, $\psi$ is a Borel function, so $\psi(Y)$ is $\sigma(Y)$-measurable, which is necessary for a conditional expectation.

Next we verify the defining property of conditional expectation. Because $\sigma(Y)$ is generated by sets of the form
$A_a=\{\omega: g(0)\le Y(\omega)\le a\}$, $a>g(0)$,
it is enough to show that for every $a>g(0)$,
$\int_{A_a} X\,dP=\int_{A_a}\psi(Y)\,dP$.

Now compute the left-hand side. Since $Y=g(X)$,
$\int_{A_a} X\,dP=\int_{\{x: g(0)\le g(x)\le a\}} x f(x)\,dx$.
Because $g$ is even and strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$, the set $\{x: g(0)\le g(x)\le a\}$ is exactly $[-h(a),h(a)]$. Hence
$\int_{A_a} X\,dP=\int_{-h(a)}^{h(a)} x f(x)\,dx$.
Split the integral at $0$:
$\int_{-h(a)}^{h(a)} x f(x)\,dx=\int_{-h(a)}^0 x f(x)\,dx+\int_0^{h(a)} x f(x)\,dx$.
In the first integral, substitute $x\mapsto -x$:
$\int_{-h(a)}^0 x f(x)\,dx=\int_{h(a)}^0 x f(-x)\,dx$.
Therefore,
$\int_{A_a} X\,dP=\int_{h(a)}^0 x f(-x)\,dx+\int_0^{h(a)} x f(x)\,dx$
$=\int_0^{h(a)} x\bigl[f(x)-f(-x)\bigr]dx$.
Now use the change of variable $y=g(x)$, so $x=h(y)$ and $dx=h'(y)dy$. Then
$\int_{A_a} X\,dP=\int_{g(0)}^a h(y)\bigl[f(h(y))-f(-h(y))\bigr]h'(y)\,dy$.

Now compute the right-hand side. The density of $Y$ is
$h'(y)\bigl[f(h(y))+f(-h(y))\bigr]I_{(g(0),\infty)}(y)$,
because for each $y>g(0)$ there are exactly two preimages $\pm h(y)$.
Hence
$\int_{A_a}\psi(Y)\,dP=\int_{g(0)}^a \psi(y)h'(y)\bigl[f(h(y))+f(-h(y))\bigr]dy$.
Substitute the definition of $\psi(y)$:
$\int_{A_a}\psi(Y)\,dP=
\int_{g(0)}^a h(y)\frac{f(h(y))-f(-h(y))}{f(h(y))+f(-h(y))}h'(y)\bigl[f(h(y))+f(-h(y))\bigr]dy$
$=\int_{g(0)}^a h(y)\bigl[f(h(y))-f(-h(y))\bigr]h'(y)\,dy$.
This is exactly the same as the expression obtained for $\int_{A_a}X\,dP$.

Therefore, for every generator set $A_a$ of $\sigma(Y)$,
$\int_{A_a} X\,dP=\int_{A_a}\psi(Y)\,dP$.
Since $\psi(Y)$ is $\sigma(Y)$-measurable, it follows that
$E(X\mid Y)=\psi(Y)$ a.s.

So the conditional expectation is
$E(X\mid Y)=h(Y)\dfrac{f(h(Y))-f(-h(Y))}{f(h(Y))+f(-h(Y))}$ a.s.

answer:
(i) For a Borel set $B$, $\{Y\in B\}=\{Z\in h^{-1}(B)\}$. Since $X$ is independent of every measurable function of $Z$ and both variables are integrable,
$$
\int_{\{Y\in B\}}XZ\,dP
=E\!\left[X\,Z I_{h^{-1}(B)}(Z)\right]
=E(X)E\!\left[Z I_{h^{-1}(B)}(Z)\right]
=E(X)\int_{\{Y\in B\}}Z\,dP.
$$
The defining property of conditional expectation gives
$$E(XZ\mid Y)=E(X)E(Z\mid Y)\quad\text{a.s.}$$

(ii) Take the bounded, continuous, strictly increasing function $r(t)=e^t/(1+e^t)$. The assumption applies to both $r$ and $r^2$. Since $Y=h(Z)$ is $\sigma(Z)$-measurable,
$$
E\{[r(X)-r(Y)]^2\mid Z\}
=E[r^2(X)\mid Z]+r^2(Y)-2r(Y)E[r(X)\mid Z]=0.
$$
Thus $r(X)=r(Y)$ a.s.; injectivity of $r$ yields $X=Y$ a.s.

(iii) Fix $c\in\mathbb R$ and choose bounded continuous nondecreasing $r_m$ with $r_m(t)\to I_{(c,\infty)}(t)$. Conditional dominated convergence and the assumption give
$$
P(X>c,Y>c)
=E\{I_{\{Y>c\}}E[I_{\{X>c\}}\mid Z]\}
\ge P(Y>c).
$$
The reverse inequality is automatic, so $P(X\le c,Y>c)=0$. Finally,
$$\{X<Y\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q}\{X\le q<Y\},$$
and every event in this countable union has probability $0$. Hence $X\ge Y$ a.s.
explanation:
For (i), test the proposed conditional-expectation identity on the generating events $\{Y\in B\}$. Because $Y=h(Z)$, their indicators are functions of $Z$, so independence factors the integral without ever integrating over the nonevent $h^{-1}(B)$ itself.

For (ii), a single bounded continuous one-to-one transform $r(t)=e^t/(1+e^t)$ is enough. Applying the hypothesis to $r$ and $r^2$ makes the conditional mean square of $r(X)-r(Y)$ equal to zero, which forces equality.

For (iii), continuous increasing approximations to $I_{(c,\infty)}$ imply $P(X\le c<Y)=0$ for every real $c$. Density of the rationals then gives
$$\{X<Y\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q}\{X\le q<Y\},$$
so the undesired event is a countable union of null events.

question: Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},\ldots$ be a sequence of identically distributed random variables with $E\left| {X}_{1}\right| < \infty$ and let ${Y}_{n} = {n}^{-1}\mathop{\max }\limits_{{1 \leq i \leq n}}\left| {X}_{i}\right|$ . Show that $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}E\left( {Y}_{n}\right) = 0$ and $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}{Y}_{n} = 0$ a.s.
keypoint: 随机变量序列的收敛性
answer:
(i) Let ${g}_{n}\left( t\right) = {n}^{-1}P\left( {\mathop{\max }\limits_{{1 \leq i \leq n}}\left| {X}_{i}\right| > t}\right)$ . Then $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}{g}_{n}\left( t\right) = 0$ for any $t$ and$$
0 \leq {g}_{n} \leq \frac{1}{n}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}P\left( {\left| {X}_{i}\right| > t}\right) = P\left( {\left| {X}_{1}\right| > t}\right) .
$$
Since $E\left| {X}_{1}\right| < \infty ,{\int }_{0}^{\infty }P\left( {\left| {X}_{1}\right| > t}\right) {dt} < \infty$ (Exercise 23). By the dominated convergence theorem,$$
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}E\left( {Y}_{n}\right) = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{g}_{n}\left( t\right) {dt} = {\int }_{0}^{\infty }\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}{g}_{n}\left( t\right) {dt} = 0.
$$
(ii) Since $E\left| {X}_{1}\right| < \infty$ ,$$
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{n = 1}}^{\infty }P\left( {\left| {X}_{n}\right| /n > \epsilon }\right) = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{n = 1}}^{\infty }P\left( {\left| {X}_{1}\right| > {\epsilon n}}\right) < \infty ,
$$
which implies that $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}\left| {X}_{n}\right| /n = 0$ a.s. (see, e.g., Theorem 1.8(v) in Shao, 2003). Let ${\Omega }^{0} = \left\{ {\omega : \mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}\left| {{X}_{n}\left( \omega \right) }\right| /n = 0}\right\}$ . Then $P\left( {\Omega }^{0}\right) = 1$ . Let $\omega \in {\Omega }^{0}$ . For any $\epsilon > 0$ , there exists an ${N}_{\epsilon ,\omega }$ such that $\left| {{X}_{n}\left( \omega \right) }\right| < {n\epsilon }$ whenever $n > \; {N}_{\epsilon ,\omega }$ . Also, there exists an ${M}_{\epsilon ,\omega } > {N}_{\epsilon ,\omega }$ such that $\mathop{\max }\limits_{{1 \leq i \leq {N}_{\epsilon \omega }}}\left| {{X}_{i}\left( \omega \right) }\right| \leq {n\epsilon }$ whenever $n > {M}_{\epsilon ,\omega }$ . Then, whenever $n > {M}_{\epsilon ,\omega }$ ,$$
{Y}_{n}\left( \omega \right) = \frac{\mathop{\max }\limits_{{1 \leq i \leq n}}\left| {{X}_{i}\left( \omega \right) }\right| }{n}
$$$$
\leq \frac{\mathop{\max }\limits_{{1 \leq i \leq {N}_{\epsilon \omega }}}\left| {{X}_{i}\left( \omega \right) }\right| }{n} + \frac{\mathop{\max }\limits_{{{N}_{\epsilon \omega } < i \leq n}}\left| {{X}_{i}\left( \omega \right) }\right| }{n}
$$$$
\leq \epsilon + \mathop{\max }\limits_{{{N}_{\epsilon \omega } < i \leq n}}\frac{\left| {X}_{i}\left( \omega \right) \right| }{i}
$$$$
\leq {2\epsilon }
$$
i.e., $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}{Y}_{n}\left( \omega \right) = 0$ . Hence, $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}{Y}_{n} = 0$ a.s., since $P\left( {\Omega }^{0}\right) = 1$ .
explanation:
This problem mainly uses the keypoints $\text{数学期望}$ and $\text{随机变量序列的收敛性}$. For the expectation part, we express $E(Y_n)$ through a tail integral and apply the dominated convergence theorem; for the almost sure convergence part, we first prove $|X_n|/n\to 0$ a.s. and then transfer this to the maximum term $Y_n$.

For $(1)$, prove $\lim_{n\to\infty}E(Y_n)=0$.

Let
$g_n(t)=\dfrac{1}{n}P\left(\max_{1\le i\le n}|X_i|>t\right),\quad t\ge 0.$
Since
$Y_n=\dfrac{1}{n}\max_{1\le i\le n}|X_i|,$
we use the tail-integral formula for a nonnegative random variable:
$E(Y_n)=\int_0^{\infty}P(Y_n>u)\,du.$
Now
$P(Y_n>u)=P\left(\max_{1\le i\le n}|X_i|>nu\right).$
By changing variable $t=nu$, $dt=n\,du$, we obtain
$E(Y_n)=\int_0^{\infty}P\left(\max_{1\le i\le n}|X_i|>nu\right)du
=\int_0^{\infty}\frac{1}{n}P\left(\max_{1\le i\le n}|X_i|>t\right)dt
=\int_0^{\infty}g_n(t)dt.$

Next fix any $t\ge 0$. Since the random variables are identically distributed,
$0\le g_n(t)=\frac{1}{n}P\left(\max_{1\le i\le n}|X_i|>t\right)
\le \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n P(|X_i|>t)
= P(|X_1|>t).$
Also, for fixed $t$, we have
$0\le P\left(\max_{1\le i\le n}|X_i|>t\right)\le 1,$
so
$0\le g_n(t)\le \frac{1}{n}\to 0.$
Hence for every fixed $t$,
$g_n(t)\to 0.$

Because $E|X_1|<\infty$, the tail-integral identity gives
$\int_0^{\infty}P(|X_1|>t)dt=E|X_1|<\infty.$
Thus $P(|X_1|>t)$ is an integrable dominating function for $g_n(t)$. By the dominated convergence theorem,
$\lim_{n\to\infty}E(Y_n)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^{\infty}g_n(t)dt
=\int_0^{\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty}g_n(t)dt
=\int_0^{\infty}0\,dt=0.$
So
$\lim_{n\to\infty}E(Y_n)=0.$

For $(2)$, prove $Y_n\to 0$ almost surely.

Since $E|X_1|<\infty$, for any $\varepsilon>0$,
$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}P\left(\frac{|X_n|}{n}>\varepsilon\right)
=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}P(|X_1|>\varepsilon n)<\infty.$
Therefore, by the Borel-Cantelli type conclusion, we get
$\frac{|X_n|}{n}\to 0\quad \text{a.s.}$
Define
$\Omega^0=\left\{\omega: \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{|X_n(\omega)|}{n}=0\right\}.$
Then $P(\Omega^0)=1$.

Now take any $\omega\in\Omega^0$. For arbitrary $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $N_{\varepsilon,\omega}$ such that whenever $n>N_{\varepsilon,\omega}$,
$|X_n(\omega)|<n\varepsilon.$
Since the finitely many values $|X_1(\omega)|,\dots,|X_{N_{\varepsilon,\omega}}(\omega)|$ are fixed, there exists $M_{\varepsilon,\omega}>N_{\varepsilon,\omega}$ such that whenever $n>M_{\varepsilon,\omega}$,
$\max_{1\le i\le N_{\varepsilon,\omega}}|X_i(\omega)|\le n\varepsilon.$

For $n>M_{\varepsilon,\omega}$,
$Y_n(\omega)=\frac{\max_{1\le i\le n}|X_i(\omega)|}{n}$
$\le \frac{\max_{1\le i\le N_{\varepsilon,\omega}}|X_i(\omega)|}{n}
+\frac{\max_{N_{\varepsilon,\omega}<i\le n}|X_i(\omega)|}{n}$
$\le \varepsilon+\max_{N_{\varepsilon,\omega}<i\le n}\frac{|X_i(\omega)|}{i}$
$\le \varepsilon+\varepsilon=2\varepsilon.$
Since $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary, this implies
$Y_n(\omega)\to 0.$
Because this holds for every $\omega\in\Omega^0$ and $P(\Omega^0)=1$, we conclude that
$Y_n\to 0\quad \text{a.s.}$

Therefore, the final results are
$\lim_{n\to\infty}E(Y_n)=0$ and $Y_n\to 0$ almost surely.

answer:
Work on $([0,1],\mathcal B,\lambda)$.

(i) Let $X=0$. For $m\ge0$, $0\le k<2^m$, and $n=2^m+k$, set
\[
X_n=I_{[k/2^m,(k+1)/2^m)}.
\]
Then $P(X_n=1)=2^{-m}\to0$, so $X_n\xrightarrow{P}0$, while almost every $\omega$ belongs to one such interval in every block and also lies outside infinitely many of them; hence $X_n(\omega)$ does not converge.

(ii) Let $X=0$ and $X_n=e^n I_{[0,1/n]}$. Then $P(X_n\ne0)=1/n\to0$, but for every $p>0$,
\[
E|X_n|^p=\frac{e^{np}}n\to\infty.
\]

(iii) Let $X=I_{[0,1/2]}$ and $X_n=1-X$. They have the same Bernoulli$(1/2)$ distribution, so $X_n\xrightarrow dX$, but $P(|X_n-X|>1/2)=1$.

(iv) Let $X_n=1/n$, $X=0$, and $g(t)=I_{\{t\ne0\}}$. Then $X_n\xrightarrow PX$, but $g(X_n)=1\not\xrightarrow P0=g(X)$.

(v) Let $N_m=m(m-1)/2$. For $1\le k\le m$, define the single sequence
\[
X_{N_m+k}=\sqrt m\,I_{((k-1)/m,k/m]}.
\]
Then $E|X_{N_m+k}|=m^{-1/2}\to0$. For every $\omega\in(0,1]$ and every $m$, one of the $m$ variables in block $m$ equals $\sqrt m$ at $\omega$. Thus any common dominating function is infinite almost everywhere and cannot be integrable.
explanation:
This problem is about modes of convergence of random variable sequences, especially $\xrightarrow{P}$ and $\xrightarrow{d}$, and about constructing counterexamples showing that different convergence notions are not equivalent. The key ideas are to verify the required convergence directly from the definitions and then show the stronger property fails by explicit calculation.

(i) Example with $X_n\xrightarrow{P}X$ but not almost surely.

Work on the probability space $([0,1],\mathcal B_{[0,1]},P)$, where $P$ is Lebesgue measure, and let $X=0$. For each positive integer $n$, write
\[
n=2^m-2+k,\qquad 0\le k<2^m.
\]
Define
\[
X_n(\omega)=
\begin{cases}
1, & \dfrac{k}{2^m}\le \omega\le \dfrac{k+1}{2^m},\\[4pt]
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
To prove convergence in probability, fix $\varepsilon>0$. Since $X=0$ and $X_n$ only takes values $0$ and $1$,
\[
P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\le P(X_n=1)=P\!\left(\left[\frac{k}{2^m},\frac{k+1}{2^m}\right]\right)=\frac{1}{2^m}\to0
\]
as $n\to\infty$. Hence $X_n\xrightarrow{P}0$.

Now show almost sure convergence fails. Fix any $\omega\in[0,1]$. For each $m$, there exists some integer $k$ with $1\le k\le 2^m$ such that
\[
\frac{k-1}{2^m}\le \omega\le \frac{k}{2^m}.
\]
Set $n_m=2^m-2+k$. Then by construction $X_{n_m}(\omega)=1$. Since this happens for infinitely many $m$, the sequence $X_n(\omega)$ does not converge to $0$. Because $\omega$ was arbitrary, $X_n$ does not converge to $X$ almost surely.

(ii) Example with $X_n\xrightarrow{P}X$ but $E|X_n-X|^p$ does not converge for any $p>0$.

Let $X=0$ and define
\[
X_n(\omega)=
\begin{cases}
0, & 1/n<\omega\le1,\\
e^n, & 0\le \omega\le 1/n.
\end{cases}
\]
Fix any $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$. Then
\[
P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)=P(X_n\ne0)=\frac{1}{n}\to0.
\]
Therefore $X_n\xrightarrow{P}0$.

Next compute the $p$th absolute moment of the error for arbitrary $p>0$:
\[
E|X_n-X|^p=E|X_n|^p=e^{np}\cdot P\left(0\le\omega\le\frac1n\right)=e^{np}\cdot\frac1n=\frac{e^{np}}{n}.
\]
Since $e^{np}/n\to\infty$, the sequence $E|X_n-X|^p$ does not converge for any $p>0$.

(iii) Example with $X_n\xrightarrow{d}X$ but not in probability.

Define
\[
X(\omega)=
\begin{cases}
1, & 0\le \omega\le 1/2,\\
0, & 1/2<\omega\le1,
\end{cases}
\qquad
X_n(\omega)=
\begin{cases}
0, & 0\le \omega\le 1/2,\\
1, & 1/2<\omega\le1.
\end{cases}
\]
Both $X$ and $X_n$ take values $0$ and $1$ with probability $1/2$ each. Thus, for every real $t$,
\[
P(X\le t)=P(X_n\le t)=
\begin{cases}
1, & t\ge1,\\
1/2, & 0\le t<1,\\
0, & t<0.
\end{cases}
\]
So the distribution functions are identical, and hence $X_n\xrightarrow{d}X$.

However,
\[
|X_n-X|=1
\]
for every $\omega\in[0,1]$. Therefore, for any $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$,
\[
P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)=1,
\]
which does not tend to $0$. Hence $X_n$ does not converge to $X$ in probability.

(iv) Example with $X_n\xrightarrow{P}X$ but $g(X_n)\not\xrightarrow{P}g(X)$.

Take
\[
g(t)=1-I_{\{0\}}(t),\qquad X=0,\qquad X_n=\frac1n.
\]
Since $X_n$ is deterministic and $1/n\to0$, clearly $X_n\xrightarrow{P}0=X$.

Now evaluate the transformed variables. Because $X_n=1/n\ne0$,
\[
g(X_n)=1-I_{\{0\}}(1/n)=1.
\]
But
\[
g(X)=g(0)=1-I_{\{0\}}(0)=0.
\]
Thus $g(X_n)$ is constantly equal to $1$, while $g(X)=0$. Hence for any $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$,
\[
P(|g(X_n)-g(X)|>\varepsilon)=1,
\]
so $g(X_n)$ does not converge to $g(X)$ in probability.

(v) Example with $\lim_n E|X_n|=0$ but no integrable common dominator.

Let $N_m=m(m-1)/2$. For each $m\ge1$ and $1\le k\le m$, define the single-indexed sequence by
\[
X_{N_m+k}(\omega)=
\begin{cases}
\sqrt m, & \dfrac{k-1}{m}<\omega\le\dfrac{k}{m},\\[4pt]
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Every positive integer has a unique representation $N_m+k$ with $1\le k\le m$, so this defines one sequence $\{X_n\}$.

For $n=N_m+k$,
\[
E|X_n|=\sqrt m\cdot\frac1m=\frac1{\sqrt m}\longrightarrow0
\]
because $m\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$.

Suppose an integrable function $f$ dominated every $|X_n|$. Fix $\omega\in(0,1]$. For every $m$, exactly one interval $((k-1)/m,k/m]$ contains $\omega$, and for its corresponding index $n=N_m+k$,
\[
|X_n(\omega)|=\sqrt m.
\]
Hence $f(\omega)\ge\sqrt m$ for every $m$, so $f(\omega)=\infty$ for all $\omega\in(0,1]$. Such an $f$ cannot be integrable. Therefore no integrable function dominates the sequence.

Conclusion: the five constructions above provide explicit examples for all requested cases, showing the distinctions among convergence in probability, almost sure convergence, convergence in distribution, moment convergence, and domination by an integrable function.

question: Let ${X}_{n}$ be a random variable and ${m}_{n}$ be a median of ${X}_{n}$ , $n = 1,2,\ldots$ Show that if ${X}_{n}{ \rightarrow }_{d}X$ for a random variable $X$ , then any limit point of ${m}_{n}$ is a median of $X$ .
answer:
Without loss of generality, assume that $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}{m}_{n} = m$ . For $\epsilon > 0$ such that $m + \epsilon$ and $m - \epsilon$ are continuity points of the distribution of $X$ , $m - \epsilon < {m}_{n} < m + \epsilon$ for sufficiently large $n$ and$$
\frac{1}{2} \leq P\left( {{X}_{n} \leq {m}_{n}}\right) \leq P\left( {{X}_{n} \leq m + \epsilon }\right)
$$
and$$
\frac{1}{2} \leq P\left( {{X}_{n} \geq {m}_{n}}\right) \leq P\left( {{X}_{n} \geq m - \epsilon }\right) .
$$
Letting $n \rightarrow \infty$ , we obtain that $\frac{1}{2} \leq P\left( {X \leq m + \epsilon }\right)$ and $\frac{1}{2} \leq P\left( {X \geq m - \epsilon }\right)$ . Letting $\epsilon \rightarrow 0$ , we obtain that $\frac{1}{2} \leq P\left( {X \leq m}\right)$ and $\frac{1}{2} \leq P\left( {X \geq m}\right)$ . Hence $m$ is a median of $X$ .
explanation:
This problem uses the notions of median, convergence in distribution, and the distribution function. The key idea is to combine the defining inequalities of a median with the preservation of probabilities at continuity points under $X_n \xrightarrow{d} X$.

Assume, without loss of generality, that a subsequence of $\{m_n\}$ converges and that
$\lim_{n\to\infty} m_n = m$.
We will show that $m$ is a median of $X$.

By definition, since $m_n$ is a median of $X_n$, for every $n$ we have
$P(X_n \le m_n) \ge \frac12$
and
$P(X_n \ge m_n) \ge \frac12$.

Now fix $\varepsilon > 0$ such that both $m+\varepsilon$ and $m-\varepsilon$ are continuity points of the distribution of $X$. Since $m_n \to m$, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$m-\varepsilon < m_n < m+\varepsilon$.

Because $m_n < m+\varepsilon$, the event $\{X_n \le m_n\}$ is contained in $\{X_n \le m+\varepsilon\}$, hence
$\frac12 \le P(X_n \le m_n) \le P(X_n \le m+\varepsilon)$.
Taking $n \to \infty$ and using $X_n \xrightarrow{d} X$ at the continuity point $m+\varepsilon$, we get
$\frac12 \le P(X \le m+\varepsilon)$.

Similarly, since $m_n > m-\varepsilon$, the event $\{X_n \ge m_n\}$ is contained in $\{X_n \ge m-\varepsilon\}$, so
$\frac12 \le P(X_n \ge m_n) \le P(X_n \ge m-\varepsilon)$.
Letting $n \to \infty$, and again using convergence in distribution at the continuity point $m-\varepsilon$, we obtain
$\frac12 \le P(X \ge m-\varepsilon)$.

Therefore, for every such $\varepsilon>0$,
$P(X \le m+\varepsilon) \ge \frac12$
and
$P(X \ge m-\varepsilon) \ge \frac12$.

Now let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. By the right-continuity/monotonicity properties of probabilities for these nested events, we get
$P(X \le m) \ge \frac12$
and
$P(X \ge m) \ge \frac12$.

These are exactly the conditions that $m$ be a median of $X$. Hence any limit point of $\{m_n\}$ is a median of $X$.
subject: Mathematical Statistics

question: Show that if ${X}_{n}{ \rightarrow }_{d}X$ and $X = c$ a.s. for a real number $c$ , then ${X}_{n}{ \rightarrow }_{p}X$ .
answer:
Note that the cumulative distribution function of $X$ has only one discontinuity point $c$ . For any $\epsilon > 0$ ,$$
P\left( {\left| {{X}_{n} - X}\right| > \epsilon }\right) = P\left( {\left| {{X}_{n} - c}\right| > \epsilon }\right)
$$$$
\leq P\left( {{X}_{n} > c + \epsilon }\right) + P\left( {{X}_{n} \leq c - \epsilon }\right)
$$$$
\rightarrow P\left( {X > c + \epsilon }\right) + P\left( {X \leq c - \epsilon }\right)
$$$$
= 0
$$
as $n \rightarrow \infty$ . Thus, ${X}_{n}{ \rightarrow }_{p}X$ .
explanation:
This problem involves the relation between convergence in distribution and convergence in probability, together with the special case that $X=c$ a.s., namely a degenerate distribution. The key idea is to use the distributional convergence of $X_n$ to the constant random variable $X$ and show that the tail probability $P(|X_n-c|>\epsilon)$ tends to $0$ for every $\epsilon>0$.

Since $X=c$ a.s., we have
$X_n-X = X_n-c$ a.s.,
so for any $\epsilon>0$,
$$P\bigl(|X_n-X|>\epsilon\bigr)=P\bigl(|X_n-c|>\epsilon\bigr).$$
Now the event $\{|X_n-c|>\epsilon\}$ implies either $X_n>c+\epsilon$ or $X_n<c-\epsilon$. Hence,
$$P\bigl(|X_n-c|>\epsilon\bigr)\le P(X_n>c+\epsilon)+P(X_n\le c-\epsilon).$$

Next use the assumption $X_n\xrightarrow{d}X$. Because $X=c$ a.s., the distribution function of $X$ is degenerate at $c$, so its only discontinuity point is $c$. Therefore, for the continuity points $c+\epsilon$ and $c-\epsilon$, convergence in distribution gives the corresponding tail probabilities converging to those of $X$. Thus,
$$P(X_n>c+\epsilon)\to P(X>c+\epsilon),$$
$$P(X_n\le c-\epsilon)\to P(X\le c-\epsilon).$$
Since $X=c$ a.s.,
$$P(X>c+\epsilon)=0,\qquad P(X\le c-\epsilon)=0.$$
Therefore,
$$P\bigl(|X_n-X|>\epsilon\bigr)
=P\bigl(|X_n-c|>\epsilon\bigr)
\le P(X_n>c+\epsilon)+P(X_n\le c-\epsilon)
\to 0+0=0.$$

Because this holds for every $\epsilon>0$, by the definition of convergence in probability,
$$X_n\xrightarrow{p}X.$$
So the conclusion is proved.
subject: Mathematical Statistics

question:
Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},\ldots$ be random variables. Show that $\left\{ \left| {X}_{n}\right| \right\}$ is uniformly integrable if one of the following condition holds:
(i) $\mathop{\sup }\limits_{n}E{\left| {X}_{n}\right| }^{1 + \delta } < \infty$ for a $\delta > 0$ ;
(ii) $P\left( {\left| {X}_{n}\right| \geq c}\right) \leq P\left( {\left| X\right| \geq c}\right)$ for all $n$ and $c > 0$ , where $X$ is an integrable random variable.
Note. A sequence of random variables $\left\{ {X}_{n}\right\}$ is uniformly integrable if $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{n}E\left( {\left| {X}_{n}\right| {I}_{\left\{ \left| {X}_{n}\right| > t\right\} }}\right) = 0.$
answer:
(i) Denote $p = 1 + \delta$ and $q = 1 + {\delta }^{-1}$ . Then$$
E\left(|X_n|I_{\{|X_n|>t\}}\right)
\leq \left(E|X_n|^p\right)^{1/p}
\left[E\left(I_{\{|X_n|>t\}}^q\right)\right]^{1/q}
$$$$
=\left(E|X_n|^p\right)^{1/p}
\left[P(|X_n|>t)\right]^{1/q}
$$$$
\leq \left(E|X_n|^p\right)^{1/p}
\left(E|X_n|^p\right)^{1/q}t^{-p/q}
$$$$
=E|X_n|^{1+\delta}t^{-\delta},
$$
where the first inequality follows from Hölder's inequality (e.g., Shao, 2003, p. 29) and the second inequality follows from$$
P\left( {\left| {X}_{n}\right| > t}\right) \leq {t}^{-p}E{\left| {X}_{n}\right| }^{p}.
$$
Hence$$
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{n}E\left( {\left| {X}_{n}\right| {I}_{\left\{ \left| {X}_{n}\right| > t\right\} }}\right) \leq \mathop{\sup }\limits_{n}E{\left| {X}_{n}\right| }^{1 + \delta }\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow \infty }}{t}^{-\delta } = 0.
$$
(ii) By Exercise 23,$$
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{n}E\left( {\left| {X}_{n}\right| {I}_{\left\{ \left| {X}_{n}\right| > t\right\} }}\right) = \mathop{\sup }\limits_{n}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }P\left( {\left| {X}_{n}\right| {I}_{\left\{ \left| {X}_{n}\right| > t\right\} } > s}\right) {ds}
$$$$
= \mathop{\sup }\limits_{n}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }P\left( {\left| {X}_{n}\right| > s,\left| {X}_{n}\right| > t}\right) {ds}
$$$$
= \mathop{\sup }\limits_{n}\left( {{tP}\left( {\left| {X}_{n}\right| > t}\right) + {\int }_{t}^{\infty }P\left( {\left| {X}_{n}\right| > s}\right) {ds}}\right)
$$$$
\leq {tP}\left( {\left| X\right| > t}\right) + {\int }_{t}^{\infty }P\left( {\left| X\right| > s}\right) {ds}
$$$$
\rightarrow 0
$$
as $t \rightarrow \infty$ when $E\left| X\right| < \infty$ . ∎
explanation:
This problem uses the notions of random variables and mathematical expectation, together with moment bounds and tail integrals. The key idea is to verify directly from the definition of uniform integrability that $\lim_{t\to\infty}\sup_n E\big(|X_n|I_{\{|X_n|>t\}}\big)=0$ under each given condition.

For (i), assume that for some $\delta>0$,
$\sup_n E|X_n|^{1+\delta}<\infty$.
Set
$ p=1+\delta, \quad q=1+\delta^{-1}, $
so that $1/p+1/q=1$.
Then by H\"older's inequality,
$ E\big(|X_n|I_{\{|X_n|>t\}}\big)
\le (E|X_n|^p)^{1/p}\Big(E\big(I_{\{|X_n|>t\}}^q\big)\Big)^{1/q}. $
Since $I_{\{|X_n|>t\}}^q=I_{\{|X_n|>t\}}$,
$ E\big(|X_n|I_{\{|X_n|>t\}}\big)
\le (E|X_n|^p)^{1/p}\,P(|X_n|>t)^{1/q}. $
Next apply Markov's inequality to $|X_n|^p$:
$ P(|X_n|>t)\le t^{-p}E|X_n|^p. $
Therefore,
$ E\big(|X_n|I_{\{|X_n|>t\}}\big)
\le (E|X_n|^p)^{1/p}\big(t^{-p}E|X_n|^p\big)^{1/q}
= (E|X_n|^p)^{1/p+1/q} t^{-p/q}. $
Because $1/p+1/q=1$ and $p/q=\delta$,
$ E\big(|X_n|I_{\{|X_n|>t\}}\big)
\le E|X_n|^{1+\delta}\, t^{-\delta}. $
Taking supremum over $n$ gives
$ \sup_n E\big(|X_n|I_{\{|X_n|>t\}}\big)
\le \Big(\sup_n E|X_n|^{1+\delta}\Big)t^{-\delta}. $
Since $\sup_n E|X_n|^{1+\delta}<\infty$ and $t^{-\delta}\to 0$ as $t\to\infty$,
$ \lim_{t\to\infty}\sup_n E\big(|X_n|I_{\{|X_n|>t\}}\big)=0. $
Hence $\{|X_n|\}$ is uniformly integrable.

For (ii), assume that
$ P(|X_n|\ge c)\le P(|X|\ge c), \quad \forall n,\ c>0, $
where $X$ is integrable, i.e. $E|X|<\infty$.
Use the tail-integral representation:
$ E\big(|X_n|I_{\{|X_n|>t\}}\big)
= \int_0^{\infty} P\big(|X_n|I_{\{|X_n|>t\}}>s\big)\,ds. $
Now,
$ \{|X_n|I_{\{|X_n|>t\}}>s\}
= \{|X_n|>s,\ |X_n|>t\}. $
So,
$ E\big(|X_n|I_{\{|X_n|>t\}}\big)
= \int_0^{\infty} P(|X_n|>s, |X_n|>t)\,ds. $
Split the integral at $t$.
For $0\le s\le t$, the event $\{|X_n|>s,|X_n|>t\}$ is just $\{|X_n|>t\}$, hence
$ \int_0^t P(|X_n|>s,|X_n|>t)\,ds = tP(|X_n|>t). $
For $s>t$, the event $\{|X_n|>s,|X_n|>t\}$ is just $\{|X_n|>s\}$, hence
$ \int_t^{\infty} P(|X_n|>s,|X_n|>t)\,ds = \int_t^{\infty} P(|X_n|>s)\,ds. $
Therefore,
$ E\big(|X_n|I_{\{|X_n|>t\}}\big)
= tP(|X_n|>t)+\int_t^{\infty}P(|X_n|>s)\,ds. $
Using the tail domination condition,
$ E\big(|X_n|I_{\{|X_n|>t\}}\big)
\le tP(|X|>t)+\int_t^{\infty}P(|X|>s)\,ds. $
Thus,
$ \sup_n E\big(|X_n|I_{\{|X_n|>t\}}\big)
\le tP(|X|>t)+\int_t^{\infty}P(|X|>s)\,ds. $
Since $E|X|<\infty$, the tail expectation of $|X|$ tends to $0$, equivalently,
$ tP(|X|>t)+\int_t^{\infty}P(|X|>s)\,ds \to 0 \quad (t\to\infty). $
Hence,
$ \lim_{t\to\infty}\sup_n E\big(|X_n|I_{\{|X_n|>t\}}\big)=0. $
So $\{|X_n|\}$ is uniformly integrable.

Therefore, under either condition (i) or condition (ii), the sequence $\{|X_n|\}$ is uniformly integrable.

question: Let $\left\{ {X}_{n}\right\}$ and $\left\{ {Y}_{n}\right\}$ be sequences of random variables such that ${X}_{n}$ diverges to $\infty$ in probability and ${Y}_{n}$ is bounded in probability. Show that ${X}_{n} + {Y}_{n}$ diverges to $\infty$ in probability.
keypoint: 随机变量序列的收敛性
answer:
By the definition of bounded in probability, for any $\epsilon > 0$ , there is ${C}_{\epsilon } > 0$ such that $\mathop{\sup }\limits_{n}P\left( {\left| {Y}_{n}\right| > {C}_{\epsilon }}\right) < \epsilon /2$ . By the definition of divergence to $\infty$ in probability, for any $M > 0$ and $\epsilon > 0$ , there is ${n}_{\epsilon } > 0$ such that $P\left( {\left| {X}_{n}\right| \leq M + {C}_{\epsilon }}\right) < \epsilon /2$ whenever $n > {n}_{\epsilon }$ . Then, for $n > {n}_{\epsilon }$ ,$$
P\left( {\left| {{X}_{n} + {Y}_{n}}\right| \leq M}\right) \leq P\left( {\left| {X}_{n}\right| \leq M + \left| {Y}_{n}\right| }\right)
$$$$
= P\left( {\left| {X}_{n}\right| \leq M + \left| {Y}_{n}\right| ,\left| {Y}_{n}\right| \leq {C}_{\epsilon }}\right)
$$
\[
+ P\left( {\left| {X}_{n}\right| \leq M + \left| {Y}_{n}\right| ,\left| {Y}_{n}\right| > {C}_{\epsilon }}\right)
 \]
$$
 \leq P\left( {\left| {X}_{n}\right| \leq M + {C}_{\epsilon }}\right) + P\left( {\left| {Y}_{n}\right| > {C}_{\epsilon }}\right)
 $$$$
 \leq \epsilon /2 + \epsilon /2
 $$$$
 = \epsilon \text{ . }
 $$
This means that ${X}_{n} + {Y}_{n}$ diverges to $\infty$ in probability.
explanation:
This problem uses the notions of divergence to $\infty$ in probability and boundedness in probability, which belong to the study of convergence of random variable sequences. The key idea is to control $Y_n$ by boundedness in probability and then use the fact that $X_n$ becomes arbitrarily large in probability.

We need to show that for every $M>0$,
\[
P\bigl(|X_n+Y_n|\le M\bigr)\to 0 \quad (n\to\infty).
\]

First, since $\{Y_n\}$ is bounded in probability, for any $\epsilon>0$, there exists a constant $C_{\epsilon}>0$ such that
\[
\sup_n P\bigl(|Y_n|>C_{\epsilon}\bigr)<\frac{\epsilon}{2}.
\]
In particular, for every $n$,
\[
P\bigl(|Y_n|>C_{\epsilon}\bigr)<\frac{\epsilon}{2}.
\]

Next, since $X_n$ diverges to $\infty$ in probability, for any given $M>0$ and the same $\epsilon>0$, there exists $n_{\epsilon}$ such that whenever $n>n_{\epsilon}$,
\[
P\bigl(|X_n|\le M+C_{\epsilon}\bigr)<\frac{\epsilon}{2}.
\]

Now for $n>n_{\epsilon}$, consider the event $\{|X_n+Y_n|\le M\}$. By the triangle inequality,
\[
|X_n|=|(X_n+Y_n)-Y_n|\le |X_n+Y_n|+|Y_n|.
\]
Therefore, on the event $\{|X_n+Y_n|\le M\}$, we must have
\[
|X_n|\le M+|Y_n|.
\]
Hence,
\[
P\bigl(|X_n+Y_n|\le M\bigr)
\le P\bigl(|X_n|\le M+|Y_n|\bigr).
\]
Split the event according to whether $|Y_n|\le C_{\epsilon}$ or $|Y_n|>C_{\epsilon}$:
\[
P\bigl(|X_n|\le M+|Y_n|\bigr)
\le P\bigl(|X_n|\le M+|Y_n|,\ |Y_n|\le C_{\epsilon}\bigr)
+P\bigl(|X_n|\le M+|Y_n|,\ |Y_n|>C_{\epsilon}\bigr).
\]
For the first term, if $|Y_n|\le C_{\epsilon}$, then $M+|Y_n|\le M+C_{\epsilon}$, so
\[
P\bigl(|X_n|\le M+|Y_n|,\ |Y_n|\le C_{\epsilon}\bigr)
\le P\bigl(|X_n|\le M+C_{\epsilon}\bigr).
\]
For the second term,
\[
P\bigl(|X_n|\le M+|Y_n|,\ |Y_n|>C_{\epsilon}\bigr)
\le P\bigl(|Y_n|>C_{\epsilon}\bigr).
\]
Thus,
\[
P\bigl(|X_n+Y_n|\le M\bigr)
\le P\bigl(|X_n|\le M+C_{\epsilon}\bigr)+P\bigl(|Y_n|>C_{\epsilon}\bigr).
\]
Using the two bounds obtained above, for $n>n_{\epsilon}$,
\[
P\bigl(|X_n+Y_n|\le M\bigr)
\le \frac{\epsilon}{2}+\frac{\epsilon}{2}=\epsilon.
\]

Since $\epsilon>0$ is arbitrary, we conclude that for every $M>0$,
\[
P\bigl(|X_n+Y_n|\le M\bigr)\to 0.
\]
Therefore,
\[
X_n+Y_n \to \infty \quad \text{in probability}.
\]

question: Let $X,{X}_{1},{X}_{2},\ldots$ be random variables. Show that if $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}{X}_{n} \; = X$ a.s., then $\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{m \geq n}}\left| {X}_{m}\right|$ is bounded in probability.
keypoint: 随机变量序列的收敛性
answer:
Since $\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{m \geq n}}\left| {X}_{m}\right| \leq \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{m \geq 1}}\left| {X}_{m}\right|$ for any $n$ , it suffices to show that for any $\epsilon > 0$ , there is a $C > 0$ such that $P\left( {\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{n > 1}}\left| {X}_{n}\right| > C}\right) \leq \epsilon$ . Note that $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}{X}_{n} = X$ implies that, for any $\epsilon > 0$ and any fixed ${c}_{1} > 0$ , there exists a sufficiently large $N$ such that $P\left( {{ \cup }_{n = N}^{\infty }\left\{ {\left| {{X}_{n} - X}\right| > {c}_{1}}\right\} }\right) < \epsilon /3$ (e.g., Lemma 1.4 in Shao,2003). For this fixed $N$ , there exist constants ${c}_{2} > 0$ and ${c}_{3} > 0$ such that$$
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{n = 1}}^{N}P\left( {\left| {X}_{n}\right| > {c}_{2}}\right) < \frac{\epsilon }{3}\;\text{ and }\;P\left( {\left| X\right| > {c}_{3}}\right) < \frac{\epsilon }{3}.
$$
Let $C = \max \left\{ {{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}\right\} + {c}_{3}$ . Then the result follows from$$
P\left( {\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{n \geq 1}}\left| {X}_{n}\right| > C}\right) = P\left( {\mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{{n = 1}}^{\infty }\left\{ {\left| {X}_{n}\right| > C}\right\} }\right)
$$$$
\leq \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{n = 1}}^{N}P\left( {\left| {X}_{n}\right| > C}\right) + P\left( {\mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{{n = N}}^{\infty }\left\{ {\left| {X}_{n}\right| > C}\right\} }\right)
$$$$
\leq \frac{\epsilon }{3} + P\left( {\left| X\right| > {c}_{3}}\right) + P\left( {\mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{{n = N}}^{\infty }\left\{ {\left| {X}_{n}\right| > C,\left| X\right| \leq {c}_{3}}\right\} }\right)
$$$$
\leq \frac{\epsilon }{3} + \frac{\epsilon }{3} + P\left( {\mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{{n = N}}^{\infty }\left\{ {\left| {{X}_{n} - X}\right| > {c}_{1}}\right\} }\right)
$$$$
\leq \frac{\epsilon }{3} + \frac{\epsilon }{3} + \frac{\epsilon }{3} = \epsilon \text{ . ∎ }
$$
explanation:
This problem uses the convergence of a sequence of random variables and basic probability bounds. The key idea is that almost sure convergence $X_n\to X$ implies that the tail deviations $\{|X_n-X|>c_1\}$ become uniformly unlikely for large $n$, and then we combine this with probability bounds for finitely many initial variables and for $X$ itself.

We need to show that $\sup_{m\ge n}|X_m|$ is bounded in probability. Since for every $n$,
\[
\sup_{m\ge n}|X_m|\le \sup_{m\ge 1}|X_m|,
\]
it is enough to prove that $\sup_{m\ge 1}|X_m|$ is bounded in probability. That is, we must show:
for every $\epsilon>0$, there exists $C>0$ such that
\[
P\left(\sup_{n\ge 1}|X_n|>C\right)\le \epsilon.
\]

Fix any $\epsilon>0$. Because $X_n\to X$ almost surely, for any fixed $c_1>0$, there exists a sufficiently large integer $N$ such that
\[
P\left(\bigcup_{n=N}^{\infty}\{|X_n-X|>c_1|\}\right)<\frac{\epsilon}{3}.
\]
This is the tail control obtained from almost sure convergence.

Now for this fixed $N$, since there are only finitely many random variables $X_1,\dots,X_N$, we can choose $c_2>0$ large enough so that
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{N}P(|X_n|>c_2)<\frac{\epsilon}{3}.
\]
Also, because $X$ is a random variable, we can choose $c_3>0$ such that
\[
P(|X|>c_3)<\frac{\epsilon}{3}.
\]

Define
\[
C=\max\{c_1,c_2\}+c_3.
\]
We now estimate the probability of the event that the whole sequence exceeds $C$:
\[
P\left(\sup_{n\ge 1}|X_n|>C\right)
= P\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}\{|X_n|>C\}\right).
\]
Split this union into the first $N$ terms and the tail:
\[
P\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}\{|X_n|>C\}\right)
\le \sum_{n=1}^{N}P(|X_n|>C)+P\left(\bigcup_{n=N}^{\infty}\{|X_n|>C\}\right).
\]
Since $C\ge c_2$, we have
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{N}P(|X_n|>C)\le \sum_{n=1}^{N}P(|X_n|>c_2)<\frac{\epsilon}{3}.
\]
Hence,
\[
P\left(\sup_{n\ge 1}|X_n|>C\right)
\le \frac{\epsilon}{3}+P\left(\bigcup_{n=N}^{\infty}\{|X_n|>C\}\right).
\]

Next, decompose the tail event according to whether $|X|>c_3$ or not:
\[
P\left(\bigcup_{n=N}^{\infty}\{|X_n|>C\}\right)
\le P(|X|>c_3)+P\left(\bigcup_{n=N}^{\infty}\{|X_n|>C,\ |X|\le c_3\}\right).
\]
Therefore,
\[
P\left(\sup_{n\ge 1}|X_n|>C\right)
\le \frac{\epsilon}{3}+P(|X|>c_3)+P\left(\bigcup_{n=N}^{\infty}\{|X_n|>C,\ |X|\le c_3\}\right).
\]
Using $P(|X|>c_3)<\epsilon/3$, we get
\[
P\left(\sup_{n\ge 1}|X_n|>C\right)
\le \frac{\epsilon}{3}+\frac{\epsilon}{3}+P\left(\bigcup_{n=N}^{\infty}\{|X_n|>C,\ |X|\le c_3\}\right).
\]

Now if $|X_n|>C$ and $|X|\le c_3$, then by the triangle inequality,
\[
|X_n-X|\ge |X_n|-|X|>C-c_3=\max\{c_1,c_2\}\ge c_1.
\]
So
\[
\{|X_n|>C,\ |X|\le c_3\}\subseteq \{|X_n-X|>c_1\}.
\]
Hence,
\[
P\left(\bigcup_{n=N}^{\infty}\{|X_n|>C,\ |X|\le c_3\}\right)
\le P\left(\bigcup_{n=N}^{\infty}\{|X_n-X|>c_1\}\right)
<\frac{\epsilon}{3}.
\]
Combining all bounds,
\[
P\left(\sup_{n\ge 1}|X_n|>C\right)
\le \frac{\epsilon}{3}+\frac{\epsilon}{3}+\frac{\epsilon}{3}=\epsilon.
\]

Thus for every $\epsilon>0$, there exists $C>0$ such that
\[
P\left(\sup_{n\ge 1}|X_n|>C\right)\le \epsilon.
\]
Therefore $\sup_{m\ge n}|X_m|$ is bounded in probability.

question: Let $\left\{ {X}_{n}\right\}$ and $\left\{ {Y}_{n}\right\}$ be two sequences of random variables such that ${X}_{n}$ is bounded in probability and, for any real number $t$ and $\epsilon > 0,\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}\left\lbrack {P\left( {{X}_{n} \leq t,{Y}_{n} \geq t + \epsilon }\right) + P\left( {{X}_{n} \geq t + \epsilon ,{Y}_{n} \leq t}\right) }\right\rbrack = 0$ . Show that ${X}_{n} - {Y}_{n}{ \rightarrow }_{p}0$ .
keypoint: 随机变量序列的收敛性
answer:
For any $\epsilon > 0$ , there exists an $M > 0$ such that $P\left( {\left| {X}_{n}\right| \geq M}\right) \leq \epsilon$ for any $n$ , since ${X}_{n}$ is bounded in probability. For this fixed $M$ , there exists an $N$ such that ${2M}/N < \epsilon /2$ . Let ${t}_{i} = - M + {2Mi}/N, i = 0,1,\ldots , N$ . Then,$$
P\left( {\left| {{X}_{n} - {Y}_{n}}\right| \geq \epsilon }\right) \leq P\left( {\left| {X}_{n}\right| \geq M}\right) + P\left( {\left| {X}_{n}\right| < M,\left| {{X}_{n} - {Y}_{n}}\right| \geq \epsilon }\right)
$$$$
\leq \epsilon + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{N}P\left( {{t}_{i - 1} \leq {X}_{n} \leq {t}_{i},\left| {{X}_{n} - {Y}_{n}}\right| \geq \epsilon }\right)
$$$$
\leq \epsilon + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{N}P\left( {{Y}_{n} \leq {t}_{i - 1} - \epsilon /2,{t}_{i - 1} \leq {X}_{n}}\right)
$$
\[
+ \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{N}P\left( {{Y}_{n} \geq {t}_{i} + \epsilon /2,{X}_{n} \leq {t}_{i}}\right)
 \]
This, together with the given condition, implies that$$
\mathop{\limsup }\limits_{n}P\left( {\left| {{X}_{n} - {Y}_{n}}\right| \geq \epsilon }\right) \leq \epsilon
$$
Since $\epsilon$ is arbitrary, we conclude that ${X}_{n} - {Y}_{n}{ \rightarrow }_{p}0$ .
explanation:
This problem uses the ideas of $\,$"bounded in probability" and convergence in probability, so the core knowledge points are $\text{依概率收敛}$ and $\text{随机变量序列的收敛性}$. The proof works by controlling the tail of $X_n$ uniformly and then partitioning a bounded interval into small subintervals, so that the given crossing-probability condition can be applied.

Fix $\epsilon>0$. Since $\{X_n\}$ is bounded in probability, there exists $M>0$ such that for all $n$,
$$
P(|X_n|\ge M)\le \epsilon.
$$
Then decompose
$$
P(|X_n-Y_n|\ge \epsilon)
\le P(|X_n|\ge M)+P(|X_n|<M,\,|X_n-Y_n|\ge \epsilon).
$$
Hence,
$$
P(|X_n-Y_n|\ge \epsilon)
\le \epsilon+P(|X_n|<M,\,|X_n-Y_n|\ge \epsilon).
$$

Now choose an integer $N$ such that
$$
\frac{2M}{N}<\frac{\epsilon}{2}.
$$
Define a partition of $[-M,M]$ by
$$
t_i=-M+\frac{2Mi}{N},\qquad i=0,1,\ldots,N.
$$
Then for $|X_n|<M$, the value of $X_n$ must lie in one of the intervals $[t_{i-1},t_i]$, so
$$
P(|X_n|<M,\,|X_n-Y_n|\ge \epsilon)
\le \sum_{i=1}^N P(t_{i-1}\le X_n\le t_i,\,|X_n-Y_n|\ge \epsilon).
$$
Therefore,
$$
P(|X_n-Y_n|\ge \epsilon)
\le \epsilon+\sum_{i=1}^N P(t_{i-1}\le X_n\le t_i,\,|X_n-Y_n|\ge \epsilon).
$$

For each fixed $i$, on the event
$$
\{t_{i-1}\le X_n\le t_i,\ |X_n-Y_n|\ge \epsilon\},
$$
we have either $Y_n\le X_n-\epsilon$ or $Y_n\ge X_n+\epsilon$.

If $Y_n\le X_n-\epsilon$, then since $X_n\ge t_{i-1}$,
$$
Y_n\le X_n-\epsilon\le t_i-\epsilon.
$$
Because $t_i-t_{i-1}=2M/N<\epsilon/2$, we have
$$
t_i-\epsilon\le t_{i-1}-\frac{\epsilon}{2}.
$$
Thus,
$$
\{t_{i-1}\le X_n\le t_i,\ Y_n\le X_n-\epsilon\}
\subseteq \{Y_n\le t_{i-1}-\epsilon/2,\ t_{i-1}\le X_n\}.
$$

If $Y_n\ge X_n+\epsilon$, then since $X_n\le t_i$,
$$
Y_n\ge X_n+\epsilon\ge t_{i-1}+\epsilon.
$$
Again using $t_i-t_{i-1}<\epsilon/2$, we get
$$
t_{i-1}+\epsilon\ge t_i+\frac{\epsilon}{2}.
$$
Hence,
$$
\{t_{i-1}\le X_n\le t_i,\ Y_n\ge X_n+\epsilon\}
\subseteq \{Y_n\ge t_i+\epsilon/2,\ X_n\le t_i\}.
$$

Combining the two cases,
$$
P(t_{i-1}\le X_n\le t_i,\,|X_n-Y_n|\ge \epsilon)
\le P(Y_n\le t_{i-1}-\epsilon/2,\ t_{i-1}\le X_n)
+P(Y_n\ge t_i+\epsilon/2,\ X_n\le t_i).
$$
So
$$
P(|X_n-Y_n|\ge \epsilon)
\le \epsilon+\sum_{i=1}^N P(Y_n\le t_{i-1}-\epsilon/2,\ t_{i-1}\le X_n)
+\sum_{i=1}^N P(Y_n\ge t_i+\epsilon/2,\ X_n\le t_i).
$$
Rewrite these terms in the form required by the assumption:
$$
P(Y_n\le t_{i-1}-\epsilon/2,\ t_{i-1}\le X_n)
= P(X_n\ge t_{i-1},\ Y_n\le t_{i-1}-\epsilon/2),
$$
which matches
$$
P(X_n\ge t+\epsilon',\ Y_n\le t)
$$
by taking $t=t_{i-1}-\epsilon/2$ and $\epsilon'=\epsilon/2$;

and
$$
P(Y_n\ge t_i+\epsilon/2,\ X_n\le t_i)
= P(X_n\le t_i,\ Y_n\ge t_i+\epsilon/2),
$$
which matches
$$
P(X_n\le t,\ Y_n\ge t+\epsilon')
$$
with $t=t_i$ and $\epsilon'=\epsilon/2$.

By the given condition, for every fixed $i$,
$$
P(X_n\ge t_{i-1},\ Y_n\le t_{i-1}-\epsilon/2)\to 0,
$$
and
$$
P(X_n\le t_i,\ Y_n\ge t_i+\epsilon/2)\to 0.
$$
Since there are only finitely many terms, both finite sums converge to $0$. Therefore,
$$
\limsup_{n\to\infty} P(|X_n-Y_n|\ge \epsilon)\le \epsilon.
$$
Because $\epsilon>0$ was arbitrary, we may replace it by any smaller positive number, and hence conclude that
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty} P(|X_n-Y_n|\ge \epsilon)=0
$$
for every $\epsilon>0$. That is,
$$
X_n-Y_n\xrightarrow{P}0.
$$
Thus the result is proved.

question: Let ${F}_{n}, n = 0,1,2,\ldots$ , be cumulative distribution functions such that ${F}_{n} \rightarrow {F}_{0}$ for every continuity point of ${F}_{0}$ . Let $U$ be a random variable having the uniform distribution on the interval $\left\lbrack {0,1}\right\rbrack$ and let ${G}_{n}\left( U\right) = \sup \left\{ {x : {F}_{n}\left( x\right) \leq U}\right\} , n = 0,1,2,\ldots$ Show that ${G}_{n}\left( U\right) { \rightarrow }_{p}{G}_{0}\left( U\right) .$
answer:
This problem uses the knowledge of distribution functions, the uniform distribution, and convergence in probability. The key idea is to express the events involving $G_n(U)$ in terms of $F_n$ and the uniform random variable $U$, then show that the probability of a discrepancy larger than a fixed gap tends to $0$.

First, recall the definition
$G_n(U)=\sup\{x:F_n(x)\le U\}, \quad n=0,1,2,\dots.$
For any real $t$, by the definition of this generalized inverse,
$G_n(U)\le t$ if and only if $F_n(t)\ge U$ almost surely.
Similarly,
$G_n(U)\ge t$ if and only if $F_n(t)\le U$ almost surely.

Now fix $t\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Consider the event that $G_n(U)$ is at most $t$ while $G_0(U)$ is at least $t+\varepsilon$. Using the equivalences above,
\[
P\bigl(G_n(U)\le t,\, G_0(U)\ge t+\varepsilon\bigr)
= P\bigl(F_n(t)\ge U,\, F_0(t+\varepsilon)\le U\bigr).
\]
Since $U\sim \mathrm{Uniform}[0,1]$, this is the probability that $U$ lies in the interval $[F_0(t+\varepsilon),F_n(t)]$ when this interval is nonempty. Hence
\[
P\bigl(G_n(U)\le t,\, G_0(U)\ge t+\varepsilon\bigr)
= \max\{0,\, F_n(t)-F_0(t+\varepsilon)\}.
\]

Likewise, for the opposite discrepancy,
\[
P\bigl(G_n(U)\ge t+\varepsilon,\, G_0(U)\le t\bigr)
= P\bigl(F_n(t+\varepsilon)\le U,\, F_0(t)\ge U\bigr).
\]
Again using that $U$ is uniform on $[0,1]$, this probability equals the length of the interval $[F_n(t+\varepsilon),F_0(t)]$ when it is nonempty, so
\[
P\bigl(G_n(U)\ge t+\varepsilon,\, G_0(U)\le t\bigr)
= \max\{0,\, F_0(t)-F_n(t+\varepsilon)\}.
\]

Assume now that both $t$ and $t+\varepsilon$ are continuity points of $F_0$. Since $F_n(x)\to F_0(x)$ at every continuity point of $F_0$, we have
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\bigl(F_n(t)-F_0(t+\varepsilon)\bigr)
= F_0(t)-F_0(t+\varepsilon)\le 0,
\]
and also
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\bigl(F_0(t)-F_n(t+\varepsilon)\bigr)
= F_0(t)-F_0(t+\varepsilon)\le 0.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty} \max\{0,\, F_n(t)-F_0(t+\varepsilon)\}=0,
\]
and
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty} \max\{0,\, F_0(t)-F_n(t+\varepsilon)\}=0.
\]
So,
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\Bigl[
P\bigl(G_n(U)\le t,\, G_0(U)\ge t+\varepsilon\bigr)
+
P\bigl(G_n(U)\ge t+\varepsilon,\, G_0(U)\le t\bigr)
\Bigr]=0.
\]

Thus, whenever both $t$ and $t+\varepsilon$ are continuity points of $F_0$, the probability that $G_n(U)$ and $G_0(U)$ lie on opposite sides of the interval $[t,t+\varepsilon]$ tends to $0$.

Finally, since a distribution function has at most countably many discontinuity points, we can choose such $t$ and $t+\varepsilon$ outside the discontinuity set of $F_0$. The two probability bounds above, together with the boundedness in probability of $G_0(U)$, give the standard convergence-in-probability criterion, so
\[
G_n(U)-G_0(U)\xrightarrow{P}0.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
G_n(U)\xrightarrow{P}G_0(U).
\]

Therefore, the required convergence in probability is proved.

question: Let $\left\{ {X}_{n}\right\}$ be a sequence of independent and identically distributed random variables. Show that there does not exist a sequence of real numbers $\left\{ {c}_{n}\right\}$ such that $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\left( {{X}_{i} - {c}_{i}}\right)$ exists a.s., unless the distribution of ${X}_{1}$ is degenerate.
answer:
Suppose that $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\left( {{X}_{i} - {c}_{i}}\right)$ exists a.s. Let $\phi$ and $g$ be the characteristic functions of ${X}_{1}$ and $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\left( {{X}_{i} - {c}_{i}}\right)$ , respectively. For any $n$ , the characteristic function of $\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\left( {{X}_{i} - {c}_{i}}\right)$ is$$
\mathop{\prod }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\phi \left( t\right) {e}^{-\sqrt{-1}t{c}_{i}} = {\left\lbrack \phi \left( t\right) \right\rbrack }^{n}{e}^{-\sqrt{-1}t\left( {{c}_{1} + \cdots + {c}_{n}}\right) },
$$
which converges to $g\left( t\right)$ for any $t$ . Then$$
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}\left| {{\left\lbrack \phi \left( t\right) \right\rbrack }^{n}{e}^{-\sqrt{-1}t\left( {{c}_{1} + \cdots + {c}_{n}}\right) }}\right| = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}{\left| \phi \left( t\right) \right| }^{n} = \left| {g\left( t\right) }\right| .
$$
Since $\left| {g\left( t\right) }\right|$ is continuous and $g\left( 0\right) = 1,\left| {g\left( t\right) }\right| \neq 0$ on a neighborhood of 0 . Hence, $\left| {\phi \left( t\right) }\right| = 1$ on this neighborhood and, thus, ${X}_{1}$ is degenerate.
explanation:
This problem uses the definition and basic properties of characteristic functions, together with the characterization of degenerate distributions by the condition $|\phi(t)|=1$ near $0$. The key idea is that if the partial sums converge almost surely, then their characteristic functions must converge pointwise, and this forces the characteristic function of $X_1$ to have modulus $1$ in a neighborhood of the origin.

Assume that there exists a real sequence $\{c_n\}$ such that
$\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-c_i)$ converges almost surely as $n\to\infty$.
Let
$S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-c_i)$,
and suppose
$S_n\to S$ a.s.
Denote by $\phi(t)$ the characteristic function of $X_1$, and by $g(t)$ the characteristic function of $S$.

Since $X_1,X_2,\dots$ are independent and identically distributed, for each $n$ the characteristic function of $S_n$ is
$E\big(e^{itS_n}\big)=\prod_{i=1}^n E\big(e^{it(X_i-c_i)}\big)$.
Because
$E\big(e^{it(X_i-c_i)}\big)=E\big(e^{itX_i}e^{-itc_i}\big)=\phi(t)e^{-itc_i}$,
we obtain
$E\big(e^{itS_n}\big)=\prod_{i=1}^n \phi(t)e^{-itc_i}=[\phi(t)]^n e^{-it(c_1+\cdots+c_n)}$.

Now $S_n\to S$ almost surely, and $|e^{itS_n}|=1$ for all $n$, so by bounded convergence,
$E\big(e^{itS_n}\big)\to E\big(e^{itS}\big)=g(t)$
for every $t$.
Hence,
$[\phi(t)]^n e^{-it(c_1+\cdots+c_n)}\to g(t), \qquad \forall t\in\mathbb{R}$.

Take absolute values. Since $\left|e^{-it(c_1+\cdots+c_n)}\right|=1$, we get
$\left|[\phi(t)]^n e^{-it(c_1+\cdots+c_n)}\right|=|\phi(t)|^n$.
Passing to the limit yields
$|\phi(t)|^n\to |g(t)|, \qquad \forall t\in\mathbb{R}$.
So for every fixed $t$,
$\lim_{n\to\infty} |\phi(t)|^n=|g(t)|$.

Next, $g$ is a characteristic function, so it is continuous, and
$g(0)=1$.
Therefore $|g(0)|=1$, and by continuity of $|g(t)|$, there exists a neighborhood of $0$ such that
$|g(t)|\neq 0$.

But if for some $t$ we had $|\phi(t)|<1$, then $|\phi(t)|^n\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$. Since in a neighborhood of $0$ we have $|g(t)|\neq 0$, it follows that in that neighborhood we cannot have $|\phi(t)|<1$. Also $|\phi(t)|\le 1$ for every characteristic function, hence on that neighborhood of $0$ we must have
$|\phi(t)|=1$.

A characteristic function having modulus $1$ on a neighborhood of $0$ implies that the corresponding random variable is degenerate. Therefore $X_1$ must be degenerate.

So, unless the distribution of $X_1$ is degenerate, there does not exist any real sequence $\{c_n\}$ such that
$\lim_{n\to\infty} \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-c_i)$ exists almost surely.

question: Let $P,{P}_{1},{P}_{2},\ldots$ be probability measures such that $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}{P}_{n}\left( O\right) \; = P\left( O\right)$ for any open set $O$ with $P\left( {\partial O}\right) = 0$ , where $\partial A$ is the boundary of the set $A$ . Show that $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}{P}_{n}\left( A\right) = P\left( A\right)$ for any Borel $A$ with $P\left( {\partial A}\right) = 0$ .
answer:
Let $A$ be a Borel set with $P\left( {\partial A}\right) = 0$ . Let ${A}_{0}$ be the interior of $A$ and ${A}_{1}$ be the closure of $A$ . Then ${A}_{0} \subset A \subset {A}_{1} = {A}_{0} \cup \partial A$ . Since $\partial {A}_{0} \subset \partial A, P\left( {\partial {A}_{0}}\right) = 0$ and, by assumption, $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}{P}_{n}\left( {A}_{0}\right) = P\left( {A}_{0}\right)$ . Since $\partial {A}_{1}^{c} \subset \partial A$ and ${A}_{1}^{c}$ is an open set, $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}{P}_{n}\left( {A}_{1}^{c}\right) = P\left( {A}_{1}^{c}\right)$ , which implies $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}{P}_{n}\left( {A}_{1}\right) = P\left( {A}_{1}\right)$ . Then,$$
P\left( A\right) \leq P\left( {A}_{0}\right) + P\left( {\partial A}\right) = P\left( {A}_{0}\right) = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}{P}_{n}\left( {A}_{0}\right) \leq \mathop{\liminf }\limits_{n}{P}_{n}\left( A\right)
$$
and$$
P\left( A\right) \geq P\left( {A}_{0}\right) = P\left( {A}_{0}\right) + P\left( {\partial A}\right) = P\left( {A}_{1}\right) = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}{P}_{n}\left( {A}_{1}\right) \geq \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{n}{P}_{n}\left( A\right) .
$$
Hence $\mathop{\liminf }\limits_{n}{P}_{n}\left( A\right) = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{n}{P}_{n}\left( A\right) = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}{P}_{n}\left( A\right) = P\left( A\right)$ .
explanation:
This problem uses the ideas of $P$-continuity on boundaries and weak convergence on continuity sets. The key is to compare a Borel set $A$ with its interior and closure, both of which can be related to open sets appearing in the assumption.

Let $A$ be a Borel set such that $P(\partial A)=0$. Denote by $A_0$ the interior of $A$, and by $A_1$ the closure of $A$. Then
$A_0\subset A\subset A_1$,
and since $A_1=A_0\cup \partial A$, we also have
$P(A_1\setminus A_0)=P(\partial A)=0$.

First, consider $A_0$.
Because $A_0$ is open and $\partial A_0\subset \partial A$, it follows that
$P(\partial A_0)=0$.
By the assumption of the problem, for every open set whose boundary has $P$-measure zero,
$\lim_{n\to\infty} P_n(A_0)=P(A_0)$.

Next, consider $A_1$.
Its complement $A_1^c$ is open. Also,
$\partial(A_1^c)\subset \partial A$,
so
$P(\partial(A_1^c))=0$.
Applying the assumption again to the open set $A_1^c$, we get
$\lim_{n\to\infty} P_n(A_1^c)=P(A_1^c)$.
Therefore,
$\lim_{n\to\infty} P_n(A_1)=\lim_{n\to\infty} \bigl(1-P_n(A_1^c)\bigr)=1-P(A_1^c)=P(A_1)$.

Now use the inclusions $A_0\subset A\subset A_1$.
For every $n$,
$P_n(A_0)\le P_n(A)\le P_n(A_1)$.
Hence,
$\liminf_{n\to\infty} P_n(A)\ge \lim_{n\to\infty} P_n(A_0)=P(A_0)$,
and
$\limsup_{n\to\infty} P_n(A)\le \lim_{n\to\infty} P_n(A_1)=P(A_1)$.

It remains to show that $P(A_0)=P(A)=P(A_1)$. Since
$A\subset A_0\cup \partial A$,
we have
$P(A)\le P(A_0)+P(\partial A)=P(A_0)$.
But also $A_0\subset A$, so by monotonicity,
$P(A_0)\le P(A)$.
Therefore,
$P(A)=P(A_0)$.

Similarly, because
$A_1=A_0\cup \partial A$,
we get
$P(A_1)=P(A_0)+P(\partial A)=P(A_0)=P(A)$.
Thus,
$P(A_0)=P(A)=P(A_1)$.

Combining these bounds,
$P(A)=P(A_0)\le \liminf_{n\to\infty} P_n(A)\le \limsup_{n\to\infty} P_n(A)\le P(A_1)=P(A)$.
So
$\liminf_{n\to\infty} P_n(A)=\limsup_{n\to\infty} P_n(A)=P(A)$,
which implies
$\lim_{n\to\infty} P_n(A)=P(A)$.

Therefore, for any Borel set $A$ with $P(\partial A)=0$, we have $\lim_{n\to\infty} P_n(A)=P(A)$.
