question:
Let $X = \left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right)$ be a random sample of random variables with probability density ${f}_{\theta }$ . Find an MLE (maximum likelihood estimator) of $\theta$ in each of the following cases.
(i) ${f}_{\theta }\left( x\right) = {\theta }^{-1}{I}_{\{ 1,\ldots ,\theta \} }\left( x\right) ,\theta$ is an integer between 1 and ${\theta }_{0}$ .
(ii) ${f}_{\theta }\left( x\right) = {e}^{-\left( {x - \theta }\right) }{I}_{\left\lbrack \theta ,\infty \right) }\left( x\right) ,\theta > 0$ .
(iii) ${f}_{\theta }\left( x\right) = \theta {\left( 1 - x\right) }^{\theta - 1}{I}_{\left( 0,1\right) }\left( x\right) ,\theta > 1$ .
(iv) ${f}_{\theta }\left( x\right) = \frac{\theta }{1 - \theta }{x}^{\left( {{2\theta } - 1}\right) /\left( {1 - \theta }\right) }{I}_{\left( 0,1\right) }\left( x\right) ,\theta \in \left( {\frac{1}{2},1}\right)$ .
(v) ${f}_{\theta }\left( x\right) = {2}^{-1}{e}^{-\left| {x - \theta }\right| },\theta \in \mathcal{R}$ .
(vi) ${f}_{\theta }\left( x\right) = \theta {x}^{-2}{I}_{\left\lbrack \theta ,\infty \right) }\left( x\right) ,\theta > 0$ .
(vii) ${f}_{\theta }\left( x\right) = {\theta }^{x}{\left( 1 - \theta \right) }^{1 - x}{I}_{\{ 0,1\} }\left( x\right) ,\theta \in \left\lbrack {\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{4}}\right\rbrack$ .
(viii) ${f}_{\theta }\left( x\right)$ is the density of $N\left( {\theta ,{\theta }^{2}}\right) ,\theta \in \mathcal{R},\theta \neq 0$ .
(ix) ${f}_{\theta }\left( x\right) = {\sigma }^{-1}{e}^{-\left( {x - \mu }\right) /\sigma }{I}_{\left\lbrack \mu ,\infty \right) }\left( x\right) ,\theta = \left( {\mu ,\sigma }\right) \in \mathcal{R} \times \left( {0,\infty }\right)$ .
(x) ${f}_{\theta }\left( x\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }{\sigma x}}{e}^{-{\left( \log x - \mu \right) }^{2}/\left( {2{\sigma }^{2}}\right) }{I}_{\left( 0,\infty \right) }\left( x\right) ,\theta = \left( {\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}}\right) \in \mathcal{R} \times \left( {0,\infty }\right)$ .
(xi) ${f}_{\theta }\left( x\right) = {I}_{\left( 0,1\right) }\left( x\right)$ if $\theta = 0$ and ${f}_{\theta }\left( x\right) = {\left( 2\sqrt{x}\right) }^{-1}{I}_{\left( 0,1\right) }\left( x\right)$ if $\theta = 1$ .
(xii) ${f}_{\theta }\left( x\right) = {\beta }^{-\alpha }\alpha {x}^{\alpha - 1}{I}_{\left( 0,\beta \right\rbrack }\left( x\right) ,\theta = \left( {\alpha ,\beta }\right) \in \left( {0,\infty }\right) \times \left( {0,\infty }\right)$ .
(xiii) ${f}_{\theta }\left( x\right) = \left( \begin{matrix} \theta \\ x \end{matrix}\right) {p}^{x}{\left( 1 - p\right) }^{\theta - x}{I}_{\{ 0,1,\ldots ,\theta \} }\left( x\right) ,\theta = 1,2,\ldots$ , where $p \in \left( {0,1}\right)$ is known.
(xiv) ${f}_{\theta }\left( x\right) = \frac{1}{2}\left( {1 - {\theta }^{2}}\right) {e}^{{\theta x} - \left| x\right| },\theta \in \left( {-1,1}\right)$ .
answer:
(i) $\hat\theta=X_{(n)}$；
(ii) $\hat\theta=X_{(1)}$；
(iii) writing $\widetilde\theta=-n/\sum_{i=1}^n\log(1-X_i)$, the MLE is $\widehat\theta=\widetilde\theta$ if $\widetilde\theta>1$; if $\widetilde\theta\le1$, no MLE exists (the supremum is approached as $\theta\downarrow1$)；
(iv) writing $\widetilde\theta=\left(1-n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\log X_i\right)^{-1}$, the MLE is $\widehat\theta=\widetilde\theta$ if $\widetilde\theta>1/2$; if $\widetilde\theta\le1/2$, no MLE exists (the supremum is approached as $\theta\downarrow1/2$)；
(v) any sample median；
(vi) $\hat\theta=X_{(1)}$；
(vii) $\hat\theta=\begin{cases}\dfrac12,&\bar X\in[0,\dfrac12)\\ \bar X,&\bar X\in[\dfrac12,\dfrac34]\\ \dfrac34,&\bar X\in(\dfrac34,1]\end{cases}$；
(viii) if $\sum_iX_i^2>0$, let $\theta_{\pm}=\dfrac{-\sum_iX_i\pm\sqrt{(\sum_iX_i)^2+4n\sum_iX_i^2}}{2n}$ and choose the one with the larger likelihood (both are MLEs in case of equality); if all $X_i=0$, no MLE exists；
(ix) if $\sum_i(X_i-X_{(1)})>0$, $\hat\mu=X_{(1)}$ and $\hat\sigma=n^{-1}\sum_i(X_i-X_{(1)})$; if all observations are equal, no MLE exists；
(x) with $Y_i=\log X_i$, if $\sum_i(Y_i-\bar Y)^2>0$, $\hat\mu=\bar Y$ and $\widehat{\sigma^2}=n^{-1}\sum_i(Y_i-\bar Y)^2$; if all $Y_i$ are equal, no MLE exists；
(xi) writing $D=2^n\prod_i\sqrt{X_i}$, $\hat\theta=1$ if $D<1$, $\hat\theta=0$ if $D>1$, and both $0$ and $1$ are MLEs if $D=1$；
(xii) if $\sum_i\log(X_{(n)}/X_i)>0$, $\hat\beta=X_{(n)}$ and $\hat\alpha=\dfrac{n}{\sum_i\log(X_{(n)}/X_i)}$; if all observations are equal, no MLE exists；
(xiii) with $R_\theta=\ell(\theta+1)/\ell(\theta)$, one MLE is $\hat\theta=\min\{\theta\ge X_{(n)}:R_\theta\le1\}$ (if $R_{\hat\theta}=1$, then $\hat\theta+1$ is also an MLE)；
(xiv) $\hat\theta=\dfrac{\bar X}{1+\sqrt{1+\bar X^2}}$, including $\hat\theta=0$ when $\bar X=0$.
explanation:
This problem uses the ideas of maximum likelihood estimation and likelihood functions. In several parts, the support of the density depends on the parameter, so order statistics such as $X_{(1)}$ and $X_{(n)}$ are needed to determine where the likelihood is nonzero and where it is maximized.

(i) Here
$\ell(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n\theta^{-1}I_{\{1,\ldots,\theta\}}(X_i)=\theta^{-n}I_{\{X_{(n)},\ldots,\theta_0\}}(\theta).$
So $\ell(\theta)=0$ for $\theta<X_{(n)}$, and on $\{X_{(n)},\ldots,\theta_0\}$ the factor $\theta^{-n}$ decreases as $\theta$ increases. Hence the maximum occurs at the smallest admissible value, namely
$\hat\theta=X_{(n)}$.

(ii) The likelihood is
$\ell(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n e^{-(X_i-\theta)}I_{(\theta,\infty)}(X_i)=\exp\left\{-\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\theta)\right\}I_{(0,X_{(1)}]}(\theta).$
Thus $\ell(\theta)=0$ for $\theta>X_{(1)}$, and on $(0,X_{(1)})$,
$\ell(\theta)=e^{-\sum X_i+n\theta}$
is increasing in $\theta$. Therefore,
$\hat\theta=X_{(1)}$.

(iii) The likelihood is
$\ell(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n \theta(1-X_i)^{\theta-1}I_{(0,1)}(X_i)=\theta^n\prod_{i=1}^n(1-X_i)^{\theta-1}I_{(0,1)}(X_i),\quad \theta>1.$
Then
$\log \ell(\theta)=n\log\theta+(\theta-1)\sum_{i=1}^n\log(1-X_i)+\text{constant},$
so
$\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log\ell(\theta)=\frac{n}{\theta}+\sum_{i=1}^n\log(1-X_i),$
and
$\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\log\ell(\theta)=-\frac{n}{\theta^2}<0.$
Hence any critical point is the unique maximizer. Solving
$\frac{n}{\theta}+\sum_{i=1}^n\log(1-X_i)=0$
gives
$\tilde\theta=-\frac{n}{\sum_{i=1}^n\log(1-X_i)}.$
If $\tilde\theta>1$, it is the MLE. If $\tilde\theta\le1$, the likelihood decreases on $(1,\infty)$ and its supremum is approached as $\theta\downarrow1$, but the boundary is not in the parameter space; hence no MLE exists in this case.

(iv) The log-likelihood derivative is given by
$\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log\ell(\theta)=\frac{n}{\theta(1-\theta)}+\frac{1}{(1-\theta)^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\log X_i.$
Setting this equal to $0$ yields the unique solution
$\tilde\theta=\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\log X_i\right)^{-1}.$
Also, the derivative is positive for $\theta<\tilde\theta$ and negative for $\theta>\tilde\theta$, so the likelihood increases up to $\tilde\theta$ and then decreases. If $\tilde\theta>1/2$, it lies in the parameter space and is the MLE. If $\tilde\theta\le1/2$, the supremum is approached as $\theta\downarrow1/2$, but the boundary is excluded, so no MLE exists.$

(v) The likelihood is
$\ell(\theta)=2^{-n}\exp\left\{-\sum_{i=1}^n|X_i-\theta|\right\}.$
Maximizing $\ell(\theta)$ is equivalent to minimizing
$\sum_{i=1}^n|X_i-\theta|.$
This is minimized by any median of the sample. Therefore any sample median is an MLE of $\theta$.

(vi) Here
$\ell(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n \theta X_i^{-2}I_{(\theta,\infty)}(X_i)=\theta^n\prod_{i=1}^nX_i^{-2}I_{(0,X_{(1)}]}(\theta).$
For $\theta>X_{(1)}$ the likelihood is $0$, and on $(0,X_{(1)})$ it is proportional to $\theta^n$, which is increasing. Hence
$\hat\theta=X_{(1)}$.

(vii) Since
$\ell(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n\theta^{X_i}(1-\theta)^{1-X_i},\quad \theta\in\left[\frac12,\frac34\right],$
we have
$\log\ell(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\log\theta+\sum_{i=1}^n(1-X_i)\log(1-\theta),$
so
$\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log\ell(\theta)=\frac{n\bar X}{\theta}-\frac{n-n\bar X}{1-\theta}.$
Setting this equal to $0$ gives the unconstrained maximizer $\tilde\theta=\bar X$. Since the derivative is positive for $\theta<\bar X$ and negative for $\theta>\bar X$, the constrained MLE is the clipped value of $\bar X$ on $\left[\frac12,\frac34\right]$:
$\hat\theta=\begin{cases}
\frac12,&\bar X\in[0,\frac12),\\
\bar X,&\bar X\in[\frac12,\frac34],\\
\frac34,&\bar X\in(\frac34,1].
\end{cases}$

(viii) For $X_i\sim N(\theta,\theta^2)$ with $\theta\ne0$, the derivative of the log-likelihood is
$\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log\ell(\theta)=-\frac{1}{\theta^3}\left(n\theta^2+\theta\sum_{i=1}^nX_i-\sum_{i=1}^nX_i^2\right).$
Thus critical points satisfy
$n\theta^2+\theta\sum_{i=1}^nX_i-\sum_{i=1}^nX_i^2=0.$
The two roots are
$\theta_{\pm}=\frac{-\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\pm\sqrt{\left(\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right)^2+4n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i^2}}{2n}.$
If $\sum_iX_i^2>0$, then
$\lim_{\theta\to0}\log\ell(\theta)=-\infty.$
Checking the sign changes of the derivative around $\theta_-$ and $\theta_+$ shows that both are local maxima. Therefore the MLE is the one giving the larger likelihood value:
$\hat\theta=\begin{cases}
\theta_-,&\ell(\theta_-)\ge\ell(\theta_+),\\
\theta_+,&\ell(\theta_-)<\ell(\theta_+).
\end{cases}$
If all $X_i=0$, the likelihood is unbounded as $\theta\to0$ with $\theta\ne0$, so no MLE exists.

(ix) The likelihood is
$\ell(\mu,\sigma)=\sigma^{-n}\exp\left\{-\frac1\sigma\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)\right\}I_{(0,X_{(1)})}(\mu).$
For fixed $\sigma$, this is $0$ when $\mu>X_{(1)}$, and on the admissible interval it increases with $\mu$. Hence
$\hat\mu=X_{(1)}$.
Substitute this into the likelihood:
$\ell(X_{(1)},\sigma)=\sigma^{-n}\exp\left\{-\frac1\sigma\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-X_{(1)})\right\}.$
The log-likelihood is
$-n\log\sigma-\sigma^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-X_{(1)}).$
Differentiate with respect to $\sigma$ and set to zero:
$-\frac{n}{\sigma}+\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-X_{(1)})=0.$
So
$\hat\sigma=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-X_{(1)}).$
Thus, when $\sum_i(X_i-X_{(1)})>0$,
$\hat\mu=X_{(1)},\quad \hat\sigma=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-X_{(1)}).$
If all observations are equal, the displayed $\hat\sigma$ is $0$, outside the parameter space, and the likelihood is unbounded; no MLE exists.

(x) Let $Y_i=\log X_i$. Then the likelihood becomes
$\ell(\mu,\sigma^2)=\frac{1}{(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma)^n}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\mu)^2-\sum_{i=1}^nY_i\right\}.$
The last term does not involve the parameter. So this is the normal likelihood for $Y_i\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$. Provided the sample variance of the $Y_i$ is positive, the MLEs are
$\hat\mu=\bar Y=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nY_i,$
$\widehat{\sigma^2}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\bar Y)^2.$
Equivalently,
$\hat\mu=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\log X_i,
\quad \widehat{\sigma^2}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\log X_i-\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\log X_j\right)^2.$
If all $Y_i$ are equal, the likelihood is unbounded as $\sigma^2\downarrow0$, so no MLE exists.

(xi) There are only two parameter values. If $\theta=0$, then
$\ell(0)=\prod_{i=1}^n I_{(0,1)}(X_i)=1$
for observed data in the support. If $\theta=1$, then
$\ell(1)=\prod_{i=1}^n (2\sqrt{X_i})^{-1}I_{(0,1)}(X_i)=\left(2^n\prod_{i=1}^n\sqrt{X_i}\right)^{-1}.$
Write $D=2^n\prod_{i=1}^n\sqrt{X_i}$. Since $\ell(1)=1/D$ and $\ell(0)=1$, we have $\hat\theta=1$ when $D<1$, $\hat\theta=0$ when $D>1$, and both parameter values maximize the likelihood when $D=1$.

(xii) The likelihood is
$\ell(\alpha,\beta)=\alpha^n\beta^{-n\alpha}\prod_{i=1}^nX_i^{\alpha-1}I_{(X_{(n)},\infty)}(\beta).$
For fixed $\alpha$, this is $0$ when $\beta<X_{(n)}$, and for $\beta\ge X_{(n)}$ it decreases in $\beta$ because of the factor $\beta^{-n\alpha}$. Hence
$\hat\beta=X_{(n)}$.
Substitute into the likelihood:
$\ell(\alpha,X_{(n)})=\alpha^nX_{(n)}^{-n\alpha}\prod_{i=1}^nX_i^{\alpha-1}.$
Then
$\log\ell(\alpha,X_{(n)})=n\log\alpha-n\alpha\log X_{(n)}+(\alpha-1)\sum_{i=1}^n\log X_i.$
Differentiate and set equal to zero:
$\frac{n}{\alpha}-n\log X_{(n)}+\sum_{i=1}^n\log X_i=0.$
Thus
$\hat\alpha=\frac{n}{n\log X_{(n)}-\sum_{i=1}^n\log X_i}=\frac{n}{\sum_{i=1}^n\log(X_{(n)}/X_i)}.$
Thus, if the denominator is positive,
$\hat\beta=X_{(n)},\quad \hat\alpha=\frac{n}{\sum_{i=1}^n\log(X_{(n)}/X_i)}.$
If all observations are equal, the denominator is $0$ and the likelihood is unbounded as $\alpha\to\infty$, so no MLE exists.

(xiii) Let $T=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$ and let $X_{(n)}=\max_iX_i$. Then
$\ell(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n\binom{\theta}{X_i}p^T(1-p)^{n\theta-T}I_{\{X_{(n)},X_{(n)}+1,\ldots\}}(\theta).$
Thus the feasible values satisfy $\theta\ge X_{(n)}$. Consider the ratio
$\frac{\ell(\theta+1)}{\ell(\theta)}=(1-p)^n\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\theta+1}{\theta+1-X_i}.$
For each $i$, the factor $\dfrac{\theta+1}{\theta+1-X_i}$ decreases in $\theta$, so the whole ratio decreases in $\theta$. Also,
$\lim_{\theta\to\infty}\frac{\ell(\theta+1)}{\ell(\theta)}=(1-p)^n<1.$
Therefore the likelihood increases while this ratio exceeds $1$ and decreases after it falls below $1$. Hence one MLE is
$\hat\theta=\min\left\{\theta\ge X_{(n)}:\frac{\ell(\theta+1)}{\ell(\theta)}\le1\right\}$.
If the ratio equals $1$ at $\hat\theta$, then $\hat\theta+1$ is also an MLE.$

(xiv) The log-likelihood derivative is
$\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log\ell(\theta)=n\bar X-\frac{2n\theta}{1-\theta^2}.$
Set it equal to zero:
$n\bar X-\frac{2n\theta}{1-\theta^2}=0
\iff \bar X=\frac{2\theta}{1-\theta^2}.$
If $\bar X\ne0$, solving gives
$$
\theta=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{1+\bar X^2}}{\bar X}.
$$
Exactly one root lies in $(-1,1)$, namely
$$
\hat\theta=\frac{\sqrt{1+\bar X^2}-1}{\bar X}
=\frac{\bar X}{1+\sqrt{1+\bar X^2}}.
$$
When $\bar X=0$, the likelihood equation gives $\hat\theta=0$.

Therefore, the MLEs for parts (i)–(xiv) are exactly those listed in the answer.

answer:
Under the density convention specified in the question, observations at either endpoint have zero likelihood.

Let $X_{(1)}=\min_iX_i$ and $X_{(n)}=\max_iX_i$.

(i) If $\theta>0$, the support is $(\theta,2\theta)$. A nonzero likelihood therefore requires
$$0<X_{(1)}\le X_{(n)},\qquad \frac{X_{(n)}}2<\theta<X_{(1)},$$
which is possible exactly when the sample is positive and $X_{(n)}<2X_{(1)}$. On this interval $L(\theta)=\theta^{-n}$, whose supremum is approached as $\theta\downarrow X_{(n)}/2$ but is not attained. Thus no MLE exists for a feasible sample.

(ii) If $\theta<0$, the support is $(\theta,0)$. A nonzero likelihood requires
$$X_{(n)}<0,\qquad \theta<X_{(1)}.$$
Then $L(\theta)=(-\theta)^{-n}$, whose supremum is approached as $\theta\uparrow X_{(1)}$ but is not attained. Hence no MLE exists for a feasible all-negative sample.

(iii) In $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, every sample that has positive likelihood under some parameter falls into one of the preceding two cases, and the supremum is not attained, so there is no MLE. For a mixed-sign or otherwise infeasible sample, $L(\theta)\equiv0$ for all $\theta\ne0$; under the literal $\operatorname{argmax}$ convention every parameter is then a maximizer, whereas under the usual convention that an MLE is reported only for samples in the model support, the MLE is left undefined.
explanation:
For positive $\theta$, every observation must lie strictly between $\theta$ and $2\theta$. Intersecting these inequalities over the sample gives $X_{(n)}/2<\theta<X_{(1)}$. The likelihood decreases with $\theta$, so its best value lies at the excluded lower endpoint.

For negative $\theta$, the interval is $(\theta,0)$, not $(\theta,2\theta)$. Thus all observations must be negative, expressed by $X_{(n)}<0$, and the remaining restriction is $\theta<X_{(1)}$. Since $(-\theta)^{-n}$ increases as $\theta$ moves upward, its supremum lies at the excluded endpoint $X_{(1)}$.

Consequently, every feasible sample has a likelihood supremum but no maximizing parameter. Samples not contained in any allowed support give the identically zero likelihood; whether all parameters are called maximizers in that zero-likelihood case is a matter of convention, which is why it is stated explicitly.

question: Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent observations from $N(\mu,1)$, where $n\ge1$ and $\mu\in\mathbb{R}$ is unknown. Instead of recording the values of the observations, one records only $Y_i=\mathbf{1}\{X_i<0\}$ for each $i$. Determine when a maximum likelihood estimator of $\mu$ exists in $\mathbb{R}$, and find it whenever it exists.
answer: Let $\Phi$ denote the standard normal distribution function, and let $T=\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{1}\{X_i<0\}$. If $0<T<n$, the unique MLE is $\hat\mu=-\Phi^{-1}(T/n)$. If $T=0$ or $T=n$, no finite MLE exists in $\mathbb{R}$: the likelihood approaches its supremum as $\mu\to+\infty$ or $\mu\to-\infty$, respectively.
explanation:
Let $Y_i=\mathbf{1}\{X_i<0\}$ denote the recorded binary observation, and let $T=\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$. Let $\Phi$ denote the standard normal distribution function. Since the $X_i$ are independent with distribution $N(\mu,1)$, the $Y_i$ are independent Bernoulli variables with
$$P_\mu(Y_i=1)=\Phi(-\mu).$$
Thus the likelihood based on the recorded observations is
$$L(\mu)=\Phi(-\mu)^T[1-\Phi(-\mu)]^{n-T}.$$

Set $p=\Phi(-\mu)$. As $\mu$ ranges over $\mathbb{R}$, $p$ ranges over the open interval $(0,1)$. The likelihood becomes
$$L(p)=p^T(1-p)^{n-T}.$$

If $0<T<n$, the log-likelihood satisfies
$$\ell'(p)=\frac{T}{p}-\frac{n-T}{1-p},\qquad
\ell''(p)=-\frac{T}{p^2}-\frac{n-T}{(1-p)^2}<0.$$
Its unique maximum is at $\hat p=T/n$. Inverting $p=\Phi(-\mu)$ gives
$$\boxed{\hat\mu=-\Phi^{-1}(T/n),\qquad 0<T<n.}$$

The boundary samples require separate treatment:

If $T=0$, then $L(\mu)=\Phi(\mu)^n$, which is strictly increasing in $\mu$ and approaches $1$ as $\mu\to+\infty$. It never attains this supremum at a finite $\mu$.

If $T=n$, then $L(\mu)=\Phi(-\mu)^n$, which is strictly decreasing in $\mu$ and approaches $1$ as $\mu\to-\infty$. Again, the supremum is not attained at a finite $\mu$.

Therefore, no MLE exists in the stated parameter space $\mathbb{R}$ when $T=0$ or $T=n$. The values $+\infty$ and $-\infty$, respectively, may be described only as extended or limiting MLEs.
subject: Mathematical Statistics

question:
Let $\left( {{Y}_{1},{Z}_{1}}\right) ,\ldots ,\left( {{Y}_{n},{Z}_{n}}\right)$ be independent and identically distributed random 2-vectors such that ${Y}_{1}$ and ${Z}_{1}$ are independently distributed as the exponential distributions on $\left( {0,\infty }\right)$ with scale parameters $\lambda > 0$ and $\mu > 0$ , respectively.
(i) Find the MLE of $\left( {\lambda ,\mu }\right)$ .
(ii) Suppose that we only observe ${X}_{i} = \min \left\{ {{Y}_{i},{Z}_{i}}\right\}$ and ${\Delta }_{i} = 1$ if ${X}_{i} = {Y}_{i}$ and ${\Delta }_{i} = 0$ if ${X}_{i} = {Z}_{i}$ . Find the MLE of $\left( {\lambda ,\mu }\right)$ .
answer:
(i) The log likelihood based on the complete pairs is
$$\ell(\lambda,\mu)=-n\log\lambda-\frac{\sum_iY_i}{\lambda}-n\log\mu-\frac{\sum_iZ_i}{\mu},$$
so $\widehat\lambda=\bar Y$ and $\widehat\mu=\bar Z$.

(ii) Put $T=\sum_iX_i$ and $D=\sum_i\Delta_i$. The observed-data likelihood is
$$L(\lambda,\mu)=\lambda^{-D}\mu^{-(n-D)}
\exp\left\{-T\left(\frac1\lambda+\frac1\mu\right)\right\}.$$
If $0<D<n$, its unique maximizer is
$$\widehat\lambda=\frac TD,\qquad\widehat\mu=\frac T{n-D}.$$
If $D=0$, $\widehat\mu=T/n$ but the likelihood increases to its supremum as $\lambda\to\infty$, so no finite MLE of $\lambda$ exists. If $D=n$, $\widehat\lambda=T/n$ and the supremum is approached as $\mu\to\infty$, so no finite MLE of $\mu$ exists.
explanation:
For complete observations the exponential likelihood separates into a $\lambda$ part and a $\mu$ part, and differentiating each gives the corresponding sample mean.

With censoring, an observation with $\Delta=1$ contributes $\lambda^{-1}e^{-x/\lambda}P(Z>x)$, while one with $\Delta=0$ contributes $\mu^{-1}e^{-x/\mu}P(Y>x)$. Multiplication gives
$$L=\lambda^{-D}\mu^{-(n-D)}e^{-T(1/\lambda+1/\mu)}.$$
The two score equations yield $T/D$ and $T/(n-D)$ when both event types occur. If one count is zero, the corresponding log term disappears and that scale parameter must tend to infinity to attain the likelihood supremum; the other scale still has the finite estimate stated in the answer.
subject: Mathematical Statistics

question: Let $\left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right)$ be a random sample from the gamma distribution with shape parameter $\alpha > 0$ and scale parameter $\gamma > 0$ . Show that almost surely the likelihood equation has a unique solution that is the MLE of $\theta = \left( {\alpha ,\gamma }\right)$ . Obtain the Newton-Raphson iteration equation and the Fisher-scoring iteration equation.
answer:
Let $\bar{X}$ be the sample mean and $Y = {n}^{-1}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\log {X}_{i}$ . The log-likelihood function is$$
\log \ell \left( \theta \right) = - {n\alpha }\log \gamma - n\log \Gamma \left( \alpha \right) + \left( {\alpha - 1}\right) {nY} - {\gamma }^{-1}n\bar{X}.
$$
Then, the likelihood equations are\[
- \log \gamma - \frac{{\Gamma }^{\prime }\left( \alpha \right) }{\Gamma \left( \alpha \right) } + Y = 0;\text{ and }; - \frac{\alpha }{\gamma } + \frac{\bar{X}}{{\gamma }^{2}} = 0.
 \]
The second equation yields $\gamma = \bar{X}/\alpha$ . Substituting $\gamma = \bar{X}/\alpha$ into the first equation we obtain that$$
h\left( \alpha \right) = \log \alpha - \frac{{\Gamma }^{\prime }\left( \alpha \right) }{\Gamma \left( \alpha \right) } + Y - \log \bar{X} = 0.
$$
From calculus,$$
\frac{{\Gamma }^{\prime }\left( \alpha \right) }{\Gamma \left( \alpha \right) } = - C + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 0}}^{\infty }\left( {\frac{1}{k + 1} - \frac{1}{k + \alpha }}\right)
$$
and$$
\frac{d}{d\alpha }\left\lbrack \frac{{\Gamma }^{\prime }\left( \alpha \right) }{\Gamma \left( \alpha \right) }\right\rbrack = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 0}}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{\left( k + \alpha \right) }^{2}},
$$
where $C$ is the Euler constant defined as$$
C = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow \infty }}\left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 0}}^{{m - 1}}\frac{1}{k + 1} - \log m}\right) .
$$
Then$$
{h}^{\prime }\left( \alpha \right) = \frac{1}{\alpha } - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 0}}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{\left( k + \alpha \right) }^{2}}
$$$$
{}< \frac{1}{\alpha } - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 0}}^{\infty }\left( {\frac{1}{k + \alpha } - \frac{1}{k + 1 + \alpha }}\right)
$$$$
= \frac{1}{\alpha }-\frac{1}{\alpha }=0\text{ . }
$$
Hence, $h\left( \alpha \right)$ is strictly decreasing. Using the recurrence $\Gamma(m)=(m-1)\Gamma(m-1)$, for $m = 2,3,\ldots$ ,$$
\frac{{\Gamma }^{\prime }\left( m\right) }{\Gamma \left( m\right) } = \frac{1}{m - 1} + \frac{1}{m - 2} + \cdots + 1 + \frac{{\Gamma }^{\prime }\left( 1\right) }{\Gamma \left( 1\right) } = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 0}}^{{m - 2}}\frac{1}{k + 1} - C.
$$
Therefore,$$
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow \infty }}\left\lbrack {\log m - \frac{{\Gamma }^{\prime }\left( m\right) }{\Gamma \left( m\right) }}\right\rbrack = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow \infty }}\left\lbrack {\log m - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 0}}^{{m - 2}}\frac{1}{k + 1} + C}\right\rbrack = 0
$$
by the definition of $C$ . Hence, $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha \rightarrow \infty }}h\left( \alpha \right) = Y - \log \bar{X}$ , which is negative by Jensen’s inequality when ${X}_{i}$ ’s are not all the same. Since$$
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha \rightarrow 0}}\left\lbrack {\log \alpha - \frac{{\Gamma }^{\prime }\left( \alpha \right) }{\Gamma \left( \alpha \right) }}\right\rbrack = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha \rightarrow 0}}\left\lbrack {\log \alpha + C - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 0}}^{\infty }\left( {\frac{1}{k + 1} - \frac{1}{k + \alpha }}\right) }\right\rbrack
$$$$
= \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha \rightarrow 0}}\left\lbrack {\log \alpha + C + \frac{1}{\alpha } - 1 + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{\infty }\frac{1 - \alpha }{\left( {k + 1}\right) \left( {k + \alpha }\right) }}\right\rbrack
$$$$
= \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha \rightarrow 0}}\left( {\log \alpha + \frac{1}{\alpha }}\right) + C - 1 + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\left( {k + 1}\right) k}
$$$$
= \infty \text{ , }
$$
we have $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha \rightarrow 0}}h\left( \alpha \right) = \infty$ . Since $h$ is continuous and decreasing, $h\left( \alpha \right)=0$ has a unique solution. Thus, the likelihood equations have a unique solution, which is the MLE of $\theta$ .
Now derive the iterative schemes. The score vector is
$s(\theta)=\frac{\partial\log\ell(\theta)}{\partial\theta}=n\left(-\log\gamma-\frac{\Gamma'(\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)}+Y,\,-\frac{\alpha}{\gamma}+\frac{\bar X}{\gamma^2}\right)$.
The matrix of second derivatives is
$R(\theta)=\frac{\partial^2\log\ell(\theta)}{\partial\theta\partial\theta^{\tau}}
=n\begin{pmatrix}
\left[\dfrac{\Gamma'(\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\right]^2-\dfrac{\Gamma''(\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)} & -\dfrac{1}{\gamma}\\[4pt]
-\dfrac{1}{\gamma} & \dfrac{\alpha}{\gamma^2}-\dfrac{2\bar X}{\gamma^3}
\end{pmatrix}$.
Its expectation gives the Fisher-scoring matrix
$F(\theta)=E[R(\theta)]
=n\begin{pmatrix}
\left[\dfrac{\Gamma'(\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\right]^2-\dfrac{\Gamma''(\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)} & -\dfrac{1}{\gamma}\\[4pt]
-\dfrac{1}{\gamma} & -\dfrac{\alpha}{\gamma^2}
\end{pmatrix}$.

Therefore the Newton-Raphson iteration is
$\hat\theta^{(k+1)}=\hat\theta^{(k)}-\left[R\big(\hat\theta^{(k)}\big)\right]^{-1}s\big(\hat\theta^{(k)}\big),\qquad k=0,1,2,\ldots$
and the Fisher-scoring iteration is
$\hat\theta^{(k+1)}=\hat\theta^{(k)}-\left[F\big(\hat\theta^{(k)}\big)\right]^{-1}s\big(\hat\theta^{(k)}\big),\qquad k=0,1,2,\ldots$.
explanation:
This problem uses the key ideas of $\Gamma$-distribution likelihood, maximum likelihood estimation, and Fisher information. We first derive the likelihood equations and reduce them to a single equation in $\alpha$, then prove that this equation has exactly one root by studying a monotone function, and finally write the Newton-Raphson and Fisher-scoring iterations from the score vector and the Hessian/expected Hessian.

Let $\bar X=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ and $Y=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \log X_i$. For a gamma distribution with shape parameter $\alpha>0$ and scale parameter $\gamma>0$, the log-likelihood is
$\log \ell(\theta)=-n\alpha\log\gamma-n\log\Gamma(\alpha)+(\alpha-1)nY-\gamma^{-1}n\bar X$.

Differentiate with respect to $\alpha$ and $\gamma$. The likelihood equations are
$-\log\gamma-\dfrac{\Gamma'(\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)}+Y=0$,
and
$-\dfrac{\alpha}{\gamma}+\dfrac{\bar X}{\gamma^2}=0$.
The second equation gives
$\gamma=\dfrac{\bar X}{\alpha}$.
Substituting this into the first equation yields a single equation for $\alpha$:
$h(\alpha)=\log\alpha-\dfrac{\Gamma'(\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)}+Y-\log\bar X=0$.

Now prove uniqueness of the solution of $h(\alpha)=0$. Use the expansion
$\dfrac{\Gamma'(\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)}=-C+\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\left(\dfrac{1}{k+1}-\dfrac{1}{k+\alpha}\right)$,
where $C$ is Euler's constant, and
$\dfrac{d}{d\alpha}\left[\dfrac{\Gamma'(\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\right]=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{(k+\alpha)^2}$.
Hence
$h'(\alpha)=\dfrac{1}{\alpha}-\psi'(\alpha)$,
where
$\psi'(\alpha)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{(k+\alpha)^2}$.
For every $k\ge0$,
$\dfrac{1}{(k+\alpha)^2}>
\dfrac{1}{k+\alpha}-\dfrac{1}{k+1+\alpha}$.
Therefore
$\psi'(\alpha)>
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\left(\dfrac{1}{k+\alpha}-\dfrac{1}{k+1+\alpha}\right)
=\dfrac{1}{\alpha}$,
and hence $h'(\alpha)<0$. So $h$ is strictly decreasing.

Next evaluate the limits at the two endpoints. For integers $m\ge2$,
$\dfrac{\Gamma'(m)}{\Gamma(m)}=\dfrac{1}{m-1}+\dfrac{1}{m-2}+\cdots+1+\dfrac{\Gamma'(1)}{\Gamma(1)}=\sum_{k=0}^{m-2}\dfrac{1}{k+1}-C$.
Therefore,
$\lim_{m\to\infty}\left[\log m-\dfrac{\Gamma'(m)}{\Gamma(m)}\right]=\lim_{m\to\infty}\left[\log m-\sum_{k=0}^{m-2}\dfrac{1}{k+1}+C\right]=0$.
Hence
$\lim_{\alpha\to\infty} h(\alpha)=Y-\log\bar X$.
By Jensen's inequality, if the $X_i$ are not all equal, then
$Y=\dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \log X_i<\log\left(\dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right)=\log\bar X$,
so $\lim_{\alpha\to\infty} h(\alpha)<0$ almost surely.

As $\alpha\to0$,
$\log\alpha-\dfrac{\Gamma'(\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)}
=\log\alpha+C-\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\left(\dfrac{1}{k+1}-\dfrac{1}{k+\alpha}\right)$
$=\log\alpha+C+\dfrac{1}{\alpha}-1+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{1-\alpha}{(k+1)(k+\alpha)}$.
Taking the limit gives
$\lim_{\alpha\to0}\left(\log\alpha+\dfrac{1}{\alpha}\right)+C-1+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{(k+1)k}=\infty$,
so
$\lim_{\alpha\to0} h(\alpha)=\infty$.

Thus $h$ is continuous, strictly decreasing, tends to $\infty$ as $\alpha\to0$, and tends to a negative number as $\alpha\to\infty$. Therefore $h(\alpha)=0$ has exactly one solution. Consequently, the likelihood equations have a unique solution, and this unique critical point is the MLE of $\theta=(\alpha,\gamma)$.

Now derive the iterative schemes. The score vector is
$s(\theta)=\frac{\partial\log\ell(\theta)}{\partial\theta}=n\left(-\log\gamma-\frac{\Gamma'(\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)}+Y,\,-\frac{\alpha}{\gamma}+\frac{\bar X}{\gamma^2}\right)$.
The matrix of second derivatives is
$R(\theta)=\frac{\partial^2\log\ell(\theta)}{\partial\theta\partial\theta^{\tau}}
=n\begin{pmatrix}
\left[\dfrac{\Gamma'(\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\right]^2-\dfrac{\Gamma''(\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)} & -\dfrac{1}{\gamma}\\[4pt]
-\dfrac{1}{\gamma} & \dfrac{\alpha}{\gamma^2}-\dfrac{2\bar X}{\gamma^3}
\end{pmatrix}$.
Its expectation gives the Fisher-scoring matrix
$F(\theta)=E[R(\theta)]
=n\begin{pmatrix}
\left[\dfrac{\Gamma'(\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\right]^2-\dfrac{\Gamma''(\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)} & -\dfrac{1}{\gamma}\\[4pt]
-\dfrac{1}{\gamma} & -\dfrac{\alpha}{\gamma^2}
\end{pmatrix}$.

Therefore the Newton-Raphson iteration is
$\hat\theta^{(k+1)}=\hat\theta^{(k)}-\left[R\big(\hat\theta^{(k)}\big)\right]^{-1}s\big(\hat\theta^{(k)}\big),\qquad k=0,1,2,\ldots$
and the Fisher-scoring iteration is
$\hat\theta^{(k+1)}=\hat\theta^{(k)}-\left[F\big(\hat\theta^{(k)}\big)\right]^{-1}s\big(\hat\theta^{(k)}\big),\qquad k=0,1,2,\ldots$.

In conclusion, the MLE is uniquely determined almost surely by $\hat\gamma=\bar X/\hat\alpha$ and the unique root $\hat\alpha$ of $\log\alpha-\Gamma'(\alpha)/\Gamma(\alpha)+Y-\log\bar X=0$, and the Newton-Raphson and Fisher-scoring updates are exactly the matrix iterations written above.
subject: Mathematical Statistics

question: Let $\left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right)$ be a random sample from a population with discrete probability density ${\left\lbrack x!\left( 1 - {e}^{-\theta }\right) \right\rbrack }^{-1}{\theta }^{x}{e}^{-\theta }{I}_{\{ 1,2,\ldots \} }\left( x\right)$ , where $\theta > 0$ is unknown. Show that the likelihood equation has a unique root when the sample mean $\bar{X} > 1$ . Show whether this root is an MLE of $\theta$ .
answer:
Let $\ell \left( \theta \right)$ be the likelihood function and$$
h\left( \theta \right) = \frac{\partial \log \ell \left( \theta \right) }{\partial \theta } = n\left( {\frac{\bar{X}}{\theta } - 1 - \frac{1}{{e}^{\theta } - 1}}\right) .
$$
Obviously, $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\theta \rightarrow \infty }}h\left( \theta \right) = - n$ . Since $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\theta \rightarrow 0}}\theta /\left( {{e}^{\theta } - 1}\right) = 1$ ,$$
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\theta \rightarrow 0}}h\left( \theta \right) = n\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\theta \rightarrow 0}}\frac{1}{\theta }\left( {\bar{X} - \frac{\theta }{{e}^{\theta } - 1}}\right) - n = \infty
$$
when $\bar{X} > 1$ . Note that $h$ is continuous. Hence, when $\bar{X} > 1, h\left( \theta \right) = 0$ has at least one solution. Note that$$
{h}^{\prime }\left( \theta \right) = n\left\lbrack {-\frac{\bar{X}}{{\theta }^{2}} + \frac{{e}^{\theta }}{{\left( {e}^{\theta } - 1\right) }^{2}}}\right\rbrack < 0
$$
because ${\left( {e}^{\theta } - 1\right) }^{2}/{e}^{\theta } = \left( {{e}^{\theta } - 1}\right) \left( {1 - {e}^{-\theta }}\right) > {\theta }^{2}$ . Hence, $h\left( \theta \right) = 0$ has a unique solution and $\log \ell \left( \theta \right)$ is strictly concave. Therefore, the unique solution is the MLE of $\theta$ .
explanation:
This problem uses the ideas of maximum likelihood estimation, the likelihood function, and the score function. We need the score equation to study existence and uniqueness of a root, and then use the sign of its derivative to determine whether that root gives the maximum of the log-likelihood.

Let $\ell(\theta)$ denote the likelihood based on the sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n$. From the given pmf,
$$
P_\theta(X=x)=\frac{\theta^x e^{-\theta}}{x!\left(1-e^{-\theta}\right)},\qquad x=1,2,\ldots,
$$
so the log-likelihood derivative is
$$
h(\theta)=\frac{\partial \log \ell(\theta)}{\partial \theta}
= n\left(\frac{\bar X}{\theta}-1-\frac{1}{e^{\theta}-1}\right).
$$
The likelihood equation is therefore
$$
h(\theta)=0.
$$

First, show existence of a root when $\bar X>1$.

Consider the behavior of $h(\theta)$ as $\theta\to\infty$. Since
$$
\frac{\bar X}{\theta}\to 0,\qquad \frac{1}{e^{\theta}-1}\to 0,
$$
we get
$$
\lim_{\theta\to\infty} h(\theta)=n(0-1-0)=-n.
$$
So for large $\theta$, $h(\theta)<0$.

Next, consider $\theta\to 0^+$. Using
$$
\lim_{\theta\to 0} \frac{\theta}{e^{\theta}-1}=1,
$$
we rewrite
$$
h(\theta)=n\left(\frac{\bar X}{\theta}-1-\frac{1}{e^{\theta}-1}\right)
= n\left[\frac{1}{\theta}\left(\bar X-\frac{\theta}{e^{\theta}-1}\right)-1\right].
$$
Since $\frac{\theta}{e^{\theta}-1}\to 1$, when $\bar X>1$ the term
$$
\bar X-\frac{\theta}{e^{\theta}-1}\to \bar X-1>0,
$$
and therefore
$$
\frac{1}{\theta}\left(\bar X-\frac{\theta}{e^{\theta}-1}\right)\to \infty.
$$
Hence
$$
\lim_{\theta\to 0^+} h(\theta)=\infty.
$$
Because $h(\theta)$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)$, and it goes from $+\infty$ near $0$ to $-n$ as $\theta\to\infty$, there is at least one solution to $h(\theta)=0$ when $\bar X>1$.

Now show uniqueness.

Differentiate $h(\theta)$:
$$
h'(\theta)=n\left(-\frac{\bar X}{\theta^2}+\frac{e^{\theta}}{(e^{\theta}-1)^2}\right).
$$
To compare the two terms, note that
$$
\frac{(e^{\theta}-1)^2}{e^{\theta}}=(e^{\theta}-1)(1-e^{-\theta})>\theta^2,
$$
so
$$
\frac{e^{\theta}}{(e^{\theta}-1)^2}<\frac{1}{\theta^2}.
$$
Since $\bar X>1$, we have
$$
-\frac{\bar X}{\theta^2}+\frac{e^{\theta}}{(e^{\theta}-1)^2}
< -\frac{1}{\theta^2}+\frac{1}{\theta^2}=0.
$$
Thus
$$
h'(\theta)<0 \qquad (\theta>0).
$$
So $h(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,\infty)$. A continuous strictly decreasing function can cross zero at most once. Since we already showed existence, the likelihood equation has a unique root.

Finally, determine whether this root is the MLE.

Because
$$
\frac{d}{d\theta}\log \ell(\theta)=h(\theta),
$$
and $h(\theta)$ decreases from positive values to negative values, the unique root is the point where $\log\ell(\theta)$ changes from increasing to decreasing. Equivalently, the log-likelihood reaches its maximum there. Hence the unique solution of the likelihood equation is indeed the MLE of $\theta$.

Therefore, when $\bar X>1$, the likelihood equation has exactly one root, and that root is the maximum likelihood estimator of $\theta$.
subject: Mathematical Statistics

question: Let $\left( {{X}_{1},{Y}_{1}}\right) ,\ldots ,\left( {{X}_{n},{Y}_{n}}\right)$ be independent and identically distributed as the bivariate normal distribution with $E\left( {X}_{1}\right) = \; E\left( {Y}_{1}\right) = 0,\operatorname{Var}\left( {X}_{1}\right) = \operatorname{Var}\left( {Y}_{1}\right) = 1$ , and an unknown correlation coefficient $\rho \in \left( {-1,1}\right)$ . Show that the likelihood equation is a cubic in $\rho$ and the probability that it has a unique root tends to 1 as $n \rightarrow \infty$ .
answer:
Let $T = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\left( {{X}_{i}^{2} + {Y}_{i}^{2}}\right)$ and $R = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{i}{Y}_{i}$ . The likelihood function is$$
\ell \left( \rho \right) = {\left( 2\pi \sqrt{1 - {\rho }^{2}}\right) }^{-n}\exp \left\{ {\frac{\rho R}{1 - {\rho }^{2}} - \frac{T}{2\left( {1 - {\rho }^{2}}\right) }}\right\} .
$$
Hence,$$
\frac{\partial \log \ell \left( \rho \right) }{\partial \rho } = \frac{n\rho }{1 - {\rho }^{2}} + \frac{1 + {\rho }^{2}}{{\left( 1 - {\rho }^{2}\right) }^{2}}R - \frac{\rho }{{\left( 1 - {\rho }^{2}\right) }^{2}}T
$$
and the likelihood equation is $h\left( \rho \right) = 0$ , where$$
h\left( \rho \right) = \rho \left( {1 - {\rho }^{2}}\right) - {n}^{-1}{T\rho } + {n}^{-1}R\left( {1 + {\rho }^{2}}\right)
$$
is a cubic in $\rho$ . Since $h$ is continuous,$$
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\rho \rightarrow 1}}h\left( \rho \right) = - {n}^{-1}\left( {T - {2R}}\right) = - \frac{1}{n}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{\left( {X}_{i} - {Y}_{i}\right) }^{2} < 0
$$
and$$
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\rho \rightarrow - 1}}h\left( \rho \right) = {n}^{-1}\left( {T + {2R}}\right) = \frac{1}{n}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{\left( {X}_{i} + {Y}_{i}\right) }^{2} > 0,
$$
the likelihood equation has at least one solution. Note that$$
{h}^{\prime }\left( \rho \right) = 1 - 3{\rho }^{2} - {n}^{-1}T + 2{n}^{-1}{R\rho }.
$$
As $n \rightarrow \infty ,{n}^{-1}T{ \rightarrow }_{p}\operatorname{Var}\left( {X}_{1}\right) + \operatorname{Var}\left( {Y}_{1}\right) = 2$ and ${n}^{-1}R{ \rightarrow }_{p}E\left( {{X}_{1}{Y}_{1}}\right) = \rho$ . Hence,$$
{h}^{\prime }\left( \rho \right) { \rightarrow }_{p}1 - 3{\rho }^{2} - 2 + 2{\rho }^{2} = - 1 - {\rho }^{2} < 0.
$$
Therefore, the probability that $h\left( \rho \right) = 0$ has a unique solution tends to 1 .
explanation:
This problem uses the likelihood function for a bivariate normal model and studies the score equation for the unknown correlation coefficient, so the key ideas are $\text{二元正态分布}$ and $\text{似然函数}$. To prove uniqueness asymptotically, we also use $\text{依概率收敛}$ for the sample averages appearing in the derivative of the cubic.

Let
$T=\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i^2+Y_i^2)$ and $R=\sum_{i=1}^n X_iY_i$.
Since $(X_i,Y_i)$ are i.i.d. bivariate normal with mean vector $(0,0)$, variances $1,1$, and correlation coefficient $\rho$, the likelihood function is
$\ell(\rho)=\left(2\pi\sqrt{1-\rho^2}\right)^{-n}\exp\left\{\frac{\rho R}{1-\rho^2}-\frac{T}{2(1-\rho^2)}\right\}$.

Take logarithms:
$\log \ell(\rho)=-n\log(2\pi)-\frac{n}{2}\log(1-\rho^2)+\frac{\rho R}{1-\rho^2}-\frac{T}{2(1-\rho^2)}$.
Differentiate with respect to $\rho$:
$\frac{\partial \log \ell(\rho)}{\partial \rho}=\frac{n\rho}{1-\rho^2}+\frac{1+\rho^2}{(1-\rho^2)^2}R-\frac{\rho}{(1-\rho^2)^2}T$.

The likelihood equation is obtained by setting this derivative equal to $0$. Multiplying by $\frac{(1-\rho^2)^2}{n}$ gives an equivalent equation
$h(\rho)=0$,
where
$h(\rho)=\rho(1-\rho^2)-n^{-1}T\rho+n^{-1}R(1+\rho^2)$.
Expanding it,
$h(\rho)=\rho-\rho^3-n^{-1}T\rho+n^{-1}R+n^{-1}R\rho^2$,
which is clearly a polynomial of degree $3$ in $\rho$. Thus the likelihood equation is a cubic in $\rho$.

Next show that there is at least one root in $(-1,1)$. Since $h$ is continuous, evaluate it near the endpoints:
$\lim_{\rho\to 1} h(\rho)=-n^{-1}(T-2R)$.
Now
$T-2R=\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i^2+Y_i^2-2X_iY_i)=\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-Y_i)^2$,
so
$\lim_{\rho\to 1} h(\rho)=-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-Y_i)^2<0$.
Similarly,
$\lim_{\rho\to -1} h(\rho)=n^{-1}(T+2R)$,
and
$T+2R=\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i^2+Y_i^2+2X_iY_i)=\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i+Y_i)^2$,
thus
$\lim_{\rho\to -1} h(\rho)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i+Y_i)^2>0$.
Therefore, by continuity, $h(\rho)=0$ has at least one solution in $(-1,1)$.

To prove asymptotic uniqueness, differentiate $h(\rho)$:
$h'(\rho)=1-3\rho^2-n^{-1}T+2n^{-1}R\rho$.
Now apply the law of large numbers in probability form:
$n^{-1}T=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i^2+Y_i^2) \xrightarrow{P} E(X_1^2+Y_1^2)=\operatorname{Var}(X_1)+\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)=2$,
because $E(X_1)=E(Y_1)=0$ and both variances are $1$.
Also,
$n^{-1}R=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_iY_i \xrightarrow{P} E(X_1Y_1)=\rho$.
Substitute these limits into $h'(\rho)$:
$h'(\rho) \xrightarrow{P} 1-3\rho^2-2+2\rho^2=-1-\rho^2$.
Since
$-1-\rho^2<0$
for every $\rho\in(-1,1)$, the derivative is asymptotically negative. Hence, with probability tending to $1$, the function $h$ is strictly decreasing on the parameter interval, so the equation $h(\rho)=0$ can have at most one root.

Combining this with the fact that there is always at least one root by the sign change at the endpoints, we conclude that the probability that the likelihood equation has a unique root tends to $1$ as $n\to\infty$.
subject: Mathematical Statistics

question: Let $\left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right)$ be a random sample from the Weibull distribution with Lebesgue density $\alpha {\theta }^{-1}{x}^{\alpha - 1}{e}^{-{x}^{\alpha }/\theta }{I}_{\left( 0,\infty \right) }\left( x\right)$ , where $\alpha > 0$ and $\theta > 0$ are unknown. Show that the likelihood equations are equivalent to $h\left( \alpha \right) = {n}^{-1}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\log {X}_{i}$ and $\theta = {n}^{-1}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{i}^{\alpha }$ , where $h\left( \alpha \right) = {\left( \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{i}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-1}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{i}^{\alpha }\log {X}_{i} - {\alpha }^{-1}$ , and that the likelihood equations have a unique solution.
answer:
The log-likelihood function is$$
\log \ell \left( {\alpha ,\theta }\right) = n\log \alpha - n\log \theta + \left( {\alpha - 1}\right) \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\log {X}_{i} - \frac{1}{\theta }\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{i}^{\alpha }.
$$
Hence, the likelihood equations are$$
\frac{\partial \log \ell \left( {\alpha ,\theta }\right) }{\partial \alpha } = \frac{n}{\alpha } + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\log {X}_{i} - \frac{1}{\theta }\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{i}^{\alpha }\log {X}_{i} = 0
$$
and$$
\frac{\partial \log \ell \left( {\alpha ,\theta }\right) }{\partial \theta } = - \frac{n}{\theta } + \frac{1}{{\theta }^{2}}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{i}^{\alpha } = 0,
$$
which are equivalent to $h\left( \alpha \right) = {n}^{-1}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\log {X}_{i}$ and $\theta = {n}^{-1}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{i}^{\alpha }$ . Note that$$
{h}^{\prime }\left( \alpha \right) = \frac{\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{i}^{\alpha }{\left( \log {X}_{i}\right) }^{2}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{i}^{\alpha } - {\left( \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{i}^{\alpha }\log {X}_{i}\right) }^{2}}{{\left( \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{i}^{\alpha }\right) }^{2}} + \frac{1}{{\alpha }^{2}} > 0
$$
by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Thus, $h\left( \alpha \right)$ is increasing. Since $h$ is continuous, $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha \rightarrow 0}}h\left( \alpha \right) = - \infty$ , and$$
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha \rightarrow \infty }}h\left( \alpha \right) = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha \rightarrow \infty }}\frac{\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{\left( \frac{{X}_{i}}{{X}_{\left( n\right) }}\right) }^{\alpha }\log {X}_{i}}{\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{\left( \frac{{X}_{i}}{{X}_{\left( n\right) }}\right) }^{\alpha }} = \log {X}_{\left( n\right) } > \frac{1}{n}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\log {X}_{i},
$$
where ${X}_{\left( n\right) }$ is the largest order statistic and the inequality holds as long as ${X}_{i}$ ’s are not identical, we conclude that the likelihood equations have a unique solution.
explanation:
This problem uses the ideas of maximum likelihood estimation and the likelihood function, because we must derive the likelihood equations for the Weibull model and study their solvability. It also uses the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality to prove that the function $h(\alpha)$ is strictly increasing, which is the key to uniqueness.

Let the sample be $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ from the Weibull density
$ f(x;\alpha,\theta)=\alpha\theta^{-1}x^{\alpha-1}e^{-x^{\alpha}/\theta}I_{(0,\infty)}(x), \quad \alpha>0,\ \theta>0. $
Then the likelihood function is
$ L(\alpha,\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n \alpha\theta^{-1}X_i^{\alpha-1}e^{-X_i^{\alpha}/\theta}. $
Taking logarithms gives
$ \log L(\alpha,\theta)=n\log\alpha-n\log\theta+(\alpha-1)\sum_{i=1}^n \log X_i-\frac{1}{\theta}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}. $

Now compute the score equations.
First, differentiate with respect to $\alpha$:
$ \frac{\partial \log L(\alpha,\theta)}{\partial \alpha}=\frac{n}{\alpha}+\sum_{i=1}^n \log X_i-\frac{1}{\theta}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}\log X_i. $
Setting this equal to $0$ gives
$ \frac{n}{\alpha}+\sum_{i=1}^n \log X_i-\frac{1}{\theta}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}\log X_i=0. $

Next, differentiate with respect to $\theta$:
$ \frac{\partial \log L(\alpha,\theta)}{\partial \theta}=-\frac{n}{\theta}+\frac{1}{\theta^2}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}. $
Setting this equal to $0$ gives
$ -\frac{n}{\theta}+\frac{1}{\theta^2}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}=0. $
Multiply by $\theta^2$:
$ -n\theta+\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}=0, $
so
$ \theta=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}. $

Substitute this expression for $\theta$ into the first likelihood equation:
$ \frac{n}{\alpha}+\sum_{i=1}^n \log X_i-\frac{n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}\log X_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}}=0. $
Divide by $n$:
$ \frac{1}{\alpha}+\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \log X_i-\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}\log X_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}}=0. $
Rearranging,
$ \left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}\right)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}\log X_i-\frac{1}{\alpha}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \log X_i. $
Therefore, if we define
$ h(\alpha)=\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}\right)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}\log X_i-\alpha^{-1}, $
then the likelihood equations are equivalent to
$ h(\alpha)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \log X_i, \qquad \theta=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}. $

It remains to show that this system has a unique solution. For that, study the monotonicity of $h(\alpha)$. Differentiate $h(\alpha)$:
$ h'(\alpha)=\frac{\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}(\log X_i)^2\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}\right)-\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}\log X_i\right)^2}{\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}\right)^2}+\frac{1}{\alpha^2}. $
By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,
$ \left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}\log X_i\right)^2 \le \left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}(\log X_i)^2\right), $
so the first fraction is nonnegative. Since $\frac{1}{\alpha^2}>0$, we get
$ h'(\alpha)>0. $
Hence $h(\alpha)$ is strictly increasing and continuous on $(0,\infty)$.

Now examine the limits at the two ends.
As $\alpha\to 0$,
$ h(\alpha)=\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}\right)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}\log X_i-\frac{1}{\alpha}. $
The first term stays finite, while $-1/\alpha\to -\infty$, so
$ \lim_{\alpha\to 0} h(\alpha)=-\infty. $

As $\alpha\to\infty$, let $X_{(n)}$ be the largest order statistic. Then
$ h(\alpha)+\frac{1}{\alpha}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}\log X_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha}}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \left(\frac{X_i}{X_{(n)}}\right)^{\alpha}\log X_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n \left(\frac{X_i}{X_{(n)}}\right)^{\alpha}}. $
When $\alpha\to\infty$, all terms with $X_i<X_{(n)}$ vanish relative to the largest one, so
$ \lim_{\alpha\to\infty} h(\alpha)=\log X_{(n)}. $
Also,
$ \log X_{(n)} > \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \log X_i $
provided the sample values are not all identical.

Therefore, the strictly increasing continuous function $h(\alpha)$ satisfies
$ \lim_{\alpha\to 0} h(\alpha)=-\infty $
and
$ \lim_{\alpha\to\infty} h(\alpha)=\log X_{(n)} > \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \log X_i. $
So the equation
$ h(\alpha)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \log X_i $
has exactly one solution in $\alpha>0$. Once this unique $\alpha$ is determined, the equation
$ \theta=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^{\alpha} $
then determines $\theta$ uniquely.

Hence the likelihood equations are equivalent to the stated system, and they have a unique solution.
subject: Mathematical Statistics

question:
Consider the one-way random effects model$$
{X}_{ij} = \mu + {A}_{i} + {e}_{ij},\;j = 1,\ldots , n, i = 1,\ldots , m,
$$
where $\mu \in \mathcal{R},{A}_{i}$ ’s are independent and identically distributed as $N\left( {0,{\sigma }_{a}^{2}}\right)$ , ${e}_{ij}$ ’s are independent and identically distributed as $N\left( {0,{\sigma }^{2}}\right) ,{\sigma }_{a}^{2}$ and ${\sigma }^{2}$ are unknown, and ${A}_{i}$ ’s and ${e}_{ij}$ ’s are independent.
(i) Find an MLE of $\left( {{\sigma }_{a}^{2},{\sigma }^{2}}\right)$ when $\mu = 0$ .
(ii) Find an MLE of $\left( {\mu ,{\sigma }_{a}^{2},{\sigma }^{2}}\right)$ .
answer: (i) If $\hat\sigma_a^2>0$, then the MLE is $\left(\hat\sigma_a^2,\hat\sigma^2\right)$ with $\hat\sigma^2=\dfrac{S_E}{m(n-1)}$ and $\hat\sigma_a^2=\dfrac{\widetilde S_A}{nm}-\dfrac{S_E}{nm(n-1)}$；if $\hat\sigma_a^2\le 0$, then the MLE is $\left(0,\widetilde\sigma^2\right)$ with $\widetilde\sigma^2=\dfrac{n\widetilde S_A+S_E}{nm+m(n-1)}$. (ii) $\hat\mu=\bar X_{\cdot\cdot}$. If $\hat\sigma_a^2>0$, then the MLE is $\left(\hat\mu,\hat\sigma_a^2,\hat\sigma^2\right)$ with $\hat\sigma^2=\dfrac{S_E}{m(n-1)}$ and $\hat\sigma_a^2=\dfrac{S_A}{n(m-1)}-\dfrac{S_E}{nm(n-1)}$；if $\hat\sigma_a^2\le 0$, then the MLE is $\left(\hat\mu,0,\widetilde\sigma^2\right)$ with $\widetilde\sigma^2=\dfrac{nS_A+S_E}{n(m-1)+m(n-1)}$
explanation:
This problem uses the likelihood function and maximum likelihood estimation for the one-way random effects model. It also uses the distributional facts that certain quadratic forms are chi-square and Basu's theorem to justify independence of the sufficient statistics involved.

For the model
$X_{ij}=\mu+A_i+e_{ij}$, where $A_i\sim N(0,\sigma_a^2)$, $e_{ij}\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$, mutually independent, define
$\bar X_{i\cdot}=\dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n X_{ij}$,
$\bar X_{\cdot\cdot}=\dfrac{1}{nm}\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n X_{ij}$,
$S_E=\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n (X_{ij}-\bar X_{i\cdot})^2$,
$S_A=n\sum_{i=1}^m (\bar X_{i\cdot}-\bar X_{\cdot\cdot})^2$.

For this model, the likelihood has the form
$\ell(\mu,\sigma_a^2,\sigma^2)=\xi\exp\left\{-\dfrac{S_E}{2\sigma^2}-\dfrac{S_A}{2(\sigma^2+n\sigma_a^2)}-\dfrac{nm}{2(\sigma^2+n\sigma_a^2)}(\bar X_{\cdot\cdot}-\mu)^2\right\}$,
where $\xi$ depends on $\sigma_a^2,\sigma^2$.

(i) Case $\mu=0$.

When $\mu=0$, the likelihood becomes
$\ell(\sigma_a^2,\sigma^2)=\xi\exp\left\{-\dfrac{S_E}{2\sigma^2}-\dfrac{\widetilde S_A}{2(\sigma^2+n\sigma_a^2)}\right\}$,
where
$\widetilde S_A=n\sum_{i=1}^m \bar X_{i\cdot}^2$.

The pair $(\widetilde S_A,S_E)$ is complete and sufficient for $(\sigma_a^2,\sigma^2)$. Also,
$\dfrac{S_E}{\sigma^2}\sim \chi^2_{m(n-1)}$,
$\dfrac{\widetilde S_A}{\sigma^2+n\sigma_a^2}\sim \chi^2_m$.
Since the distribution of $S_E$ does not involve $\sigma_a^2$, and $\widetilde S_A$ is complete and sufficient for $\sigma_a^2$ when $\sigma^2$ is known, Basu's theorem implies that $\widetilde S_A$ and $S_E$ are independent. Thus the likelihood equations can be written from the joint density of these two statistics.

Differentiate the log-likelihood with respect to $\sigma_a^2$ and $\sigma^2$:
$\dfrac{\partial \log \ell}{\partial \sigma_a^2}=\dfrac{n\widetilde S_A}{\sigma^2+n\sigma_a^2}-\dfrac{nm}{\sigma^2+n\sigma_a^2}=0,$

$\dfrac{\partial \log \ell}{\partial \sigma^2}=\dfrac{n\widetilde S_A}{\sigma^2+n\sigma_a^2}-\dfrac{nm}{\sigma^2+n\sigma_a^2}+\dfrac{S_E}{\sigma^4}-\dfrac{m(n-1)}{\sigma^2}=0.$

Solving these gives the interior critical point
$\hat\sigma^2=\dfrac{S_E}{m(n-1)},$
$\hat\sigma_a^2=\dfrac{\widetilde S_A}{nm}-\dfrac{S_E}{nm(n-1)}.$

If this value satisfies $\hat\sigma_a^2>0$, then it lies in the parameter space, so the MLE is
$\left(\hat\sigma_a^2,\hat\sigma^2\right)$.

If $\hat\sigma_a^2\le 0$, the interior solution is outside the parameter space because $\sigma_a^2\ge 0$, so the maximum must occur on the boundary $\sigma_a^2=0$. Substituting $\sigma_a^2=0$ into the log-likelihood and differentiating with respect to $\sigma^2$ gives
$\dfrac{\partial \log \ell(0,\sigma^2)}{\partial \sigma^2}=\dfrac{n\widetilde S_A}{\sigma^2}-\dfrac{nm}{\sigma^2}+\dfrac{S_E}{\sigma^4}-\dfrac{m(n-1)}{\sigma^2}=0.$
This equation has the unique solution
$\widetilde\sigma^2=\dfrac{n\widetilde S_A+S_E}{nm+m(n-1)}.$
Therefore, when $\hat\sigma_a^2\le 0$, the MLE is
$\left(0,\widetilde\sigma^2\right)$.

Hence for part (i):
- if $\hat\sigma_a^2>0$, the MLE is $\left(\hat\sigma_a^2,\hat\sigma^2\right)$ with
$\hat\sigma^2=\dfrac{S_E}{m(n-1)}$ and $\hat\sigma_a^2=\dfrac{\widetilde S_A}{nm}-\dfrac{S_E}{nm(n-1)}$;
- if $\hat\sigma_a^2\le 0$, the MLE is $\left(0,\widetilde\sigma^2\right)$ with
$\widetilde\sigma^2=\dfrac{n\widetilde S_A+S_E}{nm+m(n-1)}$.

(ii) MLE of $(\mu,\sigma_a^2,\sigma^2)$.

For fixed $\sigma_a^2$ and $\sigma^2$, the likelihood depends on $\mu$ through the term
$-\dfrac{nm}{2(\sigma^2+n\sigma_a^2)}(\bar X_{\cdot\cdot}-\mu)^2$.
This is maximized when
$\hat\mu=\bar X_{\cdot\cdot}$.

So it remains to maximize the profile likelihood obtained by substituting $\mu=\bar X_{\cdot\cdot}$:
$\ell(\bar X_{\cdot\cdot},\sigma_a^2,\sigma^2)=\xi\exp\left\{-\dfrac{S_E}{2\sigma^2}-\dfrac{S_A}{2(\sigma^2+n\sigma_a^2)}\right\}$.
This has exactly the same structure as in part (i), with $\widetilde S_A$ replaced by $S_A$. Here,
$\dfrac{S_A}{\sigma^2+n\sigma_a^2}\sim \chi^2_{m-1}$,
while still
$\dfrac{S_E}{\sigma^2}\sim \chi^2_{m(n-1)}$.
Using the same argument as in part (i), the interior likelihood equations yield
$\hat\sigma^2=\dfrac{S_E}{m(n-1)},$
$\hat\sigma_a^2=\dfrac{S_A}{n(m-1)}-\dfrac{S_E}{nm(n-1)}.$

If $\hat\sigma_a^2>0$, then the MLE is
$\left(\hat\mu,\hat\sigma_a^2,\hat\sigma^2\right)$
with
$\hat\mu=\bar X_{\cdot\cdot},\quad \hat\sigma^2=\dfrac{S_E}{m(n-1)},\quad \hat\sigma_a^2=\dfrac{S_A}{n(m-1)}-\dfrac{S_E}{nm(n-1)}.$

If $\hat\sigma_a^2\le 0$, the maximum occurs on the boundary $\sigma_a^2=0$, and the corresponding maximizer of $\sigma^2$ is
$\widetilde\sigma^2=\dfrac{nS_A+S_E}{n(m-1)+m(n-1)}.$
Thus the MLE is
$\left(\hat\mu,0,\widetilde\sigma^2\right)=\left(\bar X_{\cdot\cdot},0,\dfrac{nS_A+S_E}{n(m-1)+m(n-1)}\right)$.

Therefore, the final results are:
For part (i), use $\widetilde S_A$ and the piecewise form depending on whether $\hat\sigma_a^2>0$.
For part (ii), $\hat\mu=\bar X_{\cdot\cdot}$, and the variance-component MLEs have the same piecewise form with $\widetilde S_A$ replaced by $S_A$.
subject: Mathematical Statistics

question: Let $\left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right)$ be a random sample of random variables with Lebesgue density ${\theta f}\left( {\theta x}\right)$ , where $f$ is a Lebesgue density on $\left( {0,\infty }\right)$ or symmetric about 0, and $\theta > 0$ is an unknown parameter. Show that the likelihood equation has a unique root if $x{f}^{\prime }\left( x\right) /f\left( x\right)$ is continuous and decreasing for $x > 0$ . Verify that this condition is satisfied if $f\left( x\right) = \; {\pi }^{-1}{\left( 1 + {x}^{2}\right) }^{-1}.$
answer:
Let $\ell \left( \theta \right)$ be the likelihood function and$$
h\left( \theta \right) = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\left\lbrack {1 + \frac{\theta {X}_{i}{f}^{\prime }\left( {\theta {X}_{i}}\right) }{f\left( {\theta {X}_{i}}\right) }}\right\rbrack .
$$
Then$$
\frac{\partial \log \ell \left( \theta \right) }{\partial \theta } = \frac{1}{\theta }\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\left\lbrack {1 + \frac{\theta {X}_{i}{f}^{\prime }\left( {\theta {X}_{i}}\right) }{f\left( {\theta {X}_{i}}\right) }}\right\rbrack = 0
$$
is the same as $h\left( \theta \right) = 0$ . From the condition, $h\left( \theta \right)$ is decreasing in $\theta$ when $\theta > 0$ . Hence, the likelihood equation has at most one solution. Define $g\left( t\right) = 1 + t{f}^{\prime }\left( t\right) /f\left( t\right)$ . Suppose that $g\left( t\right) \geq 0$ for all $t \in \left( {0,\infty }\right)$ . Then ${tf}\left( t\right)$ is nondecreasing since its derivative is $f\left( t\right) g\left( t\right) \geq 0$ . Let ${t}_{0} \in \left( {0,\infty }\right)$ . Then ${tf}\left( t\right) \geq {t}_{0}f\left( {t}_{0}\right)$ for $t \in \left( {{t}_{0},\infty }\right)$ and$$
1 \geq {\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{\infty }f\left( t\right) {dt} \geq {\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{\infty }\frac{{t}_{0}f\left( {t}_{0}\right) }{t}{dt} = \infty ,
$$
which is impossible. Suppose that $g\left( t\right) \leq 0$ for all $t \in \left( {0,\infty }\right)$ . Then ${tf}\left( t\right)$ is nonincreasing and ${tf}\left( t\right) \geq {t}_{0}f\left( {t}_{0}\right)$ for $t \in \left( {0,{t}_{0}}\right)$ . Then$$
1 \geq {\int }_{0}^{{t}_{0}}f\left( t\right) {dt} \geq {\int }_{0}^{{t}_{0}}\frac{{t}_{0}f\left( {t}_{0}\right) }{t}{dt} = \infty ,
$$
which is impossible. Combining these results and the fact that $g\left( t\right)$ is nonincreasing, we conclude that$$
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\theta \rightarrow 0}}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\left\lbrack {1 + \frac{\theta {X}_{i}{f}^{\prime }\left( {\theta {X}_{i}}\right) }{f\left( {\theta {X}_{i}}\right) }}\right\rbrack > 0 > \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\theta \rightarrow \infty }}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\left\lbrack {1 + \frac{\theta {X}_{i}{f}^{\prime }\left( {\theta {X}_{i}}\right) }{f\left( {\theta {X}_{i}}\right) }}\right\rbrack
$$
and, therefore, $h\left( \theta \right) = 0$ has a unique solution.
For $f\left( x\right) = {\pi }^{-1}{\left( 1 + {x}^{2}\right) }^{-1}$ ,$$
\frac{x{f}^{\prime }\left( x\right) }{f\left( x\right) } = -\frac{2{x}^{2}}{1 + {x}^{2}},
$$
which is clearly continuous and decreasing for $x > 0$ .
explanation:
This problem uses the ideas of likelihood function, maximum likelihood estimation, and the score function. The key is to write the likelihood equation in terms of a one-variable function and then use the monotonicity assumption on $x f'(x)/f(x)$ to prove existence and uniqueness of the root.

Let $\ell(\theta)$ be the likelihood based on the sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, where the density is $\theta f(\theta x)$ and $\theta>0$. The log-likelihood is
$\log \ell(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n \log\bigl(\theta f(\theta X_i)\bigr)$.
Differentiating with respect to $\theta$ gives
$\dfrac{\partial \log \ell(\theta)}{\partial \theta}=\sum_{i=1}^n \left(\dfrac{1}{\theta}+\dfrac{X_i f'(\theta X_i)}{f(\theta X_i)}\right)$.
Factor out $1/\theta$:
$\dfrac{\partial \log \ell(\theta)}{\partial \theta}=\dfrac{1}{\theta}\sum_{i=1}^n \left[1+\dfrac{\theta X_i f'(\theta X_i)}{f(\theta X_i)}\right]$.
Define
$h(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n \left[1+\dfrac{\theta X_i f'(\theta X_i)}{f(\theta X_i)}\right]$.
Then the likelihood equation
$\dfrac{\partial \log \ell(\theta)}{\partial \theta}=0$
is equivalent to
$h(\theta)=0$.

Now define
$g(t)=1+\dfrac{t f'(t)}{f(t)}$.
Then
$h(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n g(\theta X_i)$.
By assumption, $\dfrac{x f'(x)}{f(x)}$ is continuous and decreasing for $x>0$, so $g(t)$ is also continuous and decreasing on $(0,\infty)$. Therefore each term $g(\theta X_i)$ is decreasing in $\theta$, and hence $h(\theta)$ is decreasing in $\theta$ for $\theta>0$. Thus the equation $h(\theta)=0$ can have at most one solution.

It remains to show that a solution actually exists. For this, analyze the signs of $g(t)$ near $0$ and $\infty$.

First, suppose $g(t)\ge 0$ for all $t\in(0,\infty)$. Then
$\dfrac{d}{dt}\bigl(t f(t)\bigr)=f(t)+t f'(t)=f(t)\left(1+\dfrac{t f'(t)}{f(t)}\right)=f(t)g(t)\ge 0$.
So $t f(t)$ is nondecreasing on $(0,\infty)$. Fix any $t_0>0$. Then for all $t\ge t_0$,
$t f(t)\ge t_0 f(t_0)$,
so
$f(t)\ge \dfrac{t_0 f(t_0)}{t}$.
Hence
$1\ge \int_{t_0}^{\infty} f(t)\,dt \ge \int_{t_0}^{\infty} \dfrac{t_0 f(t_0)}{t}\,dt=\infty$,
which is impossible. Therefore $g(t)$ cannot be nonnegative for all $t>0$.

Second, suppose $g(t)\le 0$ for all $t\in(0,\infty)$. Then
$\dfrac{d}{dt}\bigl(t f(t)\bigr)=f(t)g(t)\le 0$,
so $t f(t)$ is nonincreasing. Fix any $t_0>0$. Then for all $0<t\le t_0$,
$t f(t)\ge t_0 f(t_0)$,
so
$f(t)\ge \dfrac{t_0 f(t_0)}{t}$.
Hence
$1\ge \int_0^{t_0} f(t)\,dt \ge \int_0^{t_0} \dfrac{t_0 f(t_0)}{t}\,dt=\infty$,
again impossible. Therefore $g(t)$ cannot be nonpositive for all $t>0$.

Since $g$ is continuous and decreasing, and it cannot stay always nonnegative or always nonpositive, it must satisfy
$\lim_{t\to 0^+} g(t)>0, \qquad \lim_{t\to \infty} g(t)<0$.
Therefore,
$\lim_{\theta\to 0^+} h(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n \lim_{\theta\to 0^+} g(\theta X_i)>0$,
and
$\lim_{\theta\to \infty} h(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n \lim_{\theta\to \infty} g(\theta X_i)<0$.
Because $h(\theta)$ is continuous and decreasing, it changes sign from positive to negative as $\theta$ goes from $0^+$ to $\infty$. By the intermediate value theorem, there exists a root of $h(\theta)=0$. Since $h$ is decreasing, that root is unique.

So the likelihood equation has a unique root.

Now verify the condition for
$f(x)=\pi^{-1}(1+x^2)^{-1}$.
Differentiate:
$f'(x)=\pi^{-1}\cdot \left(-(1+x^2)^{-2}\cdot 2x\right)=-\dfrac{2x}{\pi(1+x^2)^2}$.
Hence
$\dfrac{x f'(x)}{f(x)}=x\cdot \dfrac{-2x}{\pi(1+x^2)^2}\cdot \dfrac{\pi(1+x^2)}{1}=-\dfrac{2x^2}{1+x^2}$.
This function is continuous for $x>0$. Its derivative is
$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(-\dfrac{2x^2}{1+x^2}\right)=-\dfrac{4x}{(1+x^2)^2}<0, \qquad x>0$,
so it is decreasing on $(0,\infty)$.

Therefore the required condition is satisfied for the Cauchy density $f(x)=\pi^{-1}(1+x^2)^{-1}$, and the likelihood equation has a unique root in this case as well.
subject: Mathematical Statistics

question:
Let $\left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right)$ be a random sample having Lebesgue density ${f}_{\theta }\left( x\right) = \theta {f}_{1}\left( x\right) + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) {f}_{2}\left( x\right)$ , where ${f}_{j}$ ’s are two different known Lebesgue densities and $\theta \in \left( {0,1}\right)$ is unknown.
(i) Provide a necessary and sufficient condition for the likelihood equation to have a unique solution and show that if there is a solution, it is the MLE of $\theta$ .
(ii) Derive the MLE of $\theta$ when the likelihood equation has no solution.
answer:
(i) Let $\ell \left( \theta \right)$ be the likelihood function. Note that$$
s\left( \theta \right) = \frac{\partial \log \ell \left( \theta \right) }{\partial \theta } = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\frac{{f}_{1}\left( {X}_{i}\right) - {f}_{2}\left( {X}_{i}\right) }{{f}_{2}\left( {X}_{i}\right) + \theta \left\lbrack {{f}_{1}\left( {X}_{i}\right) - {f}_{2}\left( {X}_{i}\right) }\right\rbrack },
$$
which has derivative$$
{s}^{\prime }\left( \theta \right) = - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\frac{{\left\lbrack {f}_{1}\left( {X}_{i}\right) - {f}_{2}\left( {X}_{i}\right) \right\rbrack }^{2}}{{\left\{ {f}_{2}\left( {X}_{i}\right) + \theta \left\lbrack {f}_{1}\left( {X}_{i}\right) - {f}_{2}\left( {X}_{i}\right) \right\rbrack \right\} }^{2}} < 0.
$$
Therefore, $s\left( \theta \right) = 0$ has at most one solution. The necessary and sufficient condition that $s\left( \theta \right) = 0$ has a solution (which is unique if it exists) is that $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\theta \rightarrow 0}}s\left( \theta \right) > 0$ and $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\theta \rightarrow 1}}s\left( \theta \right) < 0$ , which is equivalent to$$
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\frac{{f}_{1}\left( {X}_{i}\right) }{{f}_{2}\left( {X}_{i}\right) } > n\text{ and }\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\frac{{f}_{2}\left( {X}_{i}\right) }{{f}_{1}\left( {X}_{i}\right) } > n.
$$
The solution, if it exists, is the MLE since ${s}^{\prime }\left( \theta \right) < 0$ .
(ii) If $\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\frac{{f}_{2}\left( {X}_{i}\right) }{{f}_{1}\left( {X}_{i}\right) } \leq n$ , then $s\left( \theta \right) \geq 0$ and $\ell \left( \theta \right)$ is nondecreasing and, thus, the MLE of $\theta$ is 1 . Similarly, if $\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\frac{{f}_{1}\left( {X}_{i}\right) }{{f}_{2}\left( {X}_{i}\right) } \leq n$ , then the MLE of $\theta$ is 0 .
explanation:
This problem uses the key ideas of maximum likelihood estimation, the likelihood function, and the score function. We need the score equation to locate interior maximizers, and the monotonicity of the score to determine uniqueness and what happens when no interior solution exists.

Let
$L(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n \bigl[\theta f_1(X_i)+(1-\theta)f_2(X_i)\bigr]$,
with $\theta\in(0,1)$. Then the log-likelihood is
$\log L(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n \log\Bigl(f_2(X_i)+\theta\bigl[f_1(X_i)-f_2(X_i)\bigr]\Bigr)$.

(i) Condition for a unique solution of the likelihood equation and why it is the MLE.

Differentiate the log-likelihood. The score function is
$s(\theta)=\frac{\partial \log L(\theta)}{\partial \theta}
=\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{f_1(X_i)-f_2(X_i)}{f_2(X_i)+\theta\,[f_1(X_i)-f_2(X_i)]}$.

Differentiate once more:
$s'(\theta)
=-\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{[f_1(X_i)-f_2(X_i)]^2}{\{f_2(X_i)+\theta[f_1(X_i)-f_2(X_i)]\}^2}<0.$

So $s(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,1)$. Therefore the likelihood equation
$s(\theta)=0$
has at most one solution.

Since $s(\theta)$ is continuous and strictly decreasing, it has a solution in $(0,1)$ if and only if its value near $0$ is positive and its value near $1$ is negative, namely
$\lim_{\theta\to 0} s(\theta)>0$
and
$\lim_{\theta\to 1} s(\theta)<0$.

Compute these two endpoint limits.
At $\theta\to 0$,
$\lim_{\theta\to 0} s(\theta)
=\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{f_1(X_i)-f_2(X_i)}{f_2(X_i)}
=\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{f_1(X_i)}{f_2(X_i)}-n.$
Thus
$\lim_{\theta\to 0} s(\theta)>0$
is equivalent to
$\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{f_1(X_i)}{f_2(X_i)}>n.$

At $\theta\to 1$,
$\lim_{\theta\to 1} s(\theta)
=\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{f_1(X_i)-f_2(X_i)}{f_1(X_i)}
=n-\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{f_2(X_i)}{f_1(X_i)}.$
Thus
$\lim_{\theta\to 1} s(\theta)<0$
is equivalent to
$\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{f_2(X_i)}{f_1(X_i)}>n.$

Hence the necessary and sufficient condition for the likelihood equation to have a solution is
$\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{f_1(X_i)}{f_2(X_i)}>n$
and
$\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{f_2(X_i)}{f_1(X_i)}>n.$
Because $s'(\theta)<0$, the log-likelihood is strictly concave, so any interior solution of $s(\theta)=0$ is the unique maximizer. Therefore, if a solution exists, it is the MLE of $\theta$.

(ii) MLE when the likelihood equation has no solution.

If
$\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{f_2(X_i)}{f_1(X_i)}\le n$,
then
$\lim_{\theta\to 1} s(\theta)=n-\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{f_2(X_i)}{f_1(X_i)}\ge 0.$
Since $s(\theta)$ is decreasing, this implies $s(\theta)\ge 0$ for all $\theta\in(0,1)$. Therefore $\log L(\theta)$, and hence $L(\theta)$, is nondecreasing in $\theta$. So the maximum is attained at the right endpoint, and the MLE is
$\hat\theta=1.$

Similarly, if
$\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{f_1(X_i)}{f_2(X_i)}\le n$,
then
$\lim_{\theta\to 0} s(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{f_1(X_i)}{f_2(X_i)}-n\le 0.$
Because $s(\theta)$ is decreasing, we have $s(\theta)\le 0$ for all $\theta\in(0,1)$. Thus $\log L(\theta)$ and $L(\theta)$ are nonincreasing in $\theta$, so the maximum is attained at the left endpoint, giving
$\hat\theta=0.$

Therefore, the final conclusions are:
(1) an interior unique solution exists iff $\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{f_1(X_i)}{f_2(X_i)}>n$ and $\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{f_2(X_i)}{f_1(X_i)}>n$, and that solution is the MLE;
(2) if no interior solution exists, then the MLE is $1$ when $\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{f_2(X_i)}{f_1(X_i)}\le n$, and is $0$ when $\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{f_1(X_i)}{f_2(X_i)}\le n$.
subject: Mathematical Statistics

question: Let ${X}_{ij}, j = 1,\ldots , r > 1, i = 1,\ldots , n$ , be independently distributed as $N\left( {{\mu }_{i},{\sigma }^{2}}\right)$ . Find the MLE of $\theta = \left( {{\mu }_{1},\ldots ,{\mu }_{n},{\sigma }^{2}}\right)$ . Show that the MLE of ${\sigma }^{2}$ is not a consistent estimator (as $n \rightarrow \infty$ ).
answer:
Let $\ell \left( \theta \right)$ be the likelihood function. Note that$$
\log \ell \left( \theta \right) = - \frac{nr}{2}\log \left( {{2\pi }{\sigma }^{2}}\right) - \frac{1}{2{\sigma }^{2}}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{r}{\left( {X}_{ij} - {\mu }_{i}\right) }^{2},
$$$$
\frac{\partial \log \ell \left( \theta \right) }{\partial {\mu }_{i}} = \frac{1}{{\sigma }^{2}}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{r}\left( {{X}_{ij} - {\mu }_{i}}\right)
$$
and$$
\frac{\partial \log \ell \left( \theta \right) }{\partial {\sigma }^{2}} = - \frac{nr}{2{\sigma }^{2}} + \frac{1}{2{\sigma }^{4}}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{r}{\left( {X}_{ij} - {\mu }_{i}\right) }^{2}.
$$
Hence, the MLE of ${\mu }_{i}$ is ${\bar{X}}_{i \cdot } = {r}^{-1}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{r}{X}_{ij}, i = 1,\ldots , n$ , and the MLE of ${\sigma }^{2}$ is$$
{\widehat{\sigma }}^{2} = \frac{1}{nr}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{r}{\left( {X}_{ij} - {\bar{X}}_{i \cdot }\right) }^{2}.
$$
Since$$
E\left\lbrack {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{r}{\left( {X}_{ij} - {\bar{X}}_{i \cdot }\right) }^{2}}\right\rbrack = \left( {r - 1}\right) {\sigma }^{2},
$$
by the law of large numbers,$$
{\widehat{\sigma }}^{2}{ \rightarrow }_{p}\frac{r - 1}{r}{\sigma }^{2}
$$
as $n \rightarrow \infty$ . Hence, ${\widehat{\sigma }}^{2}$ is inconsistent.
explanation:
This problem uses the key ideas of $\text{maximum likelihood estimation}$ and the $\text{likelihood function}$ to derive the estimators, and then uses $\text{consistency}$ together with the law of large numbers to study the asymptotic behavior of the MLE of $\sigma^2$. The essential point is that there are $n$ nuisance means $\mu_i$, one for each group, and this affects the limit of the variance estimator.

First write the log-likelihood for
$X_{ij}\sim N(\mu_i,\sigma^2)$ independently, with $j=1,\ldots,r$ and $i=1,\ldots,n$:
$$
\log \ell(\theta)= -\frac{nr}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2)-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^r (X_{ij}-\mu_i)^2,
$$
where $\theta=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_n,\sigma^2)$.

Step 1: Find the MLE of each $\mu_i$.
Differentiate the log-likelihood with respect to $\mu_i$:
$$
\frac{\partial \log \ell(\theta)}{\partial \mu_i}
=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{j=1}^r (X_{ij}-\mu_i).
$$
Set this equal to $0$:
$$
\sum_{j=1}^r (X_{ij}-\mu_i)=0.
$$
Hence,
$$
r\mu_i=\sum_{j=1}^r X_{ij},
$$
so
$$
\hat{\mu}_i=\bar{X}_{i\cdot}=\frac{1}{r}\sum_{j=1}^r X_{ij},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.
$$

Step 2: Find the MLE of $\sigma^2$.
Differentiate the log-likelihood with respect to $\sigma^2$:
$$
\frac{\partial \log \ell(\theta)}{\partial \sigma^2}
=-\frac{nr}{2\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{2\sigma^4}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^r (X_{ij}-\mu_i)^2.
$$
Set this equal to $0$:
$$
-\frac{nr}{2\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{2\sigma^4}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^r (X_{ij}-\mu_i)^2=0.
$$
Multiply by $2\sigma^4$:
$$
-nr\sigma^2+\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^r (X_{ij}-\mu_i)^2=0.
$$
Thus,
$$
\hat{\sigma}^2=\frac{1}{nr}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^r (X_{ij}-\hat{\mu}_i)^2.
$$
Substituting $\hat{\mu}_i=\bar{X}_{i\cdot}$ gives
$$
\hat{\sigma}^2=\frac{1}{nr}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^r (X_{ij}-\bar{X}_{i\cdot})^2.
$$
So the MLEs are
$$
\hat{\mu}_i=\bar{X}_{i\cdot},\qquad
\hat{\sigma}^2=\frac{1}{nr}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^r (X_{ij}-\bar{X}_{i\cdot})^2.
$$

Step 3: Show that $\hat{\sigma}^2$ is not consistent as $n\to\infty$.
For each fixed $i$, the within-group sum of squares satisfies
$$
E\left[\sum_{j=1}^r (X_{ij}-\bar{X}_{i\cdot})^2\right]=(r-1)\sigma^2.
$$
Therefore,
$$
E(\hat{\sigma}^2)
=\frac{1}{nr}\sum_{i=1}^n E\left[\sum_{j=1}^r (X_{ij}-\bar{X}_{i\cdot})^2\right]
=\frac{1}{nr}\cdot n(r-1)\sigma^2
=\frac{r-1}{r}\sigma^2.
$$
Now define
$$
Y_i=\sum_{j=1}^r (X_{ij}-\bar{X}_{i\cdot})^2.
$$
Because the groups are independent across $i$, the variables $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$ are independent and identically distributed, with
$$
E(Y_i)=(r-1)\sigma^2.
$$
Then
$$
\hat{\sigma}^2=\frac{1}{nr}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i.
$$
By the law of large numbers,
$$
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i \xrightarrow{P} E(Y_i)=(r-1)\sigma^2.
$$
Dividing by $r$ gives
$$
\hat{\sigma}^2=\frac{1}{r}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i\right)
\xrightarrow{P} \frac{r-1}{r}\sigma^2.
$$
Since $r>1$ is fixed,
$$
\frac{r-1}{r}\sigma^2\neq \sigma^2.
$$
Hence $\hat{\sigma}^2$ does not converge in probability to the true parameter $\sigma^2$, so it is not a consistent estimator.

Conclusion:
$$
\hat{\mu}_i=\bar{X}_{i\cdot},\qquad
\hat{\sigma}^2=\frac{1}{nr}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^r (X_{ij}-\bar{X}_{i\cdot})^2,
$$
and
$$
\hat{\sigma}^2\xrightarrow{P}\frac{r-1}{r}\sigma^2,
$$
so the MLE of $\sigma^2$ is inconsistent as $n\to\infty$.
subject: Mathematical Statistics

question:
Let $\left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right)$ be a random sample from the uniform distribution on $\left( {0,\theta }\right)$ , where $\theta > 0$ is unknown. Let $\widehat{\theta }$ be the MLE of $\theta$ and $T$ be the UMVUE.
(i) Obtain the ratio of the mean squared error of $T$ over the mean squared error of $\widehat{\theta }$ and show that the MLE is inadmissible when $n \geq 2$ .
(ii) Let ${Z}_{a,\theta }$ be a random variable having the exponential distribution on $\left( {a,\infty }\right)$ with scale parameter $\theta$ . Prove $n\left( {\theta - \widehat{\theta }}\right) { \rightarrow }_{d}{Z}_{0,\theta }$ and $n\left( {\theta - T}\right) { \rightarrow }_{d} \; {Z}_{-\theta ,\theta }$ . Obtain the asymptotic relative efficiency of $\widehat{\theta }$ with respect to $T$ .
answer:
(i) Let ${X}_{\left( n\right) }$ be the largest order statistic. Then $\widehat{\theta } = {X}_{\left( n\right) }$ and $T\left( X\right) = \frac{n + 1}{n}{X}_{\left( n\right) }$ . The mean squared error of $\widehat{\theta }$ is$$
E{\left( {X}_{\left( n\right) } - \theta \right) }^{2} = \frac{2{\theta }^{2}}{\left( {n + 1}\right) \left( {n + 2}\right) }
$$
and the mean squared error of $T$ is$$
E{\left( T - \theta \right) }^{2} = \frac{{\theta }^{2}}{n\left( {n + 2}\right) }.
$$
The ratio is $\left( {n + 1}\right) /\left( {2n}\right)$ . When $n \geq 2$ , this ratio is less than 1 and, therefore, the MLE $\widehat{\theta }$ is inadmissible.
(ii) From$$
P\left( {n\left( {\theta - \widehat{\theta }}\right) \leq x}\right) = P\left( {{X}_{\left( n\right) } \geq \theta - \frac{x}{n}}\right)
$$$$
= {\theta }^{-n}{\int }_{\theta - x/n}^{\theta }n{t}^{n - 1}{dt}
$$$$
= 1 - {\left( 1 - \frac{x}{n\theta }\right) }^{n}
$$$$
\rightarrow 1 - {e}^{-x/\theta }
$$
as $n \rightarrow \infty$ , we conclude that $n\left( {\theta - \widehat{\theta }}\right) { \rightarrow }_{d}{Z}_{0,\theta }$ . From$$
n\left( {\theta - T}\right) = n\left( {\theta - \widehat{\theta }}\right) - \widehat{\theta }
$$
and Slutsky’s theorem, we conclude that $n\left( {\theta - T}\right) { \rightarrow }_{d}{Z}_{0,\theta } - \theta$ , which has the same distribution as ${Z}_{-\theta ,\theta }$ . The asymptotic relative efficiency of $\widehat{\theta }$ with respect to $T$ is $E\left( {Z}_{-\theta ,\theta }^{2}\right) /E\left( {Z}_{0,\theta }^{2}\right) = {\theta }^{2}/\left( {{\theta }^{2} + {\theta }^{2}}\right) = \frac{1}{2}$ .
explanation:
This problem uses the key ideas of maximum likelihood estimation, mean squared error comparison, and asymptotic distribution. The estimator is built from the largest order statistic of a uniform sample, and then its finite-sample MSE and limiting scaled distribution are compared with those of the UMVUE.

For a random sample from $U(0,\theta)$, let $X_{(n)}=\max\{X_1,\dots,X_n\}$. Since the likelihood is
$L(\theta)=\theta^{-n}I(\theta\ge X_{(n)})$,
it is maximized at the smallest admissible value of $\theta$, so the MLE is
$\widehat{\theta}=X_{(n)}$.
The UMVUE is
$T=\frac{n+1}{n}X_{(n)}$.

(i) Compare the mean squared errors.

First, use the known moments of the maximum order statistic from $U(0,\theta)$:
$E[X_{(n)}]=\frac{n}{n+1}\theta,$
$E[X_{(n)}^2]=\frac{n}{n+2}\theta^2.$
Hence
$\mathrm{MSE}(\widehat{\theta})=E[(X_{(n)}-\theta)^2]$
$=E[X_{(n)}^2]-2\theta E[X_{(n)}]+\theta^2$
$=\frac{n}{n+2}\theta^2-2\theta\cdot \frac{n}{n+1}\theta+\theta^2.$
Putting over the common denominator $(n+1)(n+2)$ gives
$\mathrm{MSE}(\widehat{\theta})=\frac{2\theta^2}{(n+1)(n+2)}.$

Now compute the MSE of $T=\frac{n+1}{n}X_{(n)}$. Since $T$ is unbiased,
$E[T]=\frac{n+1}{n}E[X_{(n)}]=\theta,$
so
$\mathrm{MSE}(T)=\mathrm{Var}(T)=\left(\frac{n+1}{n}\right)^2\mathrm{Var}(X_{(n)}).$
From the moments above,
$\mathrm{Var}(X_{(n)})=E[X_{(n)}^2]-\{E[X_{(n)}]\}^2$
$=\frac{n}{n+2}\theta^2-\left(\frac{n}{n+1}\theta\right)^2.$
Therefore
$\mathrm{MSE}(T)=\frac{\theta^2}{n(n+2)}.$

So the ratio is
$\frac{\mathrm{MSE}(T)}{\mathrm{MSE}(\widehat{\theta})}
=\frac{\theta^2/[n(n+2)]}{2\theta^2/[(n+1)(n+2)]}
=\frac{n+1}{2n}.$
When $n\ge2$,
$\frac{n+1}{2n}<1.$
Thus $T$ has strictly smaller mean squared error than the MLE, so $\widehat{\theta}$ is inadmissible.

(ii) Find the limiting distributions.

First consider $n(\theta-\widehat{\theta})=n(\theta-X_{(n)})$. For $x\ge0$,
$P\bigl(n(\theta-\widehat{\theta})\le x\bigr)
=P\left(X_{(n)}\ge \theta-\frac{x}{n}\right).$
Since $X_{(n)}$ has distribution function
$P(X_{(n)}\le t)=\left(\frac{t}{\theta}\right)^n,\quad 0<t<\theta,$
we get
$P\left(X_{(n)}\ge \theta-\frac{x}{n}\right)
=1-P\left(X_{(n)}<\theta-\frac{x}{n}\right)
=1-\left(1-\frac{x}{n\theta}\right)^n.$
As $n\to\infty$,
$\left(1-\frac{x}{n\theta}\right)^n\to e^{-x/\theta},$
so
$P\bigl(n(\theta-\widehat{\theta})\le x\bigr)\to 1-e^{-x/\theta},\quad x\ge0.$
This is the distribution function of an exponential random variable on $(0,\infty)$ with scale parameter $\theta$, namely
$n(\theta-\widehat{\theta})\xrightarrow{d} Z_{0,\theta}.$

Next,
$n(\theta-T)=n\left(\theta-\frac{n+1}{n}\widehat{\theta}\right)
=n(\theta-\widehat{\theta})-\widehat{\theta}.$
Since $\widehat{\theta}=X_{(n)}\xrightarrow{P}\theta$, by Slutsky’s theorem,
$n(\theta-T)\xrightarrow{d} Z_{0,\theta}-\theta.$
A shift of an exponential random variable on $(0,\infty)$ by $-\theta$ gives an exponential distribution on $(-\theta,\infty)$ with the same scale parameter $\theta$. Hence
$n(\theta-T)\xrightarrow{d} Z_{-\theta,\theta}.$

Finally, compute the asymptotic relative efficiency of $\widehat{\theta}$ with respect to $T$ using the limiting second moments of the scaled errors:
$\mathrm{ARE}(\widehat{\theta}\text{ w.r.t. }T)
=\frac{E[Z_{-\theta,\theta}^2]}{E[Z_{0,\theta}^2]}.$
Now if $Y\sim Z_{0,\theta}$, then $E[Y]=\theta$ and $\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\theta^2$, so
$E[Y^2]=\theta^2+\theta^2=2\theta^2.$
Also $Z_{-\theta,\theta}=Y-\theta$, so
$E[(Y-\theta)^2]=\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\theta^2.$
Therefore
$\mathrm{ARE}(\widehat{\theta}\text{ w.r.t. }T)=\frac{\theta^2}{2\theta^2}=\frac{1}{2}.$

Hence the conclusions are: in finite samples,
$\dfrac{\mathrm{MSE}(T)}{\mathrm{MSE}(\widehat{\theta})}=\dfrac{n+1}{2n}<1$ for $n\ge2$, so the MLE is inadmissible; and asymptotically,
$n(\theta-\widehat{\theta})\xrightarrow{d} Z_{0,\theta}$,
$n(\theta-T)\xrightarrow{d} Z_{-\theta,\theta}$,
with asymptotic relative efficiency $\frac{1}{2}$.
