question: Let $\left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right)$ be a random sample from the exponential distribution on $\left( {a,\infty }\right)$ with scale parameter $\theta$ , where $a \in \mathcal{R}$ and $\theta > 0$ are unknown. Obtain the asymptotic relative efficiency of the MLE of $a$ (or $\theta$ ) with respect to the UMVUE of $a$ (or $\theta$ ).
keypoint: 一致最小方差无偏估计
answer:
Let $X_i=a+Y_i$ with $Y_i\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\theta)$, and put
$$M=X_{(1)},\qquad R=\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-M)=n(\bar X-M).$$
The MLEs and UMVUEs are
$$\widehat a=M,\qquad \widehat\theta=\frac Rn,$$
$$\widetilde\theta=\frac R{n-1},\qquad
\widetilde a=M-\frac{R}{n(n-1)}=M-\frac{\bar X-M}{n-1}.$$
For the scale parameter, both estimators have asymptotic variance $\theta^2/n$, so
$$\operatorname{ARE}(\widehat\theta\text{ relative to }\widetilde\theta)=1.$$
For the location parameter the convergence rate is $n$, not $\sqrt n$, and the comparison is made using MSE. Since $M-a\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\theta/n)$,
$$\operatorname{MSE}(\widehat a)=\frac{2\theta^2}{n^2}.$$
Also $M-a$ is independent of $R\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(n-1,\theta)$, so
$$\operatorname{MSE}(\widetilde a)=\operatorname{Var}(\widetilde a)=\frac{\theta^2}{n(n-1)}.$$
Consequently,
$$\operatorname{ARE}(\widehat a\text{ relative to }\widetilde a)
=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{MSE}(\widetilde a)}{\operatorname{MSE}(\widehat a)}=\frac12.$$
explanation:
The minimum $M$ determines the location MLE, and the residual sum $R=\sum(X_i-M)$ determines the scale estimators. Exponential spacings give $M-a\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\theta/n)$, $R\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(n-1,\theta)$, and independence of $M-a$ and $R$. These facts make the bias and MSE calculations explicit.

The scale MLE differs from its UMVUE only by the factor $(n-1)/n$, so their first-order asymptotic variances agree. The location estimators are nonregular and converge at rate $n$; using the asymptotic MSE ratio, the UMVUE has leading MSE $\theta^2/n^2$ whereas the biased MLE has leading MSE $2\theta^2/n^2$, giving efficiency $1/2$.

question:
Let $\left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right) , n \geq 2$ , be a random sample from a distribution having Lebesgue density ${f}_{\theta , j}$ , where $\theta > 0, j = 1,2,{f}_{\theta ,1}$ is the density of $N\left( {0,{\theta }^{2}}\right)$ , and ${f}_{\theta ,2}\left( x\right) = {\left( 2\theta \right) }^{-1}{e}^{-\left| x\right| /\theta }$ .
(i) Obtain an MLE of $\left( {\theta , j}\right)$ .
(ii) Show whether the MLE of $j$ in part (i) is consistent.
(iii) Show that the MLE of $\theta$ is consistent and derive its nondegenerated asymptotic distribution.
answer:
(i) Let ${T}_{1} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{i}^{2}$ and ${T}_{2} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\left| {X}_{i}\right|$ . The likelihood function is$$
\ell \left( {\theta , j}\right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} {\left( 2\pi \right) }^{-n/2}{\theta }^{-n}{e}^{-{T}_{1}/\left( {2{\theta }^{2}}\right) } & j = 1 \\ {2}^{-n}{\theta }^{-n}{e}^{-{T}_{2}/\theta } & j = 2. \end{array}\right.
$$
Note that ${\widehat{\theta }}_{1} = \sqrt{{T}_{1}/n}$ maximizes $\ell \left( {\theta ,1}\right)$ and ${\widehat{\theta }}_{2} = {T}_{2}/n$ maximizes $\ell \left( {\theta ,2}\right)$ . Define$$
\widehat{j} = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1 & \ell \left( {{\widehat{\theta }}_{1},1}\right) \geq \ell \left( {{\widehat{\theta }}_{2},2}\right) \\ 2 & \ell \left( {{\widehat{\theta }}_{1},1}\right) < \ell \left( {{\widehat{\theta }}_{2},2}\right) \end{array}\right.
$$
which is the same as$$
\widehat{j} = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1 & \frac{{\widehat{\theta }}_{1}}{{\widehat{\theta }}_{2}} \leq \sqrt{\frac{2e}{\pi }} \\ 2 & \frac{{\widehat{\theta }}_{1}}{{\widehat{\theta }}_{2}} > \sqrt{\frac{2e}{\pi }}, \end{array}\right.
$$
and define$$
\widehat{\theta } = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} {\widehat{\theta }}_{1} & \widehat{j} = 1 \\ {\widehat{\theta }}_{2} & \widehat{j} = 2. \end{array}\right.
$$
Then$$
\ell \left( {\widehat{\theta },\widehat{j}}\right) \geq \ell \left( {\theta , j}\right)
$$
for any $\theta$ and $j$ . This shows that $\left( {\widehat{\theta },\widehat{j}}\right)$ is an MLE of $\left( {\theta , j}\right)$ .
(ii) The consistency of $\widehat{j}$ means that$$
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}P\left( {\widehat{j} = j}\right) = 1
$$
which is equivalent to$$
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}P\left( {\frac{{\widehat{\theta }}_{1}}{{\widehat{\theta }}_{2}} \leq \sqrt{\frac{2e}{\pi }}}\right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1 & \text{ if }j = 1 \\ 0 & \text{ if }j = 2. \end{array}\right.
$$
It suffices to consider the limit of ${\widehat{\theta }}_{1}/{\widehat{\theta }}_{2}$ . When $j = 1,{\widehat{\theta }}_{1}{ \rightarrow }_{p}\theta$ and ${\widehat{\theta }}_{2}{ \rightarrow }_{p} \; \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi }}\theta$ (since $E\left| {X}_{1}\right| = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi }}\theta$ ). Then ${\widehat{\theta }}_{1}/{\widehat{\theta }}_{2}{ \rightarrow }_{p}\sqrt{\frac{\pi }{2}} < \sqrt{\frac{2e}{\pi }}$ (since ${\pi }^{2} < {4e}$ ). When $j = 2,{\widehat{\theta }}_{1}{ \rightarrow }_{p}\sqrt{2}\theta$ and ${\widehat{\theta }}_{2}{ \rightarrow }_{p}\theta$ . Then ${\widehat{\theta }}_{1}/{\widehat{\theta }}_{2}{ \rightarrow }_{p}\sqrt{2} > \sqrt{\frac{2e}{\pi }}$ (since $e < \pi )$ . Therefore, $\widehat{j}$ is consistent.
(iii) When $j = 1$ , by the result in part (ii) of the solution,$$
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}P\left( {\widehat{\theta } = {\widehat{\theta }}_{1}}\right) = 1
$$
Hence, the asymptotic distribution of $\widehat{\theta }$ is the same as that of ${\widehat{\theta }}_{1}$ under the normal distribution assumption. By the central limit theorem and the $\delta$ - method, $\sqrt{n}\left( {{\widehat{\theta }}_{1} - \theta }\right) { \rightarrow }_{d}N\left( {0,{\theta }^{2}/2}\right)$ . Similarly, when $j = 2$ , the asymptotic distribution of $\widehat{\theta }$ is the same as that of ${\widehat{\theta }}_{2}$ . By the central limit theorem, $\sqrt{n}\left( {{\widehat{\theta }}_{2} - \theta }\right) { \rightarrow }_{d}N\left( {0,{\theta }^{2}}\right)$ .
explanation:
This problem uses maximum likelihood estimation to determine the joint estimator of the model index $j$ and scale parameter $\theta$, then uses consistency and asymptotic normality to study the large-sample behavior. The key points are $\,$maximum likelihood estimation$\,$ because the estimators are defined by maximizing the likelihood over two candidate families, $\,$consistency$\,$ because we must show the selected model and parameter converge to the truth, and $\,$asymptotic normality$\,$ because the limiting distribution of the MLE of $\theta$ is required.

(i) Obtain an MLE of $(\theta,j)$.

Let
$T_1=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2,\qquad T_2=\sum_{i=1}^n |X_i|.$

For $j=1$, the density is that of $N(0,\theta^2)$, so the likelihood is
$\ell(\theta,1)=\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\theta}\exp\left(-\frac{X_i^2}{2\theta^2}\right)
=(2\pi)^{-n/2}\theta^{-n}\exp\left(-\frac{T_1}{2\theta^2}\right).$

For $j=2$, the density is
$f_{\theta,2}(x)=\frac{1}{2\theta}e^{-|x|/\theta},$
so the likelihood is
$\ell(\theta,2)=\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{2\theta}e^{-|X_i|/\theta}
=2^{-n}\theta^{-n}\exp\left(-\frac{T_2}{\theta}\right).$

Now maximize each likelihood over $\theta>0$ separately.

For $j=1$, the maximizer is the usual normal scale MLE:
$\widehat{\theta}_1=\sqrt{\frac{T_1}{n}}.$

For $j=2$, the maximizer is the Laplace scale MLE:
$\widehat{\theta}_2=\frac{T_2}{n}.$

Then compare the maximized likelihood values. Define
$\widehat{j}=\begin{cases}
1,& \ell(\widehat{\theta}_1,1)\ge \ell(\widehat{\theta}_2,2),\\
2,& \ell(\widehat{\theta}_1,1)< \ell(\widehat{\theta}_2,2).
\end{cases}$

Compute the two maximized likelihoods:
$\ell(\widehat{\theta}_1,1)=(2\pi)^{-n/2}\widehat{\theta}_1^{-n}e^{-n/2},$
because $T_1/(2\widehat{\theta}_1^2)=n/2$;

and
$\ell(\widehat{\theta}_2,2)=2^{-n}\widehat{\theta}_2^{-n}e^{-n},$
because $T_2/\widehat{\theta}_2=n$.

Thus
$\ell(\widehat{\theta}_1,1)\ge \ell(\widehat{\theta}_2,2)$
iff
$(2\pi)^{-n/2}\widehat{\theta}_1^{-n}e^{-n/2}\ge 2^{-n}\widehat{\theta}_2^{-n}e^{-n}$.

Taking the $n$th root and rearranging gives
$(2\pi)^{-1/2}\widehat{\theta}_1^{-1}e^{-1/2}\ge 2^{-1}\widehat{\theta}_2^{-1}e^{-1}$,
which is equivalent to
$\frac{\widehat{\theta}_1}{\widehat{\theta}_2}\le \sqrt{\frac{2e}{\pi}}.$

So
$\widehat{j}=\begin{cases}
1,& \dfrac{\widehat{\theta}_1}{\widehat{\theta}_2}\le \sqrt{\dfrac{2e}{\pi}},\\
2,& \dfrac{\widehat{\theta}_1}{\widehat{\theta}_2}> \sqrt{\dfrac{2e}{\pi}}.
\end{cases}$

Finally define
$\widehat{\theta}=\begin{cases}
\widehat{\theta}_1,& \widehat{j}=1,\\
\widehat{\theta}_2,& \widehat{j}=2.
\end{cases}$

Since for each fixed $j$ we maximize over $\theta$, and then choose the larger of the two maximized likelihood values, we have
$\ell(\widehat{\theta},\widehat{j})\ge \ell(\theta,j)$
for every $\theta>0$ and $j\in\{1,2\}$. Therefore $(\widehat{\theta},\widehat{j})$ is an MLE of $(\theta,j)$.

(ii) Show whether the MLE of $j$ is consistent.

Consistency of $\widehat{j}$ means
$\lim_{n\to\infty}P(\widehat{j}=j)=1.$

Because $\widehat{j}$ is determined by whether
$\dfrac{\widehat{\theta}_1}{\widehat{\theta}_2}\le \sqrt{\dfrac{2e}{\pi}},$
it is enough to find the probability limit of $\widehat{\theta}_1/\widehat{\theta}_2$ under each true model.

Case 1: $j=1$.
Then $X_i\sim N(0,\theta^2)$.

By the law of large numbers,
$\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2\xrightarrow{P}E(X_1^2)=\theta^2,$
so
$\widehat{\theta}_1=\sqrt{\frac{T_1}{n}}\xrightarrow{P}\theta.$

Also,
$\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n |X_i|\xrightarrow{P}E|X_1|.$
For $N(0,\theta^2)$,
$E|X_1|=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\theta,$
so
$\widehat{\theta}_2=\frac{T_2}{n}\xrightarrow{P}\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\theta.$

Hence
$\frac{\widehat{\theta}_1}{\widehat{\theta}_2}\xrightarrow{P}\frac{\theta}{\sqrt{2/\pi}\,\theta}=\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}.$
Now
$\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}<\sqrt{\frac{2e}{\pi}}$
equivalently $\pi^2<4e$.
Therefore,
$P\left(\frac{\widehat{\theta}_1}{\widehat{\theta}_2}\le \sqrt{\frac{2e}{\pi}}\right)\to 1,$
so $P(\widehat{j}=1)\to 1$ when $j=1$.

Case 2: $j=2$.
Then $X_i$ has Laplace density $\frac{1}{2\theta}e^{-|x|/\theta}$.

For this distribution,
$E|X_1|=\theta,
\qquad E(X_1^2)=2\theta^2.$

Thus by the law of large numbers,
$\widehat{\theta}_2=\frac{T_2}{n}\xrightarrow{P}\theta,$
and
$\widehat{\theta}_1=\sqrt{\frac{T_1}{n}}\xrightarrow{P}\sqrt{2\theta^2}=\sqrt{2}\,\theta.$

Hence
$\frac{\widehat{\theta}_1}{\widehat{\theta}_2}\xrightarrow{P}\sqrt{2}.$
Now
$\sqrt{2}>\sqrt{\frac{2e}{\pi}}$
equivalently $e<\pi$.
Therefore,
$P\left(\frac{\widehat{\theta}_1}{\widehat{\theta}_2}\le \sqrt{\frac{2e}{\pi}}\right)\to 0,$
so $P(\widehat{j}=2)\to 1$ when $j=2$.

Combining the two cases,
$\lim_{n\to\infty}P(\widehat{j}=j)=1.$
Thus $\widehat{j}$ is consistent.

(iii) Show that the MLE of $\theta$ is consistent and derive its nondegenerate asymptotic distribution.

Because $\widehat{j}$ is consistent, the probability that the MLE selects the wrong model tends to $0$. Hence asymptotically $\widehat{\theta}$ behaves like the correct within-model estimator.

Case 1: $j=1$.
From part (ii),
$P(\widehat{\theta}=\widehat{\theta}_1)=P(\widehat{j}=1)\to 1.$
So the asymptotic distribution of $\widehat{\theta}$ is the same as that of $\widehat{\theta}_1$.

Now
$\widehat{\theta}_1=g\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2\right),
\qquad g(x)=\sqrt{x}.$
Under $j=1$, for $Y_i=X_i^2$,
$E(Y_i)=\theta^2,
\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=E(X_i^4)-\theta^4=3\theta^4-\theta^4=2\theta^4.$
By the central limit theorem,
$\sqrt{n}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2-\theta^2\right)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,2\theta^4).$

Since $g'(x)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}$, we have
$g'(\theta^2)=\frac{1}{2\theta}.$
By the $\delta$-method,
$\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\theta}_1-\theta)
\xrightarrow{d}N\left(0,\left(\frac{1}{2\theta}\right)^2\cdot 2\theta^4\right)
=N\left(0,\frac{\theta^2}{2}\right).$
Therefore,
$\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\theta}-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N\left(0,\frac{\theta^2}{2}\right)$
when $j=1$.

Case 2: $j=2$.
From part (ii),
$P(\widehat{\theta}=\widehat{\theta}_2)=P(\widehat{j}=2)\to 1.$
So the asymptotic distribution of $\widehat{\theta}$ is the same as that of $\widehat{\theta}_2$.

Here
$\widehat{\theta}_2=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n |X_i|.$
Under $j=2$, $|X_i|$ has mean $\theta$ and variance $\theta^2$. Hence by the central limit theorem,
$\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\theta}_2-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,\theta^2).$
Therefore,
$\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\theta}-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,\theta^2)$
when $j=2$.

Since in each case $\widehat{\theta}$ is asymptotically equivalent to a consistent estimator of $\theta$, it follows that $\widehat{\theta}$ is consistent.

Conclusion: the joint MLE is obtained by maximizing the likelihood within each model and then comparing the two maximized values; $\widehat{j}$ is consistent; and $\widehat{\theta}$ is consistent with asymptotic law $N(0,\theta^2/2)$ after $\sqrt{n}$ scaling under $j=1$, and $N(0,\theta^2)$ after $\sqrt{n}$ scaling under $j=2$.

question:
Let $\left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right) , n \geq 2$ , be a random sample from a distribution with discrete probability density ${f}_{\theta , j}$ , where $\theta \in \left( {0,1}\right) , j = \; 1,2,{f}_{\theta ,1}$ is the Poisson distribution with mean $\theta$ , and ${f}_{\theta ,2}$ is the binomial distribution with size 1 and probability $\theta$ .
(i) Obtain an MLE of $\left( {\theta , j}\right)$ .
(ii) Show whether the MLE of $j$ in part (i) is consistent.
(iii) Show that the MLE of $\theta$ is consistent and derive its nondegenerated asymptotic distribution.
answer:
(i) Let $X = \left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right) ,\bar{X}$ be the sample mean, $g\left( X\right) = \; {\left( \mathop{\prod }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{i}!\right) }^{-1}$ , and $h\left( X\right) = 1$ if all ${X}_{i}$ ’s are not larger than 1 and $h\left( X\right) = 0$ otherwise. The likelihood function is$$
\ell \left( {\theta , j}\right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} {e}^{-{n\theta }}{\theta }^{n\bar{X}}g\left( X\right) & j = 1 \\ {\theta }^{n\bar{X}}{\left( 1 - \theta \right) }^{n - n\bar{X}}h\left( X\right) & j = 2. \end{array}\right.
$$
Note that $\bar{X} = T/n$ maximizes both $\ell \left( {\theta ,1}\right)$ and $\ell \left( {\theta ,2}\right)$ . Define$$
\widehat{j} = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1 & \ell \left( {\bar{X},1}\right) > \ell \left( {\bar{X},2}\right) \\ 2 & \ell \left( {\bar{X},1}\right) \leq \ell \left( {\bar{X},2}\right) . \end{array}\right.
$$
Then$$
\ell \left( {\bar{X},\widehat{j}}\right) \geq \ell \left( {\theta , j}\right)
$$
for any $\theta$ and $j$ and, hence, $\left( {\bar{X},\widehat{j}}\right)$ is an MLE of $\left( {\theta , j}\right)$ . We now simplify the formula for $\widehat{j}$ . If at least one ${X}_{i}$ is larger than 1, then $h\left( X\right) = 0$ , $\ell \left( {\bar{X},1}\right) > \ell \left( {\bar{X},2}\right)$ , and $\widehat{j} = 1$ . If all ${X}_{i}$ ’s are not larger than 1, then $h\left( X\right) = g\left( X\right) = 1$ and$$
\frac{\ell \left( {\bar{X},2}\right) }{\ell \left( {\bar{X},1}\right) } = {\left( 1 - \bar{X}\right) }^{n - n\bar{X}}{e}^{n\bar{X}} \geq 1
$$
because of the inequality ${\left( 1 - t\right) }^{1 - t} \geq {e}^{-t}$ for any $t \in \lbrack 0,1)$ . This shows that$$
\widehat{j} = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1 & h\left( X\right) = 0 \\ 2 & h\left( X\right) = 1. \end{array}\right.
$$
(ii) If $j = 2, h\left( X\right) = 1$ always holds. Therefore, $\widehat{j}$ is consistent if we can show that if $j = 1,\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}P\left( {h\left( X\right) = 1}\right) = 0$ . Since $P\left( {{X}_{1} = 0}\right) = {e}^{-\theta }$ and $P\left( {{X}_{1} = 1}\right) = {e}^{-\theta }\theta ,$$$
P\left( {h\left( X\right) = 1}\right) = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 0}}^{n}\left( \begin{array}{l} n \\ k \end{array}\right) {\left( {e}^{-\theta }\theta \right) }^{k}{\left( {e}^{-\theta }\right) }^{n - k}
$$$$
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 0}}^{n}\left( \begin{array}{l} n \\ k \end{array}\right) {\theta }^{k}{e}^{-{n\theta }}
$$$$
\leq \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 0}}^{n}\left( \begin{array}{l} n \\ k \end{array}\right) {\theta }^{k}{\left( 1 - \theta \right) }^{n\left( {1 - \theta }\right) }.
$$
For any fixed $\theta \in \left( {0,1}\right)$ and any $\epsilon > 0$ , there exists $K$ such that ${\left( 1 - \theta \right) }^{k - \theta } < \; \epsilon$ whenever $k \geq K$ . Then, when $n > K$ ,$$
P\left( {h\left( X\right) = 1}\right) \leq \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = K}}^{n}\left( \begin{array}{l} n \\ k \end{array}\right) {\theta }^{k}{\left( 1 - \theta \right) }^{n\left( {1 - \theta }\right) } + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 0}}^{K}\left( \begin{array}{l} n \\ k \end{array}\right) {\theta }^{k}{\left( 1 - \theta \right) }^{n\left( {1 - \theta }\right) }
$$$$
\leq \epsilon + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 0}}^{K}\left( \begin{array}{l} n \\ k \end{array}\right) {\theta }^{k}{\left( 1 - \theta \right) }^{n\left( {1 - \theta }\right) }.
$$
For any fixed $K$ ,$$
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 0}}^{K}\left( \begin{array}{l} n \\ k \end{array}\right) {\theta }^{k}{\left( 1 - \theta \right) }^{n\left( {1 - \theta }\right) } = 0.
$$
Hence, $\mathop{\limsup }\limits_{n}P\left( {h\left( X\right) = 1}\right) \leq \epsilon$ and the result follows since $\epsilon$ is arbitrary. (iii) By the central limit theorem, $\sqrt{n}\left( {\bar{X} - \theta }\right) { \rightarrow }_{d}N\left( {0,\operatorname{Var}\left( {X}_{1}\right) }\right)$ , since $E\left( \bar{X}\right) = \theta$ in any case. When $j = 1,\operatorname{Var}\left( {X}_{1}\right) = \theta$ and when $j = 2$ , $\operatorname{Var}\left( {X}_{1}\right) = \theta \left( {1 - \theta }\right)$ . ∎
explanation:
This problem uses the ideas of maximum likelihood estimation, consistency, and asymptotic distribution. We first write the likelihood under the two candidate models, then compare their maximized values to obtain the MLE of $(\theta,j)$, and finally study consistency and the asymptotic law of the estimator of $\theta$.

(i) Obtain an MLE of $(\theta,j)$.

Let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ and let $\bar X=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$. Define
$g(X)=\left(\prod_{i=1}^n X_i!\right)^{-1}$,
and define
$h(X)=1$ if all $X_i\le 1$, and $h(X)=0$ otherwise.

Under $j=1$, $X_i\sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\theta)$, so the likelihood is
$L(\theta,1)=\prod_{i=1}^n e^{-\theta}\frac{\theta^{X_i}}{X_i!}=e^{-n\theta}\theta^{\sum X_i}g(X)=e^{-n\theta}\theta^{n\bar X}g(X)$.

Under $j=2$, $X_i\sim \mathrm{Bin}(1,\theta)$, so the likelihood is
$L(\theta,2)=\prod_{i=1}^n \theta^{X_i}(1-\theta)^{1-X_i}h(X)=\theta^{n\bar X}(1-\theta)^{n-n\bar X}h(X)$,
because if some $X_i>1$, then the binomial model assigns probability $0$, which is exactly represented by $h(X)=0$.

Now maximize with respect to $\theta$ for each fixed $j$.

For $j=1$, maximize $e^{-n\theta}\theta^{n\bar X}$ over $\theta\in(0,1)$. The log-likelihood part is
$-n\theta+n\bar X\log\theta$.
Differentiating gives
$-n+\frac{n\bar X}{\theta}=0 \Rightarrow \theta=\bar X$.

For $j=2$, maximize $\theta^{n\bar X}(1-\theta)^{n-n\bar X}$ over $\theta\in(0,1)$. The log-likelihood part is
$n\bar X\log\theta+(n-n\bar X)\log(1-\theta)$.
Differentiating gives
$\frac{n\bar X}{\theta}-\frac{n-n\bar X}{1-\theta}=0 \Rightarrow \theta=\bar X$.

So for both models the maximizing value is $\hat\theta=\bar X$. Hence define
$\hat j=\begin{cases}1,&L(\bar X,1)>L(\bar X,2),\\2,&L(\bar X,1)\le L(\bar X,2).\end{cases}$
Then $(\bar X,\hat j)$ maximizes the likelihood over all $(\theta,j)$, so it is an MLE.

We now simplify the form of $\hat j$.

If at least one $X_i>1$, then $h(X)=0$, so
$L(\bar X,2)=0$,
while $L(\bar X,1)>0$.
Therefore $\hat j=1$.

If all $X_i\le 1$, then necessarily each $X_i$ is either $0$ or $1$, so $h(X)=1$ and also $g(X)=1$ because $0!=1!=1$. In this case,
$\frac{L(\bar X,2)}{L(\bar X,1)}=\frac{\bar X^{n\bar X}(1-\bar X)^{n-n\bar X}}{e^{-n\bar X}\bar X^{n\bar X}}=(1-\bar X)^{n-n\bar X}e^{n\bar X}$.
Thus
$\frac{L(\bar X,2)}{L(\bar X,1)}=\left((1-\bar X)^{1-\bar X}e^{\bar X}\right)^n$.
Using the inequality
$(1-t)^{1-t}\ge e^{-t},\qquad t\in[0,1)$,
we get
$\left((1-\bar X)^{1-\bar X}e^{\bar X}\right)^n\ge 1$.
Hence $L(\bar X,2)\ge L(\bar X,1)$, so $\hat j=2$.

Therefore the MLE can be written as
$\hat\theta=\bar X,$
$\hat j=\begin{cases}1,&\exists i\text{ such that }X_i>1,\\2,&X_i\le 1\text{ for all }i.\end{cases}$

(ii) Show whether the MLE of $j$ is consistent.

We must show that $P_\theta(\hat j=j)\to 1$ under each true model.

First suppose the true model is $j=2$. Then each $X_i\sim \mathrm{Bin}(1,\theta)$, so $X_i\in\{0,1\}$ always. Hence $h(X)=1$ with probability $1$, and by the characterization above, $\hat j=2$ always. Therefore,
$P(\hat j=2)=1$ for all $n$,
so consistency holds in this case.

Now suppose the true model is $j=1$. Then each $X_i\sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\theta)$. The only way that $\hat j=2$ occurs is that all observations are at most $1$, that is, $h(X)=1$. So it suffices to show
$P(h(X)=1)\to 0$.

For a Poisson$(\theta)$ variable,
$P(X_1=0)=e^{-\theta},\qquad P(X_1=1)=e^{-\theta}\theta.$
Hence
$P(X_1\le 1)=e^{-\theta}+e^{-\theta}\theta=e^{-\theta}(1+\theta)$,
and by independence,
$P(h(X)=1)=\bigl(e^{-\theta}(1+\theta)\bigr)^n.$
Equivalently, expanding binomially,
$P(h(X)=1)=\sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}(e^{-\theta}\theta)^k(e^{-\theta})^{n-k}=e^{-n\theta}\sum_{k=0}^n\binom{n}{k}\theta^k.$
The given argument bounds this expression and shows it tends to $0$ as $n\to\infty$. Therefore,
$P(\hat j=2)=P(h(X)=1)\to 0,$
so
$P(\hat j=1)\to 1.$
Thus $\hat j$ is consistent under $j=1$ as well.

Hence the MLE $\hat j$ is consistent.

(iii) Show that the MLE of $\theta$ is consistent and derive its nondegenerated asymptotic distribution.

From part (i), the MLE of $\theta$ is
$\hat\theta=\bar X.$

Under both models,
$E(X_1)=\theta$.
Indeed, if $j=1$ and $X_1\sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\theta)$, then $E(X_1)=\theta$; if $j=2$ and $X_1\sim \mathrm{Bin}(1,\theta)$, then also $E(X_1)=\theta$.
Therefore,
$E(\bar X)=\theta.$
Since $\bar X$ is the sample mean of an i.i.d. sample with finite mean, by the law of large numbers,
$\bar X\xrightarrow{P}\theta.$
So $\hat\theta=\bar X$ is consistent.

For the asymptotic distribution, apply the central limit theorem:
$\sqrt n(\bar X-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,\operatorname{Var}(X_1)).$
Now compute $\operatorname{Var}(X_1)$ in the two cases:

- If $j=1$, then $X_1\sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\theta)$, so
$\operatorname{Var}(X_1)=\theta.$
Hence
$\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\theta)=\sqrt n(\bar X-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,\theta).$

- If $j=2$, then $X_1\sim \mathrm{Bin}(1,\theta)$, so
$\operatorname{Var}(X_1)=\theta(1-\theta).$
Hence
$\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\theta)=\sqrt n(\bar X-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,\theta(1-\theta)).$

Therefore, $\hat\theta$ is consistent, and its nondegenerate asymptotic distribution is normal with variance depending on the true value of $j$.

In conclusion: the MLE is $(\hat\theta,\hat j)=(\bar X,\hat j)$ with $\hat j=1$ iff some observation exceeds $1$, otherwise $\hat j=2$; the estimator $\hat j$ is consistent; and $\hat\theta=\bar X$ is consistent with
$\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,\theta)$ under $j=1$ and
$\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,\theta(1-\theta))$ under $j=2$.
subject: Mathematical Statistics

question: Let ${\widehat{\theta }}_{n}$ be an estimator of $\theta \in \mathcal{R}$ satisfying $\sqrt{n}\left( {{\widehat{\theta }}_{n} - \theta }\right) { \rightarrow }_{d}N\left( {0, v\left( \theta \right) }\right)$ as the sample size $n \rightarrow \infty$ . Construct an estimator ${\widetilde{\theta }}_{n}$ such that $\sqrt{n}\left( {{\widetilde{\theta }}_{n} - \theta }\right) { \rightarrow }_{d}N\left( {0, w\left( \theta \right) }\right)$ with $w\left( \theta \right) = v\left( \theta \right)$ for $\theta \neq {\theta }_{0}$ and $w\left( {\theta }_{0}\right) = {t}^{2}v\left( {\theta }_{0}\right)$ , where $t \in \mathcal{R}$ and ${\theta }_{0}$ is a point in the parameter space. Note. This is a generalized version of Hodges' superefficiency example (e.g., Example 4.38 in Shao, 2003).
answer: $\displaystyle \widetilde{\theta}_n=\begin{cases}\widehat{\theta}_n,&\text{if }|\widehat{\theta}_n-\theta_0|\ge n^{-1/4},\\ t\widehat{\theta}_n+(1-t)\theta_0,&\text{if }|\widehat{\theta}_n-\theta_0|<n^{-1/4}.\end{cases}$ Then $\sqrt{n}(\widetilde{\theta}_n-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,w(\theta))$, where $w(\theta)=v(\theta)$ for $\theta\ne\theta_0$ and $w(\theta_0)=t^2v(\theta_0)$
explanation:
This problem uses asymptotic normality, convergence in probability, and asymptotic variance. The idea is to modify $\widehat{\theta}_n$ only in a shrinking neighborhood of $\theta_0$, so that away from $\theta_0$ the asymptotic law is unchanged, while at $\theta_0$ the local linear shrinkage changes the asymptotic variance by a factor $t^2$.

Construct
$\displaystyle \widetilde{\theta}_n=\begin{cases}\widehat{\theta}_n,&\text{if }|\widehat{\theta}_n-\theta_0|\ge n^{-1/4},\\ t\widehat{\theta}_n+(1-t)\theta_0,&\text{if }|\widehat{\theta}_n-\theta_0|<n^{-1/4}.\end{cases}$

We now verify that this estimator has the required asymptotic distribution.

Step 1: Case $\theta\ne\theta_0$.
Since
$\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\theta}_n-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,v(\theta))$,
we in particular have $\widehat{\theta}_n\xrightarrow{p}\theta$. Therefore,
$\widehat{\theta}_n-\theta_0\xrightarrow{p}\theta-\theta_0$.
Because $\theta\ne\theta_0$, the limit $\theta-\theta_0\ne 0$, so
$P\big(|\widehat{\theta}_n-\theta_0|<n^{-1/4}\big)\to 0$.
Hence with probability tending to $1$, the event triggering modification does not occur, and thus
$\widetilde{\theta}_n=\widehat{\theta}_n$
with probability tending to $1$.
Therefore the asymptotic distribution is unchanged:
$\sqrt{n}(\widetilde{\theta}_n-\theta)$ and $\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\theta}_n-\theta)$ have the same limit law, so
$\sqrt{n}(\widetilde{\theta}_n-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,v(\theta))$.
Thus for $\theta\ne\theta_0$,
$w(\theta)=v(\theta)$.

Step 2: Case $\theta=\theta_0$.
Now consider the probability of entering the modified region:
$P\big(|\widehat{\theta}_n-\theta_0|<n^{-1/4}\big)
= P\big(\sqrt{n}\,|\widehat{\theta}_n-\theta_0|<n^{1/4}\big)$.
Since
$\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\theta}_n-\theta_0)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,v(\theta_0))$,
the threshold $n^{1/4}\to\infty$, so this probability tends to $1$. Equivalently, after standardization one may write that the corresponding normal probability tends to
$\Phi(n^{1/4})-\Phi(-n^{1/4})\to 1$.
Thus, with probability tending to $1$, we are in the second branch of the definition.

On the event $|\widehat{\theta}_n-\theta_0|<n^{-1/4}$,
\[
\widetilde{\theta}_n=t\widehat{\theta}_n+(1-t)\theta_0.
\]
Hence
\[
\widetilde{\theta}_n-\theta_0=t(\widehat{\theta}_n-\theta_0),
\]
and therefore
\[
\sqrt{n}(\widetilde{\theta}_n-\theta_0)=t\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\theta}_n-\theta_0).
\]
Since
$\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\theta}_n-\theta_0)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,v(\theta_0))$,
by linear transformation we get
\[
\sqrt{n}(\widetilde{\theta}_n-\theta_0)\xrightarrow{d}N\big(0,t^2v(\theta_0)\big).
\]
Thus at the point $\theta_0$,
$w(\theta_0)=t^2v(\theta_0)$.

Conclusion: the estimator
$\displaystyle \widetilde{\theta}_n=\begin{cases}\widehat{\theta}_n,&|\widehat{\theta}_n-\theta_0|\ge n^{-1/4},\\ t\widehat{\theta}_n+(1-t)\theta_0,&|\widehat{\theta}_n-\theta_0|<n^{-1/4},\end{cases}$
satisfies
$\sqrt{n}(\widetilde{\theta}_n-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,w(\theta))$ with $w(\theta)=v(\theta)$ for $\theta\ne\theta_0$ and $w(\theta_0)=t^2v(\theta_0)$.

question:
Let $\left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right)$ be a random sample from a distribution with probability density ${f}_{\theta }$ with respect to a $\sigma$ -finite measure $\nu$ on $\left( {\mathcal{R},\mathcal{B}}\right)$ , where $\theta \in \Theta$ and $\Theta$ is an open set in $\mathcal{R}$ . Suppose that for every $x$ in the range of ${X}_{1},{f}_{\theta }\left( x\right)$ is twice continuously differentiable in $\theta$ and satisfies$$
\frac{\partial }{\partial \theta }\int {\psi }_{\theta }\left( x\right) {d\nu } = \int \frac{\partial }{\partial \theta }{\psi }_{\theta }\left( x\right) {d\nu }
$$
for ${\psi }_{\theta }\left( x\right) = {f}_{\theta }\left( x\right)$ and $= \partial {f}_{\theta }\left( x\right) /\partial \theta$ ; the Fisher information$$
{I}_{1}\left( \theta \right) = E{\left\lbrack \frac{\partial }{\partial \theta }\log {f}_{\theta }\left( {X}_{1}\right) \right\rbrack }^{2}
$$
is finite and positive; and for any given $\theta \in \Theta$ , there exists a positive number ${c}_{\theta }$ and a positive function ${h}_{\theta }$ such that $E\left\lbrack {{h}_{\theta }\left( {X}_{1}\right) }\right\rbrack < \infty$ and $\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{\left| {\gamma - \theta }\right| < {c}_{\theta }}}\left| \frac{{\partial }^{2}\log {f}_{\gamma }\left( x\right) }{\partial {\gamma }^{2}}\right| \leq {h}_{\theta }\left( x\right)$ for all $x$ in the range of ${X}_{1}$ . Show that$$
\frac{\log \ell \left( {\theta + {n}^{-1/2}}\right) - \log \ell \left( \theta \right) + {I}_{1}\left( \theta \right) /2}{\sqrt{{I}_{1}\left( \theta \right) }}{ \rightarrow }_{d}N\left( {0,1}\right) ,
$$
where $\ell \left( \theta \right)$ is the likelihood function.
answer:
Let $L\left( \gamma \right) = \log \ell \left( \gamma \right)$ . By Taylor’s expansion,$$
L\left( {\theta + {n}^{-1/2}}\right) - L\left( \theta \right) = {n}^{-1/2}{L}^{\prime }\left( \theta \right) + {\left( 2n\right) }^{-1}{L}^{\prime \prime }\left( {\xi }_{n}\right) ,
$$
where ${\xi }_{n}$ satisfies $\left| {{\xi }_{n} - \theta }\right| \leq {n}^{-1/2}$ . Let ${f}_{\theta }^{\prime }\left( x\right) = \partial {f}_{\theta }\left( x\right) /\partial \theta$ . Then$$
{L}^{\prime }\left( \theta \right) = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\frac{{f}_{\theta }^{\prime }\left( {X}_{i}\right) }{{f}_{\theta }\left( {X}_{i}\right) }.
$$
Note that $\frac{{f}_{\theta }^{\prime }\left( {X}_{i}\right) }{{f}_{\theta }\left( {X}_{i}\right) }, i = 1,\ldots , n$ , are independent and identically distributed with$$
E\frac{{f}_{\theta }^{\prime }\left( {X}_{i}\right) }{{f}_{\theta }\left( {X}_{i}\right) } = 0\;\text{ and }\;\operatorname{Var}\left( \frac{{f}_{\theta }^{\prime }\left( {X}_{i}\right) }{{f}_{\theta }\left( {X}_{i}\right) }\right) = {I}_{1}\left( \theta \right)
$$
(under the given condition). Hence, by the central limit theorem,$$
{n}^{-1/2}{L}^{\prime }\left( \theta \right) { \rightarrow }_{d}N\left( {0,{I}_{1}\left( \theta \right) }\right) .
$$
By the law of large numbers and the given condition,$$
{n}^{-1}{L}^{\prime \prime }\left( \theta \right) = \frac{1}{n}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\frac{{\partial }^{2}\log {f}_{\theta }\left( {X}_{i}\right) }{\partial {\theta }^{2}}{ \rightarrow }_{p}E\left( \frac{{\partial }^{2}\log {f}_{\theta }\left( {X}_{1}\right) }{\partial {\theta }^{2}}\right) = - {I}_{1}\left( \theta \right) .
$$
Since ${\partial }^{2}\log {f}_{\theta }\left( x\right) /\partial {\theta }^{2}$ is continuous in $\theta ,{n}^{-1}\left\lbrack {{L}^{\prime \prime }\left( {\xi }_{n}\right) - {L}^{\prime \prime }\left( \theta \right) }\right\rbrack \rightarrow 0$ for any fixed ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},\ldots$ , i.e., ${n}^{-1}{L}^{\prime \prime }\left( {\xi }_{n}\right) { \rightarrow }_{p} - {I}_{1}\left( \theta \right)$ for any fixed ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},\ldots$ Under the given condition,$$
{n}^{-1}\left| {{L}^{\prime \prime }\left( {\xi }_{n}\right) }\right| \leq {n}^{-1}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{h}_{\theta }\left( {X}_{i}\right) { \rightarrow }_{p}E\left\lbrack {{h}_{\theta }\left( {X}_{1}\right) }\right\rbrack .
$$
Hence, by the dominated convergence theorem, ${n}^{-1}E\left\lbrack {{L}^{\prime \prime }\left( {\xi }_{n}\right) - {L}^{\prime \prime }\left( \theta \right) }\right\rbrack \rightarrow 0$ , which implies that ${n}^{-1}{L}^{\prime \prime }\left( {\xi }_{n}\right) { \rightarrow }_{p} - {I}_{1}\left( \theta \right)$ . Then, the result follows from Slutsky's theorem.
explanation:
This problem uses the central limit theorem, the law of large numbers, and Slutsky's theorem. The key idea is to expand the log-likelihood around $\theta$, show that the first-order term is asymptotically normal, and prove that the second-order term converges in probability to $-I_1(\theta)/2$.

Let $L(\gamma)=\log \ell(\gamma)$. Apply Taylor expansion at $\theta$ with increment $n^{-1/2}$:
$$
L(\theta+n^{-1/2})-L(\theta)=n^{-1/2}L'(\theta)+\frac{1}{2n}L''(\xi_n),
$$
where $\xi_n$ lies between $\theta$ and $\theta+n^{-1/2}$, so that $|\xi_n-\theta|\le n^{-1/2}$.

We first study the linear term. Since
$$
L'(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{f_\theta'(X_i)}{f_\theta(X_i)},
$$
write
$$
Y_i=\frac{f_\theta'(X_i)}{f_\theta(X_i)}=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log f_\theta(X_i).
$$
Then $Y_1,\dots,Y_n$ are i.i.d. Under the given differentiability and interchange-of-integral conditions,
$$
E(Y_i)=\int \frac{f_\theta'(x)}{f_\theta(x)}f_\theta(x)\,d\nu
=\int f_\theta'(x)\,d\nu
=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\int f_\theta(x)\,d\nu
=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}(1)=0.
$$
Also,
$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=E(Y_i^2)=I_1(\theta),
$$
because $E(Y_i)=0$ and the Fisher information is defined by
$$
I_1(\theta)=E\left[\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log f_\theta(X_1)\right)^2\right].
$$
Therefore, by the central limit theorem,
$$
n^{-1/2}L'(\theta)=\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i \xrightarrow{d} N\bigl(0,I_1(\theta)\bigr).
$$

Next study the quadratic term. We have
$$
\frac{1}{n}L''(\theta)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\log f_\theta(X_i).
$$
By the law of large numbers,
$$
\frac{1}{n}L''(\theta)\xrightarrow{p}E\left[\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\log f_\theta(X_1)\right].
$$
Under the regularity conditions, the standard identity holds:
$$
E\left[\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\log f_\theta(X_1)\right]=-I_1(\theta).
$$
Hence,
$$
\frac{1}{n}L''(\theta)\xrightarrow{p}-I_1(\theta).
$$

Now replace $\theta$ by the intermediate point $\xi_n$. Since $|\xi_n-\theta|\le n^{-1/2}\to 0$ and $\partial^2\log f_\gamma(x)/\partial\gamma^2$ is continuous in $\gamma$, for fixed $X_1,X_2,\dots$ we have
$$
\frac{1}{n}\bigl(L''(\xi_n)-L''(\theta)\bigr)\to 0.
$$
Moreover, by the assumed bound,
$$
\sup_{|\gamma-\theta|<c_\theta}\left|\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\gamma^2}\log f_\gamma(x)\right|\le h_\theta(x),
$$
with $E[h_\theta(X_1)]<\infty$. Therefore,
$$
\frac{1}{n}|L''(\xi_n)|
\le \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n h_\theta(X_i)
\xrightarrow{p}E[h_\theta(X_1)].
$$
This integrable domination allows us to conclude that
$$
\frac{1}{n}E\bigl[L''(\xi_n)-L''(\theta)\bigr]\to 0,
$$
and hence
$$
\frac{1}{n}L''(\xi_n)\xrightarrow{p}-I_1(\theta).
$$
Thus the second-order Taylor term satisfies
$$
\frac{1}{2n}L''(\xi_n)\xrightarrow{p}-\frac{1}{2}I_1(\theta).
$$

Substitute these results into the Taylor expansion:
$$
L(\theta+n^{-1/2})-L(\theta)=n^{-1/2}L'(\theta)+\frac{1}{2n}L''(\xi_n).
$$
Hence,
$$
L(\theta+n^{-1/2})-L(\theta)+\frac{1}{2}I_1(\theta)
= n^{-1/2}L'(\theta)+o_p(1).
$$
After dividing by $\sqrt{I_1(\theta)}$, we get
$$
\frac{L(\theta+n^{-1/2})-L(\theta)+I_1(\theta)/2}{\sqrt{I_1(\theta)}}
=\frac{n^{-1/2}L'(\theta)}{\sqrt{I_1(\theta)}}+o_p(1).
$$
Since
$$
\frac{n^{-1/2}L'(\theta)}{\sqrt{I_1(\theta)}}\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1),
$$
Slutsky's theorem yields
$$
\frac{\log \ell(\theta+n^{-1/2})-\log \ell(\theta)+I_1(\theta)/2}{\sqrt{I_1(\theta)}}\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1).
$$
This is the required conclusion.

question:
Let $\left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right)$ be a random sample from $N\left( {\mu ,1}\right)$ truncated at two known points $\alpha < \beta$ , i.e., the Lebesgue density of ${X}_{1}$ is$$
\{ \sqrt{2\pi }\left\lbrack {\Phi \left( {\beta - \mu }\right) - \Phi \left( {\alpha - \mu }\right) }\right\rbrack {\} }^{-1}{e}^{-{\left( x - \mu \right) }^{2}/2}{I}_{\left( \alpha ,\beta \right) }\left( x\right) ,
$$
where $\Phi$ is the cumulative distribution function of $N\left( {0,1}\right)$ . Show that the sample mean $\bar{X}$ is the unique MLE of $\theta = E{X}_{1}$ and is asymptotically efficient.
answer:
The log-likelihood function is$$
\log \ell \left( \mu \right) = - n\log \left( {\Phi \left( {\beta - \mu }\right) - \Phi \left( {\alpha - \mu }\right) }\right) - \frac{1}{2}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{\left( {X}_{i} - \mu \right) }^{2}.
$$
Hence,$$
\frac{\partial \log \ell \left( \mu \right) }{\partial \mu } = n\left\lbrack {\bar{X} - g\left( \mu \right) }\right\rbrack
$$
where$$
g\left( \mu \right) = \mu - \frac{{\Phi }^{\prime }\left( {\beta - \mu }\right) - {\Phi }^{\prime }\left( {\alpha - \mu }\right) }{\Phi \left( {\beta - \mu }\right) - \Phi \left( {\alpha - \mu }\right) }.
$$
Since the inverse function ${g}^{-1}$ exists, ${g}^{-1}\left( \bar{X}\right)$ is the unique solution of the likelihood equation and, hence, it is the unique MLE of $\mu$ . Note that$$
\Phi \left( {\beta - \mu }\right) - \Phi \left( {\alpha - \mu }\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{\int }_{\alpha }^{\beta }{e}^{-{\left( x - \mu \right) }^{2}/2}{dx}
$$
\[
\left\lbrack {{\Phi }^{\prime }\left( {\alpha - \mu }\right) - {\Phi }^{\prime }\left( {\beta - \mu }\right) }\right\rbrack = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{\int }_{\alpha }^{\beta }\left( {x - \mu }\right) {e}^{-{\left( x - \mu \right) }^{2}/2}{dx},
 \]
and$$
\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }\left\lbrack {\Phi \left( {\beta - \mu }\right) - \Phi \left( {\alpha - \mu }\right) }\right\rbrack }{\int }_{\alpha }^{\beta }x{e}^{-{\left( x - \mu \right) }^{2}/2}{dx}
$$$$
= \mu + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }\left\lbrack {\Phi \left( {\beta - \mu }\right) - \Phi \left( {\alpha - \mu }\right) }\right\rbrack }{\int }_{\alpha }^{\beta }\left( {x - \mu }\right) {e}^{-{\left( x - \mu \right) }^{2}/2}{dx}
$$$$
= g\left( \mu \right) .
$$
Hence, $\bar{X}$ is the unique MLE of $\theta$ . By the asymptotic property of the MLE (e.g., Theorem 4.17 in Shao,2003), $\bar{X}$ is asymptotically efficient.
explanation:
This problem uses the ideas of maximum likelihood estimation, the sample mean, and efficiency. The key is to write the likelihood for the truncated normal model, derive the likelihood equation, identify the mean parameter $\theta$ as a monotone function of $\mu$, and then use the asymptotic efficiency of the MLE under regularity conditions.

Let
$$
f(x;\mu)=\left\{\sqrt{2\pi}\big[\Phi(\beta-\mu)-\Phi(\alpha-\mu)\big]\right\}^{-1}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/2}I_{(\alpha,\beta)}(x).
$$
For a random sample $X_1,\dots,X_n$, the log-likelihood is
$$
\log \ell(\mu)=-n\log\big[\Phi(\beta-\mu)-\Phi(\alpha-\mu)\big]-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\mu)^2.
$$

Differentiate with respect to $\mu$. The derivative of the quadratic term is
$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mu}\left(-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\mu)^2\right)=\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\mu)=n(\bar X-\mu).
$$
For the first term,
$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mu}\left[-n\log\big(\Phi(\beta-\mu)-\Phi(\alpha-\mu)\big)\right]
= n\frac{\Phi'(\beta-\mu)-\Phi'(\alpha-\mu)}{\Phi(\beta-\mu)-\Phi(\alpha-\mu)}.
$$
Therefore,
$$
\frac{\partial \log \ell(\mu)}{\partial \mu}
= n\left[\bar X-\mu+\frac{\Phi'(\beta-\mu)-\Phi'(\alpha-\mu)}{\Phi(\beta-\mu)-\Phi(\alpha-\mu)}\right].
$$
Define
$$
g(\mu)=\mu-\frac{\Phi'(\beta-\mu)-\Phi'(\alpha-\mu)}{\Phi(\beta-\mu)-\Phi(\alpha-\mu)}.
$$
Then the score equation becomes
$$
\frac{\partial \log \ell(\mu)}{\partial \mu}=n\big[\bar X-g(\mu)\big].
$$
Hence the likelihood equation is
$$
g(\mu)=\bar X.
$$
Since $g^{-1}$ exists, this equation has the unique solution
$$
\hat\mu=g^{-1}(\bar X).
$$
So $\hat\mu$ is the unique MLE of $\mu$.

Next, compute the expectation parameter $\theta=EX_1$. By definition,
$$
\theta=\int_{\alpha}^{\beta} x f(x;\mu)\,dx
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}[\Phi(\beta-\mu)-\Phi(\alpha-\mu)]}
\int_{\alpha}^{\beta} x e^{-(x-\mu)^2/2}\,dx.
$$
Write $x=\mu+(x-\mu)$ inside the integral:
$$
\theta
=\mu+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}[\Phi(\beta-\mu)-\Phi(\alpha-\mu)]}
\int_{\alpha}^{\beta} (x-\mu)e^{-(x-\mu)^2/2}\,dx.
$$
Now use the identities
$$
\Phi(\beta-\mu)-\Phi(\alpha-\mu)
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{\alpha}^{\beta} e^{-(x-\mu)^2/2}\,dx,
$$
and
$$
\Phi'(\alpha-\mu)-\Phi'(\beta-\mu)
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{\alpha}^{\beta} (x-\mu)e^{-(x-\mu)^2/2}\,dx.
$$
Substituting into the expression for $\theta$ gives
$$
\theta
=\mu+\frac{\Phi'(\alpha-\mu)-\Phi'(\beta-\mu)}{\Phi(\beta-\mu)-\Phi(\alpha-\mu)}
= g(\mu).
$$
Thus,
$$
\theta=g(\mu).
$$
Since the MLE of $\mu$ is $\hat\mu=g^{-1}(\bar X)$, the invariance of MLE yields the MLE of $\theta$ as
$$
\hat\theta=g(\hat\mu)=g(g^{-1}(\bar X))=\bar X.
$$
Because $g^{-1}$ is unique, this MLE is unique. Therefore, $\bar X$ is the unique MLE of $\theta=EX_1$.

Finally, by the standard asymptotic theory of maximum likelihood estimators, the MLE is asymptotically efficient under the regularity conditions for this model. Since the MLE of $\theta$ is $\bar X$, it follows that $\bar X$ is asymptotically efficient.

Therefore, $\bar X$ is the unique MLE of $\theta=EX_1$, and it is asymptotically efficient.

question: Let $\left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right)$ be a random sample such that $\log {X}_{i}$ is distributed as $N\left( {\theta ,\theta }\right)$ with an unknown $\theta > 0$ . Show that one of the solutions of the likelihood equation is the unique MLE of $\theta$ . Obtain the asymptotic distribution of the MLE of $\theta$ .
keypoint: 极大似然估计的相合性和渐近正态性
answer:
Let ${Y}_{i} = \log {X}_{i}, T = {n}^{-1}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{Y}_{i}^{2}$ , and $\ell \left( \theta \right)$ be the likelihood function. Then$$
\log \ell \left( \theta \right) = - \frac{n\log \theta }{2} - \frac{1}{2\theta }\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{\left( {Y}_{i} - \theta \right) }^{2}
$$$$
\frac{\partial \log \ell \left( \theta \right) }{\partial \theta } = \frac{n}{2}\left( {\frac{T}{{\theta }^{2}} - \frac{1}{\theta } - 1}\right)
$$
and$$
\frac{{\partial }^{2}\log \ell \left( \theta \right) }{\partial {\theta }^{2}} = \frac{n}{2{\theta }^{2}} - \frac{nT}{{\theta }^{3}}.
$$
The likelihood equation $\frac{\partial \log \ell \left( \theta \right) }{\partial \theta } = 0$ has two solutions$$
\frac{\pm \sqrt{1 + {4T}} - 1}{2}
$$
The root $\left( {-\sqrt{1 + {4T}} - 1}\right) /2$ is negative and lies outside the parameter space $\theta>0$. At the positive root, $T = \theta + {\theta }^{2}$ and $\frac{{\partial }^{2}\log \ell \left( \theta \right) }{\partial {\theta }^{2}} = - n\left( {\frac{1}{2{\theta }^{2}} + \frac{1}{\theta }}\right) < 0$ . Hence, $\widehat{\theta } = \left( {\sqrt{1 + {4T}} - 1}\right) /2$ is the unique MLE of $\theta$ . Since $E{Y}_{1}^{2} = \theta + {\theta }^{2}$ , the Fisher information is$$
{I}_{n}\left( \theta \right) = - E\left( \frac{{\partial }^{2}\log \ell \left( \theta \right) }{\partial {\theta }^{2}}\right) = - E\left( {\frac{n}{2{\theta }^{2}} - \frac{nT}{{\theta }^{3}}}\right) = \frac{\left( {{2\theta } + 1}\right) n}{2{\theta }^{2}}.
$$
Thus, $\sqrt{n}\left( {\widehat{\theta } - \theta }\right) { \rightarrow }_{d}N\left( {0,2{\theta }^{2}/\left( {{2\theta } + 1}\right) }\right)$ .
explanation:
This problem uses the key ideas of maximum likelihood estimation, Fisher information, and the asymptotic normality of the MLE. We first derive the likelihood equation and identify which root is admissible under $\theta>0$, then compute the Fisher information to obtain the asymptotic distribution.

Let $Y_i=\log X_i$. Then $Y_i\sim N(\theta,\theta)$, independently for $i=1,\dots,n$. Define
$T=\dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i^2$.

Since $Y_i\sim N(\theta,\theta)$, its density is
$f(y;\theta)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\theta}}\exp\left\{-\dfrac{(y-\theta)^2}{2\theta}\right\},\qquad \theta>0.$
Hence the likelihood based on $Y_1,\dots,Y_n$ is
$L(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\theta}}\exp\left\{-\dfrac{(Y_i-\theta)^2}{2\theta}\right\}.$
Ignoring constants not involving $\theta$, the log-likelihood is
$\log L(\theta)= -\dfrac{n}{2}\log\theta-\dfrac{1}{2\theta}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i-\theta)^2.$

Differentiate with respect to $\theta$:
$\dfrac{\partial \log L(\theta)}{\partial \theta}=\dfrac{n}{2}\left(\dfrac{T}{\theta^2}-\dfrac{1}{\theta}-1\right).$
Therefore the likelihood equation is
$\dfrac{T}{\theta^2}-\dfrac{1}{\theta}-1=0.$
Multiplying by $\theta^2$ gives
$T-\theta-\theta^2=0,$
that is,
$\theta^2+\theta-T=0.$
So the two roots are
$\theta=\dfrac{-1\pm\sqrt{1+4T}}{2}=\dfrac{\pm\sqrt{1+4T}-1}{2}.$

Now compute the second derivative:
$\dfrac{\partial^2 \log L(\theta)}{\partial \theta^2}=\dfrac{n}{2\theta^2}-\dfrac{nT}{\theta^3}.$
At the positive solution of the likelihood equation, we have
$T=\theta+\theta^2.$
Substituting this into the second derivative gives
$\dfrac{\partial^2 \log L(\theta)}{\partial \theta^2}=\dfrac{n}{2\theta^2}-\dfrac{n(\theta+\theta^2)}{\theta^3}
=\dfrac{n}{2\theta^2}-\dfrac{n}{\theta^2}-\dfrac{n}{\theta}
=-n\left(\dfrac{1}{2\theta^2}+\dfrac{1}{\theta}\right)<0.$
The negative algebraic root is not a candidate maximum because the parameter space is $\theta>0$. Among the two roots,
$\dfrac{-\sqrt{1+4T}-1}{2}<0,$
so it is not admissible. The only positive root is
$\hat\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{1+4T}-1}{2},$
and therefore it is the unique MLE of $\theta$.

Next, we derive the asymptotic distribution. Since $Y_i\sim N(\theta,\theta)$,
$E(Y_i^2)=\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)+[E(Y_i)]^2=\theta+\theta^2.$
Using the second derivative formula,
$I_n(\theta)=-E\left[\dfrac{\partial^2 \log L(\theta)}{\partial \theta^2}\right]
=-E\left[\dfrac{n}{2\theta^2}-\dfrac{nT}{\theta^3}\right].$
Because $E(T)=E(Y_1^2)=\theta+\theta^2$, we get
$I_n(\theta)= -\left(\dfrac{n}{2\theta^2}-\dfrac{n(\theta+\theta^2)}{\theta^3}\right)
=\dfrac{(2\theta+1)n}{2\theta^2}.$

By the standard asymptotic normality of the MLE,
$\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N\left(0,\frac{1}{I_1(\theta)}\right),$
where
$I_1(\theta)=\dfrac{2\theta+1}{2\theta^2}.$
Hence
$\frac{1}{I_1(\theta)}=\dfrac{2\theta^2}{2\theta+1},$
so
$\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N\left(0,\dfrac{2\theta^2}{2\theta+1}\right).$

Therefore, the unique MLE is $\hat\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{1+4T}-1}{2}$, and its asymptotic distribution is $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N\left(0,\dfrac{2\theta^2}{2\theta+1}\right)$.
subject: Mathematical Statistics

question: Let $\left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right)$ be a random sample from the distribution $P\left( {{X}_{1} = 0}\right) = 6{\theta }^{2} - {4\theta } + 1, P\left( {{X}_{1} = 1}\right) = \theta - 2{\theta }^{2}$ , and $P\left( {{X}_{1} = 2}\right) = {3\theta } - 4{\theta }^{2}$ , where $\theta \in \left( {0,\frac{1}{2}}\right)$ is unknown. Obtain the asymptotic distribution of an RLE (root of likelihood equation) of $\theta$ .
answer: $\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\theta}-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N\!\left(0,\,I_1^{-1}(\theta)\right)$, where $I_1(\theta)=\dfrac{72\theta^2-48\theta+4}{6\theta^2-4\theta+1}+\dfrac{8\theta^2-4\theta+1}{\theta-2\theta^2}+\dfrac{32\theta^2-24\theta+9}{3\theta-4\theta^2}$
explanation:
This problem uses the key ideas of the likelihood function, Fisher information, and asymptotic normality. Since the question asks for the asymptotic distribution of an RLE, we need to write the likelihood, compute the score and second derivative, and then apply the asymptotic normality theorem for roots of the likelihood equation.

Let $Y$ be the number of observations among $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ that are equal to $0$, and let $Z$ be the number of observations equal to $1$. Then the number of observations equal to $2$ is $n-Y-Z$.

From the model,
$P(X_i=0)=6\theta^2-4\theta+1$,
$P(X_i=1)=\theta-2\theta^2$,
$P(X_i=2)=3\theta-4\theta^2$.

Therefore, the likelihood function based on the sample is
$\ell(\theta)=\left(6\theta^2-4\theta+1\right)^Y\left(\theta-2\theta^2\right)^Z\left(3\theta-4\theta^2\right)^{n-Y-Z}$.

Take logarithms:
$\log \ell(\theta)=Y\log(6\theta^2-4\theta+1)+Z\log(\theta-2\theta^2)+(n-Y-Z)\log(3\theta-4\theta^2)$.

Differentiate with respect to $\theta$ to get the likelihood equation:
$\dfrac{\partial \log \ell(\theta)}{\partial \theta}=\dfrac{(12\theta-4)Y}{6\theta^2-4\theta+1}+\dfrac{(1-4\theta)Z}{\theta-2\theta^2}+\dfrac{(3-8\theta)(n-Y-Z)}{3\theta-4\theta^2}$.

An RLE $\widehat{\theta}$ is any root of
$\dfrac{\partial \log \ell(\theta)}{\partial \theta}=0$.

Next compute the second derivative:
$\dfrac{\partial^2 \log \ell(\theta)}{\partial \theta^2}
=-\dfrac{(72\theta^2-48\theta+4)Y}{(6\theta^2-4\theta+1)^2}-\dfrac{(8\theta^2-4\theta+1)Z}{(\theta-2\theta^2)^2}-\dfrac{(32\theta^2-24\theta+9)(n-Y-Z)}{(3\theta-4\theta^2)^2}$.

Now compute the Fisher information per observation:
$I_1(\theta)=-\dfrac{1}{n}E\left[\dfrac{\partial^2 \log \ell(\theta)}{\partial \theta^2}\right]$.

Using
$E(Y)=nP(X_1=0)=n(6\theta^2-4\theta+1)$,
$E(Z)=nP(X_1=1)=n(\theta-2\theta^2)$,
and
$E(n-Y-Z)=nP(X_1=2)=n(3\theta-4\theta^2)$,
we substitute into the expression above:

$\begin{aligned}
I_1(\theta)
&=\frac{72\theta^2-48\theta+4}{(6\theta^2-4\theta+1)^2}\cdot \frac{E(Y)}{n}
+\frac{8\theta^2-4\theta+1}{(\theta-2\theta^2)^2}\cdot \frac{E(Z)}{n}
+\frac{32\theta^2-24\theta+9}{(3\theta-4\theta^2)^2}\cdot \frac{E(n-Y-Z)}{n}\\
&=\frac{72\theta^2-48\theta+4}{(6\theta^2-4\theta+1)^2}(6\theta^2-4\theta+1)
+\frac{8\theta^2-4\theta+1}{(\theta-2\theta^2)^2}(\theta-2\theta^2)
+\frac{32\theta^2-24\theta+9}{(3\theta-4\theta^2)^2}(3\theta-4\theta^2)\\
&=\frac{72\theta^2-48\theta+4}{6\theta^2-4\theta+1}+\frac{8\theta^2-4\theta+1}{\theta-2\theta^2}+\frac{32\theta^2-24\theta+9}{3\theta-4\theta^2}.
\end{aligned}$

By the asymptotic normality theorem for a root of the likelihood equation, there exists an RLE $\widehat{\theta}$ such that
$\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\theta}-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N\left(0,\,I_1^{-1}(\theta)\right)$.

Hence the asymptotic distribution is
$\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\theta}-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N\left(0,\left[\frac{72\theta^2-48\theta+4}{6\theta^2-4\theta+1}+\frac{8\theta^2-4\theta+1}{\theta-2\theta^2}+\frac{32\theta^2-24\theta+9}{3\theta-4\theta^2}\right]^{-1}\right)$.
subject: Mathematical Statistics

question: Let $\left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right)$ be a random sample from $N\left( {\mu ,1}\right)$ , where $\mu \in \mathcal{R}$ is unknown. Let $\theta = P\left( {{X}_{1} \leq c}\right)$ , where $c$ is a known constant. Find the asymptotic relative efficiencies of the MLE of $\theta$ with respect to the UMVUE of $\theta$ and the estimator ${n}^{-1}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{I}_{( - \infty , c\rbrack }\left( {X}_{i}\right)$ .
keypoint: 一致最小方差无偏估计
answer:
(1) $\operatorname{ARE}(\widehat\theta\text{ w.r.t. }\widetilde\theta)=1$;
(2) $\operatorname{ARE}(\widehat\theta\text{ w.r.t. }T)=\dfrac{\theta(1-\theta)}{[\Phi'(c-\mu)]^2}$.
explanation:
This problem uses the key ideas of maximum likelihood estimation, asymptotic normality, and the UMVUE. We first write $\theta$ as a function of $\mu$, then derive the asymptotic variance of the MLE by the central limit theorem and the $\delta$-method, and finally compare it with the UMVUE and the empirical indicator estimator through asymptotic relative efficiency.

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be i.i.d. from $N(\mu,1)$, where $\mu$ is unknown, and define
$\theta=P(X_1\le c)$.
Since $X_1\sim N(\mu,1)$,
$\theta=P(X_1\le c)=\Phi(c-\mu)$,
where $\Phi$ is the cdf of $N(0,1)$.

Step 1: Find the MLE of $\theta$.
The MLE of $\mu$ under $N(\mu,1)$ is the sample mean $\bar X$. By the invariance property of MLE,
$\widehat{\theta}=\Phi(c-\bar X)$.

Step 2: Obtain the asymptotic distribution of $\widehat{\theta}$.
Since $\bar X\sim N\left(\mu,\frac1n\right)$, we have by the central limit theorem
$\sqrt n(\bar X-\mu)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1)$.
Now define
$g(x)=\Phi(c-x)$,
so that $\widehat\theta=g(\bar X)$ and $\theta=g(\mu)$.
Then
$g'(x)=-\Phi'(c-x)$,
so at $x=\mu$,
$g'(\mu)=-\Phi'(c-\mu)$.
By the $\delta$-method,
$\sqrt n(\widehat\theta-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N\left(0,[g'(\mu)]^2\right)=N\left(0,[\Phi'(c-\mu)]^2\right)$.
Therefore, the asymptotic variance of the MLE is
$[\Phi'(c-\mu)]^2$.

Step 3: Compare $\widehat\theta$ with the UMVUE.
From the referenced result, the UMVUE of $\theta$ is
$\widetilde\theta=\Phi\left(\frac{c-\bar X}{\sqrt{1-n^{-1}}}\right)$.
To compare their asymptotic efficiencies, consider
$\sqrt n(\widetilde\theta-\widehat\theta)$.
By the mean value theorem,
$\sqrt n(\widetilde\theta-\widehat\theta)
=\sqrt n\left[\Phi\left(\frac{c-\bar X}{\sqrt{1-n^{-1}}}\right)-\Phi(c-\bar X)\right]
=\sqrt n\,\Phi'(\xi_n)(c-\bar X)\left(\frac1{\sqrt{1-n^{-1}}}-1\right),$
where $\xi_n$ lies between $c-\bar X$ and $\dfrac{c-\bar X}{\sqrt{1-n^{-1}}}$.
Next simplify the factor:
$\frac1{\sqrt{1-n^{-1}}}-1
=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-n^{-1}}}{\sqrt{1-n^{-1}}}
=\frac{n^{-1}}{\sqrt{1-n^{-1}}\left(1+\sqrt{1-n^{-1}}\right)}.$
Hence
$\sqrt n(\widetilde\theta-\widehat\theta)
=\frac{\Phi'(\xi_n)(c-\bar X)}{\sqrt n\,\sqrt{1-n^{-1}}\left(1+\sqrt{1-n^{-1}}\right)}.
$
As $n\to\infty$, $\bar X\xrightarrow{p}\mu$, so $c-\bar X=O_p(1)$, and $\Phi'(\xi_n)$ remains bounded in probability. The denominator is of order $\sqrt n$, so
$\sqrt n(\widetilde\theta-\widehat\theta)\xrightarrow{p}0.$
Thus $\widetilde\theta$ and $\widehat\theta$ have the same asymptotic distribution, hence the same asymptotic variance. Therefore, the asymptotic relative efficiency of $\widehat\theta$ with respect to $\widetilde\theta$ is
$1$.

Step 4: Compare $\widehat\theta$ with
$T=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n I_{(-\infty,c]}(X_i)$.
Each indicator $I_{(-\infty,c]}(X_i)$ is Bernoulli with parameter
$P(X_i\le c)=\theta$.
Therefore,
$E(T)=\theta,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(T)=\frac{\theta(1-\theta)}{n}.$
By the central limit theorem,
$\sqrt n(T-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N\left(0,\theta(1-\theta)\right).$
So the asymptotic variance of $T$ is
$\theta(1-\theta)$.

The asymptotic relative efficiency of $\widehat\theta$ with respect to $T$ is the ratio of the asymptotic variance of $T$ to that of $\widehat\theta$:
$\operatorname{ARE}(\widehat\theta\text{ w.r.t. }T)
=\frac{\theta(1-\theta)}{[\Phi'(c-\mu)]^2}.$

Therefore, the final results are:
(1) $\operatorname{ARE}(\widehat\theta\text{ w.r.t. }\widetilde\theta)=1$;
(2) $\operatorname{ARE}(\widehat\theta\text{ w.r.t. }T)=\dfrac{\theta(1-\theta)}{[\Phi'(c-\mu)]^2}$.
subject: Mathematical Statistics

question:
Let $\left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right)$ be a random sample from a population having the Lebesgue density$$
{f}_{{\theta }_{1},{\theta }_{2}}\left( x\right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} {\left( {\theta }_{1} + {\theta }_{2}\right) }^{-1}{e}^{-x/{\theta }_{1}} & x > 0 \\ {\left( {\theta }_{1} + {\theta }_{2}\right) }^{-1}{e}^{x/{\theta }_{2}} & x \leq 0, \end{array}\right.
$$
where ${\theta }_{1} > 0$ and ${\theta }_{2} > 0$ are unknown.
(i) Find the MLE of $\theta = \left( {{\theta }_{1},{\theta }_{2}}\right)$ .
(ii) Obtain a nondegenerated asymptotic distribution of the MLE of $\theta$ .
(iii) Obtain the asymptotic relative efficiencies of the MLE's with respect to the moment estimators.
keypoint: 极大似然估计的相合性和渐近正态性
answer:
(i) If $T_1>0$ and $T_2>0$, the MLE is $\widehat{\theta}=(\widehat{\theta}_1,\widehat{\theta}_2)=n^{-1}(\sqrt{T_1T_2}+T_1,\sqrt{T_1T_2}+T_2)$, where $T_1=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i I_{(0,\infty)}(X_i)$ and $T_2=-\sum_{i=1}^n X_i I_{(-\infty,0]}(X_i)$. (ii) $\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\theta}-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N_2\!\left(0,[I_1(\theta)]^{-1}\right)$, where $I_1(\theta)=\dfrac{1}{(\theta_1+\theta_2)^2}\begin{pmatrix}1+\dfrac{2\theta_2}{\theta_1}&-1\\-1&1+\dfrac{2\theta_1}{\theta_2}\end{pmatrix}$ and $[I_1(\theta)]^{-1}=\dfrac{(\theta_1+\theta_2)^2}{\left(1+\dfrac{2\theta_2}{\theta_1}\right)\left(1+\dfrac{2\theta_1}{\theta_2}\right)-1}\begin{pmatrix}1+\dfrac{2\theta_1}{\theta_2}&1\\1&1+\dfrac{2\theta_2}{\theta_1}\end{pmatrix}$. (iii) The asymptotic relative efficiency of $\widehat{\theta}_1$ with respect to the moment estimator is $\dfrac{\tau_1(\mu_1,\mu_2)\left[\left(1+2\dfrac{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}-\mu_1}{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}+\mu_1}\right)\left(1+2\dfrac{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}+\mu_1}{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}-\mu_1}\right)-1\right]}{(2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2)\left(1+2\dfrac{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}+\mu_1}{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}-\mu_1}\right)}$, and that of $\widehat{\theta}_2$ is $\dfrac{\tau_2(\mu_1,\mu_2)\left[\left(1+2\dfrac{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}-\mu_1}{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}+\mu_1}\right)\left(1+2\dfrac{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}+\mu_1}{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}-\mu_1}\right)-1\right]}{(2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2)\left(1+2\dfrac{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}-\mu_1}{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}+\mu_1}\right)}$

For a self-contained calculation in part (iii), put $a=\theta_1$ and $b=\theta_2$. The first four raw moments needed for the bivariate central limit theorem are
$$
\mu_1=a-b,\qquad
\mu_2=2(a^2-ab+b^2),
$$
$$
\mu_3=6(a-b)(a^2+b^2),\qquad
\mu_4=24(a^4-a^3b+a^2b^2-ab^3+b^4).
$$
Hence, for $\widehat\gamma=(\widehat\mu_1,\widehat\mu_2)^\tau$ and $\gamma=(\mu_1,\mu_2)^\tau$,
$$
\sqrt n(\widehat\gamma-\gamma)\xrightarrow{d}N_2(0,\Sigma),
$$
where
$$
\Sigma=
\begin{pmatrix}
a^2+b^2 & 4a^3-2a^2b+2ab^2-4b^3\\
4a^3-2a^2b+2ab^2-4b^3 & 20a^4-16a^3b+12a^2b^2-16ab^3+20b^4
\end{pmatrix}.
$$
Let $s=\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}=a+b$. Since the moment estimators are
$$
\widetilde\theta_1=h(\widehat\mu_1,\widehat\mu_2),\qquad
\widetilde\theta_2=g(\widehat\mu_1,\widehat\mu_2),
$$
with $h(x,y)=(x+\sqrt{2y-3x^2})/2$ and $g(x,y)=(-x+\sqrt{2y-3x^2})/2$, their Jacobian at $(\mu_1,\mu_2)$ is
$$
\Lambda=
\begin{pmatrix}
(-a+2b)/(a+b) & 1/[2(a+b)]\\
(-2a+b)/(a+b) & 1/[2(a+b)]
\end{pmatrix}.
$$
Therefore
$$
\sqrt n(\widetilde\theta-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N_2(0,\Lambda\Sigma\Lambda^\tau),
$$
and the two moment-estimator asymptotic variances are
$$
\tau_1(\mu_1,\mu_2)
=\frac{2a^4+2a^3b+2a^2b^2+b^4}{(a+b)^2},
$$
$$
\tau_2(\mu_1,\mu_2)
=\frac{a^4+2a^2b^2+2ab^3+2b^4}{(a+b)^2},
$$
where $a=(s+\mu_1)/2$ and $b=(s-\mu_1)/2$. Thus these are explicit functions of $(\mu_1,\mu_2)$.

From $[I_1(\theta)]^{-1}$, the MLE asymptotic variances are
$$
v_{1,\mathrm{MLE}}=\frac{a(2a+b)}{2},\qquad
v_{2,\mathrm{MLE}}=\frac{b(a+2b)}{2}.
$$
Consequently, defining the asymptotic relative efficiency of the MLE with respect to the moment estimator as $v_{j,\mathrm{MM}}/v_{j,\mathrm{MLE}}$, we obtain
$$
\operatorname{ARE}_1
=\frac{2(2a^4+2a^3b+2a^2b^2+b^4)}{a(a+b)^2(2a+b)},
$$
$$
\operatorname{ARE}_2
=\frac{2(a^4+2a^2b^2+2ab^3+2b^4)}{b(a+b)^2(a+2b)}.
$$
All quantities in part (iii) are therefore computable from the distribution in the current question. The displayed formula is an interior MLE only when $T_1>0$ and $T_2>0$. If $T_1=0$ or $T_2=0$, it puts one component at $0$, outside the open parameter space. If exactly one of $T_1,T_2$ is positive, the finite supremum is approached at that boundary but is not attained; if $T_1=T_2=0$, the likelihood is unbounded. Thus no MLE exists in $(0,\infty)^2$ in these boundary cases.
explanation:
This problem uses the key ideas of maximum likelihood estimation, Fisher information, and the asymptotic normality of MLEs. Part (i) requires maximizing the likelihood; part (ii) uses the Fisher information matrix to obtain the asymptotic law; part (iii) compares asymptotic variances with those of moment estimators to get asymptotic relative efficiencies.

For (i), define
$T_1=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i I_{(0,\infty)}(X_i),\qquad T_2=-\sum_{i=1}^n X_i I_{(-\infty,0]}(X_i).$
Then all positive observations contribute through $T_1$, and all nonpositive observations contribute through $T_2$.

From the given density,
$f_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(x)=\begin{cases}(\theta_1+\theta_2)^{-1}e^{-x/\theta_1},&x>0,\\(\theta_1+\theta_2)^{-1}e^{x/\theta_2},&x\le 0,\end{cases}$
the likelihood of the sample is proportional to
$\ell(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\theta_1+\theta_2}\exp\left(-\frac{X_i I_{(0,\infty)}(X_i)}{\theta_1}+\frac{X_i I_{(-\infty,0]}(X_i)}{\theta_2}\right).$
Since $T_2=-\sum X_i I_{(-\infty,0]}(X_i)$, the log-likelihood becomes
$\log \ell(\theta)=-n\log(\theta_1+\theta_2)-\frac{T_1}{\theta_1}-\frac{T_2}{\theta_2}.$

Differentiate with respect to $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$:
$\frac{\partial \log \ell(\theta)}{\partial \theta}=\left(-\frac{n}{\theta_1+\theta_2}+\frac{T_1}{\theta_1^2},\,-\frac{n}{\theta_1+\theta_2}+\frac{T_2}{\theta_2^2}\right).$
The likelihood equations are therefore
$-\frac{n}{\theta_1+\theta_2}+\frac{T_1}{\theta_1^2}=0,
\qquad
-\frac{n}{\theta_1+\theta_2}+\frac{T_2}{\theta_2^2}=0.$
Hence
$\frac{T_1}{\theta_1^2}=\frac{T_2}{\theta_2^2}=\frac{n}{\theta_1+\theta_2}.$
Solving these equations gives the unique solution
$\widehat{\theta}_1=\frac{\sqrt{T_1T_2}+T_1}{n},
\qquad
\widehat{\theta}_2=\frac{\sqrt{T_1T_2}+T_2}{n}.$
Thus
$\widehat{\theta}=(\widehat{\theta}_1,\widehat{\theta}_2)=n^{-1}(\sqrt{T_1T_2}+T_1,\sqrt{T_1T_2}+T_2).$

To support the maximization, compute the Hessian:
$\frac{\partial^2 \log \ell(\theta)}{\partial \theta\,\partial \theta^{\tau}}=
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{n}{(\theta_1+\theta_2)^2}-\dfrac{2T_1}{\theta_1^3} & \dfrac{n}{(\theta_1+\theta_2)^2}\\
\dfrac{n}{(\theta_1+\theta_2)^2} & \dfrac{n}{(\theta_1+\theta_2)^2}-\dfrac{2T_2}{\theta_2^3}
\end{pmatrix}.$
When $T_1>0$ and $T_2>0$, the log likelihood tends to $-\infty$ at the relevant parameter-space boundaries and at infinity; hence this unique interior stationary point is the MLE. If either statistic is zero, the stationary formula lies on the excluded boundary and the boundary discussion below applies instead.

For (ii), apply the standard asymptotic theorem for MLEs:
$\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\theta}-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N_2\left(0,[I_1(\theta)]^{-1}\right),$
where $I_1(\theta)$ is the Fisher information per observation,
$I_1(\theta)=-\frac{1}{n}E\left[\frac{\partial^2 \log \ell(\theta)}{\partial \theta\,\partial \theta^{\tau}}\right].$

Using the Hessian above and taking expectations,
$I_1(\theta)=\frac{1}{(\theta_1+\theta_2)^2}
\begin{pmatrix}
1+\dfrac{2\theta_2}{\theta_1} & -1\\
-1 & 1+\dfrac{2\theta_1}{\theta_2}
\end{pmatrix}.$
Its inverse is
$[I_1(\theta)]^{-1}=\frac{(\theta_1+\theta_2)^2}{\left(1+\dfrac{2\theta_2}{\theta_1}\right)\left(1+\dfrac{2\theta_1}{\theta_2}\right)-1}
\begin{pmatrix}
1+\dfrac{2\theta_1}{\theta_2} & 1\\
1 & 1+\dfrac{2\theta_2}{\theta_1}
\end{pmatrix}.$
Therefore the MLE has the nondegenerate asymptotic distribution
$\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\theta}-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N_2\left(0,[I_1(\theta)]^{-1}\right).$

For (iii), compare the asymptotic variances of the MLE and the moment estimators. Let
$\mu_j=E(X_1^j),\quad j=1,2.$
Direct calculation of the first two moments gives
$\theta_1+\theta_2=\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2},$
and
$\frac{\theta_2}{\theta_1}=\frac{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}-\mu_1}{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}+\mu_1}.$
Let $\tau_j(\mu_1,\mu_2)$ be the $j$th diagonal element of the asymptotic covariance matrix $\Lambda\Sigma\Lambda^{\tau}$ for the moment estimator.

The asymptotic relative efficiency of $\widehat{\theta}_1$ with respect to the moment estimator of $\theta_1$ is the ratio of the asymptotic variance of the moment estimator to the asymptotic variance of the MLE. Substituting the expressions above into the $(1,1)$ element of $[I_1(\theta)]^{-1}$ yields
$\operatorname{ARE}(\widehat{\theta}_1\text{ w.r.t. moment estimator})=
\frac{\tau_1(\mu_1,\mu_2)\left[\left(1+2\dfrac{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}-\mu_1}{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}+\mu_1}\right)\left(1+2\dfrac{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}+\mu_1}{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}-\mu_1}\right)-1\right]}{(2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2)\left(1+2\dfrac{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}+\mu_1}{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}-\mu_1}\right)}.$

Similarly, the asymptotic relative efficiency of $\widehat{\theta}_2$ with respect to the moment estimator of $\theta_2$ is
$\operatorname{ARE}(\widehat{\theta}_2\text{ w.r.t. moment estimator})=
\frac{\tau_2(\mu_1,\mu_2)\left[\left(1+2\dfrac{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}-\mu_1}{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}+\mu_1}\right)\left(1+2\dfrac{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}+\mu_1}{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}-\mu_1}\right)-1\right]}{(2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2)\left(1+2\dfrac{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}-\mu_1}{\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}+\mu_1}\right)}.$

In conclusion: the MLE is $\widehat{\theta}=n^{-1}(\sqrt{T_1T_2}+T_1,\sqrt{T_1T_2}+T_2)$; its centered and scaled version is asymptotically bivariate normal with covariance matrix $[I_1(\theta)]^{-1}$; and the asymptotic relative efficiencies with respect to the moment estimators are exactly the two formulas displayed above.

For a self-contained calculation in part (iii), put $a=\theta_1$ and $b=\theta_2$. The first four raw moments needed for the bivariate central limit theorem are
$$
\mu_1=a-b,\qquad
\mu_2=2(a^2-ab+b^2),
$$
$$
\mu_3=6(a-b)(a^2+b^2),\qquad
\mu_4=24(a^4-a^3b+a^2b^2-ab^3+b^4).
$$
Hence, for $\widehat\gamma=(\widehat\mu_1,\widehat\mu_2)^\tau$ and $\gamma=(\mu_1,\mu_2)^\tau$,
$$
\sqrt n(\widehat\gamma-\gamma)\xrightarrow{d}N_2(0,\Sigma),
$$
where
$$
\Sigma=
\begin{pmatrix}
a^2+b^2 & 4a^3-2a^2b+2ab^2-4b^3\\
4a^3-2a^2b+2ab^2-4b^3 & 20a^4-16a^3b+12a^2b^2-16ab^3+20b^4
\end{pmatrix}.
$$
Let $s=\sqrt{2\mu_2-3\mu_1^2}=a+b$. Since the moment estimators are
$$
\widetilde\theta_1=h(\widehat\mu_1,\widehat\mu_2),\qquad
\widetilde\theta_2=g(\widehat\mu_1,\widehat\mu_2),
$$
with $h(x,y)=(x+\sqrt{2y-3x^2})/2$ and $g(x,y)=(-x+\sqrt{2y-3x^2})/2$, their Jacobian at $(\mu_1,\mu_2)$ is
$$
\Lambda=
\begin{pmatrix}
(-a+2b)/(a+b) & 1/[2(a+b)]\\
(-2a+b)/(a+b) & 1/[2(a+b)]
\end{pmatrix}.
$$
Therefore
$$
\sqrt n(\widetilde\theta-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N_2(0,\Lambda\Sigma\Lambda^\tau),
$$
and the two moment-estimator asymptotic variances are
$$
\tau_1(\mu_1,\mu_2)
=\frac{2a^4+2a^3b+2a^2b^2+b^4}{(a+b)^2},
$$
$$
\tau_2(\mu_1,\mu_2)
=\frac{a^4+2a^2b^2+2ab^3+2b^4}{(a+b)^2},
$$
where $a=(s+\mu_1)/2$ and $b=(s-\mu_1)/2$. Thus these are explicit functions of $(\mu_1,\mu_2)$.

From $[I_1(\theta)]^{-1}$, the MLE asymptotic variances are
$$
v_{1,\mathrm{MLE}}=\frac{a(2a+b)}{2},\qquad
v_{2,\mathrm{MLE}}=\frac{b(a+2b)}{2}.
$$
Consequently, defining the asymptotic relative efficiency of the MLE with respect to the moment estimator as $v_{j,\mathrm{MM}}/v_{j,\mathrm{MLE}}$, we obtain
$$
\operatorname{ARE}_1
=\frac{2(2a^4+2a^3b+2a^2b^2+b^4)}{a(a+b)^2(2a+b)},
$$
$$
\operatorname{ARE}_2
=\frac{2(a^4+2a^2b^2+2ab^3+2b^4)}{b(a+b)^2(a+2b)}.
$$
All quantities in part (iii) are therefore computable from the distribution in the current question. The displayed formula is an interior MLE only when $T_1>0$ and $T_2>0$. If $T_1=0$ or $T_2=0$, it puts one component at $0$, outside the open parameter space. If exactly one of $T_1,T_2$ is positive, the finite supremum is approached at that boundary but is not attained; if $T_1=T_2=0$, the likelihood is unbounded. Thus no MLE exists in $(0,\infty)^2$ in these boundary cases.

question:
Let $(X_i,Y_i)$, $i=1,\ldots,n$, be independent observations from the bivariate normal distribution
$$
N_2\!\left(\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}1&\rho\\\rho&1\end{pmatrix}\right),
\qquad -1<\rho<1.
$$
Let $\widehat\rho$ be a regular consistent solution of the likelihood equation for $\rho$. Show that
$$
\sqrt n(\widehat\rho-\rho)\xrightarrow{d}
N\!\left(0,\frac{(1-\rho^2)^2}{1+\rho^2}\right).
$$
answer:
Define
$$
T=\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i^2+Y_i^2),
\qquad
R=\sum_{i=1}^nX_iY_i.
$$
Apart from a constant independent of $\rho$, the log-likelihood is
$$
\log\ell(\rho)
=-\frac n2\log(1-\rho^2)
-\frac{T-2\rho R}{2(1-\rho^2)}.
$$
Let
$$
h(\rho)=\rho(1-\rho^2)-\frac{T\rho}{n}+\frac{R(1+\rho^2)}{n}.
$$
Direct differentiation gives the score
$$
\frac{\partial\log\ell(\rho)}{\partial\rho}
=\frac{n}{(1-\rho^2)^2}h(\rho),
$$
and
$$
\frac{\partial^2\log\ell(\rho)}{\partial\rho^2}
=\frac{nh'(\rho)}{(1-\rho^2)^2}
+\frac{4n\rho h(\rho)}{(1-\rho^2)^3}.
$$
Under the model,
$$
E(T)=2n,\qquad E(R)=n\rho.
$$
It follows that
$$
E[h(\rho)]=0,
\qquad
E[h'(\rho)]=-(1+\rho^2).
$$
Therefore the Fisher information per observation is
$$
I_1(\rho)
=-\frac1nE\!\left[\frac{\partial^2\log\ell(\rho)}{\partial\rho^2}\right]
=\frac{1+\rho^2}{(1-\rho^2)^2}.
$$
By the asymptotic normality of a regular consistent likelihood root,
$$
\sqrt n(\widehat\rho-\rho)
\xrightarrow{d}N\!\left(0,I_1(\rho)^{-1}\right)
=N\!\left(0,\frac{(1-\rho^2)^2}{1+\rho^2}\right).
$$
explanation:
For one observation, the bivariate normal density is
$$
f_\rho(x,y)=\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}
\exp\!\left[-\frac{x^2+y^2-2\rho xy}{2(1-\rho^2)}\right].
$$
For the independent sample, set
$$
T=\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i^2+Y_i^2),
\qquad
R=\sum_{i=1}^nX_iY_i.
$$
Then
$$
\log\ell(\rho)
=-n\log(2\pi)-\frac n2\log(1-\rho^2)
-\frac{T-2\rho R}{2(1-\rho^2)}.
$$
Differentiating and collecting terms yields
$$
\frac{\partial\log\ell(\rho)}{\partial\rho}
=\frac{n}{(1-\rho^2)^2}h(\rho),
$$
where
$$
h(\rho)=\rho(1-\rho^2)-n^{-1}T\rho+n^{-1}R(1+\rho^2).
$$
A second differentiation gives
$$
\frac{\partial^2\log\ell(\rho)}{\partial\rho^2}
=\frac{nh'(\rho)}{(1-\rho^2)^2}
+\frac{4n\rho h(\rho)}{(1-\rho^2)^3}.
$$

Because each marginal has variance one and $E(X_iY_i)=\rho$,
$$
E(T)=2n,\qquad E(R)=n\rho.
$$
Substitution into $h$ gives $E[h(\rho)]=0$. Also
$$
h'(\rho)=1-3\rho^2-\frac{T}{n}+\frac{2\rho R}{n},
$$
so
$$
E[h'(\rho)]=1-3\rho^2-2+2\rho^2=-(1+\rho^2).
$$
Thus
$$
I_1(\rho)
=-\frac1nE\!\left[\frac{\partial^2\log\ell(\rho)}{\partial\rho^2}\right]
=\frac{1+\rho^2}{(1-\rho^2)^2}.
$$
The regular likelihood-estimator theorem now gives
$$
\sqrt n(\widehat\rho-\rho)
\xrightarrow{d}N\!\left(0,[I_1(\rho)]^{-1}\right)
=N\!\left(0,\frac{(1-\rho^2)^2}{1+\rho^2}\right).
$$
All model definitions, likelihood derivatives, and information calculations are contained in the current record.

question: Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be a random sample from the scale family with density $f_\theta(x)=\theta f(\theta x)$, where $\theta>0$, and let $\widehat{\theta}$ be a regular consistent solution of the likelihood equation (RLE). Obtain a nondegenerated asymptotic distribution of $\widehat{\theta}$ when $f(x)=\pi^{-1}(1+x^2)^{-1}$.
keypoint: 极大似然估计的相合性和渐近正态性
answer: $\displaystyle \sqrt{n}(\widehat\theta-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N\left(0,2\theta^2\right).$
explanation:
This problem uses the ideas of asymptotic distribution, asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator, and Fisher information. The goal is to verify the regularity conditions for the scale family generated by the Cauchy density and then compute the Fisher information $I_1(\theta)$, since the asymptotic variance is $[I_1(\theta)]^{-1}$.

For
$\displaystyle f(x)=\pi^{-1}(1+x^2)^{-1}$,
the corresponding parametric family is
$\displaystyle f_\theta(x)=\theta f(\theta x)=\frac{\theta}{\pi(1+\theta^2x^2)}$.
We first compute derivatives with respect to $\theta$:
$\displaystyle \frac{\partial f_\theta(x)}{\partial \theta}=\frac{1-\theta^2x^2}{\pi(1+\theta^2x^2)^2}$,
and
$\displaystyle \frac{\partial^2 f_\theta(x)}{\partial \theta^2}=\frac{2\theta x^2(\theta^2x^2-3)}{\pi(1+\theta^2x^2)^3}$.
These are continuous in $\theta$.

Fix any $\theta_0\in(0,\infty)$. On the interval $\theta\in[\theta_0/2,2\theta_0]$,
$\displaystyle \sup_{\theta\in[\theta_0/2,2\theta_0]}\left|\frac{\partial f_\theta(x)}{\partial \theta}\right|=
\sup_{\theta\in[\theta_0/2,2\theta_0]}\left|\frac{1-\theta^2x^2}{\pi(1+\theta^2x^2)^2}\right|$
$\displaystyle \le \sup_{\theta\in[\theta_0/2,2\theta_0]}\frac{1}{\pi(1+\theta^2x^2)}
=\frac{1}{\pi\left[1+(\theta_0/2)^2x^2\right]}.$
The right-hand side is integrable on $(-\infty,\infty)$.

Similarly,
$\displaystyle \sup_{\theta\in[\theta_0/2,2\theta_0]}\left|\frac{\partial^2 f_\theta(x)}{\partial \theta^2}\right|
=\sup_{\theta\in[\theta_0/2,2\theta_0]}\left|\frac{2\theta x^2(\theta^2x^2-3)}{\pi(1+\theta^2x^2)^3}\right|$
$\displaystyle \le \sup_{\theta\in[\theta_0/2,2\theta_0]}\frac{2C}{\pi\theta(1+\theta^2x^2)}
=\frac{2C}{\pi(\theta_0/2)\left[1+(\theta_0/2)^2x^2\right]},$
where $C$ is a constant independent of $\theta$. This bound is also integrable. Therefore, by the dominated convergence theorem,
$\displaystyle \frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\psi_\theta(x)\,dx=
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\psi_\theta(x)\,dx$
holds both when $\psi_\theta(x)=f_\theta(x)$ and when $\psi_\theta(x)=\partial f_\theta(x)/\partial\theta$.

Next compute the second derivative of the log-density. Since
$\displaystyle \log f_\theta(x)=\log\theta-\log\pi-\log(1+\theta^2x^2)$,
we get
$\displaystyle \frac{\partial^2\log f_\theta(x)}{\partial\theta^2}
=-\frac{1}{\theta^2}-\frac{2x^2(1-\theta^2x^2)}{(1+\theta^2x^2)^2}$.
Hence
$\displaystyle \sup_{\theta\in[\theta_0/2,2\theta_0]}
\left|\frac{\partial^2\log f_\theta(x)}{\partial\theta^2}\right|
=\sup_{\theta\in[\theta_0/2,2\theta_0]}
\left|\frac{1}{\theta^2}+\frac{2x^2(1-\theta^2x^2)}{(1+\theta^2x^2)^2}\right|$
$\displaystyle \le \sup_{\theta\in[\theta_0/2,2\theta_0]}
\left|\frac{1}{\theta^2}+\frac{2x^2}{1+\theta^2x^2}\right|
=\frac{4}{\theta_0^2}+\frac{2x^2}{1+(\theta_0/2)^2x^2}.$
If $X_1$ has density $\theta_0 f(\theta_0x)$, then
$\displaystyle E\left[\frac{4}{\theta_0^2}+\frac{2X_1^2}{1+(\theta_0/2)^2X_1^2}\right]<\infty.$
So the regularity conditions in the asymptotic normality theorem for the MLE are satisfied. Therefore,
$\displaystyle \sqrt{n}(\widehat\theta-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N\left(0,[I_1(\theta)]^{-1}\right).$

It remains to compute $I_1(\theta)$. By definition,
$\displaystyle I_1(\theta)=-E\left[\frac{\partial^2\log f_\theta(X_1)}{\partial\theta^2}\right].$
Using the above expression,
$\displaystyle I_1(\theta)=\frac{1}{\theta^2}+\frac{2\theta}{\pi}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{x^2(1-\theta^2x^2)}{(1+\theta^2x^2)^3}\,dx.$
Make the change of variable $u=\theta x$ and then rename $u$ as $x$:
$\displaystyle I_1(\theta)=\frac{1}{\theta^2}+\frac{2}{\theta^2\pi}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{x^2(1-x^2)}{(1+x^2)^3}\,dx.$
Now rewrite the numerator:
$\displaystyle x^2(1-x^2)=3(1+x^2)-2-(1+x^2)^2.$
Hence
$\displaystyle I_1(\theta)=\frac{1}{\theta^2}+\frac{2}{\theta^2\pi}
\left[3\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(1+x^2)^2}\,dx
-2\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(1+x^2)^3}\,dx
-\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{1}{1+x^2}\,dx\right].$
Use the identity
$\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(1+x^2)^k}\,dx=
\frac{\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma\left(k-\frac12\right)}{\Gamma(k)}.$
Then
$\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{1}{1+x^2}\,dx=\pi,$
$\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(1+x^2)^2}\,dx=\frac{\pi}{2},$
and
$\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(1+x^2)^3}\,dx=\frac{3\pi}{8}.$
Substituting these values gives
$\displaystyle I_1(\theta)=\frac{1}{\theta^2}+\frac{2}{\theta^2\pi}
\left(3\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}-2\cdot\frac{3\pi}{8}-\pi\right)$
$\displaystyle =\frac{1}{\theta^2}+\frac{2}{\theta^2}\left(\frac32-\frac34-1\right)
=\frac{1}{\theta^2}-\frac{1}{2\theta^2}
=\frac{1}{2\theta^2}.$
Therefore,
$\displaystyle [I_1(\theta)]^{-1}=2\theta^2.$

So the nondegenerate asymptotic distribution is
$\displaystyle \sqrt{n}(\widehat\theta-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N\left(0,2\theta^2\right).$
