question:
Let ${\widehat{\theta }}_{n}$ be an estimator of a real-valued parameter $\theta$ such that ${V}_{n}^{-1/2}\left( {{\widehat{\theta }}_{n} - \theta }\right) { \rightarrow }_{d}N\left( {0,1}\right)$ for any $\theta$ and let ${\widehat{V}}_{n}$ be a consistent estimator of ${V}_{n}$ . Suppose that ${V}_{n} \rightarrow 0$ .
(i) Show that the test with rejection region ${\widehat{V}}_{n}^{-1/2}\left( {{\widehat{\theta }}_{n} - {\theta }_{0}}\right) > {z}_{\alpha }$ is a consistent asymptotic level $\alpha$ test for testing ${H}_{0} : \theta \leq {\theta }_{0}$ versus ${H}_{1} : \theta > {\theta }_{0}$ , where ${z}_{\alpha }$ is the $\left( {1 - \alpha }\right)$ th quantile of $N\left( {0,1}\right)$ .
(ii) Apply the result in (i) to show that the one-sample one-sided t-test for the testing problem in (i) is a consistent asymptotic level $\alpha$ test.
answer:
(i) Under ${H}_{1} : \theta > {\theta }_{0},{\widehat{V}}_{n}^{-1/2}\left( {{\widehat{\theta }}_{n} - \theta }\right) { \rightarrow }_{d}N\left( {0,1}\right)$ . Therefore, the test with rejection region ${\widehat{V}}_{n}^{-1/2}\left( {{\widehat{\theta }}_{n} - {\theta }_{0}}\right) > {z}_{\alpha }$ is an asymptotic level $\alpha$ test. Also,$$
P\left( {{\widehat{V}}_{n}^{-1/2}\left( {{\widehat{\theta }}_{n} - {\theta }_{0}}\right) > {z}_{\alpha }}\right) = P\left( {{\widehat{V}}_{n}^{-1/2}\left( {{\widehat{\theta }}_{n} - \theta }\right) > {z}_{\alpha } - {\widehat{V}}_{n}^{-1/2}\left( {\theta - {\theta }_{0}}\right) }\right) \rightarrow 1
$$
as $n \rightarrow \infty$ , since ${\widehat{V}}_{n}^{-1/2}\left( {\theta - {\theta }_{0}}\right) { \rightarrow }_{p}\infty$ . Hence, the test is consistent.
(ii) Let $\left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right)$ be a random sample from a population with finite mean $\theta$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}$ . For testing ${H}_{0} : \theta \leq {\theta }_{0}$ versus ${H}_{1} : \theta > {\theta }_{0}$ , the one-sample t-test rejects ${H}_{0}$ if and only if $t\left( X\right) = \sqrt{n}\left( {\bar{X} - {\theta }_{0}}\right) /S > \; {t}_{n - 1,\alpha }$ , where $\bar{X}$ and ${S}^{2}$ are the sample mean and variance and ${t}_{n - 1,\alpha }$ is the $\left( {1 - \alpha }\right)$ th quantile of the t-distribution ${t}_{n - 1}$ . By the central limit theorem, $\sqrt{n}\left( {\bar{X} - \theta }\right) { \rightarrow }_{d}N\left( {0,{\sigma }^{2}}\right)$ . Hence ${V}_{n} = {\sigma }^{2}/n \rightarrow 0$ . By the law of large numbers, ${S}^{2}{ \rightarrow }_{p}{\sigma }^{2}$ . Hence ${\widehat{V}}_{n} = {S}^{2}/n$ is a consistent estimator of ${V}_{n}$ . Note that the t-distribution ${t}_{n - 1}$ converges to $N\left( {0,1}\right)$ . Then, by the result in Exercise 28 of Chapter 5, $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}{t}_{n - 1,\alpha } = {z}_{\alpha }$ . From the result in (i), the one-sample t-test is a consistent asymptotic level $\alpha$ test.
explanation:
This problem uses the ideas of hypothesis testing and asymptotic normality. In part (i), we verify asymptotic level and consistency from the asymptotic distribution of the standardized estimator and the consistency of $\widehat V_n$; in part (ii), we identify the one-sample $t$-test as a special case with $\widehat\theta_n=\bar X$ and $\widehat V_n=S^2/n$.

For (i), we are given that for any $\theta$,
$V_n^{-1/2}(\widehat\theta_n-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1)$,
and that $\widehat V_n$ is a consistent estimator of $V_n$, with $V_n\to 0$.

First show the asymptotic level $\alpha$ property. Consider the test statistic
$T_n=\widehat V_n^{-1/2}(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)$,
and reject when $T_n>z_\alpha$.
Under the boundary case $\theta=\theta_0$ of $H_0:\theta\le \theta_0$, we have
$\widehat V_n^{-1/2}(\widehat\theta_n-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1)$.
Because $\widehat V_n$ is consistent for $V_n$, replacing $V_n$ by $\widehat V_n$ preserves the same asymptotic standard normal limit, so under $\theta=\theta_0$,
$T_n\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1)$.
Therefore,
$P_{\theta_0}(T_n>z_\alpha)\to P(Z>z_\alpha)=\alpha,$
where $Z\sim N(0,1)$.
Since for testing $H_0:\theta\le \theta_0$ against $H_1:\theta>\theta_0$, the largest rejection probability under the null occurs at the boundary $\theta=\theta_0$, the test is an asymptotic level $\alpha$ test.

Next show consistency. Fix any $\theta>\theta_0$. Then
$T_n=\widehat V_n^{-1/2}(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)
=\widehat V_n^{-1/2}(\widehat\theta_n-\theta)+\widehat V_n^{-1/2}(\theta-\theta_0).$
Hence
$P_\theta(T_n>z_\alpha)
=P\left(\widehat V_n^{-1/2}(\widehat\theta_n-\theta)>z_\alpha-\widehat V_n^{-1/2}(\theta-\theta_0)\right).$
Now $\theta-\theta_0>0$ is a fixed positive constant. Since $\widehat V_n\xrightarrow{p}V_n$ and $V_n\to 0$, we have $\widehat V_n\xrightarrow{p}0$, so
$\widehat V_n^{-1/2}(\theta-\theta_0)\xrightarrow{p}\infty.$
Therefore the threshold on the right-hand side,
$z_\alpha-\widehat V_n^{-1/2}(\theta-\theta_0),$
converges in probability to $-\infty$.
At the same time,
$\widehat V_n^{-1/2}(\widehat\theta_n-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1)$,
so a random variable with an asymptotically standard normal distribution exceeds a threshold tending to $-\infty$ with probability tending to $1$. Thus,
$P_\theta(T_n>z_\alpha)\to 1.$
So for every fixed $\theta>\theta_0$, the power tends to $1$, which proves consistency.

Therefore, the rejection region $\widehat V_n^{-1/2}(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)>z_\alpha$ defines a consistent asymptotic level $\alpha$ test.

For (ii), let $(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ be a random sample from a population with finite mean $\theta$ and variance $\sigma^2$. We test
$H_0:\theta\le \theta_0\quad\text{versus}\quad H_1:\theta>\theta_0.$
The one-sample one-sided $t$-test rejects $H_0$ when
$t(X)=\frac{\sqrt n(\bar X-\theta_0)}{S}>t_{n-1,\alpha},$
where $\bar X$ is the sample mean, $S^2$ is the sample variance, and $t_{n-1,\alpha}$ is the $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of the $t_{n-1}$ distribution.

To apply part (i), take
$\widehat\theta_n=\bar X,\qquad V_n=\frac{\sigma^2}{n},\qquad \widehat V_n=\frac{S^2}{n}.$
By the central limit theorem,
$\sqrt n(\bar X-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,\sigma^2).$
Equivalently,
$V_n^{-1/2}(\widehat\theta_n-\theta)=\left(\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)^{-1/2}(\bar X-\theta)=\frac{\sqrt n(\bar X-\theta)}{\sigma}\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1).$
Also,
$V_n=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\to 0.$
By the law of large numbers,
$S^2\xrightarrow{p}\sigma^2,$
so
$\widehat V_n=\frac{S^2}{n}$
is a consistent estimator of
$V_n=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}$.
Thus all assumptions of part (i) are satisfied.

Now compare the rejection rule in part (i) with the $t$-test statistic:
$\widehat V_n^{-1/2}(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)=\left(\frac{S^2}{n}\right)^{-1/2}(\bar X-\theta_0)=\frac{\sqrt n(\bar X-\theta_0)}{S}=t(X).$
So the rejection region from part (i) is
$t(X)>z_\alpha.$
The actual one-sample $t$-test uses the cutoff $t_{n-1,\alpha}$ instead of $z_\alpha$. Since the $t$-distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom converges to $N(0,1)$, its quantiles satisfy
$t_{n-1,\alpha}\to z_\alpha.$
Therefore replacing $z_\alpha$ by $t_{n-1,\alpha}$ does not change the asymptotic level or consistency.

Hence the one-sample one-sided $t$-test is a consistent asymptotic level $\alpha$ test for testing $H_0:\theta\le \theta_0$ versus $H_1:\theta>\theta_0$.

question: Let $\left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right)$ be a random sample from the gamma distribution with shape parameter $\theta$ and scale parameter $\gamma$ , where $\theta > 0$ and $\gamma > 0$ are unknown. Let ${T}_{n} = n\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{i}^{2}/{\left( \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{i}\right) }^{2}$ . Show how to use ${T}_{n}$ to obtain an asymptotic level $\alpha$ and consistent test for testing ${H}_{0} : \theta = 1$ versus ${H}_{1} : \theta \neq 1$ .
keypoint: 独立同分布下的中心极限定理
answer:
From the central limit theorem,$$
\sqrt{n}\left\lbrack {\left( \begin{matrix} \frac{1}{n}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{i} \\ \frac{1}{n}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{i}^{2} \end{matrix}\right) - \left( \begin{matrix} E\left( {X}_{1}\right) \\ E\left( {X}_{1}^{2}\right) \end{matrix}\right) }\right\rbrack { \rightarrow }_{d}{N}_{2}\left( {0,\sum }\right) ,
$$
where$$
\sum = \left( \begin{matrix} E\left( {X}_{1}^{2}\right) - {\left\lbrack E\left( {X}_{1}\right) \right\rbrack }^{2} & E\left( {X}_{1}^{3}\right) - E\left( {X}_{1}\right) E\left( {X}_{1}^{2}\right) \\ E\left( {X}_{1}^{3}\right) - E\left( {X}_{1}\right) E\left( {X}_{1}^{2}\right) & E\left( {X}_{1}^{4}\right) - {\left\lbrack E\left( {X}_{1}^{2}\right) \right\rbrack }^{2} \end{matrix}\right) .
$$
Since the moment generating function of the gamma distribution is $g\left( t\right) = \; {\left( 1 - \gamma t\right) }^{-\theta },$$$
E\left( {X}_{1}\right) = {g}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) = {\theta \gamma }
$$$$
E\left( {X}_{1}^{2}\right) = {g}^{\prime \prime }\left( 0\right) = \theta \left( {\theta + 1}\right) {\gamma }^{2},
$$$$
E\left( {X}_{1}^{3}\right) = {g}^{\prime \prime \prime }\left( 0\right) = \theta \left( {\theta + 1}\right) \left( {\theta + 2}\right) {\gamma }^{3},
$$
and$$
E\left( {X}_{1}^{4}\right) = {g}^{\prime \prime \prime \prime }\left( 0\right) = \theta \left( {\theta + 1}\right) \left( {\theta + 2}\right) \left( {\theta + 3}\right) {\gamma }^{4}.
$$
Hence,$$
\sum = \left( \begin{matrix} \theta {\gamma }^{2} & {2\theta }\left( {\theta + 1}\right) {\gamma }^{3} \\ {2\theta }\left( {\theta + 1}\right) {\gamma }^{3} & {2\theta }\left( {\theta + 1}\right) \left( {{2\theta } + 3}\right) {\gamma }^{4} \end{matrix}\right) .
$$
Note that$$
T = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{i}^{2}}{{\left( \frac{1}{n}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{i}\right) }^{2}} = h\left( {\frac{1}{n}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{i},\frac{1}{n}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{i}^{2}}\right)
$$
with $h\left( {x, y}\right) = y/{x}^{2}$ ,$$
H\left( {x, y}\right) = \left( \begin{matrix} \frac{\partial h}{\partial x} \\ \frac{\partial h}{\partial y} \end{matrix}\right) = \left( \begin{matrix} - \frac{2y}{{x}^{3}} \\ \frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \end{matrix}\right) ,
$$
and$$
H\left( {E\left( {X}_{1}\right) , E\left( {X}_{1}^{2}\right) }\right) = H\left( {{\theta \gamma },\theta \left( {\theta + 1}\right) {\gamma }^{2}}\right) = \left( \begin{matrix} - \frac{2\left( {\theta + 1}\right) }{{\theta }^{2}\gamma } \\ \frac{1}{{\theta }^{2}{\gamma }^{2}} \end{matrix}\right) .
$$
By the $\delta$ -method,$$
\sqrt{n}\left\lbrack {T - h\left( {E\left( {X}_{1}\right) , E\left( {X}_{1}^{2}\right) }\right) }\right\rbrack { \rightarrow }_{d}N\left( {0,{\sigma }^{2}}\right) ,
$$
where$$
{\sigma }^{2} = {\left\lbrack H\left( \theta \gamma ,\theta \left( \theta + 1\right) {\gamma }^{2}\right) \right\rbrack }^{\tau }{\sum H}\left( {{\theta \gamma },\theta \left( {\theta + 1}\right) {\gamma }^{2}}\right)
$$$$
= \frac{4{\left( \theta + 1\right) }^{2}}{{\theta }^{3}} + \frac{2\left( {\theta + 1}\right) \left( {{2\theta } + 3}\right) }{{\theta }^{3}} - \frac{8{\left( \theta + 1\right) }^{2}}{{\theta }^{3}}
$$$$
= \frac{2\left( {\theta + 1}\right) }{{\theta }^{3}}.
$$
Note that$$
h\left( {E\left( {X}_{1}\right) , E\left( {X}_{1}^{2}\right) }\right) = h\left( {{\theta \gamma },\theta \left( {\theta + 1}\right) {\gamma }^{2}}\right) = \frac{\theta \left( {\theta + 1}\right) {\gamma }^{2}}{{\theta }^{2}{\gamma }^{2}} = 1 + \frac{1}{\theta }.
$$
Combining all the results, we obtain that$$
{V}_{n}^{-1/2}\left( {T - 1 - \frac{1}{\theta }}\right) { \rightarrow }_{d}N\left( {0,1}\right)
$$
with ${V}_{n} = 2\left( {\theta + 1}\right) /\left( {{\theta }^{3}n}\right)$ . From the asymptotic normality of $T$ ,$$
\frac{1}{T - 1}{ \rightarrow }_{p}\theta
$$
Hence, a consistent estimator of ${V}_{n}$ is$$
{\widehat{V}}_{n} = \frac{2\left( {\frac{1}{T - 1} + 1}\right) }{\frac{n}{{\left( T - 1\right) }^{3}}} = \frac{{2T}{\left( T - 1\right) }^{2}}{n}.
$$
From Theorem 6.12 in Shao (2003), an asymptotic level $\alpha$ and consistent test for ${H}_{0} : \theta = 1$ versus ${H}_{1} : \theta \neq 1$ rejects ${H}_{0}$ if and only if$$
{\widehat{V}}_{n}^{-1}{\left( T - 2\right) }^{2} > {\chi }_{1,\alpha }^{2},
$$
which is the same as$$
\frac{n{\left( T - 2\right) }^{2}}{{2T}{\left( T - 1\right) }^{2}} > {\chi }_{1,\alpha }^{2}
$$
where ${\chi }_{1,\alpha }^{2}$ is the $\left( {1 - \alpha }\right)$ th quantile of the chi-square distribution ${\chi }_{1}^{2}$ . ∎
explanation:
This problem uses the keypoints of hypothesis testing, asymptotic distribution, and the central limit theorem for i.i.d. samples. The idea is to derive the asymptotic distribution of $T_n$ under the gamma model, then standardize it to construct a large-sample test for $H_0:\theta=1$.

Let
$\displaystyle \bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i,\qquad \overline{X^2}_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2.$
Then
$\displaystyle T_n=n\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2}{\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right)^2}=\frac{\overline{X^2}_n}{\bar X_n^2}.$
So $T_n$ is a function of the sample moments $(\bar X_n,\overline{X^2}_n)$.

Step 1: Apply the multivariate central limit theorem.
Since $X_1,\dots,X_n$ are i.i.d.,
$\displaystyle \sqrt n\left[\begin{pmatrix}\bar X_n\\ \overline{X^2}_n\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}E(X_1)\\E(X_1^2)\end{pmatrix}\right]\xrightarrow{d}N_2(0,\Sigma),$
where
$\displaystyle \Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}
E(X_1^2)-[E(X_1)]^2 & E(X_1^3)-E(X_1)E(X_1^2)\\
E(X_1^3)-E(X_1)E(X_1^2) & E(X_1^4)-[E(X_1^2)]^2
\end{pmatrix}.$

Step 2: Compute the moments of the gamma distribution.
The mgf is
$\displaystyle g(t)=(1-\gamma t)^{-\theta}.$
Differentiating at $t=0$ gives
$\displaystyle E(X_1)=g'(0)=\theta\gamma,$
$\displaystyle E(X_1^2)=g''(0)=\theta(\theta+1)\gamma^2,$
$\displaystyle E(X_1^3)=g'''(0)=\theta(\theta+1)(\theta+2)\gamma^3,$
$\displaystyle E(X_1^4)=g''''(0)=\theta(\theta+1)(\theta+2)(\theta+3)\gamma^4.$
Therefore,
$\displaystyle \Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}
\theta\gamma^2 & 2\theta(\theta+1)\gamma^3\\
2\theta(\theta+1)\gamma^3 & 2\theta(\theta+1)(2\theta+3)\gamma^4
\end{pmatrix}.$

Step 3: Express $T_n$ as a smooth function and use the $\delta$-method.
Define
$\displaystyle h(x,y)=\frac{y}{x^2},$
so that
$\displaystyle T_n=h(\bar X_n,\overline{X^2}_n).$
Its gradient is
$\displaystyle H(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\\ \frac{\partial h}{\partial y}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-\frac{2y}{x^3}\\ \frac1{x^2}\end{pmatrix}.$
Evaluate at the population values:
$\displaystyle H\big(E(X_1),E(X_1^2)\big)=H\big(\theta\gamma,\theta(\theta+1)\gamma^2\big)=\begin{pmatrix}-\frac{2(\theta+1)}{\theta^2\gamma}\\ \frac1{\theta^2\gamma^2}\end{pmatrix}.$
By the $\delta$-method,
$\displaystyle \sqrt n\left[T_n-h\big(E(X_1),E(X_1^2)\big)\right]\xrightarrow{d}N(0,\sigma^2),$
where
$\displaystyle \sigma^2=H^\top\Sigma H.$
Substituting the expressions above,
$\displaystyle \sigma^2=\frac{4(\theta+1)^2}{\theta^3}+\frac{2(\theta+1)(2\theta+3)}{\theta^3}-\frac{8(\theta+1)^2}{\theta^3}
=\frac{2(\theta+1)}{\theta^3}.$
Also,
$\displaystyle h\big(E(X_1),E(X_1^2)\big)=\frac{\theta(\theta+1)\gamma^2}{\theta^2\gamma^2}=1+\frac1\theta.$
Hence,
$\displaystyle \sqrt n\left(T_n-1-\frac1\theta\right)\xrightarrow{d}N\left(0,\frac{2(\theta+1)}{\theta^3}\right).$
Equivalently,
$\displaystyle V_n^{-1/2}\left(T_n-1-\frac1\theta\right)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1),$
with
$\displaystyle V_n=\frac{2(\theta+1)}{\theta^3 n}.$

Step 4: Estimate the asymptotic variance.
Since $T_n\to_p 1+\frac1\theta$, we have
$\displaystyle \frac1{T_n-1}\to_p \theta.$
So a consistent estimator of $V_n$ is obtained by replacing $\theta$ with $\frac1{T_n-1}$:
$\displaystyle \widehat V_n=\frac{2\left(\frac1{T_n-1}+1\right)}{n\left(\frac1{T_n-1}\right)^3}
=\frac{2T_n(T_n-1)^2}{n}.$

Step 5: Construct the asymptotic test under $H_0:\theta=1$.
Under $H_0$, the centering constant is
$\displaystyle 1+\frac1\theta=2.$
Thus the Wald-type statistic is
$\displaystyle \frac{(T_n-2)^2}{\widehat V_n}.$
By asymptotic theory,
$\displaystyle \frac{(T_n-2)^2}{\widehat V_n}\xrightarrow{d}\chi_1^2\qquad (H_0).$
Therefore, an asymptotic level $\alpha$ test rejects $H_0$ when
$\displaystyle \frac{(T_n-2)^2}{\widehat V_n}>\chi^2_{1,\alpha},$
where $\chi^2_{1,\alpha}$ is the $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of $\chi_1^2$.
Substituting $\widehat V_n=\frac{2T_n(T_n-1)^2}{n}$ gives the rejection region
$\displaystyle \frac{n(T_n-2)^2}{2T_n(T_n-1)^2}>\chi^2_{1,\alpha}.$

Therefore, using the statistic
$\displaystyle \frac{n(T_n-2)^2}{2T_n(T_n-1)^2}$
and rejecting for large values yields an asymptotic level $\alpha$ and consistent test for $H_0:\theta=1$ versus $H_1:\theta\neq 1$.

question:
Let $\left( {{X}_{i1},{X}_{i2}}\right) , i = 1,\ldots , n$ , be a random sample from the bivariate normal distribution with unknown ${\mu }_{j} = E\left( {X}_{1j}\right) ,{\sigma }_{j}^{2} = \; \operatorname{Var}\left( {X}_{1j}\right) , j = 1,2$ , and ${\sigma }_{12} = \operatorname{Cov}\left( {{X}_{11},{X}_{12}}\right)$ . Let $\theta = {\mu }_{2}/{\mu }_{1}$ be the parameter of interest $\left( {{\mu }_{1} \neq 0}\right) ,{Y}_{i}\left( \theta \right) = {X}_{i2} - \theta {X}_{i1}$ , and$$
{S}^{2}\left( \theta \right) = \frac{1}{n - 1}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{\left\lbrack {Y}_{i}\left( \theta \right) - \bar{Y}\left( \theta \right) \right\rbrack }^{2} = {S}_{2}^{2} - {2\theta }{S}_{12} + {\theta }^{2}{S}_{1}^{2},
$$
where $\bar{Y}\left( \theta \right)$ is the average of ${Y}_{i}\left( \theta \right)$ ’s and ${S}_{i}^{2}$ and ${S}_{12}$ are sample variances and covariance based on ${X}_{ij}$ ’s. Discuss when Fieller’s confidence set for $\theta$ ,$$
C\left( X\right) = \left\{ {\theta : n{\left\lbrack \bar{Y}\left( \theta \right) \right\rbrack }^{2}/{S}^{2}\left( \theta \right) \leq {t}_{n - 1,\alpha /2}^{2}}\right\} ,
$$
is a finite interval, the complement of a finite interval, or the whole real line.
answer:
Put $t=t_{n-1,\alpha/2}$, $\bar X_j=n^{-1}\sum_iX_{ij}$, and expand
$$t^2S^2(\theta)-n[\bar Y(\theta)]^2\ge0.$$
Since $\bar Y(\theta)=\bar X_2-\theta\bar X_1$, the confidence set is
$$C(X)=\{\theta:q(\theta)=a\theta^2+b\theta+c\ge0\},$$
where
$$a=t^2S_1^2-n\bar X_1^2,$$
$$b=2\bigl(n\bar X_1\bar X_2-t^2S_{12}\bigr),$$
$$c=t^2S_2^2-n\bar X_2^2,$$
and $\Delta=b^2-4ac$.

If $a<0$ and $\Delta>0$, $C(X)$ is the closed finite interval between the two roots; for $a<0,\Delta=0$ it is the singleton at the double root, and for $a<0,\Delta<0$ it is empty. If $a>0$ and $\Delta>0$, it is
$$(-\infty,\theta_-]\cup[\theta_+,\infty),$$
the complement of the open finite interval $(\theta_-,\theta_+)$; if $a>0$ and $\Delta\le0$, it is all of $\mathbb R$. If $a=0$, the inequality is linear: it gives a half-line when $b\ne0$, all of $\mathbb R$ when $b=0,c\ge0$, and the empty set when $b=0,c<0$.
explanation:
Starting from the Fieller inequality, multiply by $S^2(\theta)$ and move the left side to the right:
$$t^2\{S_2^2-2\theta S_{12}+\theta^2S_1^2\}
-n(\bar X_2-\theta\bar X_1)^2\ge0.$$
Collecting powers of $\theta$ gives
$$q(\theta)=a\theta^2+b\theta+c,$$
with
$$a=t^2S_1^2-n\bar X_1^2,\quad
b=2(n\bar X_1\bar X_2-t^2S_{12}),\quad
c=t^2S_2^2-n\bar X_2^2.$$

The form of the confidence set is therefore exactly the sign set of a quadratic. A downward-opening quadratic is nonnegative between its real roots, producing a finite interval (a singleton for a double root); without real roots it is everywhere negative. An upward-opening quadratic is nonnegative outside two real roots, producing the complement of an open finite interval; with no two distinct real roots it is nonnegative everywhere. If the quadratic coefficient vanishes, the remaining linear or constant inequality gives the stated half-line, whole-line, or empty-set boundary cases.

question: Let $X = \left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right)$ be a random sample from $N\left( {\theta ,\theta }\right)$ with an unknown $\theta > 0$ . Find a pivotal quantity and use it to construct a confidence interval for $\theta$ .
answer: A pivotal quantity is $R(X,\theta)=\dfrac{n(\bar{X}-\theta)^2}{\theta}\sim \chi_1^2$. Hence a $(1-\alpha)$ confidence set for $\theta$ is $C(X)=\left\{\theta:\dfrac{n(\bar{X}-\theta)^2}{\theta}\le \chi_{1,\alpha}^2\right\}$, that is, $C(X)=\left\{\theta:\theta^2-2(\bar{X}+c)\theta+\bar{X}^2\le 0\right\}$ with $c=\dfrac{\chi_{1,\alpha}^2}{2n}$. If $\bar{X}\ge -c/2$, this becomes $\left[\bar{X}+c-\sqrt{2c\bar{X}+c^2},\ \bar{X}+c+\sqrt{2c\bar{X}+c^2}\right]$；if $\bar{X}< -c/2$, the confidence set is empty
explanation:
This problem uses the ideas of confidence intervals, the pivotal quantity method, and the $\chi^2$ distribution. The key is to find a function of the sample and parameter whose distribution does not depend on the unknown parameter, and then invert the resulting probability statement to obtain a confidence set.

Let $\bar{X}$ be the sample mean. Since $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are i.i.d. from $N(\theta,\theta)$, the sample mean has distribution
$\bar{X}\sim N\left(\theta,\frac{\theta}{n}\right)$.

Standardizing $\bar{X}$ gives
$\frac{\bar{X}-\theta}{\sqrt{\theta/n}}\sim N(0,1)$.
Therefore,
$R(X,\theta)=\left(\frac{\bar{X}-\theta}{\sqrt{\theta/n}}\right)^2=\frac{n(\bar{X}-\theta)^2}{\theta}\sim \chi_1^2$.
Because its distribution does not depend on $\theta$, $R(X,\theta)$ is a pivotal quantity.

Now let $\chi_{1,\alpha}^2$ denote the $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of $\chi_1^2$. Then
$P\left(R(X,\theta)\le \chi_{1,\alpha}^2\right)=1-\alpha$.
Hence a $(1-\alpha)$ confidence set for $\theta$ is obtained by solving
$\frac{n(\bar{X}-\theta)^2}{\theta}\le \chi_{1,\alpha}^2$.

Define
$c=\frac{\chi_{1,\alpha}^2}{2n}$.
Then the inequality becomes
$(\bar{X}-\theta)^2\le \frac{\chi_{1,\alpha}^2}{n}\theta=2c\theta$.
Expand the left-hand side:
$\bar{X}^2-2\bar{X}\theta+\theta^2\le 2c\theta$.
Move all terms to one side:
$\theta^2-2(\bar{X}+c)\theta+\bar{X}^2\le 0$.
So
$C(X)=\left\{\theta:\theta^2-2(\bar{X}+c)\theta+\bar{X}^2\le 0\right\}$.

This is a quadratic inequality in $\theta$. Its roots are
$\theta=(\bar{X}+c)\pm \sqrt{(\bar{X}+c)^2-\bar{X}^2}$.
Simplify the discriminant:
$(\bar{X}+c)^2-\bar{X}^2=\bar{X}^2+2c\bar{X}+c^2-\bar{X}^2=2c\bar{X}+c^2$.
Thus the roots are
$\theta=(\bar{X}+c)\pm \sqrt{2c\bar{X}+c^2}$.

Therefore, if the discriminant is nonnegative, i.e.
$2c\bar{X}+c^2\ge 0$,
which is equivalent to
$\bar{X}\ge -\frac{c}{2}$,
then the confidence set is the interval between the two roots:
$C(X)=\left[\bar{X}+c-\sqrt{2c\bar{X}+c^2},\ \bar{X}+c+\sqrt{2c\bar{X}+c^2}\right]$.

If $\bar{X}< -\frac{c}{2}$, then $2c\bar{X}+c^2<0$, so the quadratic has no real roots and the inequality cannot hold for any $\theta$. In that case,
$C(X)=\varnothing$.

Hence the pivotal quantity is $R(X,\theta)=\dfrac{n(\bar{X}-\theta)^2}{\theta}\sim \chi_1^2$, and the corresponding $(1-\alpha)$ confidence set is the interval above when $\bar{X}\ge -c/2$, and the empty set otherwise.

question: Let $T$ be a random variable having cumulative distribution function $F$ . For any $t \in \left( {0,1}\right)$ , show that $P\left( {F\left( T\right) < t}\right) \leq t$ and $P\left( {F\left( {T - }\right) > 1 - t}\right) \leq t$ , where $F\left( {x - }\right)$ denotes the left limit of $F$ at $x$ .
answer:
Let ${F}^{-1}\left( t\right) = \inf \{ x : F\left( x\right) \geq t\}$ . If $F\left( T\right) < t$ , then, by definition, $T < {F}^{-1}\left( t\right)$ . Thus,$$
P\left( {F\left( T\right) < t}\right) \leq P\left( {T < {F}^{-1}\left( t\right) }\right) = F\left( {{F}^{-1}\left( t\right) - }\right) \leq t,
$$
since $F\left( x\right) < t$ for all $x < {F}^{-1}\left( t\right)$ so that the left limit of $F$ at ${F}^{-1}\left( t\right)$ is no larger than $t$ . Similarly, $F\left( {T - }\right) > 1 - t$ implies $T > {F}^{-1}\left( {1 - t}\right)$ and, hence,$$
P\left( {F\left( {T - }\right) > 1 - t}\right) \leq P\left( {T > {F}^{-1}\left( {1 - t}\right) }\right) = 1 - F\left( {{F}^{-1}\left( {1 - t}\right) }\right) \leq t,
$$
since $F\left( {{F}^{-1}\left( {1 - t}\right) }\right) \geq 1 - t$ .
explanation:
This problem uses the distribution function and its basic properties, together with the quantile-type inverse $F^{-1}(t)=\inf\{x:F(x)\ge t\}$. The key idea is to convert the events involving $F(T)$ and $F(T-)$ into events involving $T$, and then bound their probabilities by properties of $F$ and its left limits.

Define
$F^{-1}(t)=\inf\{x:F(x)\ge t\}$.
We prove the two inequalities separately.

(1) Prove that $P\big(F(T)<t\big)\le t$.

If $F(T)<t$, then by the definition of $F^{-1}(t)$, we must have
$T<F^{-1}(t)$.
Indeed, if $T\ge F^{-1}(t)$, then by the definition of the infimum point where $F$ reaches level $t$, it would contradict $F(T)<t$.
Therefore,
$\{F(T)<t\}\subseteq \{T<F^{-1}(t)\}$,
so
$P\big(F(T)<t\big)\le P\big(T<F^{-1}(t)\big)$.

Now use the definition of the left limit of the cdf:
$P\big(T<F^{-1}(t)\big)=F\big(F^{-1}(t)-\big)$.

Next, for every $x<F^{-1}(t)$, the definition of $F^{-1}(t)$ implies
$F(x)<t$.
Hence the left limit at $F^{-1}(t)$ also satisfies
$F\big(F^{-1}(t)-\big)\le t$.
Thus,
$P\big(F(T)<t\big)\le F\big(F^{-1}(t)-\big)\le t$.
So the first inequality is proved.

(2) Prove that $P\big(F(T-)>1-t\big)\le t$.

If $F(T-)>1-t$, then necessarily
$T>F^{-1}(1-t)$.
To see this, if $T\le F^{-1}(1-t)$, then the left limit before $T$ could not exceed the level $1-t$ in a way consistent with the definition of $F^{-1}(1-t)$ as the first point where $F$ reaches at least $1-t$.
Therefore,
$\{F(T-)>1-t\}\subseteq \{T>F^{-1}(1-t)\}$,
so
$P\big(F(T-)>1-t\big)\le P\big(T>F^{-1}(1-t)\big)$.

Now compute
$P\big(T>F^{-1}(1-t)\big)=1-F\big(F^{-1}(1-t)\big)$.
By the definition of $F^{-1}(1-t)$,
$F\big(F^{-1}(1-t)\big)\ge 1-t$.
Hence,
$1-F\big(F^{-1}(1-t)\big)\le 1-(1-t)=t$.
Therefore,
$P\big(F(T-)>1-t\big)\le t$.

Combining the two parts, we obtain
$P\big(F(T)<t\big)\le t$ and $P\big(F(T-)>1-t\big)\le t$ for all $t\in(0,1)$.
subject: Mathematical Statistics

question:
Let $\left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right)$ be a random sample of random variables having Lebesgue density $\frac{a}{\theta }{\left( \frac{x}{\theta }\right) }^{a - 1}{I}_{\left( 0,\theta \right) }\left( x\right)$ , where $a \geq 1$ is known and $\theta > 0$ is unknown.
(i) Construct a confidence interval for $\theta$ with confidence coefficient $1 - \alpha$ using the cumulative distribution function of the largest order statistic ${X}_{\left( n\right) }$ . (ii) Show that the confidence interval in (i) can also be obtained using a pivotal quantity.
answer:
(i) The cumulative distribution function of ${X}_{\left( n\right) }$ is$$
{F}_{\theta }\left( t\right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 0 & t \leq 0 \\ {\left( t/\theta \right) }^{na} & 0 < t < \theta \\ 1 & t \geq \theta , \end{array}\right.
$$
which is decreasing in $\theta$ for any fixed $t \in \left( {0,\theta }\right)$ . Also, for $t > 0,\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\theta \rightarrow 0}}{F}_{\theta }\left( t\right) \; = 1$ and $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\theta \rightarrow \infty }}{F}_{\theta }\left( t\right) = 0$ . By Theorem 7.1 in Shao (2003), a $1 - \alpha$ confidence interval for $\theta$ has upper limit being the unique solution of ${F}_{\theta }\left( T\right) = {\alpha }_{1}$ and lower limit being the unique solution of ${F}_{\theta }\left( T\right) = 1 - {\alpha }_{2}$ , where ${\alpha }_{1} + {\alpha }_{2} = \; \alpha$ . Consequently, this confidence interval is $\left\lbrack {T/{\left( 1 - {\alpha }_{2}\right) }^{{\left( na\right) }^{-1}}, T/{\alpha }_{1}^{{\left( na\right) }^{-1}}}\right\rbrack$ . (ii) Note that $U\left( \theta \right) = {\left( {X}_{\left( n\right) }/\theta \right) }^{na}$ has the uniform distribution on $\left( {0,1}\right)$ and, hence, is a pivotal quantity. The $1 - \alpha$ confidence interval constructed using $U\left( \theta \right)$ is the same as that in part (i) of the solution.
explanation:
This problem uses the distribution of the largest order statistic and the method of confidence intervals, and part (ii) additionally uses a pivotal quantity. The key idea is that $X_{(n)}$ has a distribution depending on $\theta$ in a monotone way, and the transformed statistic $\left(X_{(n)}/\theta\right)^{na}$ has a parameter-free distribution.

For a single observation, the density is
$ f(x;\theta)=\dfrac{a}{\theta}\left(\dfrac{x}{\theta}\right)^{a-1}I_{(0,\theta)}(x), \quad a\ge 1,\ \theta>0. $
Hence for $0<x<\theta$,
$ F_X(x)=\int_0^x \frac{a}{\theta}\left(\frac{t}{\theta}\right)^{a-1}dt=\left(\frac{x}{\theta}\right)^a. $
So each $X_i$ has cdf
$ F_X(x)=\begin{cases}
0, & x\le 0,\\
\left(\dfrac{x}{\theta}\right)^a, & 0<x<\theta,\\
1, & x\ge \theta.
\end{cases} $

(i) Construct a confidence interval from the cdf of $X_{(n)}$.

Since $X_{(n)}=\max\{X_1,\dots,X_n\}$, its cdf is
$ F_{\theta}(t)=P_\theta(X_{(n)}\le t)=[F_X(t)]^n. $
Therefore,
$ F_{\theta}(t)=\begin{cases}
0, & t\le 0,\\
\left(\dfrac{t}{\theta}\right)^{na}, & 0<t<\theta,\\
1, & t\ge \theta.
\end{cases} $

For fixed $t\in(0,\theta)$,
$ F_{\theta}(t)=\left(\dfrac{t}{\theta}\right)^{na} $
is decreasing in $\theta$. Also, for each fixed $t>0$,
$ \lim_{\theta\to 0}F_{\theta}(t)=1, \qquad \lim_{\theta\to\infty}F_{\theta}(t)=0. $
Thus we can invert the cdf to obtain a confidence interval.

Let $T=X_{(n)}$. For numbers $\alpha_1,\alpha_2>0$ with $\alpha_1+\alpha_2=\alpha$, define the upper endpoint by solving
$ F_{\theta}(T)=\alpha_1, $
and the lower endpoint by solving
$ F_{\theta}(T)=1-\alpha_2. $
Using
$ F_{\theta}(T)=\left(\frac{T}{\theta}\right)^{na}, $
we solve each equation:

1. Upper endpoint:
$ \left(\frac{T}{\theta_U}\right)^{na}=\alpha_1 $
so
$ \theta_U=\frac{T}{\alpha_1^{1/(na)}}. $

2. Lower endpoint:
$ \left(\frac{T}{\theta_L}\right)^{na}=1-\alpha_2 $
so
$ \theta_L=\frac{T}{(1-\alpha_2)^{1/(na)}}. $

Hence a $1-\alpha$ confidence interval for $\theta$ is
$ \left[\frac{T}{(1-\alpha_2)^{1/(na)}},\frac{T}{\alpha_1^{1/(na)}}\right]
=\left[\frac{X_{(n)}}{(1-\alpha_2)^{1/(na)}},\frac{X_{(n)}}{\alpha_1^{1/(na)}}\right], $
where $\alpha_1+\alpha_2=\alpha$.

If one chooses equal tails, $\alpha_1=\alpha_2=\alpha/2$, then the interval becomes
$ \left[\frac{X_{(n)}}{(1-\alpha/2)^{1/(na)}},\frac{X_{(n)}}{(\alpha/2)^{1/(na)}}\right]. $

(ii) Show the same interval can be obtained from a pivotal quantity.

Consider
$ U(\theta)=\left(\frac{X_{(n)}}{\theta}\right)^{na}. $
For $0<u<1$,
\begin{align*}
P(U(\theta)\le u)
&=P\left(\left(\frac{X_{(n)}}{\theta}\right)^{na}\le u\right)\\
&=P\left(X_{(n)}\le \theta u^{1/(na)}\right)\\
&=F_{\theta}(\theta u^{1/(na)})\\
&=\left(\frac{\theta u^{1/(na)}}{\theta}\right)^{na}\\
&=u.
\end{align*}
Thus
$ U(\theta)\sim \mathrm{Unif}(0,1), $
which does not depend on $\theta$, so it is a pivotal quantity.

Now choose $\alpha_1,\alpha_2>0$ with $\alpha_1+\alpha_2=\alpha$. Then
$ P\big(\alpha_1\le U(\theta)\le 1-\alpha_2\big)=1-\alpha. $
Substituting $U(\theta)=\left(X_{(n)}/\theta\right)^{na}$,
$ P\left(\alpha_1\le \left(\frac{X_{(n)}}{\theta}\right)^{na}\le 1-\alpha_2\right)=1-\alpha. $
Since all quantities are positive, take the $1/(na)$ power:
$ P\left(\alpha_1^{1/(na)}\le \frac{X_{(n)}}{\theta}\le (1-\alpha_2)^{1/(na)}\right)=1-\alpha. $
Now solve the inequalities for $\theta$:
$ P\left(\frac{X_{(n)}}{(1-\alpha_2)^{1/(na)}}\le \theta\le \frac{X_{(n)}}{\alpha_1^{1/(na)}}\right)=1-\alpha. $
Therefore the confidence interval obtained by the pivot method is
$ \left[\frac{X_{(n)}}{(1-\alpha_2)^{1/(na)}},\frac{X_{(n)}}{\alpha_1^{1/(na)}}\right], $
which is exactly the same as the interval found in part (i).

So the final conclusion is that both methods give the same $1-\alpha$ confidence interval for $\theta$.

question:
Let $\left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right)$ be a random sample from the exponential distribution on $\left( {a,\infty }\right)$ with scale parameter 1, where $a \in \mathcal{R}$ is unknown.
(i) Construct a confidence interval for $a$ with confidence coefficient $1 - \alpha$ by using the cumulative distribution function of the smallest order statistic ${X}_{\left( 1\right) }$ .
(ii) Show that the confidence interval in (i) can also be obtained using a pivotal quantity.
answer:
Let $T=X_{(1)}$. Since each $X_i-a$ has the exponential distribution with scale $1$,
$$
F_a(t)=P_a(T\le t)=
\begin{cases}
0,&t\le a,\\
1-e^{-n(t-a)},&t>a.
\end{cases}
$$
For fixed $t>a$, $F_a(t)$ is decreasing in $a$.

Choose $\alpha_1,\alpha_2\ge0$ with $\alpha_1+\alpha_2=\alpha$. Solving
$$
F_a(T)=\alpha_1
$$
gives
$$
a=T+\frac1n\log(1-\alpha_1),
$$
the upper endpoint. Solving
$$
F_a(T)=1-\alpha_2
$$
gives
$$
a=T+\frac1n\log\alpha_2,
$$
the lower endpoint. Thus a $(1-\alpha)$ confidence interval is
$$
\boxed{\left[T+\frac1n\log\alpha_2,\;
T+\frac1n\log(1-\alpha_1)\right]}.
$$

For the pivotal construction, define
$$
W(a)=n(T-a).
$$
For $w>0$,
$$
P_a\{W(a)\le w\}
=P_a\left\{T\le a+\frac wn\right\}=1-e^{-w},
$$
and the probability is $0$ for $w\le0$. Hence
$$
W(a)\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)\quad\text{on }(0,\infty),
$$
so $W(a)$ is pivotal. Moreover,
$$
P\{W\le-\log(1-\alpha_1)\}=\alpha_1,
\qquad
P\{W\ge-\log\alpha_2\}=\alpha_2.
$$
Therefore
$$
P\{-\log(1-\alpha_1)\le W(a)\le-\log\alpha_2\}=1-\alpha.
$$
Substituting $W(a)=n(T-a)$ and reversing the inequalities when solving for $a$ gives
$$
T+\frac1n\log\alpha_2
\le a\le
T+\frac1n\log(1-\alpha_1),
$$
which is exactly the interval obtained from $F_a$ in part (i).
explanation:
Let $T=X_{(1)}$. Since each $X_i-a$ has the exponential distribution with scale $1$,
$$
F_a(t)=P_a(T\le t)=
\begin{cases}
0,&t\le a,\\
1-e^{-n(t-a)},&t>a.
\end{cases}
$$
For fixed $t>a$, $F_a(t)$ is decreasing in $a$.

Choose $\alpha_1,\alpha_2\ge0$ with $\alpha_1+\alpha_2=\alpha$. Solving
$$
F_a(T)=\alpha_1
$$
gives
$$
a=T+\frac1n\log(1-\alpha_1),
$$
the upper endpoint. Solving
$$
F_a(T)=1-\alpha_2
$$
gives
$$
a=T+\frac1n\log\alpha_2,
$$
the lower endpoint. Thus a $(1-\alpha)$ confidence interval is
$$
\boxed{\left[T+\frac1n\log\alpha_2,\;
T+\frac1n\log(1-\alpha_1)\right]}.
$$

For the pivotal construction, define
$$
W(a)=n(T-a).
$$
For $w>0$,
$$
P_a\{W(a)\le w\}
=P_a\left\{T\le a+\frac wn\right\}=1-e^{-w},
$$
and the probability is $0$ for $w\le0$. Hence
$$
W(a)\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)\quad\text{on }(0,\infty),
$$
so $W(a)$ is pivotal. Moreover,
$$
P\{W\le-\log(1-\alpha_1)\}=\alpha_1,
\qquad
P\{W\ge-\log\alpha_2\}=\alpha_2.
$$
Therefore
$$
P\{-\log(1-\alpha_1)\le W(a)\le-\log\alpha_2\}=1-\alpha.
$$
Substituting $W(a)=n(T-a)$ and reversing the inequalities when solving for $a$ gives
$$
T+\frac1n\log\alpha_2
\le a\le
T+\frac1n\log(1-\alpha_1),
$$
which is exactly the interval obtained from $F_a$ in part (i).

question:
Let $X$ be a single observation from the uniform distribution on $\left( {\theta - \frac{1}{2},\theta + \frac{1}{2}}\right)$ , where $\theta \in \mathcal{R}$ is unknown.
(i) Show that $X - \theta$ is a pivotal quantity and that a confidence interval of the form $\left\lbrack {X + c, X + d}\right\rbrack$ with some constants $- \frac{1}{2} < c < d < \frac{1}{2}$ has confidence coefficient $1 - \alpha$ if and only if its length is $1 - \alpha$ .
(ii) Show that the cumulative distribution function ${F}_{\theta }\left( x\right)$ of $X$ is nonincreasing in $\theta$ for any $x$ and it can be used to construct a confidence interval for $\theta$ with confidence coefficient $1 - \alpha$ .
answer:
(i) The distribution of $\theta - X$ is the uniform distribution on $\left( {-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}}\right)$ . Hence, $\theta - X$ is a pivotal quantity. For $- \frac{1}{2} < c < d < \frac{1}{2}$ ,$$
P\left( {X + c < \theta < X + d}\right) = P\left( {c < \theta - X < d}\right) = d - c.
$$
Hence, $\left\lbrack {X + c, X + d}\right\rbrack$ is a confidence interval with confidence coefficient $1 - \alpha$ if and only if $d - c = 1 - \alpha$ , i.e., the length of $\left\lbrack {X + c, X + d}\right\rbrack$ is $1 - \alpha$ . (ii) For $x\in\mathbb R$,
$$
F_\theta(x)=\begin{cases}
1,&\theta\le x-\frac12,\\
x+\frac12-\theta,&x-\frac12<\theta<x+\frac12,\\
0,&\theta\ge x+\frac12,
\end{cases}
$$
which is nonincreasing in $\theta$. Let $\alpha_1,\alpha_2\ge0$ with $\alpha_1+\alpha_2=\alpha$. Solving
$$F_\theta(X)=1-\alpha_2\quad\text{and}\quad F_\theta(X)=\alpha_1$$
on the middle branch gives the lower and upper limits
$$L(X)=X+\alpha_2-\frac12,\qquad U(X)=X+\frac12-\alpha_1.$$
The coverage can be verified directly, without invoking an external theorem:
$$
\{L(X)\le\theta\le U(X)\}
=\left\{\alpha_2-\frac12\le\theta-X\le\frac12-\alpha_1\right\}.
$$
Since $\theta-X\sim U(-1/2,1/2)$, this event has probability
$$\left(\frac12-\alpha_1\right)-\left(\alpha_2-\frac12\right)=1-\alpha.$$
Thus $[L(X),U(X)]$ is a $1-\alpha$ confidence interval for $\theta$.
explanation:
This problem uses the ideas of uniform distribution, distribution functions, and confidence intervals. In part (i), the key is to identify a pivot and compute the coverage probability directly; in part (ii), the key is to write down $F_{\theta}(x)$ explicitly and use its monotonicity in $\theta$ to invert it into confidence bounds.

(i) Since $X\sim U\left(\theta-\frac12,\theta+\frac12\right)$, subtracting $\theta$ gives
$X-\theta\sim U\left(-\frac12,\frac12\right)$.
Equivalently,
$\theta-X\sim U\left(-\frac12,\frac12\right)$.
Its distribution does not depend on the unknown parameter $\theta$, so $X-\theta$ (or $\theta-X$) is a pivotal quantity.

Now consider an interval of the form $[X+c,X+d]$, where $-\frac12<c<d<\frac12$. Its coverage probability is
$P\bigl(X+c<\theta<X+d\bigr)$.
Rewrite the event in terms of the pivot:
$X+c<\theta<X+d$
if and only if
$c<\theta-X<d$.
Therefore,
$P\bigl(X+c<\theta<X+d\bigr)=P\bigl(c<\theta-X<d\bigr)$.
Because $\theta-X\sim U\left(-\frac12,\frac12\right)$, the probability of falling in $(c,d)$ is just the interval length:
$P\bigl(c<\theta-X<d\bigr)=d-c$.
Hence the confidence coefficient of $[X+c,X+d]$ is $d-c$. So this interval has confidence coefficient $1-\alpha$ if and only if
$d-c=1-\alpha$.
But $d-c$ is exactly the length of the interval $[X+c,X+d]$. Thus $[X+c,X+d]$ has confidence coefficient $1-\alpha$ if and only if its length is $1-\alpha$.

(ii) For fixed $x\in\mathbb{R}$, since $X\sim U\left(\theta-\frac12,\theta+\frac12\right)$, the distribution function of $X$ is
$F_{\theta}(x)=P_{\theta}(X\le x)$.
By the geometry of the uniform distribution,
$F_{\theta}(x)=\begin{cases}
1, & \theta\le x-\frac12,\\
x+\frac12-\theta, & x-\frac12<\theta<x+\frac12,\\
0, & x+\frac12\le \theta.
\end{cases}$
From this piecewise expression, as $\theta$ increases, the value of $F_{\theta}(x)$ never increases. Therefore $F_{\theta}(x)$ is nonincreasing in $\theta$ for every fixed $x$.

Because of this monotonicity, we can invert the equations involving $F_{\theta}(X)$ to obtain confidence limits. Let $\alpha_1+\alpha_2=\alpha$. The upper confidence limit is defined as the unique solution of
$F_{\theta}(X)=\alpha_1$.
Using the middle branch of the cdf,
$X+\frac12-\theta=\alpha_1$,
so
$\theta=X+\frac12-\alpha_1$.
Thus the upper limit is
$U(X)=X+\frac12-\alpha_1$.

Similarly, the lower confidence limit is defined as the unique solution of
$F_{\theta}(X)=1-\alpha_2$.
Again using the middle branch,
$X+\frac12-\theta=1-\alpha_2$,
so
$\theta=X+\alpha_2-\frac12$.
Thus the lower limit is
$L(X)=X+\alpha_2-\frac12$.

Therefore a confidence interval with confidence coefficient $1-\alpha$ is
$\left[X+\alpha_2-\frac12,\,X+\frac12-\alpha_1\right]$,
where $\alpha_1+\alpha_2=\alpha$.

In conclusion: in part (i), the pivot is $X-\theta$ and the interval $[X+c,X+d]$ has confidence coefficient $1-\alpha$ exactly when its length is $1-\alpha$; in part (ii), the cdf $F_{\theta}(x)$ is nonincreasing in $\theta$ and yields the confidence interval $\left[X+\alpha_2-\frac12,\,X+\frac12-\alpha_1\right]$.

question:
Let ${X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}$ be a random sample of random variables with Lebesgue density $\theta {a}^{\theta }{x}^{-\left( {\theta + 1}\right) }{I}_{\left( a,\infty \right) }\left( x\right)$ , where $\theta > 0$ and $a > 0$ .
(i) When $\theta$ is known, derive a confidence interval for $a$ with confidence coefficient $1 - \alpha$ by using the cumulative distribution function of the smallest order statistic ${X}_{\left( 1\right) }$ .
(ii) When both $a$ and $\theta$ are unknown and $n \geq 2$ , derive a confidence interval for $\theta$ with confidence coefficient $1 - \alpha$ by using the cumulative distribution function of $T = \mathop{\prod }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\left( {{X}_{i}/{X}_{\left( 1\right) }}\right)$ .
(iii) Show that the confidence intervals in (i) and (ii) can be obtained using pivotal quantities.
(iv) When both $a$ and $\theta$ are unknown, construct a confidence set for $\left( {a,\theta }\right)$ with confidence coefficient $1 - \alpha$ by using a pivotal quantity.
answer:
(i) The cumulative distribution function of ${X}_{\left( 1\right) }$ is$$
{F}_{a}\left( x\right) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1 - {a}^{n\theta }/{x}^{n\theta } & a < x \\ 0 & a > x, \end{array}\right.
$$
which is nonincreasing in $a$ . By Theorem 7.1 in Shao (2003), a $1 - \alpha$ confidence interval for $a$ has upper limit being the unique solution of ${F}_{a}\left( {X}_{\left( 1\right) }\right) = \; {\alpha }_{1}$ and lower limit being the unique solution of ${F}_{a}\left( {X}_{\left( 1\right) }\right) = 1 - {\alpha }_{2}$ , where ${\alpha }_{1} + {\alpha }_{2} = \alpha$ . This leads to the interval $\left\lbrack {{\alpha }_{2}^{{\left( n\theta \right) }^{-1}}{X}_{\left( 1\right) },{\left( 1 - {\alpha }_{1}\right) }^{{\left( n\theta \right) }^{-1}}{X}_{\left( 1\right) }}\right\rbrack$ .
(ii) Consider ${Y}_{i} = \log {X}_{i}$ . Then $\left( {{Y}_{1},\ldots ,{Y}_{n}}\right)$ is a random sample from the exponential distribution on the interval $\left( {b,\infty }\right)$ with scale parameter ${\theta }^{-1}$ , where $b = \log a$ . From the result in Exercise 7 of Chapter 2 and the fact that ${Y}_{\left( 1\right) } = \log {X}_{\left( 1\right) }$ is the smallest order statistic of the $Y$ sample, ${2\theta }\log T = {2\theta }\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\left( {{Y}_{i} - {Y}_{\left( 1\right) }}\right)$ has the chi-square distribution ${\chi }_{2\left( {n - 1}\right) }^{2}$ . Hence, the cumulative distribution function of $T$ is$$
P\left( {T \leq t}\right) = P\left( {{2\theta }\log T \leq {2\theta }\log t}\right) = {F}_{2\left( {n - 1}\right) }\left( {{2\theta }\log t}\right)
$$
for $t > 1$ , where ${F}_{2\left( {n - 1}\right) }$ denotes the cumulative distribution function of the chi-square distribution ${\chi }_{2\left( {n - 1}\right) }^{2}$ . From Theorem 7.1 in Shao (2003), a $1 - \alpha$ confidence interval for $\theta$ has upper limit being the unique solution of ${F}_{2\left( {n - 1}\right) }\left( {{2\theta }\log T}\right) = 1 - {\alpha }_{2}$ and lower limit being the unique solution of ${F}_{2\left( {n - 1}\right) }\left( {{2\theta }\log T}\right) = {\alpha }_{1}$ , where ${\alpha }_{1} + {\alpha }_{2} = \alpha$ . The resulting interval is $\left\lbrack {{\chi }_{2\left( {n - 1}\right) ,1 - {\alpha }_{1}}^{2}/\left( {2\log T}\right) ,{\chi }_{2\left( {n - 1}\right) ,{\alpha }_{2}}^{2}/\left( {2\log T}\right) }\right\rbrack$ , where ${\chi }_{2\left( {n - 1}\right) ,\alpha }^{2}$ denotes the $\left( {1 - \alpha }\right)$ th quantile of ${\chi }_{2\left( {n - 1}\right) }^{2}$ .
(iii) When $\theta$ is known, ${X}_{\left( 1\right) }/a$ is a pivotal quantity. The confidence interval constructed using ${X}_{\left( 1\right) }/a$ is the same as that in part (i) of the solution.
When both $a$ and $\theta$ are unknown, it follows from part (ii) of the solution that ${2\theta }\log T$ is a pivotal quantity. The confidence interval constructed using ${2\theta }\log T$ is the same as that in part (ii) of the solution.
(iv) From part (i) of the solution,$$
P\left( {\frac{{X}_{\left( 1\right) }^{\theta }}{{a}^{\theta }} \leq t}\right) = P\left( {{X}_{\left( 1\right) } \leq a{t}^{1/\theta }}\right) = 1 - \frac{1}{{t}^{n}}.
$$
Hence, a pivotal quantity is ${X}_{\left( 1\right) }^{\theta }/{a}^{\theta }$ . Let $1 \le {c}_{1} < {c}_{2}$ be constants such that ${c}_{1}^{-n} - {c}_{2}^{-n} = 1 - \alpha$ . Then, a $1 - \alpha$ confidence set for $\left( {a,\theta }\right)$ is$$
C\left( X\right) = \left\{ {\left( {a,\theta }\right) : {c}_{1}{a}^{\theta } \leq {X}_{\left( 1\right) }^{\theta } \leq {c}_{2}{a}^{\theta }}\right\} .
$$
explanation:
This problem uses the distribution of the smallest order statistic and the pivotal quantity method to construct confidence intervals and a confidence set. The key ideas are: first derive the distribution of $X_{(1)}$ and of $T=\prod_{i=1}^n(X_i/X_{(1)})$, then invert these distributions or use pivots to obtain confidence procedures.

(i) Confidence interval for $a$ when $\theta$ is known.
The density is
$ f(x; a,\theta)=\theta a^{\theta}x^{-(\theta+1)}I_{(a,\infty)}(x), \quad \theta>0,\ a>0. $
For one observation,
$ P(X_i>x)=\int_x^{\infty}\theta a^{\theta}u^{-(\theta+1)}\,du=\frac{a^{\theta}}{x^{\theta}}, \quad x>a. $
Hence for the smallest order statistic,
$ P(X_{(1)}>x)=P(X_1>x,\ldots,X_n>x)=\left(\frac{a^{\theta}}{x^{\theta}}\right)^n=\frac{a^{n\theta}}{x^{n\theta}}, \quad x>a. $
Therefore its cumulative distribution function is
$ F_a(x)=P(X_{(1)}\le x)=\begin{cases}1-\dfrac{a^{n\theta}}{x^{n\theta}}, & x>a,\\ 0, & x\le a.\end{cases} $
For fixed observed $X_{(1)}$, $F_a(X_{(1)})$ is nonincreasing in $a$. Let $\alpha_1+\alpha_2=\alpha$. The lower and upper confidence limits are obtained by solving
$ F_a(X_{(1)})=1-\alpha_2 $
and
$ F_a(X_{(1)})=\alpha_1 $.
Now solve these equations:
$ 1-\frac{a^{n\theta}}{X_{(1)}^{n\theta}}=1-\alpha_2 \Rightarrow \frac{a^{n\theta}}{X_{(1)}^{n\theta}}=\alpha_2 \Rightarrow a=\alpha_2^{1/(n\theta)}X_{(1)}. $
Similarly,
$ 1-\frac{a^{n\theta}}{X_{(1)}^{n\theta}}=\alpha_1 \Rightarrow \frac{a^{n\theta}}{X_{(1)}^{n\theta}}=1-\alpha_1 \Rightarrow a=(1-\alpha_1)^{1/(n\theta)}X_{(1)}. $
Thus a $1-\alpha$ confidence interval for $a$ is
$ \left[\alpha_2^{1/(n\theta)}X_{(1)},\,(1-\alpha_1)^{1/(n\theta)}X_{(1)}\right]. $

(ii) Confidence interval for $\theta$ when both $a$ and $\theta$ are unknown.
Define
$ Y_i=\log X_i. $
Since $X_i>a$, we have $Y_i>\log a=:b$. By transformation, $(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)$ is a random sample from an exponential distribution shifted by $b$, with scale parameter $1/\theta$. Also,
$ Y_{(1)}=\log X_{(1)}. $
Now
$ T=\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{X_i}{X_{(1)}} $
so
$ \log T=\sum_{i=1}^n(\log X_i-\log X_{(1)})=\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-Y_{(1)}). $
Using the known result for shifted exponential samples,
$ 2\theta\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-Y_{(1)})=2\theta\log T \sim \chi^2_{2(n-1)}. $
Therefore, for $t>1$,
$ P(T\le t)=P(2\theta\log T\le 2\theta\log t)=F_{2(n-1)}(2\theta\log t), $
where $F_{2(n-1)}$ is the cdf of $\chi^2_{2(n-1)}$.
Again let $\alpha_1+\alpha_2=\alpha$. Inverting the cdf gives the lower and upper confidence limits for $\theta$ from
$ F_{2(n-1)}(2\theta\log T)=\alpha_1 $
and
$ F_{2(n-1)}(2\theta\log T)=1-\alpha_2. $
Equivalently,
$ 2\theta\log T=\chi^2_{2(n-1),1-\alpha_1} $
for the lower limit, and
$ 2\theta\log T=\chi^2_{2(n-1),\alpha_2} $
for the upper limit, where $\chi^2_{\nu,\gamma}$ denotes the $(1-\gamma)$th quantile of $\chi^2_\nu$.
Hence the confidence interval is
$ \left[\frac{\chi^2_{2(n-1),1-\alpha_1}}{2\log T},\,\frac{\chi^2_{2(n-1),\alpha_2}}{2\log T}\right]. $

(iii) Showing the intervals can be obtained from pivotal quantities.
When $\theta$ is known, from part (i), the distribution of $X_{(1)}/a$ does not depend on $a$, so
$ \frac{X_{(1)}}{a} $
is a pivotal quantity. Inverting inequalities involving this pivot yields exactly the same confidence interval for $a$ as in part (i).
When both $a$ and $\theta$ are unknown, part (ii) shows that
$ 2\theta\log T \sim \chi^2_{2(n-1)} $
and its distribution does not depend on unknown parameters other than through the pivot itself. Therefore
$ 2\theta\log T $
is a pivotal quantity. Inverting the corresponding probability statement gives the same confidence interval for $\theta$ as in part (ii).

(iv) Confidence set for $(a,\theta)$ using a pivotal quantity.
From part (i), for $t>1$,
$ P\left(\frac{X_{(1)}^{\theta}}{a^{\theta}}\le t\right)=P\left(X_{(1)}\le a t^{1/\theta}\right). $
Using the cdf of $X_{(1)}$,
$ P\left(X_{(1)}\le a t^{1/\theta}\right)=1-\frac{a^{n\theta}}{(a t^{1/\theta})^{n\theta}}=1-\frac{1}{t^n}. $
So $X_{(1)}^{\theta}/a^{\theta}$ is a pivotal quantity. Choose constants $1\le c_1<c_2$ such that
$ c_1^{-n}-c_2^{-n}=1-\alpha. $
Then
$ P\left(c_1\le \frac{X_{(1)}^{\theta}}{a^{\theta}}\le c_2\right)=1-\alpha. $
Rewriting this event in terms of $(a,\theta)$ gives the confidence set
$ C(X)=\left\{(a,\theta): c_1 a^{\theta}\le X_{(1)}^{\theta}\le c_2 a^{\theta}\right\}. $

Therefore, the required results are exactly the interval in part (i), the interval in part (ii), the pivots identified in part (iii), and the confidence set in part (iv).

question: Let $X = \left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right)$ be a random sample from the Weibull distribution with Lebesgue density $\frac{a}{\theta }{x}^{a - 1}{e}^{-{x}^{a}/\theta }{I}_{\left( 0,\infty \right) }\left( x\right)$ , where $a > 0$ and $\theta > 0$ are unknown. Show that $R\left( {X, a,\theta }\right) = \mathop{\prod }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\left( {{X}_{i}^{a}/\theta }\right)$ is pivotal. Construct a confidence set for $\left( {a,\theta }\right)$ with confidence coefficient $1 - \alpha$ by using $R\left( {X, a,\theta }\right)$ .
answer:
Let ${Y}_{i} = {X}_{i}^{a}/\theta$ . Then ${Y}_{i}$ has the exponential distribution on $\left( {0,\infty }\right)$ with scale parameter 1 . Since ${Y}_{1},\ldots ,{Y}_{n}$ are independent, $R\left( {X, a,\theta }\right) = \; \mathop{\prod }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\left( {{X}_{i}^{a}/\theta }\right)$ is pivotal. Since the distribution of $R\left( {X, a,\theta }\right)$ is known, we can find positive constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ such that $P\left( {{c}_{1} \leq R\left( {X, a,\theta }\right) \leq {c}_{2}}\right) = 1 - \alpha$ . A confidence set for $\left( {a,\theta }\right)$ with confidence coefficient $1 - \alpha$ is$$
C\left( X\right) = \left\{ {\left( {a,\theta }\right) : a>0,\ \theta>0,\ {c}_{1}{\theta }^{n} \leq \mathop{\prod }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{i}^{a} \leq {c}_{2}{\theta }^{n}}\right\} .
$$
explanation:
This problem uses the key ideas of the Weibull distribution, the exponential distribution, and the pivotal quantity method. The main step is to transform the Weibull sample into variables with a distribution free of the unknown parameters, so that a pivot can be constructed and then inverted to obtain a confidence set.

Let
$Y_i=\dfrac{X_i^a}{\theta}$, $i=1,\dots,n$.
We first determine the distribution of $Y_i$.

Since $X_i$ has density
$f_X(x)=\dfrac{a}{\theta}x^{a-1}e^{-x^a/\theta}I_{(0,\infty)}(x)$,
consider the transformation
$x=(\theta y)^{1/a}, \quad y>0$.
Then
$\dfrac{dx}{dy}=\dfrac{1}{a}\theta^{1/a}y^{1/a-1}$.
Also,
$x^{a-1}=\big((\theta y)^{1/a}\big)^{a-1}=\theta^{(a-1)/a}y^{(a-1)/a}$,
and
$e^{-x^a/\theta}=e^{-y}$.
Therefore the density of $Y_i$ is
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_Y(y)
&=f_X\big((\theta y)^{1/a}\big)\left|\frac{dx}{dy}\right|\\
&=\frac{a}{\theta}\,\theta^{(a-1)/a}y^{(a-1)/a}e^{-y}\cdot \frac{1}{a}\theta^{1/a}y^{1/a-1}\\
&=e^{-y}, \quad y>0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence $Y_i\sim \mathrm{Exp}(1)$, the exponential distribution with scale parameter $1$.

Because $X_1,\dots,X_n$ are a random sample, they are independent, so the transformed variables $Y_1,\dots,Y_n$ are also independent. Now
$R(X,a,\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n\left(\frac{X_i^a}{\theta}\right)=\prod_{i=1}^n Y_i$.
Thus $R(X,a,\theta)$ is a function only of independent $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ variables, so its distribution does not depend on the unknown parameters $a$ and $\theta$. Therefore $R(X,a,\theta)$ is a pivotal quantity.

Next, use this pivot to construct a confidence set. Since the distribution of $R(X,a,\theta)$ is known and parameter-free, we can choose constants $c_1>0$ and $c_2>0$ such that
$P\big(c_1\le R(X,a,\theta)\le c_2\big)=1-\alpha$.
Substitute the expression for $R$:
\[
P\left(c_1\le \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{X_i^a}{\theta}\le c_2\right)=1-\alpha.
\]
Because
$\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{X_i^a}{\theta}=\frac{\prod_{i=1}^n X_i^a}{\theta^n}$,
this becomes
\[
P\left(c_1\le \frac{\prod_{i=1}^n X_i^a}{\theta^n}\le c_2\right)=1-\alpha.
\]
Multiplying through by $\theta^n>0$, we obtain
\[
P\left(c_1\theta^n\le \prod_{i=1}^n X_i^a\le c_2\theta^n\right)=1-\alpha.
\]
Therefore a confidence set for $(a,\theta)$ with confidence coefficient $1-\alpha$ is
\[
C(X)=\left\{(a,\theta): c_1\theta^n\le \prod_{i=1}^n X_i^a\le c_2\theta^n\right\}.
\]

So the final conclusion is that $R(X,a,\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n(X_i^a/\theta)$ is pivotal, and the above set is a $(1-\alpha)$ confidence set for $(a,\theta)$. Here the displayed set is understood to be intersected with the parameter space $a>0$ and $\theta>0$.

question: Let $F$ and $G$ be two known cumulative distribution functions on $\mathcal{R}$ and $X$ be a single observation from the cumulative distribution function ${\theta F}\left( x\right) + \left( {1 - \theta }\right) G\left( x\right)$ , where $\theta \in \left\lbrack {0,1}\right\rbrack$ is unknown. Construct a level $1 - \alpha$ confidence interval for $\theta$ based on the observation $X$ . Find a condition under which the derived confidence interval has confidence coefficient $1 - \alpha$ .
answer: A level $1-\alpha$ confidence interval for $\theta$ is $\left[\underline{\theta},\overline{\theta}\right]$, where $\overline{\theta}=\sup\left\{\theta:\,F_{Y,\theta}(Y(X))\ge \alpha_1\right\}$, $\underline{\theta}=\inf\left\{\theta:\,F_{Y,\theta}(Y(X)-)\le 1-\alpha_2\right\}$, and $\alpha_1+\alpha_2=\alpha$, with $Y(X)=f(X)/g(X)$. A sufficient condition for the confidence coefficient to be exactly $1-\alpha$ is that $F_{Y,\theta}(y)$ is continuous in $y$；in particular, this is implied if $F'$ and $G'$ exist and for every fixed $c$, the set $\{x:\,F'(x)=cG'(x)\}$ has Lebesgue measure $0$
explanation:
This problem uses the ideas of $\text{单调似然比分布族}$ and $\text{置信区间}$. The key is to identify a statistic with monotone likelihood ratio, then apply the inversion theorem for one-parameter monotone families to obtain a confidence interval; the continuity condition is used to guarantee that the confidence coefficient is exactly $1-\alpha$ rather than only at least $1-\alpha$.

Let $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ denote the densities of $F$ and $G$, respectively, with respect to the measure induced by $F+G$. Then the distribution of $X$ under parameter $\theta\in[0,1]$ has density
$\theta f(x)+(1-\theta)g(x)$.

From the referenced result in Chapter 6, the family
$\{\theta f(x)+(1-\theta)g(x):\theta\in[0,1]\}$
has monotone likelihood ratio in the statistic
$Y(X)=\dfrac{f(X)}{g(X)}$.
This means that $Y(X)$ is the natural statistic to use for confidence set construction.

Now let $F_{Y,\theta}$ be the cumulative distribution function of $Y(X)$ when the parameter is $\theta$. By the monotone likelihood ratio property together with the cited lemma, for every fixed observed value, $F_{Y,\theta}(y)$ is nonincreasing in $\theta$. Therefore the family is stochastically monotone in $\theta$, and Theorem 7.1 for monotone families applies.

Hence a level $1-\alpha$ confidence interval for $\theta$ is obtained by inverting the tail probabilities of the distribution of $Y(X)$. Let $\alpha_1,\alpha_2\ge 0$ with
$\alpha_1+\alpha_2=\alpha$.
Then define the upper and lower endpoints by
$\overline{\theta}=\sup\left\{\theta:\,F_{Y,\theta}(Y(X))\ge \alpha_1\right\}$,
$\underline{\theta}=\inf\left\{\theta:\,F_{Y,\theta}(Y(X)-)\le 1-\alpha_2\right\}$.
So the confidence interval is
$\left[\underline{\theta},\overline{\theta}\right]$.

The role of the left limit $F_{Y,\theta}(Y(X)-)$ in the lower endpoint is to cover the possible discontinuity of the distribution of $Y(X)$, which is the standard form for confidence bounds in possibly noncontinuous models.

Next, we determine when the resulting interval has confidence coefficient exactly $1-\alpha$. A sufficient condition is that the distribution function $F_{Y,\theta}(y)$ be continuous in $y$. Under continuity, the tail probabilities match the nominal tail areas exactly, so the coverage probability becomes exactly
$P_\theta\{\underline{\theta}\le \theta\le \overline{\theta}\}=1-\alpha$.
Without continuity, the interval is still level $1-\alpha$, but the actual confidence coefficient may be larger than $1-\alpha$ because of jumps in the distribution.

Finally, the given explanation provides a concrete sufficient condition ensuring this continuity: if $F'$ and $G'$ exist, and for every fixed constant $c$, the set
$\{x:\,F'(x)=cG'(x)\}$
has Lebesgue measure $0$, then $F_{Y,\theta}(y)$ is continuous in $y$. Under this condition, the derived confidence interval has confidence coefficient exactly $1-\alpha$.

Therefore, the required confidence interval is obtained by inverting the cdf of $Y(X)=f(X)/g(X)$ as above, and a sufficient condition for exact confidence coefficient $1-\alpha$ is the continuity of $F_{Y,\theta}$ in $y$, which is implied by the stated derivative-measure condition.

question:
Let $\left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right)$ be a random sample of binary random variables with $P\left( {{X}_{i} = 1}\right) = p$ . Using the cumulative distribution function of $T = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{X}_{i}$ , show that a level $1 - \alpha$ confidence interval for $p$ is$$
\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{1 + \frac{n - T + 1}{T}{F}_{2\left( {n - T + 1}\right) ,{2T},{\alpha }_{2}}},\frac{\frac{T + 1}{n - T}{F}_{2\left( {T + 1}\right) ,2\left( {n - T}\right) ,{\alpha }_{1}}}{1 + \frac{T + 1}{n - T}{F}_{2\left( {T + 1}\right) ,2\left( {n - T}\right) ,{\alpha }_{1}}}}\right\rbrack ,
$$
where ${\alpha }_{1} + {\alpha }_{2} = \alpha ,{F}_{a, b,\alpha }$ is the $\left( {1 - \alpha }\right)$ th quantile of the F-distribution ${F}_{a, b}$ , and ${F}_{a,0,\alpha }$ is defined to be $\infty$ .
answer:
Since $T$ has the binomial distribution with size $n$ and probability $p$ and the binomial family has monotone likelihood ratio in $T$ , the cumulative distribution function of $T,{F}_{T, p}\left( t\right)$ , is decreasing in $p$ for fixed $t$ . By Theorem 7.1 in Shao (2003), a level $1 - \alpha$ confidence interval for $p$ is $\left\lbrack {p,\bar{p}}\right\rbrack$ , where $\bar{p}$ is the solution to ${F}_{T, p}\left( T\right) = {\alpha }_{1}$ and $p$ is the solution to ${F}_{T, p}\left( {T - }\right) = 1 - {\alpha }_{2}$ . Let $Y$ be a random variable having the beta distribution with parameter $\left( {t, n - t + 1}\right)$ . Using integral by parts, we obtain that$$
P\left( {Y \leq p}\right) = {\int }_{0}^{p}\frac{n!}{\left( {t - 1}\right) !\left( {n - t}\right) !}{y}^{t - 1}{\left( 1 - y\right) }^{n - t}{dy}
$$$$
= \frac{n!}{t!\left( {n - t}\right) !}{p}^{t}{\left( 1 - p\right) }^{n - t} + {\int }_{0}^{p}\frac{n!}{t!\left( {n - t - 1}\right) !}{y}^{t}{\left( 1 - y\right) }^{n - t - 1}{dy}
$$$$
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = t}}^{n}\frac{n!}{i!\left( {n - i}\right) !}{p}^{i}{\left( 1 - p\right) }^{n - i}
$$$$
= 1 - {F}_{T, p}\left( {t - }\right) .
$$
Therefore, $p$ is the ${\alpha }_{2}$ th quantile of the beta distribution with parameter $\left( {T, n - T + 1}\right)$ if $T > 0$ and is equal to 0 if $T = 0$ . For $\bar{p}$ , it is the solution to $1 - {\alpha }_{1} = 1 - {F}_{T, p}\left( {T + 1 - }\right)$ . Hence, $\bar{p}$ is the $\left( {1 - {\alpha }_{1}}\right)$ th quantile of the beta distribution with parameter $\left( {T + 1, n - T}\right)$ if $T < n$ and is equal to 1 if $T = n$ . Let ${F}_{a, b}$ be a random variable having the F-distribution ${F}_{a, b}$ . Then, $\frac{\left( {a/b}\right) {F}_{a, b}}{1 + \left( {a/b}\right) {F}_{a, b}}$ has the beta distribution with parameter $\left( {a/2, b/2}\right)$ . Hence$$
\bar{p} = \frac{\frac{T + 1}{n - T}{F}_{2\left( {T + 1}\right) ,2\left( {n - T}\right) ,{\alpha }_{1}}}{1 + \frac{T + 1}{n - T}{F}_{2\left( {T + 1}\right) ,2\left( {n - T}\right) ,{\alpha }_{1}}}
$$
when ${F}_{a,0,\alpha }$ is defined to be $\infty$ . Similarly,$$
\underline{p} = \frac{\frac{T}{n - T + 1}{F}_{{2T},2\left( {n - T + 1}\right) ,1 - {\alpha }_{2}}}{1 + \frac{T}{n - T + 1}{F}_{{2T},2\left( {n - T + 1}\right) ,1 - {\alpha }_{2}}}.
$$
Note that ${F}_{a, b}^{-1}$ has the F-distribution ${F}_{b, a}$ . Hence,$$
\underline{p} = \frac{1}{1 + \frac{n - T + 1}{T}{F}_{2\left( {n - T + 1}\right) ,{2T},{\alpha }_{2}}}.
$$
explanation:
This problem uses the binomial distribution of the statistic $T=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$, the relation between binomial tail probabilities and beta distributions, and the transformation from beta quantiles to $F$-distribution quantiles. These tools are needed because the confidence limits are obtained by inverting the cumulative distribution function of $T$.

First, since $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are i.i.d. Bernoulli$(p)$ random variables, the statistic
$T=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$
has the binomial distribution with parameters $n$ and $p$:
$T\sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$.
For fixed $t$, the binomial family has monotone likelihood ratio in $T$, so the cumulative distribution function
$F_{T,p}(t)=P_p(T\le t)$
is decreasing in $p$.

By the general inversion theorem for monotone families, a level $1-\alpha$ confidence interval for $p$ is $[\underline p,\bar p]$, where the endpoints are defined by
$F_{T,p}(T)=\alpha_1$
and
$F_{T,p}(T-)=1-\alpha_2$,
with $\alpha_1+\alpha_2=\alpha$.
Thus $\bar p$ solves the upper-tail inversion equation, and $\underline p$ solves the lower-tail inversion equation.

Now derive the lower endpoint. Let $Y\sim \mathrm{Beta}(t,n-t+1)$. Its density is
$f_Y(y)=\dfrac{n!}{(t-1)!(n-t)!}y^{t-1}(1-y)^{n-t},\quad 0<y<1.$
Then
$P(Y\le p)=\int_0^p \dfrac{n!}{(t-1)!(n-t)!}y^{t-1}(1-y)^{n-t}\,dy.$
Using integration by parts, this becomes
$P(Y\le p)=\dfrac{n!}{t!(n-t)!}p^t(1-p)^{n-t}+\int_0^p \dfrac{n!}{t!(n-t-1)!}y^t(1-y)^{n-t-1}\,dy.$
Repeating this expansion yields
$P(Y\le p)=\sum_{i=t}^n \dfrac{n!}{i!(n-i)!}p^i(1-p)^{n-i}.$
But
$\sum_{i=t}^n \binom ni p^i(1-p)^{n-i}=P_p(T\ge t)=1-F_{T,p}(t-).$
Therefore,
$P(Y\le p)=1-F_{T,p}(t-).$

Set $t=T$. Since the lower endpoint satisfies
$F_{T,p}(T-)=1-\alpha_2$,
we get
$1-F_{T,p}(T-)=\alpha_2.$
Hence $\underline p$ is the $\alpha_2$ quantile of the beta distribution with parameters $(T,n-T+1)$ when $T>0$; if $T=0$, then $\underline p=0$.

Next derive the upper endpoint. For $\bar p$, we use
$F_{T,p}(T)=\alpha_1.$
Equivalently,
$1-\alpha_1=1-F_{T,p}(T)=1-F_{T,p}(T+1-).$
By the same beta-binomial relationship, this shows that $\bar p$ is the $(1-\alpha_1)$ quantile of the beta distribution with parameters $(T+1,n-T)$ when $T<n$; if $T=n$, then $\bar p=1$.

Now convert the beta quantiles to $F$ quantiles. If $W\sim F_{a,b}$, then
$\dfrac{(a/b)W}{1+(a/b)W}$
has the beta distribution with parameters $(a/2,b/2)$.

Apply this to the upper endpoint. Since $\bar p$ is the $(1-\alpha_1)$ quantile of $\mathrm{Beta}(T+1,n-T)$, take $a=2(T+1)$ and $b=2(n-T)$. Then
$\bar p=\frac{\dfrac{T+1}{n-T}F_{2(T+1),2(n-T),\alpha_1}}{1+\dfrac{T+1}{n-T}F_{2(T+1),2(n-T),\alpha_1}}.$
This also covers the case $T=n$ if we define $F_{a,0,\alpha}=\infty$, because then the fraction equals $1$.

For the lower endpoint, since $\underline p$ is the $\alpha_2$ quantile of $\mathrm{Beta}(T,n-T+1)$, we first write
$\underline p=\frac{\dfrac{T}{n-T+1}F_{2T,2(n-T+1),1-\alpha_2}}{1+\dfrac{T}{n-T+1}F_{2T,2(n-T+1),1-\alpha_2}}.$
Now use the reciprocal property of the $F$ distribution: if $U\sim F_{a,b}$, then $U^{-1}\sim F_{b,a}$. Therefore,
$F_{2T,2(n-T+1),1-\alpha_2}^{-1}=F_{2(n-T+1),2T,\alpha_2},$
and the lower endpoint can be rewritten as
$\underline p=\frac{1}{1+\dfrac{n-T+1}{T}F_{2(n-T+1),2T,\alpha_2}}.$
This also gives $\underline p=0$ when $T=0$.

Hence the required level $1-\alpha$ confidence interval for $p$ is
$\left[\frac{1}{1+\frac{n-T+1}{T}F_{2(n-T+1),2T,\alpha_2}},\frac{\frac{T+1}{n-T}F_{2(T+1),2(n-T),\alpha_1}}{1+\frac{T+1}{n-T}F_{2(T+1),2(n-T),\alpha_1}}\right],$
where $\alpha_1+\alpha_2=\alpha$ and $F_{a,0,\alpha}=\infty$.

question:
Let $X$ be a sample of size 1 from the negative binomial distribution with a known size $r$ and an unknown probability $p \in \left( {0,1}\right)$ . Using the cumulative distribution function of $T = X - r$ , show that a level $1 - \alpha$ confidence interval for $p$ is$$
\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{1 + \frac{T + 1}{r}{F}_{2\left( {T + 1}\right) ,{2r},{\alpha }_{2}}},\frac{\frac{r}{T}{F}_{{2r},{2T},{\alpha }_{1}}}{1 + \frac{r}{T}{F}_{{2r},{2T},{\alpha }_{1}}}}\right\rbrack ,
$$
where ${\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{2}=\alpha$ and ${F}_{a,b,\gamma}$ denotes the upper-tail $\gamma$ critical value of the central $F$ distribution with $a$ and $b$ degrees of freedom, i.e., $P(F_{a,b}>{F}_{a,b,\gamma})=\gamma$. The displayed interval applies when $T>0$; when $T=0$, its upper endpoint is $1$, and the interval is $\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{r}{F}_{2,2r,{\alpha }_{2}}},1}\right\rbrack$.
answer:
This problem uses the keypoints of negative binomial distribution, beta distribution, and confidence intervals. The main idea is to construct an exact confidence interval by inverting the cumulative distribution function of $T=X-r$, and then express the resulting beta quantiles through $F$-distribution quantiles.

Let $T=X-r$. Since the negative binomial family has a monotone likelihood ratio in $-T$, for each fixed $t$, the distribution function $F_{T,p}(t)=P_p(T\le t)$ is increasing in $p$. Therefore, by the standard inversion theorem for one-parameter discrete families with monotone likelihood ratio, a level $1-\alpha$ confidence interval for $p$ is of the form $[\underline p,\bar p]$, where $\underline p$ solves
$F_{T,p}(T)=\alpha_2,$
and $\bar p$ solves
$F_{T,p}(T-)=1-\alpha_1,$
with $\alpha_1+\alpha_2=\alpha$.

Next compute the distribution function of $T$. For any integer $t\ge 0$,
$F_{T,p}(t)=P(T\le t)=P(X-r\le t)=P(X\le t+r).$
Using the negative binomial interpretation, this is equivalent to
$F_{T,p}(t)=P(B_{t+r,p}>r-1)=P(B_{t+r,p}\ge r),$
where $B_{m,p}$ is a binomial random variable with parameters $(m,p)$.

Now use the binomial-beta relationship:
$P(B_{t+r,p}\ge r)=P(\beta_{r,t+1}\le p),$
where $\beta_{a,b}$ denotes a beta random variable with parameters $(a,b)$. Hence,
$F_{T,p}(t)=P(\beta_{r,t+1}\le p).$

Therefore, the lower endpoint $\underline p$ is the $\alpha_2$-quantile of the beta distribution $\beta_{r,T+1}$, because it is defined by
$F_{T,p}(T)=\alpha_2.$
So
$\underline p=q_{\alpha_2}(\beta_{r,T+1}).$

For the upper endpoint, note that in the discrete case
$F_{T,p}(T-)=F_{T,p}(T-1).$
Thus $\bar p$ is determined by
$F_{T,p}(T-1)=1-\alpha_1.$
From the beta representation, this means that when $T>0$, $\bar p$ is the $(1-\alpha_1)$-quantile of $\beta_{r,T}$. If $T=0$, then clearly the upper endpoint is $1$. Hence, for $T>0$,
$\bar p=q_{1-\alpha_1}(\beta_{r,T}).$

Now convert these beta quantiles into $F$-distribution quantiles using the standard beta-$F$ relationship. If $Y\sim \beta_{a,b}$, then its lower-tail quantile can be written as
$q_{\gamma}(Y)=\frac{1}{1+\frac{b}{a}F_{2b,2a,\gamma}}.$
Applying this with $a=r$, $b=T+1$, and $\gamma=\alpha_2$, we get
$\underline p=\frac{1}{1+\frac{T+1}{r}F_{2(T+1),2r,\alpha_2}}.$

Similarly, for the upper endpoint corresponding to the $(1-\alpha_1)$-quantile of $\beta_{r,T}$, the equivalent expression in terms of the upper-tail $F$-quantile is
$\bar p=\frac{\frac{r}{T}F_{2r,2T,\alpha_1}}{1+\frac{r}{T}F_{2r,2T,\alpha_1}}, \qquad T>0.$
When $T=0$, the upper endpoint is defined separately as $1$; the expression containing $r/T$ is not used.

Combining the two endpoints, when $T>0$ the level $1-\alpha$ confidence interval for $p$ is
$\left[\frac{1}{1+\frac{T+1}{r}F_{2(T+1),2r,\alpha_2}},\frac{\frac{r}{T}F_{2r,2T,\alpha_1}}{1+\frac{r}{T}F_{2r,2T,\alpha_1}}\right].$
When $T=0$, the interval is
$\left[\frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{r}F_{2,2r,\alpha_2}},1\right].$

So the required confidence interval has been shown.

question: Let $T$ be a statistic having the noncentral chi-square distribution ${\chi }_{r}^{2}\left( \theta \right)$ , where the noncentrality parameter $\theta \geq 0$ is unknown and $r$ is a known positive integer. Show that the cumulative distribution function of $T,{F}_{\theta }\left( t\right)$ , is nonincreasing in $\theta$ for each fixed $t > 0$ and use this result to construct a confidence interval for $\theta$ with confidence coefficient $1 - \alpha$ .
answer:
From Exercise 27 of Chapter 1,$$
{F}_{\theta }\left( t\right) = {e}^{-\theta /2}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 0}}^{\infty }\frac{{\left( \theta /2\right) }^{j}}{j!}{G}_{{2j} + r}\left( t\right) ,
$$
where ${G}_{{2j} + r}\left( t\right)$ is the cumulative distribution function of the central chi-square distribution ${\chi }_{{2j} + r}^{2}, j = 0,1,2,\ldots$ From the definition of the chi-square distribution ${\chi }_{{2j} + r}^{2}$ , it is the distribution of the sum of ${2j} + r$ independent and identically distributed ${\chi }_{1}^{2}$ random variables. Hence, ${G}_{{2j} + r}\left( t\right)$ is decreasing in $j$ for any fixed $t > 0$ . Let $Y$ be a random variable having the Poisson distribution with mean $\theta /2$ and $h\left( j\right) = {G}_{{2j} + r}\left( t\right) , t > 0, j = 0,1,2,\ldots$ Then ${F}_{\theta }\left( t\right) = {E}_{\theta }\left\lbrack {h\left( Y\right) }\right\rbrack$ , where ${E}_{\theta }$ is the expectation with respect to the distribution of $Y$ . Since the family of distributions of $Y$ has monotone likelihood ratio in $Y$ and $h\left( Y\right)$ is decreasing in $Y$ , by Lemma 6.3 in Shao (2003), ${E}_{\theta }\left\lbrack {h\left( Y\right) }\right\rbrack$ is nonincreasing in $\theta$ . By Theorem 7.1 in Shao (2003), a $1 - \alpha$ confidence interval for $\theta$ is $\left\lbrack {\underline{\theta },\overline{\theta }}\right\rbrack$ with$$
\overline{\theta } = \sup \left\{ {\theta : {F}_{\theta }\left( T\right) \geq {\alpha }_{1}}\right\} \;\text{ and }\;\underline{\theta } = \inf \left\{ {\theta : {F}_{\theta }\left( T\right) \leq 1 - {\alpha }_{2}}\right\} ,
$$
where ${\alpha }_{1} + {\alpha }_{2} = \alpha$ .
explanation:
This problem uses the distribution function of the noncentral chi-square distribution and the method of constructing confidence intervals from a monotone family. The key is to show that for each fixed $t>0$, the cdf $F_{\theta}(t)$ decreases as the noncentrality parameter $\theta$ increases, and then apply the general inversion rule for confidence sets.

First, use the mixture representation of the noncentral chi-square cdf:
$$
F_{\theta}(t)=e^{-\theta/2}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{(\theta/2)^j}{j!}G_{2j+r}(t),
$$
where $G_{2j+r}(t)$ is the cdf of the central chi-square distribution $\chi^2_{2j+r}$.

Now fix $t>0$. For each $j$, the distribution $\chi^2_{2j+r}$ is the distribution of the sum of $2j+r$ independent $\chi^2_1$ random variables. As the degrees of freedom increase, the sum becomes stochastically larger, so for fixed $t>0$,
$$
G_{2j+r}(t)
$$
is decreasing in $j$.

Let $Y\sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\theta/2)$ and define
$$
h(j)=G_{2j+r}(t),\qquad j=0,1,2,\ldots
$$
Then the above series can be written as
$$
F_{\theta}(t)=E_{\theta}[h(Y)].
$$
Since $h(j)$ is decreasing in $j$, and the Poisson family with mean $\theta/2$ has monotone likelihood ratio in $Y$, it follows from the monotone likelihood ratio result that
$$
E_{\theta}[h(Y)]
$$
is nonincreasing in $\theta$. Therefore,
$$
F_{\theta}(t)
$$
is nonincreasing in $\theta$ for every fixed $t>0$.

With this monotonicity established, we invert the family of cdfs to obtain a confidence interval for $\theta$. By the standard construction for a stochastically monotone family, a $(1-\alpha)$ confidence interval is
$$
[\underline{\theta},\overline{\theta}],
$$
where
$$
\overline{\theta}=\sup\{\theta:F_{\theta}(T)\ge \alpha_1\},
$$
and
$$
\underline{\theta}=\inf\{\theta:F_{\theta}(T)\le 1-\alpha_2\},
$$
with
$$
\alpha_1+\alpha_2=\alpha.
$$
This interval has confidence coefficient $1-\alpha$.

Hence the final conclusion is that $F_{\theta}(t)$ is nonincreasing in $\theta$ for fixed $t>0$, and the corresponding $(1-\alpha)$ confidence interval for $\theta$ is exactly the interval defined above.
