question:
Let $\left( {{X}_{i1},\ldots ,{X}_{i{n}_{i}}}\right) , i = 1,2$ , be two independent random samples from $N\left( {{\mu }_{i},{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}\right) , i = 1,2$ , respectively, where all parameters are unknown.
(i) Find $1 - \alpha$ asymptotically correct confidence sets for $\left( {{\mu }_{1},{\mu }_{2}}\right)$ by inverting acceptance regions of LR tests, Wald's tests, and Rao's score tests.
(ii) Repeat (i) for the parameter $\left( {{\mu }_{1},{\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{1}^{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}}\right)$ .
(iii) Repeat (i) under the assumption that ${\sigma }_{1}^{2} = {\sigma }_{2}^{2} = {\sigma }^{2}$ .
(iv) Repeat (iii) for the parameter $\left( {{\mu }_{1},{\mu }_{2},{\sigma }^{2}}\right)$ .
answer: (i) For $(\mu_1,\mu_2)$: LR set $\left\{(\mu_1,\mu_2): [\sigma_1^2(\mu_1)]^{n_1/2}[\sigma_2^2(\mu_2)]^{n_2/2} \le \widehat{\sigma}_1^{n_1}\widehat{\sigma}_2^{n_2} e^{\chi^2_{2,\alpha}/2}\right\}$；Wald set $\left\{(\mu_1,\mu_2): \dfrac{n_1(\bar X_1-\mu_1)^2}{\widehat{\sigma}_1^2}+\dfrac{n_2(\bar X_2-\mu_2)^2}{\widehat{\sigma}_2^2}\le \chi^2_{2,\alpha}\right\}$；Score set $\left\{(\mu_1,\mu_2): \dfrac{n_1(\bar X_1-\mu_1)^2}{\sigma_1^2(\mu_1)}+\dfrac{n_2(\bar X_2-\mu_2)^2}{\sigma_2^2(\mu_2)}\le \chi^2_{2,\alpha}\right\}$. (ii) For $\theta=(\mu_1,\mu_2,\sigma_1^2,\sigma_2^2)$: LR set $\left\{\theta: \sigma_1^{n_1}\sigma_2^{n_2} e^{n_1\sigma_1^2(\mu_1)/(2\sigma_1^2)+n_2\sigma_2^2(\mu_2)/(2\sigma_2^2)}\le \widehat{\sigma}_1^{n_1}\widehat{\sigma}_2^{n_2} e^{(n_1+n_2+\chi^2_{4,\alpha})/2}\right\}$；Wald set $\left\{\theta: \sum_{i=1}^2\left[\dfrac{n_i(\bar X_i-\mu_i)^2}{\widehat{\sigma}_i^2}+\dfrac{n_i(\widehat{\sigma}_i^2-\sigma_i^2)^2}{2\widehat{\sigma}_i^4}\right]\le \chi^2_{4,\alpha}\right\}$；Score set $\left\{\theta: \sum_{i=1}^2\left[\dfrac{n_i(\bar X_i-\mu_i)^2}{\sigma_i^2}+\dfrac{2\sigma_i^4}{n_i}\left(\dfrac{n_i\sigma_i^2(\mu_i)}{2\sigma_i^4}-\dfrac{n_i}{2\sigma_i^2}\right)^2\right]\le \chi^2_{4,\alpha}\right\}$. (iii) Under $\sigma_1^2=\sigma_2^2=\sigma^2$, for $(\mu_1,\mu_2)$: LR set $\left\{(\mu_1,\mu_2): \sigma^2(\mu_1,\mu_2)\le e^{\chi^2_{2,\alpha}/(n_1+n_2)}\widehat{\sigma}^2\right\}$；Wald set $\left\{(\mu_1,\mu_2): n_1(\bar X_1-\mu_1)^2+n_2(\bar X_2-\mu_2)^2\le \widehat{\sigma}^2\chi^2_{2,\alpha}\right\}$；Score set $\left\{(\mu_1,\mu_2): n_1(\bar X_1-\mu_1)^2+n_2(\bar X_2-\mu_2)^2\le \sigma^2(\mu_1,\mu_2)\chi^2_{2,\alpha}\right\}$. (iv) For $\theta=(\mu_1,\mu_2,\sigma^2)$: LR set $\left\{\theta: \sigma^2 e^{\sigma^2(\mu_1,\mu_2)/\sigma^2}\le \widehat{\sigma}^2 e^{1+\chi^2_{3,\alpha}/(n_1+n_2)}\right\}$；Wald set $\left\{\theta: \sum_{i=1}^2\dfrac{n_i(\bar X_i-\mu_i)^2}{\widehat{\sigma}^2}+\dfrac{(n_1+n_2)(\widehat{\sigma}^2-\sigma^2)^2}{2\widehat{\sigma}^4}\le \chi^2_{3,\alpha}\right\}$；Score set $\left\{\theta: \sum_{i=1}^2\dfrac{n_i(\bar X_i-\mu_i)^2}{\sigma^2}+\dfrac{n_1+n_2}{2}\left[\dfrac{\sigma^2(\mu_1,\mu_2)}{\sigma^2}-1\right]^2\le \chi^2_{3,\alpha}\right\}$
explanation:
This problem uses the ideas of joint confidence regions, likelihood ratio tests, and large-sample Wald/score procedures. The confidence sets are obtained by inverting the corresponding asymptotic acceptance regions, with the test statistics converging to chi-square distributions whose degrees of freedom equal the dimension of the parameter of interest.

For convenience, define for each sample
$\bar X_i=\dfrac1{n_i}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}X_{ij}$,
$\widehat{\sigma}_i^2=\dfrac1{n_i}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}(X_{ij}-\bar X_i)^2$,
and when a candidate mean $t$ is imposed,
$\sigma_i^2(t)=\dfrac1{n_i}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}(X_{ij}-t)^2$, $i=1,2$.

(i) Confidence sets for $(\mu_1,\mu_2)$ when $(\mu_1,\mu_2,\sigma_1^2,\sigma_2^2)$ are all unknown.
The likelihood is proportional to
$L\propto \sigma_1^{-n_1}\sigma_2^{-n_2}\exp\left\{-\sum_{i=1}^2\frac1{2\sigma_i^2}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}(X_{ij}-\mu_i)^2\right\}$.
The MLE of the full parameter vector is
$(\bar X_1,\widehat{\sigma}_1^2,\bar X_2,\widehat{\sigma}_2^2)$.
If $(\mu_1,\mu_2)$ are fixed, the constrained MLEs of the variances are $\sigma_i^2(\mu_i)$.

For the LR region, use the asymptotic criterion
$-2\log \Lambda(\mu_1,\mu_2)\le \chi^2_{2,\alpha}$.
Substituting the unrestricted and restricted maximized likelihoods gives the acceptance region
$\left\{(\mu_1,\mu_2): [\sigma_1^2(\mu_1)]^{n_1/2}[\sigma_2^2(\mu_2)]^{n_2/2}\le \widehat{\sigma}_1^{n_1}\widehat{\sigma}_2^{n_2}e^{\chi^2_{2,\alpha}/2}\right\}$.

For the Wald region, use the asymptotic covariance from Fisher information. The Fisher information matrix for $(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2,\mu_2,\sigma_2^2)$ is diagonal with entries
$\dfrac{n_1}{\sigma_1^2},\ \dfrac{n_1}{2\sigma_1^4},\ \dfrac{n_2}{\sigma_2^2},\ \dfrac{n_2}{2\sigma_2^4}$.
Hence for the subvector $(\mu_1,\mu_2)$, the Wald statistic is
$\dfrac{n_1(\bar X_1-\mu_1)^2}{\widehat{\sigma}_1^2}+\dfrac{n_2(\bar X_2-\mu_2)^2}{\widehat{\sigma}_2^2}$,
so the confidence region is
$\left\{(\mu_1,\mu_2): \dfrac{n_1(\bar X_1-\mu_1)^2}{\widehat{\sigma}_1^2}+\dfrac{n_2(\bar X_2-\mu_2)^2}{\widehat{\sigma}_2^2}\le \chi^2_{2,\alpha}\right\}$.

For the score region, evaluate the score under the constrained parameter. The score components relevant to the means are
$\dfrac{n_1(\bar X_1-\mu_1)}{\sigma_1^2}$ and $\dfrac{n_2(\bar X_2-\mu_2)}{\sigma_2^2}$.
Using the constrained variance estimates $\sigma_i^2(\mu_i)$ in the score statistic leads to
$\left\{(\mu_1,\mu_2): \dfrac{n_1(\bar X_1-\mu_1)^2}{\sigma_1^2(\mu_1)}+\dfrac{n_2(\bar X_2-\mu_2)^2}{\sigma_2^2(\mu_2)}\le \chi^2_{2,\alpha}\right\}$.

(ii) Confidence sets for $\theta=(\mu_1,\mu_2,\sigma_1^2,\sigma_2^2)$.
Now the parameter dimension is $4$, so the asymptotic cutoff is $\chi^2_{4,\alpha}$.

For the LR region, compare the likelihood at a generic $\theta$ with the maximized likelihood at the full MLE. After simplification, the acceptance region is
$\left\{\theta: \sigma_1^{n_1}\sigma_2^{n_2}\exp\left(\frac{n_1\sigma_1^2(\mu_1)}{2\sigma_1^2}+\frac{n_2\sigma_2^2(\mu_2)}{2\sigma_2^2}\right)\le \widehat{\sigma}_1^{n_1}\widehat{\sigma}_2^{n_2}\exp\left(\frac{n_1+n_2+\chi^2_{4,\alpha}}{2}\right)\right\}$.

For the Wald region, use the inverse Fisher information evaluated at the MLE. Since the information matrix is diagonal, the quadratic form separates into two samples and two parameters per sample:
$\sum_{i=1}^2\left[\frac{n_i(\bar X_i-\mu_i)^2}{\widehat{\sigma}_i^2}+\frac{n_i(\widehat{\sigma}_i^2-\sigma_i^2)^2}{2\widehat{\sigma}_i^4}\right]\le \chi^2_{4,\alpha}$.
Therefore the Wald confidence set is exactly
$\left\{\theta: \sum_{i=1}^2\left[\frac{n_i(\bar X_i-\mu_i)^2}{\widehat{\sigma}_i^2}+\frac{n_i(\widehat{\sigma}_i^2-\sigma_i^2)^2}{2\widehat{\sigma}_i^4}\right]\le \chi^2_{4,\alpha}\right\}$.

For the score region, use the score vector at the candidate $\theta$ and the Fisher information at $\theta$. The variance component of the score for sample $i$ is
$\frac{n_i\sigma_i^2(\mu_i)}{2\sigma_i^4}-\frac{n_i}{2\sigma_i^2}$.
Thus the score statistic becomes
$\sum_{i=1}^2\left[\frac{n_i(\bar X_i-\mu_i)^2}{\sigma_i^2}+\frac{2\sigma_i^4}{n_i}\left(\frac{n_i\sigma_i^2(\mu_i)}{2\sigma_i^4}-\frac{n_i}{2\sigma_i^2}\right)^2\right]$,
so the score confidence set is
$\left\{\theta: \sum_{i=1}^2\left[\frac{n_i(\bar X_i-\mu_i)^2}{\sigma_i^2}+\frac{2\sigma_i^4}{n_i}\left(\frac{n_i\sigma_i^2(\mu_i)}{2\sigma_i^4}-\frac{n_i}{2\sigma_i^2}\right)^2\right]\le \chi^2_{4,\alpha}\right\}$.

(iii) Confidence sets for $(\mu_1,\mu_2)$ under the restriction $\sigma_1^2=\sigma_2^2=\sigma^2$.
Now the model has common variance. The MLE of $(\mu_1,\mu_2,\sigma^2)$ is
$(\bar X_1,\bar X_2,\widehat{\sigma}^2)$,
where
$\widehat{\sigma}^2=\frac1{n_1+n_2}\sum_{i=1}^2\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}(X_{ij}-\bar X_i)^2$.
If $(\mu_1,\mu_2)$ are fixed, the constrained MLE of the common variance is
$\sigma^2(\mu_1,\mu_2)=\frac1{n_1+n_2}\sum_{i=1}^2\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}(X_{ij}-\mu_i)^2$.

For the LR region, use $-2\log\Lambda(\mu_1,\mu_2)\le \chi^2_{2,\alpha}$. This yields
$\left\{(\mu_1,\mu_2): \sigma^2(\mu_1,\mu_2)\le e^{\chi^2_{2,\alpha}/(n_1+n_2)}\widehat{\sigma}^2\right\}$.

For Wald and score, first compute the score vector for $(\mu_1,\mu_2,\sigma^2)$:
$\left(\frac{n_1(\bar X_1-\mu_1)}{\sigma^2},\frac{n_2(\bar X_2-\mu_2)}{\sigma^2},\frac{(n_1+n_2)\sigma^2(\mu_1,\mu_2)}{2\sigma^4}-\frac{n_1+n_2}{2\sigma^2}\right)$.
The Fisher information matrix is diagonal with entries
$\dfrac{n_1}{\sigma^2},\ \dfrac{n_2}{\sigma^2},\ \dfrac{n_1+n_2}{2\sigma^4}$.
Therefore, for the two-dimensional mean parameter, the Wald statistic is
$\frac{n_1(\bar X_1-\mu_1)^2}{\widehat{\sigma}^2}+\frac{n_2(\bar X_2-\mu_2)^2}{\widehat{\sigma}^2}$,
which is equivalent to
$n_1(\bar X_1-\mu_1)^2+n_2(\bar X_2-\mu_2)^2\le \widehat{\sigma}^2\chi^2_{2,\alpha}$.
So the Wald confidence set is
$\left\{(\mu_1,\mu_2): n_1(\bar X_1-\mu_1)^2+n_2(\bar X_2-\mu_2)^2\le \widehat{\sigma}^2\chi^2_{2,\alpha}\right\}$.

For the score test, use the candidate-dependent information, giving
$n_1(\bar X_1-\mu_1)^2+n_2(\bar X_2-\mu_2)^2\le \sigma^2(\mu_1,\mu_2)\chi^2_{2,\alpha}$.
Hence the score confidence set is
$\left\{(\mu_1,\mu_2): n_1(\bar X_1-\mu_1)^2+n_2(\bar X_2-\mu_2)^2\le \sigma^2(\mu_1,\mu_2)\chi^2_{2,\alpha}\right\}$.

(iv) Confidence sets for $\theta=(\mu_1,\mu_2,\sigma^2)$ under the common-variance assumption.
Now the parameter dimension is $3$, so the cutoff is $\chi^2_{3,\alpha}$.

For the LR region, compare the likelihood at a generic $\theta$ with the maximized likelihood at $(\bar X_1,\bar X_2,\widehat{\sigma}^2)$. The resulting acceptance region is
$\left\{\theta: \sigma^2\exp\left(\frac{\sigma^2(\mu_1,\mu_2)}{\sigma^2}\right)\le \widehat{\sigma}^2\exp\left(1+\frac{\chi^2_{3,\alpha}}{n_1+n_2}\right)\right\}$.

For the Wald region, use the information matrix at the MLE. The quadratic form becomes
$\sum_{i=1}^2\frac{n_i(\bar X_i-\mu_i)^2}{\widehat{\sigma}^2}+\frac{(n_1+n_2)(\widehat{\sigma}^2-\sigma^2)^2}{2\widehat{\sigma}^4}\le \chi^2_{3,\alpha}$.
Therefore the Wald confidence set is
$\left\{\theta: \sum_{i=1}^2\frac{n_i(\bar X_i-\mu_i)^2}{\widehat{\sigma}^2}+\frac{(n_1+n_2)(\widehat{\sigma}^2-\sigma^2)^2}{2\widehat{\sigma}^4}\le \chi^2_{3,\alpha}\right\}$.

For the score region, use the score vector and the Fisher information at the candidate $\theta$. This gives the statistic
$\sum_{i=1}^2\frac{n_i(\bar X_i-\mu_i)^2}{\sigma^2}+\frac{n_1+n_2}{2}\left[\frac{\sigma^2(\mu_1,\mu_2)}{\sigma^2}-1\right]^2$,
so the score confidence set is
$\left\{\theta: \sum_{i=1}^2\frac{n_i(\bar X_i-\mu_i)^2}{\sigma^2}+\frac{n_1+n_2}{2}\left[\frac{\sigma^2(\mu_1,\mu_2)}{\sigma^2}-1\right]^2\le \chi^2_{3,\alpha}\right\}$.

In conclusion, each subproblem is solved by forming the LR, Wald, and score test acceptance regions and then inverting them, with chi-square degrees of freedom $2$, $4$, $2$, and $3$ for parts (i)–(iv), respectively.
subject: Mathematical Statistics

question: Let $X$ be a vector of $n$ observations having distribution ${N}_{n}\left( {{Z\beta },{\sigma }^{2}{I}_{n}}\right)$ , where $Z$ is a known $n \times p$ matrix of rank $r \leq p < n,\beta$ is an unknown $p$ -vector, and ${\sigma }^{2} > 0$ is unknown. Find $1 - \alpha$ asymptotically correct confidence sets for $\theta = {L\beta }$ by inverting acceptance regions of LR tests, Wald’s tests, and Rao’s score tests, where $L$ is an $s \times p$ matrix of rank $s$ and all rows of $L$ are in $\mathcal{R}\left( Z^{\tau}\right)$ .
answer:
Let $\widehat\beta$ be an unrestricted least-squares solution, define
$$R=\|X-Z\widehat\beta\|^2,$$
and, under the restriction $L\beta=\theta$, define
$$R_\theta=\min_{\beta:L\beta=\theta}\|X-Z\beta\|^2,
\qquad \widehat\sigma^2=R/n.$$
With a generalized inverse where needed,
$$R_\theta-R=(L\widehat\beta-\theta)^\tau
[L(Z^\tau Z)^{-}L^\tau]^{-1}(L\widehat\beta-\theta).$$
Define the partial-$F$ statistic
$$W(X,\theta)=\frac{(R_\theta-R)/s}{R/(n-r)}.$$

The Wald confidence set is
$$\left\{\theta:(L\widehat\beta-\theta)^\tau[L(Z^\tau Z)^{-}L^\tau]^{-1}
(L\widehat\beta-\theta)\le\widehat\sigma^2\chi^2_{s,\alpha}\right\}.$$
If $\widehat\beta(\theta)$ is the constrained least-squares solution, the Rao score set is
$$\left\{\theta:n[X-Z\widehat\beta(\theta)]^\tau Z(Z^\tau Z)^{-}Z^\tau
[X-Z\widehat\beta(\theta)]\le R_\theta\chi^2_{s,\alpha}\right\}.$$
Finally,
$$\lambda(\theta)=\left(\frac R{R_\theta}\right)^{n/2}
=\left[1+\frac{sW(X,\theta)}{n-r}\right]^{-n/2},$$
so the LR confidence set is
$$\left\{\theta:sW(X,\theta)\le(n-r)
[e^{\chi^2_{s,\alpha}/n}-1]\right\}.$$
All quantities needed to compute the three sets are defined above.
explanation:
Because every row of $L$ lies in $\mathcal R(Z^\tau)$, the linear function $L\beta$ is estimable. Let $\widehat\beta$ be an unrestricted least-squares solution and put
\[
R=\|X-Z\widehat\beta\|^2,
\qquad
\widehat\sigma^2=R/n.
\]
For a proposed value $\theta$, let $\widehat\beta(\theta)$ minimize the residual sum of squares subject to $L\beta=\theta$, and write
\[
R_\theta=\|X-Z\widehat\beta(\theta)\|^2.
\]

Set
\[
C=L(Z^\tau Z)^{-}L^\tau.
\]
The constrained least-squares identity gives
\[
R_\theta-R
=(L\widehat\beta-\theta)^\tau C^{-1}(L\widehat\beta-\theta).
\]
This identity converts each test acceptance region into a confidence set for $\theta$.

For the Wald test, the asymptotic quadratic statistic is
\[
\frac{(L\widehat\beta-\theta)^\tau C^{-1}(L\widehat\beta-\theta)}
{\widehat\sigma^2}.
\]
Inverting its acceptance region gives
\[
\left\{\theta:(L\widehat\beta-\theta)^\tau C^{-1}
(L\widehat\beta-\theta)\le\widehat\sigma^2\chi^2_{s,\alpha}\right\}.
\]

For Rao's score test, the score is evaluated at the constrained estimator. With
\[
P_Z=Z(Z^\tau Z)^{-}Z^\tau,
\]
the acceptance condition is
\[
n[X-Z\widehat\beta(\theta)]^\tau P_Z[X-Z\widehat\beta(\theta)]
\le R_\theta\chi^2_{s,\alpha},
\]
which gives the score confidence set stated in the answer.

For the LR test, maximizing over $\sigma^2$ under the unrestricted and restricted models gives
\[
\lambda(\theta)=\left(\frac R{R_\theta}\right)^{n/2}.
\]
If
\[
W(X,\theta)=\frac{(R_\theta-R)/s}{R/(n-r)},
\]
then
\[
\lambda(\theta)=\left[1+\frac{sW(X,\theta)}{n-r}\right]^{-n/2}.
\]
Inverting the asymptotic LR acceptance condition yields
\[
\left\{\theta:sW(X,\theta)\le(n-r)
[e^{\chi^2_{s,\alpha}/n}-1]\right\}.
\]
Thus the three confidence regions arise by applying the Wald, score, and likelihood-ratio quadratic restrictions to the same constrained least-squares decomposition.
subject: Mathematical Statistics

question:
Let $\left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right)$ be a random sample from a continuous cumulative distribution function $F$ on $\mathcal{R}$ that is twice differentiable at $\theta = {F}^{-1}\left( p\right) ,0 < p < 1$ , with ${F}^{\prime }\left( \theta \right) > 0$ .
(i) Let $\left\{ {k}_{n}\right\}$ be a sequence of integers satisfying ${k}_{n}/n = p + c{n}^{-1/2} + o\left( {n}^{-1/2}\right)$ with a constant $c$ . Show that$$
\sqrt{n}\left( {{X}_{\left( {k}_{n}\right) } - \widehat{\theta }}\right) = c/{F}^{\prime }\left( \theta \right) + o\left( 1\right) \text{ a.s., }
$$
where ${X}_{\left( j\right) }$ is the $j$ th order statistic and $\widehat{\theta }$ is the sample $p$ th quantile.
(ii) Show that $\sqrt{n}\left( {{X}_{\left( {k}_{n}\right) } - \theta }\right) {F}^{\prime }\left( \theta \right) { \rightarrow }_{d}N\left( {c, p\left( {1 - p}\right) }\right)$ .
(iii) Let $\left\{ {k}_{1n}\right\}$ and $\left\{ {k}_{2n}\right\}$ be two sequences of integers satisfying $1 \leq {k}_{1n} < \; {k}_{2n} \leq n$$$
{k}_{1n}/n = p - {z}_{\alpha /2}\sqrt{p\left( {1 - p}\right) /n} + o\left( {n}^{-1/2}\right) ,
$$
and$$
{k}_{2n}/n = p + {z}_{\alpha /2}\sqrt{p\left( {1 - p}\right) /n} + o\left( {n}^{-1/2}\right) ,
$$
where ${z}_{\alpha }$ is the $\left( {1 - \alpha }\right)$ th quantile of $N\left( {0,1}\right)$ . Let $C\left( X\right) = \left\lbrack {{X}_{\left( {k}_{1n}\right) },{X}_{\left( {k}_{2n}\right) }}\right\rbrack$ . Show that $\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}P\left( {\theta \in C\left( X\right) }\right) = 1 - \alpha$ , using the result in part (ii).
(iv) Construct a consistent estimator of the asymptotic variance of the sample median, using the interval $C\left( X\right)$ .
keypoint: 样本分位数与样本中位数
answer:
(i) By the Bahadur representation (e.g., Theorem 7.8 in Shao, 2003),$$
{X}_{\left( {k}_{n}\right) } = \theta + \frac{\left( {{k}_{n}/n}\right) - {F}_{n}\left( \theta \right) }{{F}^{\prime }\left( \theta \right) } + o\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \text{ a.s., }
$$
where ${F}_{n}$ is the empirical distribution. For the $p$ th sample quantile, the Bahadur representation is$$
\widehat{\theta } = \theta + \frac{p - {F}_{n}\left( \theta \right) }{{F}^{\prime }\left( \theta \right) } + o\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \text{ a.s. }
$$
The result follows by taking the difference of the two previous equations. (ii) Note that$$
\sqrt{n}\left( {{X}_{\left( {k}_{n}\right) } - \theta }\right) {F}^{\prime }\left( \theta \right) = \sqrt{n}\left( {{X}_{\left( {k}_{n}\right) } - \widehat{\theta }}\right) {F}^{\prime }\left( \theta \right) + \sqrt{n}\left( {\widehat{\theta } - \theta }\right) {F}^{\prime }\left( \theta \right) .
$$
By (i),$$
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{n}\sqrt{n}\left( {{X}_{\left( {k}_{n}\right) } - {\widehat{\theta }}_{p}}\right) {F}^{\prime }\left( \theta \right) = c\text{ a.s. }
$$
By Theorem 5.10 in Shao (2003),$$
\sqrt{n}\left( {\widehat{\theta } - \theta }\right) {F}^{\prime }\left( \theta \right) { \rightarrow }_{d}N\left( {0, p\left( {1 - p}\right) }\right) .
$$
Then, by Slusky's Theorem,$$
\sqrt{n}\left( {{X}_{\left( {k}_{n}\right) } - \theta }\right) {F}^{\prime }\left( \theta \right) { \rightarrow }_{d}N\left( {c, p\left( {1 - p}\right) }\right) .
$$
(iii) By (ii),$$
\sqrt{n}\left( {{X}_{\left( {k}_{1n}\right) } - \theta }\right) {F}^{\prime }\left( \theta \right) { \rightarrow }_{d}N\left( {-{z}_{\alpha /2}\sqrt{p\left( {1 - p}\right) }, p\left( {1 - p}\right) }\right)
$$
and$$
\sqrt{n}\left( {{X}_{\left( {k}_{2n}\right) } - \theta }\right) {F}^{\prime }\left( \theta \right) { \rightarrow }_{d}N\left( {{z}_{\alpha /2}\sqrt{p\left( {1 - p}\right) }, p\left( {1 - p}\right) }\right) .
$$
Let $\Phi$ be the cumulative distribution function of $N\left( {0,1}\right)$ . Then$$
P\left( {{X}_{\left( {k}_{1n}\right) } > \theta }\right) = P\left( {\sqrt{n}\left( {{X}_{\left( {k}_{1n}\right) } - \theta }\right) {F}^{\prime }\left( \theta \right) > 0}\right) \rightarrow 1 - \Phi \left( {z}_{\alpha /2}\right) = \alpha /2
$$
and$$
P\left( {{X}_{\left( {k}_{2n}\right) } < \theta }\right) = P\left( {\sqrt{n}\left( {{X}_{\left( {k}_{2n}\right) } - \theta }\right) {F}^{\prime }\left( \theta \right) < 0}\right) \rightarrow \Phi \left( {-{z}_{\alpha /2}}\right) = \alpha /2.
$$
The result follows from$$
P\left( {\theta \in C\left( X\right) }\right) = 1 - P\left( {{X}_{\left( {k}_{1n}\right) } > \theta }\right) - P\left( {{X}_{\left( {k}_{2n}\right) } < \theta }\right) .
$$
(iv) Let $p = \frac{1}{2}$ . If ${F}^{\prime }$ exists and is positive at $\theta$ , the median of $F$ , then the asymptotic variance of the sample median is ${\left\{ 4n{\left\lbrack {F}^{\prime }\left( \theta \right) \right\rbrack }^{2}\right\} }^{-1}$ . The length of the interval $C\left( X\right)$ is ${X}_{\left( {k}_{2n}\right) } - {X}_{\left( {k}_{1n}\right) }$ . By the result in (i), this length is equal to$$
\frac{{z}_{\alpha /2}}{\sqrt{n}{F}^{\prime }\left( \theta \right) } + o\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \text{ a.s., }
$$
i.e.,$$
\frac{{\left\lbrack {X}_{\left( {k}_{2n}\right) } - {X}_{\left( {k}_{1n}\right) }\right\rbrack }^{2}}{4{z}_{\alpha /2}^{2}} = \frac{1}{{4n}{\left\lbrack {F}^{\prime }\left( \theta \right) \right\rbrack }^{2}} + o\left( \frac{1}{n}\right) \text{ a.s. }
$$
Therefore, ${\left\lbrack {X}_{\left( {k}_{2n}\right) } - {X}_{\left( {k}_{1n}\right) }\right\rbrack }^{2}/\left( {4{z}_{\alpha /2}^{2}}\right)$ is a consistent estimator of the asymptotic variance of the sample median.
explanation:
This problem uses the asymptotic theory of order statistics and sample quantiles, especially the Bahadur representation, and then applies asymptotic distribution ideas together with Slutsky's theorem. It also uses confidence-interval construction from order statistics and the asymptotic variance formula for the sample median.

(i) We first compare the order statistic $X_{(k_n)}$ with the sample $p$th quantile $\widehat\theta$. By the Bahadur representation for order statistics,
$X_{(k_n)}=\theta+\dfrac{k_n/n-F_n(\theta)}{F'(\theta)}+o\!\left(\dfrac1{\sqrt n}\right)$ a.s.,
where $F_n$ is the empirical distribution function.

For the sample $p$th quantile $\widehat\theta$, the corresponding Bahadur representation is
$\widehat\theta=\theta+\dfrac{p-F_n(\theta)}{F'(\theta)}+o\!\left(\dfrac1{\sqrt n}\right)$ a.s.

Subtracting the second expansion from the first gives
$X_{(k_n)}-\widehat\theta=\dfrac{k_n/n-p}{F'(\theta)}+o\!\left(\dfrac1{\sqrt n}\right)$ a.s.

Now use the assumption
$\dfrac{k_n}{n}=p+cn^{-1/2}+o\!\left(n^{-1/2}\right)$,
so that
$\dfrac{k_n}{n}-p=cn^{-1/2}+o\!\left(n^{-1/2}\right)$.
Multiplying by $\sqrt n$ yields
$\sqrt n\bigl(X_{(k_n)}-\widehat\theta\bigr)=\dfrac{c}{F'(\theta)}+o(1)$ a.s.
This proves part (i).

(ii) Write
$\sqrt n\bigl(X_{(k_n)}-\theta\bigr)F'(\theta)=\sqrt n\bigl(X_{(k_n)}-\widehat\theta\bigr)F'(\theta)+\sqrt n\bigl(\widehat\theta-\theta\bigr)F'(\theta)$.

By part (i),
$\sqrt n\bigl(X_{(k_n)}-\widehat\theta\bigr)F'(\theta)\to c$ a.s.
Hence this term converges in probability to the constant $c$.

For the sample $p$th quantile, the standard asymptotic normality result gives
$\sqrt n\bigl(\widehat\theta-\theta\bigr)F'(\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N\bigl(0,\,p(1-p)\bigr)$.

Therefore, by Slutsky's theorem, the sum converges in distribution to a normal law with mean shifted by $c$:
$\sqrt n\bigl(X_{(k_n)}-\theta\bigr)F'(\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N\bigl(c,\,p(1-p)\bigr)$.
This proves part (ii).

(iii) Now apply part (ii) to the two sequences $k_{1n}$ and $k_{2n}$. From
$\dfrac{k_{1n}}{n}=p-z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}}+o\!\left(n^{-1/2}\right)$,
we identify
$c=-z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{p(1-p)}$.
Hence, by part (ii),
$\sqrt n\bigl(X_{(k_{1n})}-\theta\bigr)F'(\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N\Bigl(-z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{p(1-p)},\,p(1-p)\Bigr)$.

Similarly, from
$\dfrac{k_{2n}}{n}=p+z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}}+o\!\left(n^{-1/2}\right)$,
we have
$c=z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{p(1-p)}$,
so
$\sqrt n\bigl(X_{(k_{2n})}-\theta\bigr)F'(\theta)\xrightarrow{d}N\Bigl(z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{p(1-p)},\,p(1-p)\Bigr)$.

Let $\Phi$ denote the standard normal distribution function. Then
$P\bigl(X_{(k_{1n})}>\theta\bigr)=P\Bigl(\sqrt n\bigl(X_{(k_{1n})}-\theta\bigr)F'(\theta)>0\Bigr)$.
Under the limiting normal distribution, standardizing gives the limit
$1-\Phi(z_{\alpha/2})=\alpha/2$.
Thus,
$P\bigl(X_{(k_{1n})}>\theta\bigr)\to \alpha/2$.

Likewise,
$P\bigl(X_{(k_{2n})}<\theta\bigr)=P\Bigl(\sqrt n\bigl(X_{(k_{2n})}-\theta\bigr)F'(\theta)<0\Bigr)\to \Phi(-z_{\alpha/2})=\alpha/2$.

Since $C(X)=[X_{(k_{1n})},X_{(k_{2n})}]$, the event $\{\theta\in C(X)\}$ is equivalent to
$\{X_{(k_{1n})}\le \theta\le X_{(k_{2n})}\}$.
Therefore,
$P\bigl(\theta\in C(X)\bigr)=1-P\bigl(X_{(k_{1n})}>\theta\bigr)-P\bigl(X_{(k_{2n})}<\theta\bigr)$.
Taking limits gives
$\lim_{n\to\infty}P\bigl(\theta\in C(X)\bigr)=1-\alpha/2-\alpha/2=1-\alpha$.
This proves part (iii).

(iv) To estimate the asymptotic variance of the sample median, set $p=\tfrac12$. If $\theta$ is the population median and $F'(\theta)>0$, then the asymptotic variance of the sample median is
$\dfrac{1}{4n[F'(\theta)]^2}$.

Now consider the interval length
$X_{(k_{2n})}-X_{(k_{1n})}$.
Using the result of part (i), the spacing between these two order statistics is asymptotically determined by the difference of the corresponding $c$ values. For $p=\tfrac12$, those values are $\pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{p(1-p)}=\pm z_{\alpha/2}/2$. Hence the interval length satisfies
$X_{(k_{2n})}-X_{(k_{1n})}=\dfrac{z_{\alpha/2}}{\sqrt n\,F'(\theta)}+o\!\left(\dfrac1{\sqrt n}\right)$ a.s.

Squaring both sides,
$\bigl[X_{(k_{2n})}-X_{(k_{1n})}\bigr]^2=\dfrac{z_{\alpha/2}^2}{n[F'(\theta)]^2}+o\!\left(\dfrac1n\right)$ a.s.
Dividing by $4z_{\alpha/2}^2$ yields
$\dfrac{\bigl[X_{(k_{2n})}-X_{(k_{1n})}\bigr]^2}{4z_{\alpha/2}^2}=\dfrac{1}{4n[F'(\theta)]^2}+o\!\left(\dfrac1n\right)$ a.s.

The right-hand side is exactly the asymptotic variance of the sample median plus a term tending to $0$. Therefore,
$\dfrac{\left[X_{(k_{2n})}-X_{(k_{1n})}\right]^2}{4z_{\alpha/2}^2}$
is a consistent estimator of the asymptotic variance of the sample median.

In conclusion: part (i) follows from subtracting two Bahadur representations; part (ii) follows by adding the quantile fluctuation term and using Slutsky's theorem; part (iii) gives an asymptotic $(1-\alpha)$ confidence interval for $\theta$ based on order statistics; and part (iv) constructs a consistent estimator of the asymptotic variance of the sample median from the squared interval length.

question: Let ${C}_{t,\alpha }\left( X\right)$ be a confidence interval for ${\theta }_{t}$ with confidence coefficient $1 - \alpha , t = 1,\ldots , k$ . Suppose that ${C}_{1,\alpha }\left( X\right) ,\ldots ,{C}_{k,\alpha }\left( X\right)$ are independent for any $\alpha$ . Show how to construct simultaneous confidence intervals for ${\theta }_{t}, t = 1,\ldots , k$ , with confidence coefficient $1 - \alpha$ .
keypoint: 多个事件的相互独立性
answer:
Let ${a}_{k} = 1 - {\left( 1 - \alpha \right) }^{1/k}$ . By the independence of ${C}_{t,{a}_{k}}\left( X\right)$ , $t = 1,\ldots , k,$$$
P\left( {{\theta }_{t} \in {C}_{t,{a}_{k}}\left( X\right) ,\;t = 1,\ldots , k}\right) = \mathop{\prod }\limits_{{t = 1}}^{k}P\left( {{\theta }_{t} \in {C}_{t,{a}_{k}}\left( X\right) }\right)
$$$$
= \mathop{\prod }\limits_{{t = 1}}^{k}{\left( 1 - \alpha \right) }^{1/k}
$$$$
= 1 - \alpha \text{ . }
$$
Hence, ${C}_{t,{a}_{k}}\left( X\right) , t = 1,\ldots , k$ , are simultaneous confidence intervals for ${\theta }_{t}$ , $t = 1,\ldots , k$ , with confidence coefficient $1 - \alpha$ .
explanation:
This problem uses the ideas of confidence intervals and confidence level, together with mutual independence of events. The key is to choose the individual confidence level so that the probability that all $k$ intervals cover their respective parameters simultaneously is exactly $1-\alpha$.

For each $t=1,\ldots,k$, we are given a confidence interval $C_{t,\alpha}(X)$ for $\theta_t$ with confidence coefficient $1-\alpha$. That means if we replace $\alpha$ by some value $a$, then
$P\bigl(\theta_t\in C_{t,a}(X)\bigr)=1-a.$

We want to construct simultaneous confidence intervals for $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_k$ such that
$P\bigl(\theta_t\in I_t(X),\ t=1,\ldots,k\bigr)=1-\alpha.$

Let the individual error probability be $a_k$, chosen so that the product of the individual coverage probabilities equals $1-\alpha$. Define
$a_k=1-(1-\alpha)^{1/k}.$
Then
$1-a_k=(1-\alpha)^{1/k}.$

Now take the intervals
$C_{t,a_k}(X),\quad t=1,\ldots,k.$
Since these intervals are independent for any $\alpha$, in particular the events
$\{\theta_t\in C_{t,a_k}(X)\},\quad t=1,\ldots,k,$
are independent. Therefore,
\[
P\bigl(\theta_t\in C_{t,a_k}(X),\ t=1,\ldots,k\bigr)
=\prod_{t=1}^k P\bigl(\theta_t\in C_{t,a_k}(X)\bigr).
\]
For each $t$,
\[
P\bigl(\theta_t\in C_{t,a_k}(X)\bigr)=1-a_k=(1-\alpha)^{1/k}.
\]
Hence,
\[
P\bigl(\theta_t\in C_{t,a_k}(X),\ t=1,\ldots,k\bigr)
=\prod_{t=1}^k (1-\alpha)^{1/k}
=(1-\alpha)^{k\cdot (1/k)}
=1-\alpha.
\]
So the collection $C_{t,a_k}(X)$, $t=1,\ldots,k$, gives simultaneous confidence intervals for $\theta_t$, $t=1,\ldots,k$, with overall confidence coefficient $1-\alpha$.

Therefore, the required construction is to use for each parameter the individual confidence interval with level $1-a_k= (1-\alpha)^{1/k}$, where $a_k=1-(1-\alpha)^{1/k}$.

question:
Let $x \in {\mathcal{R}}^{k}$ and $A$ be a $k \times k$ positive definite matrix. Show that$$
{x}^{\tau }{A}^{-1}x = \mathop{\max }\limits_{{y \in {\mathcal{R}}^{k}, y \neq 0}}\frac{{\left( {y}^{\tau }x\right) }^{2}}{{y}^{\tau }{Ay}}.
$$
answer:
If $x = 0$ , then the equality holds. Assume that $x \neq 0$ . By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,$$
{\left( {y}^{\tau }x\right) }^{2} = {\left( {y}^{\tau }{A}^{1/2}{A}^{-1/2}x\right) }^{2} \leq \left( {{y}^{\tau }{Ay}}\right) \left( {{x}^{\tau }{A}^{-1}x}\right) .
$$
Hence,$$
{x}^{\tau }{A}^{-1}x \geq \mathop{\max }\limits_{{y \in {\mathcal{R}}^{k}, y \neq 0}}\frac{{\left( {y}^{\tau }x\right) }^{2}}{{y}^{\tau }{Ay}}.
$$
Let ${y}_{ * } = {A}^{-1}x$ . Then$$
\frac{{\left( {y}_{ * }^{\tau }x\right) }^{2}}{{y}_{ * }^{\tau }A{y}_{ * }} = \frac{{\left( {x}^{\tau }{A}^{-1}x\right) }^{2}}{{x}^{\tau }{A}^{-1}A{A}^{-1}x} = {x}^{\tau }{A}^{-1}x.
$$
Hence,$$
{x}^{\tau }{A}^{-1}x \leq \mathop{\max }\limits_{{y \in {\mathcal{R}}^{k}, y \neq 0}}\frac{{\left( {y}^{\tau }x\right) }^{2}}{{y}^{\tau }{Ay}}
$$
and, thus, the equality holds.
explanation:
This problem uses the keypoint $\text{施瓦兹不等式}$, because the main step is to bound $(y^{\tau}x)^2$ by rewriting it into a form suitable for the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality. It is also related to $\text{置信域}$ in the sense that quadratic forms of the type $x^{\tau}A^{-1}x$ frequently appear in ellipsoidal confidence sets, and this identity gives an extremal characterization of such quadratic forms.

We prove the identity in two parts.

First, consider the case $x=0$. Then for every $y\neq 0$,
$$(y^{\tau}x)^2=0,$$
so
$$\frac{(y^{\tau}x)^2}{y^{\tau}Ay}=0.$$
Hence
$$\max_{y\in\mathcal{R}^k,\,y\neq 0}\frac{(y^{\tau}x)^2}{y^{\tau}Ay}=0=x^{\tau}A^{-1}x,$$
and the equality holds.

Now assume $x\neq 0$. Since $A$ is positive definite, $A^{1/2}$ exists and is invertible. For any $y\in\mathcal{R}^k$ with $y\neq 0$, write
$$y^{\tau}x=y^{\tau}A^{1/2}A^{-1/2}x.$$
Applying the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality to the vectors $A^{1/2}y$ and $A^{-1/2}x$, we get
$$\left(y^{\tau}x\right)^2=\left(y^{\tau}A^{1/2}A^{-1/2}x\right)^2\leq \left(y^{\tau}Ay\right)\left(x^{\tau}A^{-1}x\right).$$
Since $A$ is positive definite and $y\neq 0$, we have $y^{\tau}Ay>0$. Dividing both sides by $y^{\tau}Ay$ yields
$$\frac{(y^{\tau}x)^2}{y^{\tau}Ay}\leq x^{\tau}A^{-1}x.$$
Because this is true for every $y\neq 0$, we obtain
$$\max_{y\in\mathcal{R}^k,\,y\neq 0}\frac{(y^{\tau}x)^2}{y^{\tau}Ay}\leq x^{\tau}A^{-1}x.$$

Next, we show that this upper bound is attained. Choose
$$y_*=A^{-1}x.$$
Since $x\neq 0$ and $A$ is invertible, we have $y_*\neq 0$. Substitute this choice into the ratio:
$$\frac{(y_*^{\tau}x)^2}{y_*^{\tau}Ay_*} = \frac{(x^{\tau}A^{-1}x)^2}{(A^{-1}x)^{\tau}A(A^{-1}x)}.$$
Now simplify the denominator:
$$(A^{-1}x)^{\tau}A(A^{-1}x)=x^{\tau}A^{-1}AA^{-1}x=x^{\tau}A^{-1}x.$$
Therefore,
$$\frac{(y_*^{\tau}x)^2}{y_*^{\tau}Ay_*}=\frac{(x^{\tau}A^{-1}x)^2}{x^{\tau}A^{-1}x}=x^{\tau}A^{-1}x.$$
So there exists a nonzero vector $y_*=A^{-1}x$ such that the ratio equals $x^{\tau}A^{-1}x$. Hence,
$$\max_{y\in\mathcal{R}^k,\,y\neq 0}\frac{(y^{\tau}x)^2}{y^{\tau}Ay}\geq x^{\tau}A^{-1}x.$$

Combining the two inequalities,
$$\max_{y\in\mathcal{R}^k,\,y\neq 0}\frac{(y^{\tau}x)^2}{y^{\tau}Ay}=x^{\tau}A^{-1}x.$$
Thus the required identity is proved.

question:
Let $x \in {\mathcal{R}}^{k}$ and $A$ be a $k \times k$ positive definite matrix.
(i) Suppose that ${y}^{\tau }{A}^{-1}x = 0$ , where $y \in {\mathcal{R}}^{k}$ . Show that$$
{x}^{\tau }{A}^{-1}x = \mathop{\max }\limits_{{c \in {\mathcal{R}}^{k}, c \neq 0,{c}^{\tau }y = 0}}\frac{{\left( {c}^{\tau }x\right) }^{2}}{{c}^{\tau }{Ac}}.
$$
(ii) Let $X$ be a vector of $n$ observations having distribution ${N}_{n}\left( {{Z\beta },{\sigma }^{2}{I}_{n}}\right)$ , where $Z$ is a known $n \times p$ matrix of rank $p < n,\beta$ is an unknown $p$ -vector, and ${\sigma }^{2} > 0$ is unknown. Using the result in (i), construct simultaneous confidence intervals (with confidence coefficient $1 - \alpha$ ) for ${c}^{\tau }\beta , c \in {\mathcal{R}}^{p}$ , $c \neq 0,{c}^{\tau }y = 0$ , where $y \in {\mathcal{R}}^{p}$ satisfies ${Z}^{\tau }{Zy} = 0$ .
answer:
This problem uses the ideas of joint confidence regions and simultaneous confidence intervals in the normal linear model, together with the $F$ distribution. Part (i) is a constrained maximization identity, and part (ii) applies that identity to the least squares estimator to convert an ellipsoidal confidence region into simultaneous confidence intervals.

For (i), we need to prove
$\displaystyle x^{\tau}A^{-1}x=\max_{c\in\mathcal{R}^k,\,c\neq 0,\,c^{\tau}y=0}\frac{(c^{\tau}x)^2}{c^{\tau}Ac}$
under the condition $y^{\tau}A^{-1}x=0$.

First consider the trivial case $x=0$. Then the left-hand side is $0$, and for every $c$ we have $(c^{\tau}x)^2=0$, so the maximum on the right-hand side is also $0$. Hence the equality holds.

Now assume $x\neq0$. If $y=0$, the constraint $c^\tau y=0$ is vacuous, and the standard generalized Rayleigh-quotient identity gives the maximum $x^\tau A^{-1}x$, attained at $c=A^{-1}x$. It remains to consider $y\neq0$. Define the subspace
$\mathcal{Y}=\{c\in\mathcal{R}^k: c^{\tau}y=0\}$.
Choose a $k\times (k-1)$ matrix $D$ whose columns form a basis of $\mathcal{Y}$. Then every nonzero $c\in\mathcal{Y}$ can be written as
$c=Dt$ for some $t\in\mathcal{R}^{k-1}$, $t\neq 0$.

Because $y^{\tau}A^{-1}x=0$, we have $A^{-1}x\in\mathcal{Y}$. Therefore there exists some nonzero vector $l\in\mathcal{R}^{k-1}$ such that
$A^{-1}x=Dl$,
which is equivalent to
$x=ADl$.

Now maximize over the constrained set $\mathcal{Y}$:
$\displaystyle \max_{c\in\mathcal{R}^k,\,c\neq 0,\,c^{\tau}y=0}\frac{(c^{\tau}x)^2}{c^{\tau}Ac}
=\max_{c\in\mathcal{Y},\,c\neq 0}\frac{(c^{\tau}x)^2}{c^{\tau}Ac}$.
Substitute $c=Dt$ and $x=ADl$:
$\displaystyle \max_{t\in\mathcal{R}^{k-1},\,t\neq 0}\frac{(t^{\tau}D^{\tau}ADl)^2}{t^{\tau}D^{\tau}ADt}$.

Let $M=D^{\tau}AD$ and $u=D^{\tau}ADl$. Since $A$ is positive definite and the columns of $D$ are linearly independent, $M$ is positive definite and hence invertible. Using the standard maximization result
$\displaystyle \max_{t\neq 0}\frac{(t^{\tau}u)^2}{t^{\tau}Mt}=u^{\tau}M^{-1}u$,
we get
$\displaystyle \max_{t\neq 0}\frac{(t^{\tau}D^{\tau}ADl)^2}{t^{\tau}D^{\tau}ADt}
=(D^{\tau}ADl)^{\tau}(D^{\tau}AD)^{-1}(D^{\tau}ADl)$.
Since $(D^{\tau}ADl)$ is exactly $Ml$, this becomes
$l^{\tau}(D^{\tau}AD)l$.
Now use $x=ADl$ and $A^{-1}x=Dl$:
$x^{\tau}A^{-1}x=(ADl)^{\tau}A^{-1}(ADl)=l^{\tau}D^{\tau}ADl.
$
Thus
$\displaystyle \max_{c\in\mathcal{R}^k,\,c\neq 0,\,c^{\tau}y=0}\frac{(c^{\tau}x)^2}{c^{\tau}Ac}=x^{\tau}A^{-1}x$,
which proves part (i).

For (ii), let $X\sim N_n(Z\beta,\sigma^2I_n)$, where $Z$ is $n\times p$ with rank $p<n$. Let $\widehat{\beta}$ be the least squares estimator of $\beta$, and define
$\widehat{\sigma}^2=\|X-Z\widehat{\beta}\|^2/(n-p)$.

In the normal linear model, the quadratic form
$\displaystyle \frac{(\widehat{\beta}-\beta)^{\tau}(Z^{\tau}Z)(\widehat{\beta}-\beta)}{p\widehat{\sigma}^2}$
has the $F$ distribution with degrees of freedom $(p,n-p)$, that is,
$\displaystyle \frac{(\widehat{\beta}-\beta)^{\tau}(Z^{\tau}Z)(\widehat{\beta}-\beta)}{p\widehat{\sigma}^2}\sim F_{p,n-p}$.

Now apply part (i) with
$x=\widehat{\beta}-\beta,\qquad A=(Z^{\tau}Z)^{-1}.$
Then
$A^{-1}=Z^{\tau}Z$.
The condition given in the problem is $Z^{\tau}Zy=0$, which implies
$y^{\tau}A^{-1}x=y^{\tau}(Z^{\tau}Z)(\widehat{\beta}-\beta)$,
and the result from part (i) is applied to the constrained family $c^{\tau}y=0$. Therefore,
$\displaystyle \max_{c\in\mathcal{R}^p,\,c\neq 0,\,c^{\tau}y=0}\frac{[c^{\tau}(\widehat{\beta}-\beta)]^2}{\widehat{\sigma}^2\,c^{\tau}(Z^{\tau}Z)^{-1}c}
=\frac{(\widehat{\beta}-\beta)^{\tau}(Z^{\tau}Z)(\widehat{\beta}-\beta)}{\widehat{\sigma}^2}.
$
Divide both sides by $p$:
$\displaystyle \max_{c\in\mathcal{R}^p,\,c\neq 0,\,c^{\tau}y=0}\frac{[c^{\tau}(\widehat{\beta}-\beta)]^2}{p\widehat{\sigma}^2\,c^{\tau}(Z^{\tau}Z)^{-1}c}
=\frac{(\widehat{\beta}-\beta)^{\tau}(Z^{\tau}Z)(\widehat{\beta}-\beta)}{p\widehat{\sigma}^2}.
$
Since the right-hand side has distribution $F_{p,n-p}$, if $F_{p,n-p,\alpha}$ denotes the $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of $F_{p,n-p}$, then
$\displaystyle P\left(\frac{(\widehat{\beta}-\beta)^{\tau}(Z^{\tau}Z)(\widehat{\beta}-\beta)}{p\widehat{\sigma}^2}\leq F_{p,n-p,\alpha}\right)=1-\alpha.$
Equivalently,
$\displaystyle P\left(\max_{c\neq 0,\,c^{\tau}y=0}\frac{[c^{\tau}(\widehat{\beta}-\beta)]^2}{p\widehat{\sigma}^2\,c^{\tau}(Z^{\tau}Z)^{-1}c}\leq F_{p,n-p,\alpha}\right)=1-\alpha.$

This means that with probability $1-\alpha$, for every $c\in\mathcal{R}^p$ such that $c\neq 0$ and $c^{\tau}y=0$,
$\displaystyle [c^{\tau}(\widehat{\beta}-\beta)]^2\leq p\widehat{\sigma}^2F_{p,n-p,\alpha}\,c^{\tau}(Z^{\tau}Z)^{-1}c.$
Taking square roots gives
$\displaystyle |c^{\tau}(\widehat{\beta}-\beta)|\leq \widehat{\sigma}\sqrt{pF_{p,n-p,\alpha}\,c^{\tau}(Z^{\tau}Z)^{-1}c}.$
So the simultaneous confidence intervals are
$\displaystyle \mathcal{I}_c=\left[c^{\tau}\widehat{\beta}-\widehat{\sigma}\sqrt{pF_{p,n-p,\alpha}\,c^{\tau}(Z^{\tau}Z)^{-1}c},\;c^{\tau}\widehat{\beta}+\widehat{\sigma}\sqrt{pF_{p,n-p,\alpha}\,c^{\tau}(Z^{\tau}Z)^{-1}c}\right],$
for all $c\in\mathcal{R}^p$ with $c\neq 0$ and $c^{\tau}y=0$.

Finally,
$\displaystyle P\big(c^{\tau}\beta\in \mathcal{I}_c\text{ for all }c\neq 0,\,c^{\tau}y=0\big)=1-\alpha.$
Hence these are the required $1-\alpha$ simultaneous confidence intervals.

question:
Let $\left( {{X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{n}}\right)$ be independently distributed as $N\left( {{\beta }_{0} + {\beta }_{1}{z}_{i},{\sigma }^{2}}\right) , i = 1,\ldots , n$ , where ${\beta }_{0},{\beta }_{1}$ , and ${\sigma }^{2}$ are unknown and ${z}_{i}$ ’s are known constants satisfying ${S}_{z} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{\left( {z}_{i} - \bar{z}\right) }^{2} > 0,\bar{z} = {n}^{-1}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{z}_{i}$ . Show that$$
{\mathcal{I}}_{z} = \left\lbrack {{\widehat{\beta }}_{0} + {\widehat{\beta }}_{1}z - \widehat{\sigma }\sqrt{2{F}_{2, n - 2,\alpha }D\left( z\right) },{\widehat{\beta }}_{0} + {\widehat{\beta }}_{1}z + \widehat{\sigma }\sqrt{2{F}_{2, n - 2,\alpha }D\left( z\right) }}\right\rbrack ,\;z \in \mathcal{R},
$$
are simultaneous confidence intervals for ${\beta }_{0} + {\beta }_{1}z, z \in \mathcal{R}$ , with confidence coefficient $1 - \alpha$ , where $\left( {{\widehat{\beta }}_{0},{\widehat{\beta }}_{1}}\right)$ is the LSE of $\left( {{\beta }_{0},{\beta }_{1}}\right) , D\left( z\right) = {\left( z - \bar{z}\right) }^{2}/{S}_{z} + \; {n}^{-1}$ , and ${\widehat{\sigma }}^{2} = {\left( n - 2\right) }^{-1}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{\left( {X}_{i} - {\widehat{\beta }}_{0} - {\widehat{\beta }}_{1}{z}_{i}\right) }^{2}$ .
answer:
Let $\beta = \left( {{\beta }_{0},{\beta }_{1}}\right)$ and $\widehat{\beta } = \left( {{\widehat{\beta }}_{0},{\widehat{\beta }}_{1}}\right)$ . Scheffé’s $1 - \alpha$ simultaneous confidence intervals for ${t}^{\tau }\beta , t \in {\mathcal{R}}^{2}$ are$$
\left\lbrack {{t}^{\tau }\widehat{\beta } - \widehat{\sigma }\sqrt{2{F}_{2, n - 2,\alpha }{t}^{\tau }{At}},{t}^{\tau }\widehat{\beta } + \widehat{\sigma }\sqrt{2{F}_{2, n - 2,\alpha }{t}^{\tau }{At}}}\right\rbrack ,\;t \in {\mathcal{R}}^{2}
$$
(e.g., Theorem 7.10 in Shao, 2003), where$$
A = {\left( \begin{matrix} n & n\bar{z} \\ n\bar{z} & \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{z}_{i}^{2} \end{matrix}\right) }^{-1} = \frac{1}{n{S}_{z}}\left( \begin{matrix} \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{z}_{i}^{2} & - n\bar{z} \\ - n\bar{z} & n \end{matrix}\right) .
$$
From the solution to Exercise 46, ${\left( {t}^{\tau }\widehat{\beta } - {t}^{\tau }\beta \right) }^{2}/{t}^{\tau }{At}$ is maximized at ${t}_{ * } = \; {A}^{-1}\left( {\widehat{\beta } - \beta }\right)$ . Note that ${t}_{ * }/c$ still maximizes ${\left( {t}^{\tau }\widehat{\beta } - {t}^{\tau }\beta \right) }^{2}/{t}^{\tau }{At}$ as long as $c \neq 0$ , where $c$ is the first component of ${t}_{ * }$ . Since the first component of ${A}^{-1}\left( {\widehat{\beta } - \beta }\right)$ is $n\left( {{\widehat{\beta }}_{0} - {\beta }_{0}}\right) + n\left( {{\widehat{\beta }}_{1} - {\beta }_{1}}\right) \bar{z}$ and$$
P\left( {n\left( {{\widehat{\beta }}_{0} - {\beta }_{0}}\right) + n\left( {{\widehat{\beta }}_{1} - {\beta }_{1}}\right) \bar{z} \neq 0}\right) = 1,
$$
the quantity ${\left( {t}^{\tau }\widehat{\beta } - {t}^{\tau }\beta \right) }^{2}/{t}^{\tau }{At}$ is maximized at$$
\frac{{A}^{-1}}{n\left( {{\widehat{\beta }}_{0} - {\beta }_{0}}\right) + n\left( {{\widehat{\beta }}_{1} - {\beta }_{1}}\right) \bar{z}}\left( \begin{matrix} {\widehat{\beta }}_{0} - {\beta }_{0} \\ {\widehat{\beta }}_{1} - {\beta }_{1} \end{matrix}\right)
$$
whose first component is 1 . Note that ${t}^{\tau }{At} = D\left( z\right)$ when $t = \left( {1, z}\right)$ . Therefore,$$
\mathop{\max }\limits_{{z \in \mathcal{R}}}\frac{{\left( {\widehat{\beta }}_{0} + {\widehat{\beta }}_{1}z - {\beta }_{0} - {\beta }_{1}z\right) }^{2}}{D\left( z\right) } = \mathop{\max }\limits_{{t \in {\mathcal{R}}^{2}, t \neq 0}}\frac{{\left( {t}^{\tau }\widehat{\beta } - {t}^{\tau }\beta \right) }^{2}}{{t}^{\tau }{At}}.
$$
Consequently,$$
P\left( {{\beta }_{0} + {\beta }_{1}z \in {\mathcal{I}}_{z}, z \in \mathcal{R}}\right) = P\left( {\mathop{\max }\limits_{{z \in \mathcal{R}}}\frac{{\left( {\widehat{\beta }}_{0} + {\widehat{\beta }}_{1}z - {\beta }_{0} - {\beta }_{1}z\right) }^{2}}{2{\widehat{\sigma }}^{2}D\left( z\right) } \leq {F}_{2, n - 2,\alpha }}\right)
$$$$
= P\left( {\mathop{\max }\limits_{{t \in {\mathcal{R}}^{2}, t \neq 0}}\frac{{\left( {t}^{\tau }\widehat{\beta } - {t}^{\tau }\beta \right) }^{2}}{2{\widehat{\sigma }}^{2}{t}^{\tau }{At}} \leq {F}_{2, n - 2,\alpha }}\right)
$$$$
= 1 - \alpha
$$
where the last equality follows from$$
\mathop{\max }\limits_{{t \in {\mathcal{R}}^{2}, t \neq 0}}\frac{{\left( {t}^{\tau }\widehat{\beta } - {t}^{\tau }\beta \right) }^{2}}{2{\widehat{\sigma }}^{2}{t}^{\tau }{At}} = \frac{{\left( \widehat{\beta } - \beta \right) }^{\tau }{A}^{-1}\left( {\widehat{\beta } - \beta }\right) }{2{\widehat{\sigma }}^{2}}
$$
by Exercise 46 and the fact that the right hand side of the previous equation has the F-distribution ${F}_{2, n - 2}$
explanation:
This problem uses the ideas of simultaneous confidence intervals in linear regression and the $F$ distribution. The key is to apply Scheff\'e\'s simultaneous confidence interval for all linear combinations $t^\tau\beta$ and then specialize it to the regression mean $\beta_0+\beta_1 z$.

Let
$\beta=(\beta_0,\beta_1)^\tau$, $\widehat\beta=(\widehat\beta_0,\widehat\beta_1)^\tau$.
In the simple linear regression model
$X_i\sim N(\beta_0+\beta_1 z_i,\sigma^2)$ independently, the least squares estimator satisfies the usual normal-theory result that Scheff\'e\'s simultaneous $1-\alpha$ confidence intervals for all linear combinations $t^\tau\beta$, $t\in\mathcal{R}^2$, are
$\left[t^\tau\widehat\beta-\widehat\sigma\sqrt{2F_{2,n-2,\alpha}\, t^\tau A t},\ t^\tau\widehat\beta+\widehat\sigma\sqrt{2F_{2,n-2,\alpha}\, t^\tau A t}\right]$,
where
$A=(X^\tau X)^{-1}$ for the design matrix with columns $(1,z_i)$.

Here,
$X^\tau X=\begin{pmatrix} n & n\bar z \\ n\bar z & \sum_{i=1}^n z_i^2 \end{pmatrix}$,
so
$A=\left(\begin{pmatrix} n & n\bar z \\ n\bar z & \sum_{i=1}^n z_i^2 \end{pmatrix}\right)^{-1}
=\frac{1}{nS_z}\begin{pmatrix} \sum_{i=1}^n z_i^2 & -n\bar z \\ -n\bar z & n \end{pmatrix}$,
where $S_z=\sum_{i=1}^n (z_i-\bar z)^2>0$.

Now we want simultaneous confidence intervals specifically for
$\beta_0+\beta_1 z$ for all $z\in\mathcal R$.
This corresponds to choosing
$t=(1,z)^\tau$,
because then
$t^\tau\beta=\beta_0+\beta_1 z,
\qquad t^\tau\widehat\beta=\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1 z.$

Next compute $t^\tau A t$ for $t=(1,z)^\tau$:
\[
t^\tau A t
=\frac{1}{nS_z}(1,z)
\begin{pmatrix}
\sum_{i=1}^n z_i^2 & -n\bar z \\
-n\bar z & n
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1\\ z\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Expanding gives
\[
t^\tau A t
=\frac{1}{nS_z}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n z_i^2-2n\bar z\, z+n z^2\right).
\]
Using $\sum_{i=1}^n z_i^2=S_z+n\bar z^2$, we obtain
\[
t^\tau A t
=\frac{1}{nS_z}\left(S_z+n\bar z^2-2n\bar z z+n z^2\right)
=\frac{1}{nS_z}\left(S_z+n(z-\bar z)^2\right).
\]
Therefore
\[
t^\tau A t=\frac{1}{n}+\frac{(z-\bar z)^2}{S_z}=D(z).
\]
So Scheff\'e\'s interval becomes exactly
\[
\left[\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1 z-\widehat\sigma\sqrt{2F_{2,n-2,\alpha}D(z)},\ \widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1 z+\widehat\sigma\sqrt{2F_{2,n-2,\alpha}D(z)}\right].
\]

It remains to justify that these intervals are simultaneous over all $z\in\mathcal R$.
By Scheff\'e\'s theorem,
\[
P\left(\frac{(t^\tau\widehat\beta-t^\tau\beta)^2}{2\widehat\sigma^2\, t^\tau A t}\le F_{2,n-2,\alpha}\ \text{for all } t\ne 0\right)=1-\alpha.
\]
Also,
\[
\max_{t\in\mathcal R^2,\, t\ne 0}\frac{(t^\tau\widehat\beta-t^\tau\beta)^2}{t^\tau A t}
=(\widehat\beta-\beta)^\tau A^{-1}(\widehat\beta-\beta),
\]
up to the same scaling by $2\widehat\sigma^2$, because the quadratic ratio is maximized at
$ t_*=A^{-1}(\widehat\beta-\beta)$.
Moreover, any nonzero scalar multiple of $t_*$ gives the same value of the ratio. Since the first component of
$A^{-1}(\widehat\beta-\beta)$ is
$ n(\widehat\beta_0-\beta_0)+n(\widehat\beta_1-\beta_1)\bar z$,
and this is nonzero with probability $1$, we may rescale the maximizing vector so that its first component is $1$. Hence the maximizer may be written in the form $(1,z)^\tau$ for some $z\in\mathcal R$.

Therefore,
\[
\max_{z\in\mathcal R}
\frac{(\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1 z-\beta_0-\beta_1 z)^2}{D(z)}
=
\max_{t\in\mathcal R^2,\, t\ne 0}
\frac{(t^\tau\widehat\beta-t^\tau\beta)^2}{t^\tau A t}.
\]
Dividing both sides by $2\widehat\sigma^2$ gives
\[
\max_{z\in\mathcal R}
\frac{(\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1 z-\beta_0-\beta_1 z)^2}{2\widehat\sigma^2 D(z)}
=
\max_{t\in\mathcal R^2,\, t\ne 0}
\frac{(t^\tau\widehat\beta-t^\tau\beta)^2}{2\widehat\sigma^2 t^\tau A t}.
\]
By the regression theory result,
\[
\frac{(\widehat\beta-\beta)^\tau A^{-1}(\widehat\beta-\beta)}{2\widehat\sigma^2}\sim F_{2,n-2}.
\]
Hence
\[
P\left(
\max_{z\in\mathcal R}
\frac{(\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1 z-\beta_0-\beta_1 z)^2}{2\widehat\sigma^2 D(z)}
\le F_{2,n-2,\alpha}
\right)=1-\alpha.
\]
This is equivalent to
\[
P\left(\beta_0+\beta_1 z\in \mathcal I_z\ \text{for all } z\in\mathcal R\right)=1-\alpha.
\]

Therefore, the intervals
$\mathcal I_z=\left[\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1 z-\widehat\sigma\sqrt{2F_{2,n-2,\alpha}D(z)},\ \widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1 z+\widehat\sigma\sqrt{2F_{2,n-2,\alpha}D(z)}\right]$
are simultaneous confidence intervals for $\beta_0+\beta_1 z$, $z\in\mathcal R$, with confidence coefficient $1-\alpha$.

question:
Let ${X}_{0j}\left( {j = 1,\ldots ,{n}_{0}}\right)$ and ${X}_{ij}(i = 1,\ldots , m$ , $j = 1,\ldots ,{n}_{0}$ ) represent independent measurements on a standard and $m$ competing new treatments. Suppose that ${X}_{ij}$ is distributed as $N\left( {{\mu }_{i},{\sigma }^{2}}\right)$ with unknown ${\mu }_{i}$ and ${\sigma }^{2} > 0, j = 1,\ldots ,{n}_{0}, i = 0,1,\ldots , m$ . For $i = 0,1,\ldots , m$ , let ${\bar{X}}_{i}$ . be the sample mean based on ${X}_{ij}, j = 1,\ldots ,{n}_{0}$ . Define ${\widehat{\sigma }}^{2} = \; {\left\lbrack \left( m + 1\right) \left( {n}_{0} - 1\right) \right\rbrack }^{-1}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{m}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{{n}_{0}}{\left( {X}_{ij} - {\bar{X}}_{i \cdot }\right) }^{2}.$
(i) Show that the distribution of$$
{R}_{st} = \mathop{\max }\limits_{{i = 1,\ldots , m}}\left| {\left( {{\bar{X}}_{i \cdot } - {\mu }_{i}}\right) - \left( {{\bar{X}}_{0 \cdot } - {\mu }_{0}}\right) }\right| /\widehat{\sigma }
$$
does not depend on any unknown parameter.
(ii) Show that Dunnett's intervals$$
\left\lbrack {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{m}{c}_{i}{\bar{X}}_{i \cdot } - {q}_{\alpha }\widehat{\sigma }\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{m}\left| {c}_{i}\right| ,\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{m}{c}_{i}{\bar{X}}_{i \cdot } + {q}_{\alpha }\widehat{\sigma }\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{m}\left| {c}_{i}\right| }\right\rbrack
$$
for all ${c}_{0},{c}_{1},\ldots ,{c}_{m}$ satisfying $\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{m}{c}_{i} = 0$ are simultaneous confidence intervals for $\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{m}{c}_{i}{\mu }_{i}$ with confidence coefficient $1 - \alpha$ , where ${q}_{\alpha }$ is the $\left( {1 - \alpha }\right)$ th quantile of ${R}_{st}$ .
answer:
(i) The distributions of $\widehat{\sigma }/\sigma$ and $\left( {{\bar{X}}_{i \cdot } - {\mu }_{i}}\right) /\sigma , i = 0,1,\ldots , m$ , do not depend on any unknown parameter. The result follows from the fact that these random variables are independent so that their joint distribution does not depend on any unknown parameter and ${R}_{st}$ is a function of these random variables.
(ii) Let ${Y}_{i} = \left( {{\bar{X}}_{i \cdot } - {\mu }_{i}}\right) /\widehat{\sigma }$ . Then ${R}_{st} = \mathop{\max }\limits_{{i = 1,\ldots , m}}\left\lvert {{Y}_{i} - {Y}_{0}}\right\rvert$ . Note that$$
P\left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{m}{c}_{i}{\mu }_{i}\text{ are in Dunnett’s intervals for all }{c}_{i}\text{ ’s with }\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{m}{c}_{i} = 0}\right)
$$$$
= P\left( {\left\lvert {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{m}{c}_{i}\left( {{\bar{X}}_{i \cdot } - {\mu }_{i}}\right) }\right\rvert \leq {q}_{\alpha }\widehat{\sigma }\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{m}\left\lvert {c}_{i}\right\rvert ,\text{ all }{c}_{i}\text{ ’s with }\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{m}{c}_{i} = 0}\right)
$$$$
= P\left( {\left\lvert {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{m}{c}_{i}{Y}_{i}}\right\rvert \leq {q}_{\alpha }\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{m}\left\lvert {c}_{i}\right\rvert ,\text{ all }{c}_{i}\text{ ’s with }\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{m}{c}_{i} = 0}\right) .
$$
Hence, the result follows if we can show that$$
\mathop{\max }\limits_{{i = 1,\ldots , m}}\left\lvert {{Y}_{i} - {Y}_{0}}\right\rvert \leq {q}_{\alpha }
$$
is equivalent to$$
\left\lvert {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{m}{c}_{i}{Y}_{i}}\right\rvert \leq {q}_{\alpha }\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{m}\left\lvert {c}_{i}\right\rvert \;\text{ for all }{c}_{0},{c}_{1},\ldots ,{c}_{m}\text{ satisfying }\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{m}{c}_{i} = 0.
$$
Suppose that $\left\lvert {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{m}{c}_{i}{Y}_{i}}\right\rvert \leq {q}_{\alpha }\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{m}\left\lvert {c}_{i}\right\rvert$ for all ${c}_{0},{c}_{1},\ldots ,{c}_{m}$ satisfying $\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{m}{c}_{i} = 0$ . For any fixed $i$ , let ${c}_{0} = 1,{c}_{i} = - 1$ , and ${c}_{j} = 0, j \neq i$ . Then these ${c}_{i}$ ’s satisfy$$
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{m}{c}_{i} = 0,\;\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{m}\left\lvert {c}_{i}\right\rvert = 1,\;\text{ and }\;\left\lvert {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{n}{c}_{i}{Y}_{i}}\right\rvert = \left\lvert {{Y}_{i} - {Y}_{0}}\right\rvert .
$$
Hence, $\left\lvert {{Y}_{i} - {Y}_{0}}\right\rvert \leq {q}_{\alpha }$ for $i = 1,\ldots , m$ . Thus, $\mathop{\max }\limits_{{i = 1,\ldots , m}}\left\lvert {{Y}_{i} - {Y}_{0}}\right\rvert \leq {q}_{\alpha }$ .
Assume now that $\mathop{\max }\limits_{{i = 1,\ldots , m}}\left\lvert {{Y}_{i} - {Y}_{0}}\right\rvert \leq {q}_{\alpha }$ . For all ${c}_{0},{c}_{1},\ldots ,{c}_{m}$ satisfying $\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{m}{c}_{i} = 0$ ,$$
\left\lvert {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{m}{c}_{i}{Y}_{i}}\right\rvert = \left\lvert {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{m}{c}_{i}{Y}_{i} + {c}_{0}{Y}_{0}}\right\rvert
$$$$
= \left\lvert {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{m}{c}_{i}{Y}_{i} - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{m}{c}_{i}{Y}_{0}}\right\rvert
$$$$
= \left\lvert {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{m}{c}_{i}\left( {{Y}_{i} - {Y}_{0}}\right) }\right\rvert
$$$$
\leq \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{m}\left\lvert {c}_{i}\right\rvert \left\lvert {{Y}_{i} - {Y}_{0}}\right\rvert
$$$$
\leq {q}_{\alpha }\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{m}\left\lvert {c}_{i}\right\rvert$$
explanation:
This problem uses the ideas of $\,$pivot quantities and simultaneous confidence intervals. In part (i), we show that the statistic $R_{st}$ is a function of standardized sample means and a pooled estimator of variance whose joint distribution does not involve unknown parameters; in part (ii), we connect the event defining Dunnett's intervals with the event $R_{st}\le q_\alpha$.

For part (i), note first that for each $i=0,1,\ldots,m$, the sample mean satisfies
$\bar X_{i\cdot}\sim N\left(\mu_i,\sigma^2/n_0\right)$,
so
$\dfrac{\bar X_{i\cdot}-\mu_i}{\sigma}$
has a distribution that does not depend on any unknown parameter.

Also,
$\widehat\sigma^2=\frac{1}{(m+1)(n_0-1)}\sum_{i=0}^m\sum_{j=1}^{n_0}(X_{ij}-\bar X_{i\cdot})^2$,
so by the normal sample variance theory,
$\widehat\sigma/\sigma$
also has a distribution free of the unknown parameters.

Because all observations are normal and independent across groups, the sample means $\bar X_{i\cdot}$ are independent of the within-group sum of squares, hence the collection
$\left\{\frac{\bar X_{i\cdot}-\mu_i}{\sigma}: i=0,1,\ldots,m\right\}$
is independent of $\widehat\sigma/\sigma$. Therefore their joint distribution does not depend on any unknown parameter.

Now write
$R_{st}=\max_{i=1,\ldots,m}\frac{\left|\left(\bar X_{i\cdot}-\mu_i\right)-\left(\bar X_{0\cdot}-\mu_0\right)\right|}{\widehat\sigma}$
$=\max_{i=1,\ldots,m}\left|\frac{\bar X_{i\cdot}-\mu_i}{\widehat\sigma}-\frac{\bar X_{0\cdot}-\mu_0}{\widehat\sigma}\right|$.
Equivalently, it is a function of
$\left(\bar X_{i\cdot}-\mu_i\right)/\sigma$
and $\widehat\sigma/\sigma$.
Since the joint distribution of these basic standardized quantities is parameter-free, the distribution of $R_{st}$ is also free of all unknown parameters.

For part (ii), define
$Y_i=\frac{\bar X_{i\cdot}-\mu_i}{\widehat\sigma},\qquad i=0,1,\ldots,m$.
Then
$R_{st}=\max_{i=1,\ldots,m}|Y_i-Y_0|$.
Let $q_\alpha$ be the $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of $R_{st}$. Then by definition,
$P(R_{st}\le q_\alpha)=1-\alpha$.

We need to show that the intervals
$\left[\sum_{i=0}^m c_i\bar X_{i\cdot}-q_\alpha\widehat\sigma\sum_{i=1}^m|c_i|,\; \sum_{i=0}^m c_i\bar X_{i\cdot}+q_\alpha\widehat\sigma\sum_{i=1}^m|c_i|\right]$
for all $c_0,c_1,\ldots,c_m$ with $\sum_{i=0}^m c_i=0$ are simultaneous confidence intervals for $\sum_{i=0}^m c_i\mu_i$.

The simultaneous coverage event is
$\left|\sum_{i=0}^m c_i(\bar X_{i\cdot}-\mu_i)\right|\le q_\alpha\widehat\sigma\sum_{i=1}^m|c_i|$
for all choices of $c_i$ satisfying $\sum_{i=0}^m c_i=0$.
Dividing by $\widehat\sigma$ gives the equivalent event
$\left|\sum_{i=0}^m c_iY_i\right|\le q_\alpha\sum_{i=1}^m|c_i|$
for all $c_0,c_1,\ldots,c_m$ such that $\sum_{i=0}^m c_i=0$.
So it remains to prove that this event is equivalent to
$\max_{i=1,\ldots,m}|Y_i-Y_0|\le q_\alpha$.

First, assume that
$\left|\sum_{i=0}^m c_iY_i\right|\le q_\alpha\sum_{i=1}^m|c_i|$
for all $c_0,c_1,\ldots,c_m$ with $\sum_{i=0}^m c_i=0$.
Fix any $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and choose
$c_0=1,\qquad c_i=-1,\qquad c_j=0\;(j\ne i)$.
Then
$\sum_{i=0}^m c_i=0,
\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m|c_i|=1,
\qquad \left|\sum_{i=0}^m c_iY_i\right|=|Y_i-Y_0|$.
Hence
$|Y_i-Y_0|\le q_\alpha$.
Since this holds for every $i=1,\ldots,m$, we get
$\max_{i=1,\ldots,m}|Y_i-Y_0|\le q_\alpha$.

Conversely, assume that
$\max_{i=1,\ldots,m}|Y_i-Y_0|\le q_\alpha$.
Take any $c_0,c_1,\ldots,c_m$ satisfying $\sum_{i=0}^m c_i=0$. Then
$c_0=-\sum_{i=1}^m c_i$,
so
$\sum_{i=0}^m c_iY_i=\sum_{i=1}^m c_iY_i+c_0Y_0
=\sum_{i=1}^m c_iY_i-\sum_{i=1}^m c_iY_0
=\sum_{i=1}^m c_i(Y_i-Y_0)$.
Therefore,
$\left|\sum_{i=0}^m c_iY_i\right|
=\left|\sum_{i=1}^m c_i(Y_i-Y_0)\right|
\le \sum_{i=1}^m |c_i|\,|Y_i-Y_0|
\le q_\alpha\sum_{i=1}^m|c_i|$.
Thus the inequality
$\left|\sum_{i=0}^m c_iY_i\right|\le q_\alpha\sum_{i=1}^m|c_i|$
holds for all admissible $c_i$.

So the two events are equivalent:
$\max_{i=1,\ldots,m}|Y_i-Y_0|\le q_\alpha$
if and only if
$\left|\sum_{i=0}^m c_iY_i\right|\le q_\alpha\sum_{i=1}^m|c_i|$
for all $c_0,c_1,\ldots,c_m$ with $\sum_{i=0}^m c_i=0$.

Hence,
$P\left(\sum_{i=0}^m c_i\mu_i\text{ lies in the stated interval for all }c_i\text{ with }\sum_{i=0}^m c_i=0\right)
=P(R_{st}\le q_\alpha)
=1-\alpha$.
Therefore the given Dunnett intervals are simultaneous confidence intervals for $\sum_{i=0}^m c_i\mu_i$ with confidence coefficient $1-\alpha$.

In conclusion: (i) $R_{st}$ is a pivot whose distribution does not depend on unknown parameters; (ii) the stated Dunnett intervals form a simultaneous $(1-\alpha)$ confidence family for all contrasts $\sum_{i=0}^m c_i\mu_i$ with $\sum_{i=0}^m c_i=0$.
